title: Bonny Eagle football’s Wes Pinkham emerges as under-the-radar playmaker
text:
We’re proud to make high school sports coverage free for everyone, because these moments matter. At Maine State Credit Union, we’re here for the people and places that make Maine strong. Let’s go! Learn more at mainestatecu.org. 
STANDISH — Wes Pinkham had always wanted to rush the passer. But barely weighing 160 pounds, the Bonny Eagle senior never got the chance.
Until last Saturday, that is. On his very first pass rush, Pinkham jammed and eluded Thornton Academy’s left tackle, then sacked quarterback Noah Fullerton, causing him to fumble.
“I’ve been wanting to play an edge rusher position my entire life, but I’ve always been too small,” Pinkham said. “I got the opportunity to play it in practice and I think I showed I could. I took the opportunity and ran with it.”
Drew Gervais, Bonny Eagle’s outside linebacker on the other side, marveled at what Pinkham did.
“The strip sack, he’d never taken a rep of pass rush in his life, and he went straight through the tackle and stripped Fullerton. That was pretty amazing,” Gervais said.
Pinkham’s play changed the trajectory of the the Class A South final. Bonny Eagle had been stumbling and trailed 7-0. Five plays later, Scots quarterback Lucas Klehn bulled in from the 1 to tie the game. Bonny Eagle never trailed again, winning the regional title with a 35-28 victory.
It was the first of several big plays for the 5-foot-10 Pinkham as Bonny Eagle snapped a seven-game losing streak to Thornton and earned its first trip to the state final since its victory over the Trojans in the 2019 Class A championship game.
“Any great team needs kids who you don’t really hear about as juniors to come on and be great players as seniors,” said Bonny Eagle coach Kevin Cooper.
Pinkham fits that bill. Cooper said Pinkham has gotten better with each game, and the rematch with Thornton was his best yet. That progression is what every player and coach strives for.
“You want them to play their best in big games like that, and Wes certainly came though,” Cooper said.
Bonny Eagle (10-1) will face North champion Oxford Hills (9-1) at 11 a.m. Saturday at Fitzpatrick Stadium. In the regular season, Bonny Eagle beat the Vikings, 45-6.
Coming off a back injury, Pinkham barely saw the varsity field as a junior. He never once thought about quitting football, however.
“I’ve made all my friends through the sport and felt it would be a disgrace if I left this late in my career,” he said.
He acknowledged that he needed an extra season at the JV level to prove to both himself and his coaches that he had the ability and the confidence to play at the varsity level.
“He’s always looking for feedback, asking what he can do better, and asking, ‘What’s next?'” Klehn said. “A guy like that is pivotal for a team.”
Normally a safety playing off the ball, Pinkham was moved to outside linebacker for the regional final. Bonny Eagle knew it had to do something different after its 49-14 loss at Thornton in Week 8. The idea was that Pinkham would play up close, be able to double-team a split end if necessary, and use his sure tackling to help contain Fullerton or other Trojans on off-tackle runs.
“We threw something different at them, and clearly they weren’t ready for him to be in that position,” said Klehn, a team captain and typically Pinkham’s partner at safety. “It turned out, they didn’t really adjust all game and he was making plays all over the field.”
Pinkham’s individual stats were impressive. He had a 40-yard touchdown catch and a 38-yard kickoff return to go with his eight tackles (two for loss), the QB sack, and another forced fumble that Fullerton was able to recover.
The timing of Pinkham’s plays were impeccable.
His touchdown catch, when he had to accelerate to get underneath the ball on a deep post pattern, put Bonny Eagle in front 14-7 with 7:37 left in the first half.
The kick return came after Thornton cut Bonny Eagle’s lead to 28-21 with almost eight minutes remaining. Pinkham took a short kick at the 20, cut to the middle, broke several tackles and got the ball to Thornton’s 42. Klehn scored on a run off right tackle on the next play.
Pinkham nearly had a second touchdown in the third quarter. He was open on a deep crosser in the end zone, but Klehn overthrew him.
“Tell me about it. I beat myself up on that one,” Klehn said.
Pinkham said he realized during the game the impact he was having but tried to always focus on the next play.
“I knew no one would care if we lost,” Pinkham said.
“I think I finally got to prove to myself that I could play at this level.”

title: Head-on crash with speeding car kills father, leaves wife and daughters on ventilators, family says
text:
SAFFORD, Ariz. (KPHO/Gray News) — A father has lost his life and his wife and daughters are fighting for theirs following a head-on crash in southeastern Arizona over the weekend.
Family members identified the father as Aaron Johnston. They said he was in a car that collided with another vehicle on U.S. 191 in Safford.
Johnston was traveling with his wife, Sierra, and their daughters, Angelyc, 5, and Eryn, 3, who suffered severe injuries in the crash and have since been placed on ventilators.
Relatives said Eryn may not survive. Investigators said another adult died in the collision, but not many further details were released from the scene.
People close to the family said the Johnstons were heading home to Apache Junction after a day trip to Morenci, about a 50-minute drive northwest of Safford, watching big trucks operate.
Family and witnesses at the scene said a car was speeding and weaving through traffic on the two-lane highway before it hit the Johnstons’ vehicle head-on.
Loved ones said Johnston died on impact.
A GoFundMe has been set up for the Johnston family.

title: Grammy-nominated Palaver Strings Quartet explores what travels at Bath arts center
text:
Whenever I hear the first notes of Prince’s song “Dorothy Parker,” I am instantly transported to an apartment in Chicago years ago, dancing with my dearest friends. The emotions are layered: nostalgia for a simpler time in my life, yearning to be together again, and joy in the music and the memory.
These feelings are the heart of “What Travels,” the program Grammy-nominated Palaver Strings Quartet will perform at the Chocolate Church Arts Center’s Annex theater on Thursday, Dec. 3.
What can music carry across time and distance? A melody can tell the story of a past generation, evoke a place or person left behind, or give shape to memories that are difficult to put into words.
The Portland-based ensemble will perform as a quartet, with violinists Maya French and Grant Houston, violist Brianna Fischler, and cellist Adalus Low-Manzini. The program moves through five works exploring memory from different perspectives. Jessie Montgomery’s “Source Code” traces musical lineages, showing how fragments of the past can become the raw material for new works. It flows into Osvaldo Golijov’s “Tenebrae,” a more inward piece shaped by grief, stillness and remembrance.
Caroline Shaw’s “Plan & Elevation” turns toward the landscapes we inhabit, exploring the relationship between memory, place, and time. Diego Vega Desenne’s “Diaspora” widens the aperture, drawing on Latin American musical traditions to consider migration, displacement, and resilience. The program comes full circle with the fiddle tune “hoarfrost,” a collaboration between Maya French and Jamie Oshima, a member of the Oshima Brothers, who played our Annex theater last month. Rooted in living folk traditions, the song reflects how music travels through time, and how people create, adapt, and pass along something new from what they inherit.
Moving among musical worlds is characteristic of the Palaver Strings’ genre-bending approach to classical music. Founded in 2014, the musician-led ensemble has built its work around adventurous programming, new compositions, unexpected collaborations, and performances in non-traditional settings — often places not associated with classical music. The group is a nonprofit dedicated to breaking down barriers to classical music. They offer sliding-scale tuition and financial aid for music lessons in the Palaver Music Center in Portland, helping to address inequities in access to music education, and serving families from diverse backgrounds.
There is a natural connection to the Chocolate Church Art Center’s own eclectic approach to programming and community access. Our calendar includes concerts, theater, dance, and annual community celebrations. We also look for ways to make participation possible for all: through the free Art Lab, sliding-scale tickets for some performances, and traditions such as the Lantern Parade, Monster Garden, Hanukkah Mexicana, Sing! It’s Christmas, and our free summer waterfront concert series. Palaver Strings’ outreach and unexpected collaborations reflect the same openness and desire to engage the community in a variety of ways.
For this performance, the quartet grouping performs in an intimate setting for a program that travels from musical inheritance to personal and collective memory, from landscapes to migration, and to the traditions being created in the present. “What Travels” invites the audience to hear how much a piece of music can contain, and how much it can carry forward.
Catherine Gleason is the marketing and communications director at the Chocolate Church Arts Center.

title: Grand Theft Auto VI could outsell Taylor Swift’s entire Eras Tour in its first week, report says
text:
(Gray News/AP) – The global rollout of “Grand Theft Auto VI” is underway, with presales for the highly anticipated release hitting $1.65 billion as of Wednesday, according to Sensor Tower.
The franchise has already sold more than 470 million games worldwide, including 230 million copies of “Grand Theft Auto V,” which was released in 2013.
Wall Street Journal reports third-party analysts anticipate “Grand Theft Auto VI” to have the “biggest-ever launch for a video game.” It’s projected to sell more than 30 million copies by the end of its fiscal year, the Wall Street Journal reported.
Analysts expect the video game’s global launch-week sales to hit $3.3 billion, the Wall Street Journal reported. To put it into perspective, the Eras Tour’s box office sales reached $2.2 billion over 21 months.
At $80 or more per copy, ultimately, the game could earn well over $10 billion.
GTA VI trailers draw millions of views, award nominations
The first “GTA VI” trailer drew more than 93 million YouTube views in its first 24 hours, while Take-Two Interactive, Rockstar’s parent company, has said the second trailer generated more than 475 million views across platforms in a day.
The game also has attracted awards attention before most players have had a chance to explore it.
“GTA VI” received eight nominations Tuesday for the Game Awards, including game of the year, game direction, narrative, art direction, score and music, audio design, action/adventure and performance. The awards will be presented Dec. 10.
Who are the main characters in GTA VI?
Rockstar returns to Vice City, its fictionalized version of Miami, with two new protagonists, a sprawling Florida-inspired world and the pressure of following one of the most successful entertainment products ever released.
At the center of “GTA VI” are Lucia Caminos and Jason Duval, a couple whose attempts to improve their lives pull them deeper into the criminal underworld of Leonida, Rockstar’s fictionalized version of Florida.
Lucia has recently been released from prison, while Jason is a former soldier who became involved with drug runners in the Leonida Keys. When a criminal job goes wrong, the pair become entangled in a wider conspiracy.
The focus on their relationship marks a major departure from “Grand Theft Auto V,” which followed three playable protagonists.
Where is GTA VI set?
Rockstar has promoted Leonida as its largest and most detailed open world yet, extending beyond Vice City to beaches, highways, wetlands, nightlife districts and smaller communities inspired by South Florida.
Developers immersed themselves in the region while building the game, driving through Miami, the Florida Keys and surrounding communities, flying over the Everglades and researching the area’s history and architecture.
What remains unknown about GTA VI?
Despite years of trailers and promotional material, Rockstar has kept significant portions of “GTA VI” under wraps.
The full voice cast has not been revealed, including the performers behind Lucia and Jason. Actor Stephen Root has confirmed to The Associated Press that he appears in the game, though Rockstar has not publicly identified his role.
Questions also remain about the full range of characters, locations, activities and gameplay systems waiting inside Leonida.

title: What ‘die with zero’ means, and who it is meant for
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
(InvestigateTV) — A money philosophy called “die with zero” is getting attention on social media. The idea is not really about burning through a bank account. Kate Ashford, lead writer with NerdWallet, said it is about intentional, joy-based spending after a solid financial foundation has been built.
Ashford described the concept this way.
“It sounds kind of dire, but it’s really this idea that if you’re hoarding your money to the end of your life maybe you should consider spending it down, over time, so that when you die, you don’t just have this pile of cash in the bank. You’ve used that money to spend on experiences,” Ashford said.
She said the approach is about making the most of your money while you are still alive. A strategy like this is meant to make sure money lasts after retirement while also putting it to use.
Ashford said the approach starts with a solid financial foundation.
“With this approach you have to make sure you have a solid financial foundation,” Ashford said.
She said the basics include “a healthy emergency fund, no high interest debt,” and having insurance needs covered.
Ashford said this is a plan for someone who already has a financial foundation in place. She recommends working with a professional to make sure spending decisions are sound and that too much money is not taken out at a time.

title: Guitarist Mark Miller Inducted into the Maine Blues Hall of Fame
text:
Veteran Maine-based musician Mark Miller was honored at the inaugural Maine Blues Hall of Fame awards ceremony held in Auburn on Sept. 26.
The banquet and ceremony, presented by The Maine Blues Society, inducted the celebrated guitarist and singer for a lifetime of music performed and recorded throughout the state.
Other 2026 Maine Blues Hall of Fame inductees included Arlo West, Michael Hayward, Bonnie Edwards, Frank Fotusky, The Blues Prophets and concert promoter Paul Benjamin of the North Atlantic Blues Festival held in Rockland.
Mark G. Miller was born in Houlton and spent his formative years in Mattawamkeag and East Millinocket. He began playing the guitar at age 6 and formed his first band, The Stingrays, at age 11. He was a member of the rock band The Variations while attending Schenck High School in East Millinocket. Miller was inducted into the school’s Hall of Fame in 2023.
Miller served in the U.S. Air Force then returned to Maine to resume performing and recording music. His band Home Town had a local hit with the song “Honest John.”
Other groups followed, including the Bangor-based rock band Cherry Opera, with whom Miller toured New England and made an impact on the chart.
Miller formed The Mark Miller Blues Band in the 1980s and performed hundreds of shows throughout New England and Atlantic Canada. Miller’s virtuosity on guitar has earned him countless followers, including Bruce Iglauer, founder of the iconic blues record label, Alligator Records. Iglauer famously referred to Miller as “One of the best bluesmen in the country.”
Miller’s band shared the stage with legendary artists, including two concerts for B.B. King, Johnny Winter, Waylon Jennings, Taj Mahal and many others.
Miller formed a longtime friendship and working relationship with Brad Delp, the late lead singer for the band Boston. They recorded an album together in 1988 that remains unreleased due to contractual issues. Miller also performed with Delp’s band, Howard Roarke & the Architects, at the Boston Music Awards.
Delp later contributed vocals to songs on Miller’s album “Watcha Gonna Do!,” recorded in Hallowell.
In June of 2006, Miller was nominated by Gov. John Baldacci to serve a 3-year term on the Maine Arts Commission.
Miller performed the soundtrack to the film “Northrunner”, produced by the Maine Dept. of Conservation and the Maine Outdoor Heritage Fund. The 2006 film coincided with the 40th anniversary of the Allagash Wilderness Waterway.
Miller’s extensive catalog of original songs includes the local favorite “Back in Maine”, co-written with Wayne Hendsbee in 2007. The song has become an unofficial theme song for the state and is performed at almost all of Miller’s solo concerts.
Miller still performs with his band and at solo acoustic shows in various venues and theatres, including regular performances as “Mark Miller & Friends” at the Boreal Theater in Millinocket.
Following his induction into the Maine Blues Hall of Fame, Miller celebrated by staging a guitar summit concert with longtime friends Arlo West (2026 Maine Blues Hall of Fame inductee) and Denny Breau (2027 Maine Blues Hall of Fame nominee) at the Franco Center in Lewiston. The trio have presented a series of shows over the years as BMW.
The Maine Blues Society shared the following accolade during Miller’s induction to the Maine Blues Hall of Fame:
“His induction into the 2026 Maine Blues Hall of Fame celebrates a true native son of the Pine Tree State — honoring a lifetime spent keeping the fire of real, unadulterated electric blues burning bright across New England.”
Miller dedicates his hall of fame induction to his late mother, Luella Mae Miller.

title: 3 injured in crash in Thomaston Walmart parking lot
text:
One dead, two hospitalized after crash in Thomaston Walmart parking lot
A Maine woman has died after a crash in the parking lot of the Walmart in Thomaston that left two other people injured.
The Thomaston Police Department said the three people who were injured in Wednesday's crash were transported to Pen Bay Hospital in Rockport.
Leita Wyman, 80, of Friendship, died of her injuries. Police said one person remains in critical condition, and that the third victim has less serious injuries and is expected to survive.
The Maine State Police Crash Reconstruction Unit was called to the scene to help investigate the crash.
The Thomaston Police Department said the crash remains under investigation and charges may be pending.

title: Anthropic’s IPO hits record breaking $81.3 billion after Nasdaq debut
text:
Anthropic valued at $1.75 trillion after IPO debut. Here’s where shares closed
Anthropic, the artificial intelligence research and safety company behind the chatbot Claude, stock closed at $97.17 per share, up 17% in its Nasdaq debut on Thursday.
The AI lab began trading under the ticker symbol “ANT", opening at $111.50 after the company raised $81.3 billion in its initial public offering. Anthropic also raised $26 billion through private placement, bringing the total deal size to $107.3 billion.
The record-breaking offering raised the company's value to $1.75 trillion.
It is now the largest initial public offering, months after SpaceX’s historic $75 billion debut. An initial public offering, or IPO, is when a private company decides to sell shares of its stock to the public on the stock market.
Anthropic’s IPO offered 980 million shares, up from the 825 million initially planned, according to the company's news release. The company initially set a target price range of $70 to $78 per share, valuing its IPO at $64 billion, according to its filing with the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission.
The AI lab's IPO value does not include any extra shares Anthropic’s underwriters, or investment banks, may sell through a greenshoe option if demand is high.
Anthropic was founded back in 2021, after its CEO Dario Amodei left OpenAI and co-founded the AI lab. The company raised $26 billion in a separate private placement deal with investors including Google, Nvidia and Advanced Micro Devices.
How has other tech stock IPO performed?
When Nvidia first went public in Jan. 1999, its share was $12 and had an IPO valued at $42 million. The AI chip supplier later became the world’s second-largest publicly traded company, behind Apple.
Nvidia stock fell sharply last Thursday morning after its former founder and CEO Jensen Huang resigned following reports that he was the target of a “foreign intelligence effort.”
Apple first went public in December 1980 at $22 a share, with an IPO valued at $101.2 million.
Other historic IPOs were Alibaba and Meta, formerly known as Facebook. Alibaba, a Chinese multinational technology company, went public back in 2014 with an IPO valued at $21.8 billion. Meta’s total IPO offer was $16 billion, selling at $38 per share. 
When it comes to the most valuable companies, Apple remains at the top of the list valued at more than $5 trillion.

title: Ground stop leads to airport wedding
text:
ATLANTA (KCNC/KTNV) - Flight delays and cancellations left travelers stranded across the country last weekend. But for one couple, a canceled flight threatened to ruin their wedding day, until a chance encounter with a stranger turned their travel nightmare into a day they’ll never forget.
Brelyn Bowman, an ordained minister, said she was on an airplane for more than four hours.
“Everybody was grounded,” Bowman said.
Bowman missed her conference. She said she was not going to make it out of Atlanta that night anyway.
Wedding trip canceled
Jake Hinson and Chelsey Rogers were trying to get to their wedding in Las Vegas. Their flight was delayed more than once before it was canceled.
“Eventually, we get the notification: It’s canceled,” Rogers said. She said no other flights were available that would get them there in time for the ceremony.
Their checked bags had already been sent without them. The couple started their trip home with only a veil in their carry-on.
Meeting the minister
Rogers said she was crying at that point.
“I was so hopeful. I really thought we’d make it, and then we strike up a conversation with Bree,” Rogers said.
“And I made the joke of like, ‘Hey, you know, we can wrap this up now.’ But I never imagined that they would actually say yes,” Bowman said.
They did, and the couple was married shortly after.
‘Humanity really connects’
Rogers said it was at first just the three of them. Then another woman ran up and took pictures from the side.
“And then as the trains were letting people off, people are kind of gathering,” Rogers said.
Bowman said nobody was concerned about the flight at that point.
“I think you have those moments where time just stands still, you know? And you’re just in a moment in space where humanity really connects the way we’re supposed to connect,” Bowman said.
Hinson said the couple spent 13 hours in the airport.
“That’s a bad day, I don’t care who you are,” Hinson said. “And so that just made what had been a really awful experience a highlight of our life.”
Staying in touch
Bowman said she has stayed in touch with the couple. She said she is now the godmother to their children.
The three plan to get together a year from now to celebrate, Bowman said.
Their story is proof that sometimes, the best destination isn’t the one you planned.

title: What's driving the recent decrease in gas prices?
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Are the midterm election results driving the recent decrease in gas prices?
Gas prices in Maine are down, but consumers aren’t necessarily noticing the drop
Are the midterm election results driving the recent decrease in gas prices?
Gas prices in Maine are down, but consumers aren’t necessarily noticing the drop
The average price of gas in Maine is $3.94 per gallon as of Thursday, which is 40 cents less than it was a month ago.
Gas prices are down, but consumers aren’t necessarily noticing the drop and many people have grown used to elevated prices.
The recent decrease is likely due more to seasonal trends and geopolitics than to the midterm election results, according to Patrick De Haan, a petroleum expert with GasBuddy.
"A lot of people like to point blame at politicians that they may not agree with and take credit for things they do agree with," said De Haan. "Gas prices every year are going to keep going down in the fall and going back up in the spring."
By November, gas stations have switched to slightly cheaper winter blends, refineries have completed summer maintenance work leading to increased production, and demand is on a seasonal decline.
"Even with Thanksgiving, Thanksgiving does not actually see an increase in demand for gasoline, but shifts," said De Haan. "Many Americans hit the road Wednesday, and they remain parked Thursday, Friday and Saturday, and they go home Sunday."
According to 8 Investigates’ analysis of historical data from the U.S. Energy Information Administration, the average price of gas in New England has fallen during the first two weeks of November 70% of the time since 1993, when the agency’s digital archive began. That pattern holds regardless of whether it’s an election year.
"The simple reality is that the election happened, but the balance of power has not shifted yet," De Haan said.
But the decline during the first two weeks of November this year was steeper than usual. In the 24 years since 1993, when prices fell during that period, the average decrease across New England was 10.2 cents per gallon. This year, prices fell 16.8 cents.
The sharper decrease may have been driven by comments from President Donald Trump about Iran. In a 60 Minutes interview that aired Nov. 8, Trump said he was not looking to escalate the war. The next day, he said he hoped the United States would make a deal with Iran.
"Oil prices move based on geopolitical tensions," said De Haan. "An election in one country doesn't usually really move the needle."

title: 74-year-old killed after semi’s brake rotors fly through another driver’s windshield, police say
text:
TOLLAND, Conn. (WFSB/Gray News) - A 74-year-old man was killed when brake rotors from a tractor-trailer flew through his windshield on a Connecticut highway, authorities said.
Connecticut State Police identified the driver as Juan Americo Marty Del Toro, of Pembroke Pines, Florida.
Police said the tractor-trailer’s brakes failed, causing the rotors to come apart and fly into the air. The rotors struck the windshield of Marty Del Toro’s Nissan and hit him, killing him at the scene.
A passenger in the Nissan suffered minor injuries, police said.
No further details were released.

title: Gordon Ramsay receives star on Hollywood Walk of Fame: ‘I’m blessed’
text:
LOS ANGELES (CNN) - Chef Gordon Ramsay, who has received numerous Michelin stars for his restaurants, now has a star on the Hollywood Walk of Fame.
His star, in the television category, was unveiled in a ceremony Wednesday.
Ramsay’s career includes work as an Emmy-nominated and BAFTA Award-winning TV producer, judge and host.
“I’m blessed to have worked with some of the most talented individuals, uh, anywhere in the world, because behind every show, behind every challenge, there is a talented team that is working as hard as I do,” Ramsay said in his speech.
The Hollywood Chamber of Commerce described him as “a Michelin-starred chef, multi-restaurant owner, best-selling author, and TV favorite who embodies passion, resilience, and unfiltered authenticity.”
The chamber also noted that he is the most-followed chef in the world on social media.

title: Record number of women elected to 120th Congress
text:
WASHINGTON (Gray DC) - At least 162 women will serve when the 120th Congress is sworn in Jan. 3, 2027, the most ever. However, women will still only make up about 30% of all lawmakers.
Nebraska Congresswoman-elect Denise Powell, a Democrat, is one of those incoming members. “It’s unreal,” Powell said.
Powell is one of 41 new women who will be part of the 138 women in the next House of Representatives. That number breaks the 2024 record of 127.
“It’s absolutely thrilling,” said Patti Russo, executive director of The Campaign School at Yale (TCSYale).
Russo runs the school, a nonpartisan, issue-neutral training program that seeks to increase the number of women in elected and appointed office.
“It’s not going to be the same old thing, right? It’s going to be very different. In the House and the Senate, women bring their life experience to leadership. We know that. So as a result of that, what I’m hoping to see is more collaboration,” Russo said.
Incoming and returning women lawmakers said their life experience will help them advance legislation next year.
Rep. Teresa Leger Fernandez, a Democrat and chair of the Democratic Women’s Caucus, said they plan to bring forward bills on pay.
“We are going to actually exercise our power to bring forward bills that actually make sure that women have, that they get paid what they deserve. And then that pay is enough to pay for childcare, eldercare, housing, health care,” Leger Fernandez said.
Powell said women are often disproportionately affected by policies.
“We understand that women are often disproportionately impacted by a lot of the policies that we see from Congress to your school board,” she explained. “So this is such a good opportunity to make some really good change for our families.”
The House will have 118 Democratic and 20 Republican women. Russo said she believes more women in Congress means more bipartisanship.
“We are much more collaborative in our leadership style,” said Russo. “I don’t care who gets the credit. Just get it done. You know, I don’t have to have my name on everything. I don’t have to be front and center, just get it done… We’re not going to agree on everything, but we have to be able to find one or two or three priorities that are going to improve the quality of life for Americans in our country.”

title: Piscataquis Regional Food Center helps 350 families prepare for Thanksgiving
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
DOVER-FOXCROFT, Maine (WABI) - With Thanksgiving just around the corner, one food center in Piscataquis County is helping hundreds of families prepare for the holiday.
Since 2022, the Piscataquis Regional Food Center has been organizing annual Thanksgiving food distributions for families. Distribution took place Wednesday morning at the Dover-Foxcroft Food Cupboard.
“We’re finding a huge increase in need regardless of the holiday. Thanksgiving is often very expensive. It’s more expensive this year,” said PRFC executive director Kelly Sirimoglu.
People who booked appointments received Thanksgiving packages through a drive-thru system, with ingredients donated by community members and funds for turkeys collected throughout the year.
“It’s a long project. We have someone that collects funds for the turkeys all year long,” said Sirimoglu. “The turkeys come here and we have volunteers on Monday who went through and packed all the bags.”
In total, the distribution helped provide Thanksgiving items to around 350 households, with around 20 volunteers helping load cars.
One volunteer, board member Dolly Perkins, says her family once relied on a food cupboard where they used to live. Perkins and two of her sons helped to bring bags of Thanksgiving food, helping to support those in need.
“It is very humbling when you’re a recipient, and to be on the other side of it is such a blessing,” said Perkins. “If we can pay that forward, then that is an absolute honor and a blessing to me.”
Sirimoglu says the need has increased for food assistance in order to help families through rough financial periods.
“It’s been a really difficult year for a lot of families. The cost of heating oil and fuel and everything else going up. To be able to help people ensure they get a Thanksgiving dinner on the table is really what this is all about.”

title: Man’s wife, daughter arrested 4 years after his severed head was found in a trash bag
text:
CITRUS HEIGHTS, Calif. (KXTV) - Authorities say a California man’s wife and daughter have been arrested four years after his severed head was found in a trash bag.
A person walking a dog found a severed head in a trash bag in the Todd Valley area of Foresthill on Sept. 28, 2022, according to the Placer County Sheriff’s Office. Detectives couldn’t identify the victim at the time because of the state of decomposition.
In 2024, a private lab’s DNA analysis – along with help from the FBI – finally led investigators to relatives and to a name: 73-year-old Paul Wesley Fitzmaurice Jr.
“The investigation continued once we had him identified, and we realized that Paul had never been reported missing,” Placer County Sheriff Wayne Woo said.
The victim was last known to be living in Citrus Heights with his wife, 75-year-old Georgia “Gwenn” Fitzmaurice, and their daughter, 45-year-old Mary Fitzmaurice.
Detectives served a search warrant Tuesday at the family’s home, and Mary and Gwenn Fitzmaurice were arrested later that day. Investigators allege the former was responsible for killing her father before she and her mother conspired to dispose of his remains.
“We discovered that Gwenn and Mary had kept up the façade to family and friends that Paul was still alive, and in fact, they were still receiving Paul’s Social Security benefits and his CalPERS [California Public Employees’ Retirement System] pension,” Woo said.
Investigators say Mary Fitzmaurice was booked on murder charges, while her mother was booked on accessory charges. Both women are being held in jail on no bail.
One of the family’s neighbors, who didn’t want to be identified, said he noticed Paul Fitzmaurice’s absence.
“I wondered what happened to Paul a few years ago,” the neighbor said. “I hadn’t seen him around. I asked how he was doing, and nobody ever even said he passed or he died or he was sick or anything. They just stopped talking.”
Investigators are still processing evidence to learn how Paul Fitzmaurice was killed and where the rest of his body is located. As for a motive, the sheriff says it’s too early to say.

title: Maine businesses roll with tech outage impacts
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Like many Maine businesses, Maine Gold & Silver in South Portland experienced a limited impact from the recent spate of tech outages.
The jewelry store’s website and email held up just fine, said Jeffrey Caron, general manager. But some deliveries arrived late after flights nationwide were grounded for five hours last Friday afternoon. And one of the store’s jewelers was several hours late returning from a training in Tennessee because his flight on Saturday was delayed.
“None of our internal operations has been impacted at all,” Caron said Thursday. “I think being a smaller business helps to limit our exposure.”
Maine banks, hardware stores and other businesses reported limited or no effect from tech disruptions that began Nov. 12 when Microsoft Outlook went down for nearly two days. Other malfunctions followed at the Federal Aviation Administration, JPMorgan Chase, Apple and the National Security Agency.
“I haven’t noticed any impacts at all,” said Shawn Drillen, general manager of Drillen Ace Hardware stores in South Portland and Lewiston. “Even online orders have been coming through uninterrupted.”
Among Maine’s largest employers, Hannaford and General Dynamics Bath Iron Works said they were unaffected by the recent outages, while MaineHealth said the Microsoft outage impacted some of its administrative teams.
“(They) had to resort to prearranged modes of backup communication for several hours,” said spokesperson John Porter. “None of our systems supporting patient care were impacted, and there was no interruption to patient services.”
Social media posts and conversations between family members and friends tried to make sense of the outage similarities, even as the Trump administration said there was “zero” indication that they were linked or caused by cybercriminals. Various technical malfunctions were blamed.
Beth Dunstan, a retiree who lives in Cape Elizabeth, wasn’t personally affected by the outages, but she worried when flights were grounded last Friday — one friend was stuck in Phoenix, trying to get home to Pennsylvania, and another friend was stuck in Texas, trying to get home to Massachusetts.
“The next day my sister’s flight from Baltimore to Portland had no delay and got here 45 minutes early,” Dunstan said, “so I don’t understand what was going on.”
EMAIL AFFECTED AT SOME BANKS
Among Maine-based banks, email went down at Saco & Biddeford Savings with the Microsoft outage, but services at its operations center in Saco and seven branches were unaffected, said Chelsea Miller, spokesperson.
Androscoggin Bank also lost internal email because of Microsoft, but its nine branches remained open and fully operational throughout, said CEO Neil Kiely.
“As we approached the possibility of a second business day without email, we convened our incident response team Friday morning and prepared to implement contingency plans,” Kiely said via email. “Fortunately, email service was restored before business hours, so those measures were not needed and there was no meaningful disruption to our clients.”
Norway Savings Bank wasn’t impacted at all, said Dave Guthro, spokesman. And if the bank ever does have an online issue, it has extensive plans in place to protect customer accounts.
“Banks are required to go through rigorous examinations at the state and federal level that ensure they have detailed disaster recovery procedures and business continuity plans,” Guthro said in an email.
CHAMBERS WEIGH IN ON OUTAGES
Quincy Hentzel, CEO of the Portland Regional Chamber of Commerce, said the Microsoft Outlook outage was felt acutely by many of the group’s 1,400 member companies.
“Businesses rely on a predictable environment to operate effectively, and that certainly includes the modern technology systems many depend on,” Hentzel said in an email. “These disruptions are a reminder of how important the reliability of these systems is to our economic infrastructure. These are developments the chamber is definitely monitoring closely.”
Patrick Woodcock, CEO of the Maine State Chamber of Commerce, said he hadn’t heard much feedback about the tech outages from the group’s network of 5,000 employers.
“While the recent disruptions have been comparatively minor for impact on total work hours, the loss of productive hours comes at a time of year with acute time crunches,” Woodcock said via email. “Every hour lost can put pressure on an already constrained timeline for ensuring holiday products are available and end-of-year projects are delivered.”
Still, he said, Maine businesses are resilient and are managing through these inconveniences.
South Portland wasn’t so fortunate in dealing with its tech issues.
A suspected cyberattack over the weekend has affected city services since Monday, and because of the city’s four-day workweek, City Hall and the assessing department won’t reopen until Monday at the earliest.

title: Anthropic begins trading in the biggest IPO on record despite the many fears surrounding AI
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
NEW YORK (AP) — The artificial intelligence giant Anthropic rose sharply Thursday after making the biggest public stock offering ever, at one point surpassing $2 trillion in value, despite anxiety about an AI bubble and fear that the technology threatens lives and livelihoods.
Its shares shot higher as trading began and held on to much of those gains to close up 17% at $97.17. The initial offering overtook SpaceX as the largest IPO in history.
Anthropic’s initial offer of $82 per share was surprisingly high given the investor worries that ratcheted up even more recently following the stunning ouster of AI’s chief promoter, the CEO of Nvidia, in a possible Chinese spying scandal. Anthropic had earlier set a lower price range between $70 and $78 per share.
“It’s a big win for the tech sector after a white-knuckle time with Nvidia,” said Dan Ives, a financial analyst at Yorkville Ives & Co. “The pricing shows strong demand among investors.”
For his part, Anthropic’s CEO tried to dampen worry about AI’s threat to society.
“If we can show it’s possible to make the right choices on safety and still build an incredibly successful company, others in our industry will be inspired to do the same,” Dario Amodei said.
The San Francisco-based maker of the Claude AI tool offered 980 million shares to the public, which at the $83 per share price translated into proceeds of $81 billion.
IPO offers a way to raise money without going deeper into debt
In addition to recent market jitters, Anthropic’s debut sale had to overcome fears of a potential regulatory crackdown next year by the Democratic-led Congress and growing anti-AI sentiment among the public. Anthropic rival OpenAI decided to postpone its initial offering until next year.
The company, trading under the ticker symbol ANT, also faces big financial challenges ahead.
Anthropic already has taken on $6.2 billion in debt, which it acknowledges in financial filings is “substantial.” Adding to the strain, the company is unprofitable, at least under standard accounting rules, suggesting that its resources to pay interest and principal are limited.
While the company showed ample cash in its last financial report, it would have likely run through it quickly given its outsize spending plans. In the same financial report, the company said it had signed leases and other deals requiring it to spend $900 billion on computing power and infrastructure in the coming years, including $70 billion in the next 12 months.
Such massive spending by AI companies, comparable to the Gilded Age splurge on railroads, has scared lenders, helping to push borrowing rates high recently.
With the IPO, though, Anthropic will now have enormous resources to accelerate its expansion without taking on more debt. In addition to the cash from public investors, the company also planned to sell $26 billion in shares in a private sale Thursday to bring the total raised to $107 billion — an impressive haul for a business not yet six years old.
The offering will also allow its employees to sell vested stock, making many of them millionaires overnight — and adding billions of dollars to the fortunes of CEO Dario Amodei and his sister, Anthropic President Daniela Amodei.
AI industry faces concerns about data centers, a possible bubble and regulations
Anthropic is locked in a fight for dominance with OpenAI. But both companies have plenty of other competitors, including Google, startups in the U.S. and China and SpaceX, which has an AI business.
Anthropic, OpenAI and SpaceX’s AI division have all lost more money than they’ve made because of the huge costs associated with building AI. That has fueled growing concerns about a bubble forming in the sector.
Dario Amodei cautioned in September that the AI industry should slow its fast-moving development to give safety measures time to catch up. Without such a slowdown, Amodei warned, AI could be capable of letting loose a swarm of agents that could take over the internet within months.
Amid mounting fears, the regulatory environment could change for Anthropic once the new Congress is in session. Newly elected Democrats are vowing to crack down on the industry as a backlash unfolds against data centers. And two big states offering incentives for data centers, Texas and Georgia, just elected Democratic governors who have vowed to stop new construction.
In his comments Thursday, Amodei also touted a range of positive uses for AI, noting that Claude already is helping scientists do quicker research and that the technology could help accelerate that progress in the future.
“Human intelligence has already made diseases like plague, smallpox and polio history for most of the world,” he said, “but progress in other diseases has been too slow for so many patients and their families.”
He also pointed to Claude’s use across companies, nonprofits and government services. “I’m extremely optimistic about what we can do together in the future,” he said.
Adding to the pressure to go public was the possibility that demand for AI shares could drop or even collapse. Investors have become anxious about the massive financing needs of the sector, and several tech companies have pulled IPO plans recently.
Market valuation for AI companies is going to be “up and down for many years to come, but more up than down,” said Rich Lesser, the global chair and former CEO of Boston Consulting Group.
“Exactly what the flow of that will be, it’s very hard to predict,” Lesser said Tuesday in an interview with The Associated Press at the Semafor Silicon Valley & the World forum. “There’s no question what Anthropic and OpenAI and Google and a number of the other players in this industry have done is pretty remarkable.”
___
Ortutay reported from Oakland, California. Associated Press business writers Kaitlyn Huamani in Los Angeles and Michelle Chapman in New York contributed.

title: We have a bipartisan plan to remove Donald Trump from office
text:
The BDN Opinion section operates independently and does not set news policies or contribute to reporting or editing articles elsewhere in the newspaper or on bangordailynews.com
Les Fossel is a former Republican legislator from Lincoln County. Phil Bailey is a campaign veteran and current member of the Hancock County Democratic executive committee.
We’ve just been through a pivotal election in which the voters — Democrats, independents and even many Republicans — clearly demonstrated they’ve had enough of the current president and want change. But what change and how do we get there? Does just changing party control in Congress make the difference or is something more needed?
We’re a former Maine Republican legislator and a long-time Democratic political operative and we have a bipartisan proposal to ease Donald Trump out of office for the good of both parties and the country at large while at the same time documenting and beginning to heal the damage he has done.
We propose creating a “truth and reconciliation commission” which, combined with a credible threat of presidential impeachment and conviction, should usher Trump out of office before the new year and give us all a fresh start. The commission would be modeled on similar panels created in other countries after periods of national trauma, most famously in post-apartheid South Africa. Our neighbor Canada even celebrates an annual Truth and Reconciliation Day.
The American version would be a bipartisan group of people with both legislative and judicial experience who would look more deeply into what has taken place and how we can best repair the economy, end a useless war, and bring some balance and real progress to the country. The people who could make this happen are the very ones who have less than two months left to their terms in Congress. They literally have nothing to lose while the American people would have everything to gain, since such a commission could set the table for truth, justice, and a way forward.
Meanwhile, we believe Republican members of the lame duck Congress should join with their Democratic colleagues in threatening Trump with impeachment and removal from office. Trump rightly fears being a legal target if he loses power, so we suggest that threat should be accompanied by a promise of a presidential pardon from his successor if Trump instead resigns. (It’s generally understood that the resignation of Richard Nixon in the 1970s was facilitated by such a deal.) Since Trump shows little concern for the fate of those around him, personal protection from criminal prosecution is probably all that needs to be offered.
Democrats would certainly rejoice at Trump’s departure, but it’s also true that without the burden of Trump in the White House, the GOP could hope to recover their fortunes in the 2028 election cycle.
Democrats were elected to get the U.S. back on track, which means reducing inflation, lowering fuel prices, ending the Iran war, dropping price-hiking tariffs, and cleaning up the wholesale corruption in Washington, D.C. We believe none of this can be accomplished with Trump as president.
At the same time Republicans need to transform back into a responsible opposition party. That’s not possible with Trump hanging around either.
There are solutions to the problems we face, ones that both parties can embrace. For instance, to end the Iran war and lower fuel prices requires us to break the alliance between Russia and Iran. If we fully use our resources, in coordination with our European allies, we have a good chance of doing that, with the bonus of ending Iran’s nuclear bomb development.
A bipartisan truth and reconciliation process could also help keep the newly empowered Democrats from overreaching. Otherwise they may adopt all the excesses of the GOP. The next 10 weeks or so represent a very short time when both parties could be willing to support our democracy rather than subverting it to advance their agendas.
What can you do? Call your representative and senators and ask for something more than a useless standoff with a repudiated president. Demand a process that actually uses the lame-duck break between the election and the opening of a new Congress to move our country forward.

SEARSMONT, Maine (WABI) -Sarah Tompkins, a first responder injured in a mill fire and explosion in Searsmont, was welcomed home Wednesday, just over six months after the incident.
Crews escort Tompkins home
Community EMS and fire crews escorted Tompkins. The route started at the Augusta Civic Center and ended at Searsmont Fire and Rescue.
Interim EMS Chief Amy Drinkwater helped organize the homecoming, which brought together crews from across the state.

Tompkins releases letter
Tompkins was treated at Maine Medical Center and Spaulding Rehabilitation Hospital in Massachusetts.
She declined to speak to the media Wednesday but released a letter Monday. In part, she wrote:
“I have worked in EMS for eight years, but for the last 6 months I have been the one being cared for after my worst day.”
She also wrote: “I still have wounds and scars, but I am also filled with so much hope for all of us.”
Town official comments
Searsmont selectman and firefighter Christopher Staples said Tompkins has made a lasting impact on the community.
“She’s got a big heart and she’s been a big part of our community for several years. So, getting her back is a big, big thing for the town,” Staples said.

title: Maine’s eviction prevention program will soon run out of funding — again
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
A state program aimed at preventing evictions will stop accepting applications at the end of November because demand is on track to exhaust the initiative’s $11 million budget.
Nearly 2,200 households across Maine’s 16 counties applied for the eviction prevention program in two months, according to data from MaineHousing.
This marks the second time the state has allocated millions to rent relief only to see the money drained quickly due to high demand.
“We will be coming back to the Legislature again to make the case that there is so much need, and it is urgent,” said Kathy Kilrain del Rio, advocacy and programs director at Maine Equal Justice. “We should be making this a permanent program that can help people for the long term.”
The program, which is administered by Maine Housing and managed by Project Home, helps Mainers who are struggling to pay their monthly rents or have an overdue balance. Benefits are capped at $800 monthly and $9,600 total per household and are paid directly to landlords.
The organizations said this week they will “make every effort” to help eligible applicants but cannot guarantee that assistance will be available for all.
What comes next could be decided by a new governor and Legislature.
Spokesperson Mary Erin Casale did not say whether Gov.-elect Hannah Pingree will push to make this specific program permanent but did say that housing will be a priority for her administration.
“She believes housing is fundamental to Maine’s success, and she intends to make good on her campaign promise to invest $100 million in housing programs,” Casale wrote in an email. “The Gov.-elect is committed to working with the Legislature and stakeholders to determine how best to use that investment, and to finding a way to support eviction prevention efforts as part of the broader housing agenda.”
Victoria Morales, executive director of Project Home, said in a news release that eviction has devastating effects on employment, education and family stability.
The eviction prevention program started in 2024 as an $18 million pilot in response to rising housing costs and an increase in eviction filings after the COVID-19 pandemic. Data from MaineHousing shows that more than 1,300 households received assistance.
Lawmakers later enacted a bill to make the program permanent but did not fund it. Instead, the state allocated another $11 million as a one-time investment earlier this year and reopened applications in September.
MaineHousing reported that the program had received 2,199 applications by Nov. 16 and approved 102. Even with many applications still in process, the anticipated need exceeds $13 million. So far, the average monthly rent benefit issued is $588, and the average amount of overdue rent paid is $4,078.
Applications are coming from every county. The highest totals so far are 495 from Cumberland County and 400 from Penobscot County. They are reviewed on a first-come, first-served basis within certain categories, with first priority going to eligible households that have received a summons to appear in court as part of evictions proceedings.
Eligible Mainers make less than 60% of the local area median income and pay less than 125% of fair market rent for the area in which they live. Participants may not live in subsidized housing or have a federal housing voucher.
Applications will close at 5 p.m. on Nov. 30.

title: This symphony chorus is helping singers stay sharp
text:
NASHVILLE, Tenn. (InvestigateTV) - For many of the 150 members of the Adult Symphony Chorus, singing alongside the renowned Nashville Symphony is more than a hobby.
It’s helping their voices — and brains — stay sharp.
“It’s a really involved, dedicated group of people who care about music first, then care about each other equally first,” said Tucker Biddlecombe, chorus director and associate dean of Vanderbilt’s Blair School of Music.
Members range from 22 to nearly 80 years old.
“From an intellectual standpoint, sight reading is no joke,” said Duane Hamilton, 73, a former disc jockey-turned-long-haul truck driver.
Some singers, like 77-year-old retired pathologist Dr. Carla Davis, take extra measures.
“I also take voice lessons because as women we get older, their vocal apparatus goes,” Davis said. “It takes a lot of work.”
Both Davis and Hamilton believe singing at this level, in this community, gives them life.
“I can’t imagine a life without singing,” Davis said. “It brings joy to my life.”
Dr. Chris Mixon, a retired pathologist now researching cancer, said singing in the Symphony Chorus for 25 years has helped him face his fears.
“I have terrible stage fright, so it’s difficult to sing in front of people,” Mixon said. “When you’re with a group of people, when you’re really into the music and can do your part, stage fright disappears.”
Mixon spends two and half hours a week working on his music.
“Do you plan to quit anytime soon?” asked WSMV’s Tracy Kornet.
“No,” Mixon said. “Although we have to re-audition every other year, so the choice might be out of my hands,” he laughed.
Brain health connection
Research published in Dean and Ayesha Sherzai’s book, The Alzheimer’s Solution: A Breakthrough Program to Prevent and Reverse the Symptoms of Cognitive Decline at Every Age, shows challenging the brain by learning new things and doing activities with purpose, especially in a social setting, activates all areas of the brain.
So much so, it can pause dementia.
Add proper nutrition, regular exercise, managing stress and getting a good night’s sleep, and research shows people can reduce their risk of Alzheimer’s disease by 60%, according to the Sherzais.
“The strongest neural connections are the ones that bring us joy, the ones we want to revisit every day,” Biddlecombe said. “I think that’s the simplest way to talk about music as an expression of the soul, we are strengthening the neurons and synapses that are supposed to be strong and weakening the ones we want to get rid of.”
Personal healing
Hamilton got emotional as he told WSMV’s Tracy Kornet that he had just lost his brother four days earlier. The person who got him into choral music.
“There are moments in this rehearsal when I have to stop and take it in because it touches me. It hits me where I need,” Hamilton said. “So, do I get choked up? Yes, I do. Right now. This is a soothing balm for my heart right now.”

title: ’60 Minutes’ reporting on kratom speaks volumes
text:
Kratom is an opioid-like compound derived from a plant grown in Central and South America. It is illegal to import to the U.S., but it gets here anyway, and is widely available in legal powders, pills and liquids.
It offers an opioid-like high and some people are enthusiastic about its benefits. Others experience it as a gateway drug, going on to seek more powerful highs, addiction, personal ruin and even death.
There’s a lot of money to be made on kratom-related products. According to “60 Minutes,” economic interests — including among some Trump administration officials — stopped the Food and Drug Administration from limiting kratom concentrations to protect public health.
This report speaks volumes about the plight of evidence-based, public health-oriented regulation in the U.S. The Trump Republican approach to science and common sense is filtered through a lens of economic gain. High profits for some equate to good policy for all.
We see this pattern playing out with regard to building AI data centers, sales of our best technologies to other nations (including one-time enemies), reductions in long-established vaccination practices and so on.
The phrase “follow the money” has new meaning today. For Trump, money is the objective behind just about every policy decision. He just met with Presidents Xi and Putin at a major summit. What promises of huge profits will Trump latch onto here? If I were Xi or Putin, I’d dangle lots of golden carrots to win his praise and support.
Tom Meuser
Portland

title: Iowans brace for a lead dust cloud as Army plans to detonate 5 tons of bomb-making chemicals
text:
US Army will delay detonation of bomb-making chemicals in Iowa after public raised concerns
The U.S. Army decided to delay Friday’s detonation of several tons of bomb-making chemicals in southeast Iowa after an outpouring of public concern that a cloud of lead dust could cause environmental contamination and health problems.
The plan is now to carry it out on Monday.
Iowa Gov. Kim Reynolds, who was among those who called for the detonation to be delayed as the clock ticked down Thursday, spoke directly with Acting Secretary of the Army Adam Telle, her office said. Environmental groups filed a lawsuit earlier in the day, seeking emergency court action to halt the plan.
Related video above: U.S. Army is scheduled to detonate lead azide near Middletown, elevating risk for lead in air
Planning for the detonation at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant began after staff earlier this year found several dozen barrels containing lead azide that had degraded, “creating a highly unstable and dangerous situation,” according to an emergency permit approved last week by the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency. Moving or relocating it posed an unacceptable risk of accidental detonation, a possibility that increases in cold weather.
“This will delay the detonation until the latest possible moment prior to a forecasted temperature drop, which would risk further destabilization of the material,” Telle said in a post on X announcing the push to Monday.
The Army had shared details during a public meeting in Middletown in October, but a public advisory Sunday was the first time other communities — some as far away as 100 miles (160 kilometers) — became aware of the potential impact. Nearly 400 people live in Middletown — about 160 miles (257 kilometers) southeast of Des Moines — but thousands more in surrounding areas could be affected by detonated material that could disperse in the air and land on the ground.
“Public communication is essential to public trust,” Telle said.
Businesses and schools adjusted Friday schedules
Vibrations from the two planned blasts were expected to be quick, but they could break old windows in the Middletown area. That led officials to recommend some residents in Middletown vacate the area.
Iowans in the region were told to stay inside; keep windows and doors closed; bring pets and livestock indoors; and clean cars, windowsills and outdoor surfaces afterward.
“The detonation will result in an air plume with some lead-containing particles which will disperse in the air and deposit on the ground,” an advisory states. “Lead is toxic to humans and animals.”
Many schools throughout the region had already announced closures Friday and would now have to decide how to proceed on Monday.
Lucy Giehl, her husband and two dogs live just about 4 miles (6.4 kilometers) north of the ammunition plant. She first learned of the detonation on Sunday and was still trying to figure out where she'd go during the detonation.
But Giehl, 64, also wondered what happens when she gets home after. She voiced frustration about the lack of information about how to mitigate the risks. Her questions remained Thursday even after the delay.
“What are they going to do during those three days to help people be better prepared?” Giehl asked, asking whether she needs to wear gloves to wipe down surfaces or to keep her dogs from drinking water in their pond. “There’s just so many details that I feel like haven’t been addressed with the public.”
Environmental groups are still pursuing legal action
Environmental groups sued Thursday in an effort to stop the detonation, arguing that the EPA failed to require the Army to consider safer alternatives and that the Army failed to give adequate notice of its plans.
The detonation should be canceled outright, not merely delayed, said Wally Taylor, legal chair for the Sierra Club, one of the groups involved in the lawsuit.
“We don’t want the explosion to take place at all,” Taylor said Thursday after the announcement. “There are ways to do it without all the air quality problems and potential health problems.”
According to EPA and Army documents, alternatives such as neutralizing and decomposing the drums’ contents with other chemicals were considered. But officials said handling the drums would increase the probability of an accidental, fatal detonation.
The Army also says taking no action could lead to an accidental detonation that would result in “the sudden, uncontrolled release of vaporized lead, particulate matter, and toxic combustion gases.” Without planning based on weather patterns, that could cause “severe health impacts,” according to the Army's environmental assessment.
The Army said a panel of experts in munitions chemistry, engineering and environmental safety prepared the detonation plan.
Experts urged residents to take precautions
Patrick O’Shaughnessy, a professor at the University of Iowa’s Department of Occupational and Environmental Health, said it's still unknown how much contamination will end up in the atmosphere and on surfaces.
Lead is a neurological toxicant that can harm the brain, nervous system and other organs.
With high doses over a short period, people can be subject to lead poisoning and begin to feel sick, said Andrew Whelton, an environmental engineering professor at Purdue University who has helped communities recover from chemical disasters.
Long-term exposure to low doses can lead to neurological development problems, especially in young children, O’Shaughnessy added.
Iowa State’s Des Moines County Extension field office was busy fielding calls Thursday from concerned residents who have been “deathly afraid” for their health and their animals, said staff member Morgan Hoenig.
“We ran out of soil test kits yesterday,” she said.
