title: Jewish WWI soldiers originally buried under crosses get corrected headstones
text:
Jewish WWI soldiers get corrected headstones after originally being buried under crosses
Three Jewish soldiers who fought and died in World War I were honored this week at Arlington National Cemetery with new headstones engraved with the Star of David, correcting a century-old mistake that had marked their graves with Christian crosses.
The ceremony included the recitation of the Mourner’s Kaddish, the Jewish memorial prayer, for Corporal Jacob Leifer, whose headstone now reflects his Jewish faith. Leifer, along with Private David Latken and Private First Class Benjamin Yarish, had been mistakenly buried with crosses on their headstones.
Shalom Lamm, co-founder and chief historian of Operation Benjamin, explained the origins of the error.
"The complexity, the number of soldiers that they were dealing with at an age before computers, clerical errors crept in — because they were buried initially on the battlefield in a shallow grave by their comrades, and then they were taken to a collection area, and they were moved to a larger regional cemetery, and only ultimately four or five burials later did they end up in a national cemetery," Lamm said.
Leifer’s great-nephew, William Taubman, who is 85 years old, said he only recently learned of his great-uncle’s existence.
"That he's remembered, and his service is remembered, and the sacrifice of him and others is remembered, and that is wonderful," Taubman said.
Leifer, Latken and Yarish served in the U.S. Army during the Meuse-Argonne offensive in France in 1918, one of the bloodiest battles of World War I. They died within six days of each other, just a month before the war ended.
The effort to research and correct the religious symbols on their headstones was led by Operation Benjamin, a nonprofit dedicated to honoring fallen Jewish service members. The organization has corrected more than 70 headstones of Jewish American soldiers from World Wars I and II.
"We get to introduce families to their loved ones who they never knew," Lamm said.
Of the three soldiers honored, only the family of David Latken had a photograph of him. His great-grandniece, Illa Moskowitz, said she had never heard of him before.
"Oh, I'm proud to know the family history. It was very moving to be here for this," Moskowitz said.
Also honored during the ceremony was Private First-Class Johann Kasten, a non-Jewish servicemember who was taken prisoner by the German army during the Battle of the Bulge in World War II. When the Germans demanded that Kasten identify Jewish soldiers in his unit, he refused.
"He was starving, he was beaten, he was tortured, and still he wouldn't yield. I don't know where that sort of inner strength comes from, but I'm so glad he was on our side," Lamm said.
Kasten’s granddaughters placed memorial stones on his headstone during the ceremony.
Even with the gratification surrounding the new Jewish headstones, Operation Benjamin’s work is far from complete. Lamm said the organization still aims to correct the headstones of between 600 and 800 American Jewish soldiers from World Wars I and II.

title: Susan Smith denied parole again 32 years after drowning her sons in a South Carolina lake
text:
Susan Smith denied parole again 32 years after drowning her sons in a South Carolina lake
Susan Smith, who rolled her car into a South Carolina lake more than 30 years ago, killing her sons who were still strapped in their car seats, was denied parole again Thursday.
Video above: Susan Smith's attorney speaks during her 2024 parole hearing
Smith, 55, was sentenced to life in prison for the 1994 drownings of 3-year-old Michael and 14-month-old Alex after the jury that convicted her chose not to give her the death penalty.
But under South Carolina law at the time, she could ask for parole after 30 years and if refused, every two years after that. The parole board unanimously denied her parole request in 2024. The parole board voted unanimously Thursday to deny parole.
The boys' father David Smith, who vowed at the first hearing to oppose his ex-wife's release as long as he can, and the original prosecutors in the case planned an early morning trip to Columbia to again ask that Smith remain in prison. Smith pinned to his jacket over his heart the same photo of his young sons that was once sent around the world when people thought they were kidnapped by a carjacker.
David Smith asked the parole board to look into his heart. He said 32 years may seem like a long time, but to him it seems like it was yesterday when he buried his boys. He said he was there to advocate for his sons, who could never stand up for themselves.
“She took away one of the greatest gifts God gives us – life. She did that deliberately. It wasn’t an accident, it wasn’t a mistake. She did it deliberately,” he said in testimony Thursday.
Smith appeared by video before board that often rejects inmates
Susan Smith’s hearing before the state Department of Probation, Parole and Pardon Services took place virtually with Smith joining by a video call from prison. She needed two-thirds support from the seven-member board to be released.
Smith said her sons were innocent children who did not deserve to die. She said she has so much remorse for killing them and asked the board to give her a chance to get out of prison and do good for the world.
“I know that David didn’t get to see Michael and Alex grow up. You didn’t get to see him ride a bike or go to school. And I’m really, really sorry for that, and I would go back and change all of that if I could, I would, OK? I’m not the same person I was 32 years ago,” Smith said.
Odds for parole were against her. The board granted parole in only 4% of cases before it and the majority were in non-violent cases, according to the agency's statistics.
And Smith's case is one of the most notorious cases to come before the board. She made international headlines in 1994 when she insisted for nine days that a Black carjacker drove away with her sons when the boys were at the bottom of John D. Long Lake in Union County.
The claims by Smith, who is white, played into a centuries-old racist trope of Black men being a danger to white women and stoked concerns about crime that were prevalent in 1990s America and remain so today.
Prosecutors blame affair while defense blames mental health
Prosecutors have long argued that Smith killed her sons because she believed they were the reason the wealthy son of the owner of the business where she worked broke off their affair.
Smith and her attorneys blamed her mental health at her trial 30 years ago, saying she planned to go into the lake with her sons but changed her mind at the last moment. Her lawyer likely will also make the same argument from her first parole hearing that she has no other criminal history and would be a low risk to ever commit a crime again.
Psychologist Jessie Hill said at the parole hearing Thursday that Smith’s roiling mental illness has been greatly subdued thanks to medicine, hormonal changes from menopause and the deaths of her mother and stepfather, who admitted in court he sexually abused his stepdaughter from before she was a teenager.
Smith at her first parole hearing said God has forgiven her and she asked for the same mercy. She cried, said what she did was horrible and she would give anything to bring her sons back.
Smith made tearful pleas for days before confessing
For nine days in 1994, Smith made numerous and sometimes tearful pleas asking that Michael and Alex be returned safely. But she would eventually confess.
A re-creation by investigators showed it took six minutes for Smith's Mazda to dip below the surface, while cameras inside the vehicle showed water pouring in through the vents and steadily rising. The boys’ bodies were found dangling upside-down in their car seats, one tiny hand pressed against a window.

title: Albin Boija’s resurgence in net powering UMaine hockey’s success
text:
ORONO, Maine — Entering the season, University of Maine sixth-year men’s hockey coach Ben Barr knew he needed a bounceback year from senior goaltender Albin Boija if his team was going to vie for a third NCAA Tournament appearance in four years.
So far, so good.
Boija will enter this weekend’s home series against Boston College ranked seventh in the country in goals-against average (1.51) among 62 Division I starting goaltenders. He’s 19th in save percentage (.932).
He’s the reigning Hockey East Goaltender of the Week after stopping 42 of 43 shots in a 0-0 tie and a 3-1 win at nationally-ranked Vermont last weekend.
“I’m just trying to play my game, nothing too crazy,” Boija said. “I’m trying to be calm, trying to be the rock the team needs. I’m doing my best out there.”
Boija was a second-team All-American two years ago when he led the Black Bears to their second-straight NCAA Tournament appearance. His 1.83 GAA was the fifth best in the country. His .928 save percentage was tied for eighth and was fourth among goalies who played in at least 30 games.
He was a finalist for the Mike Richter Award, which goes to the nation’s top Division I goalie.
He also had an impressive freshman season, winning the starting job from senior Victor Ostman and going 10-6-1 with a 2.01 GAA and a .916 save percentage to lead UMaine to its first NCAA Tournament appearance since 2012.
But Boija struggled last season, posting a 2.59 GAA and an .899 save percentage on a 10-7-3 record, and he lost his starting job to freshman Mathis Rousseau, who transferred to Cornell after the season.
In his last six starts this season. Boija has registered a GAA under 1.00 (.987) and a .952 save percentage with three shutouts. He’s just the third UMaine goalie since 2000 to rack up three shutouts through his first 10 games, joining Matt Lundin (2005-2006) and Jimmy Howard (2002-03).
He currently leads all active Division I goaltenders in career wins (48) and shutouts (13).
“He is more composed and poised than he was last year,” Barr said. “He is making saves and holding onto the puck. He is a little more patient in the net, and he is competing. He is in a better place mentally.”
Barr said the pressure of coming off an All-American season contributed to Boija’s 2025-26 season, adding that he didn’t have any roadblocks, obstacles, or expectations his first two seasons.
“He comes back last year, and the world is expected of him because he was an All-American. It’s easier to play when no one cares, and no one expects anything of you,” Barr said. “It’s good that he came back and he’s putting himself through this.”
Boija admitted he felt pressure last year.
“It wasn’t really external, necessarily,” said Boija, a Sundsvall, Sweden native. “It was more in my head and everything. I’m just trying to have a better outlook, in general.”
Assistant and goalie coach Alfie Michaud praised Boija’s growth.
“He is more mature this year,” said UMaine assistant coach and goalie coach Alfie Michaud, who was the goalie for UMaine for the program’s last NCAA championship in 1999. “It was a great learning year for him last season. When you go through something like that, you have to grow up. He is working hard and he just has to keep getting better.”
Boija and the Black Bears, 6-5-1 overall and 2-3-1 in Hockey East, will have their hands full Friday and Saturday nights at 7 against a 4-5-2 (3-2-1 Hockey East) Boston College team with six first- and second-round NHL draft picks in their 14-man roster.
“You have to see it as an opportunity to do something, so it’s going to be fun,” Boija said.
The Black Bears have been led by right wing Lee Parks (5 goals, 5 assists), left wing Tanner Klimpke (5 goals, 4 assists), center Max Scott (2 goals, 6 assists) and left wing and captain Owen Fowler (3 goals, 3 assists). Center Jaden Lipinski has points in four of his last five games (2 goals, 2 assists).
The Eagles, coming off a sweep of UMass, feature 6-foot-7 center and Boston Bruins first-round draft pick Dean Letourneau (7 goals, 6 assists) along with defenseman Luka Radivojevic (9 assists), left wing Oscar Hemming (3 goals, 5 assists), right wing Ryan Conmy (3 goals, 4 assists) and center Teddy Stiga (5 goals, 2 assists).
Goalie Louka Cloutier is 4-3-2 with a 2.33 GAA and a .912 save percentage.

title: Chase Bank announces cyberattack, says hackers may have obtained customers’ personal information
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
(Gray News) — Chase Bank said Thursday that some customers’ information was compromised during a cyberattack.
In a post on X, the bank said third parties that provide services to the firm were the target of a cyberattack.
Chase Bank said investigators found that the attackers accessed “certain marketing data held by those vendors, which may include some customer names and email addresses.”
The bank said there was no disruption to its services.
Any customers affected will be contacted directly by Chase Bank. The bank said it will offer support, including free credit monitoring.
The cyberattack is not believed to be connected to technical problems at multiple major banks earlier this week.
Thousands of customers reported difficulty accessing online accounts at several major U.S. banks and the money transfer service Zelle on Monday after a technical issue at JPMorgan Chase caused ripple effects throughout the financial system.
However, JPMorgan Chase said Monday that the technical problems were not the result of a cyberattack.
“JPMorgan Chase has experienced a temporary issue related to a software bug in an on-premises hardware system — it is not cyber-related,” said spokesman Joe Evangelisti.

title: Mental competency at issue in US criminal case against Meghan Markle’s father
text:
TAMPA, Fla. (AP) — A judge scheduled a mental competency hearing Thursday for the 82-year-old estranged father of Meghan, the Duchess of Sussex, two weeks after he was arrested in Florida and charged with storing child sexual abuse material in California.
Thomas Markle was released after his arrest at a senior care center but was ordered to jail four days later, on Nov. 10, when authorities accused him of cutting off his electronic ankle monitor. A judge also ordered him to be examined by a mental health professional.
A hearing was set for Thursday afternoon in federal court in Tampa, Florida. Prosecutors declined to comment Wednesday. Markle’s lawyer did not reply to an email seeking comment.
Markle’s arrest in Lakeland, Florida, followed the seizure of approximately 78 items from storage units in the Los Angeles area, including slides, film negatives and books that contained suspected child sexual abuse images, the FBI said in a court filing.
Some images appear to depict him with children, the FBI said.
Markle had a stroke earlier this year while living in the Philippines and had to have his left leg amputated. That forced him to return to the U.S. and settle in Florida.

title: UMaine women’s basketball tops VCU in overtime
text:
Kaliyah Sain scored 15 of her career-high 29 points in overtime, lifting UMaine to an 85-80 win over Virginia Commonwealth in a women’s basketball game Thursday night in Orono.
Maine (4-1) was leading 62-60 with 4:31 remaining in regulation when sophomore guard Lala Woods, the team’s second leading scorer so far this season, left the game because of an apparent knee injury. Woods finished with 17 points, as all five starters for the Black Bears scored in double figures.
With the game tied 69-69 after regulation, Sain took over in overtime. The senior forward from Iowa scored 15 of Maine’s 16 points in the extra session as she surpassed her career high of 26 points, set last season against VCU.
Lizzy Gruber posted a double-double with 14 points and 13 rebounds, to go with five assists and four blocked shots. Maddie Fitzpatrick added 15 points, eight rebounds and eight assists before fouling out in overtime, and Olivia Alvarez scored 10 points.
Macy Spencer led VCU (2-2) with 19 points, including 10 in overtime.

title: Reports: 'Days of Our Lives' and 'General Hospital' actor dies at 66
text:
'Days of Our Lives' and 'General Hospital' actor Larry Poindexter dies at 66, report says
Larry Poindexter, an actor who has appeared in almost 200 movies and TV series, died at the age of 66 days after he was reportedly hit by a vehicle.
Deadline reported that the actor died on Nov. 18, four days after he was hit by a car while crossing the street to pick up food in his Studio City neighborhood in California. 
The outlet said Poindexter was scheduled to have surgery for broken ribs, but died suddenly in the early morning hours.
It is unclear if any arrests have been made or if the driver stayed on the scene following the incident.
Paul Iacono, who played Poindexter's son in their MTV comedy series "The Hard Times of RJ Berger," issued a statement on Instagram following his on-screen father's passing.
"When I was in my early twenties, Larry looked out for me in ways I didn’t fully appreciate at the time. He offered wisdom I wasn’t always ready to hear, and it took me a few years to realize just how right he was about so many things. He taught me that being a good person and collaborator mattered just as much as being a great actor," Iacono said. "I’m forever honored to have played his son, and I’ll always cherish him as my second father."
In addition to "The Hard Times of RJ Berger," Poindexter also appeared in 30 episodes of daytime drama "Days Of Our Lives," playing two different characters, first in 1984 as Ben Welch, and as Father Louis from 2014-2018. He also did a 23-episode stint on Santa Barbara and 12 episodes of "General Hospital."

title: MaineHousing awards $12.7M in tax credits to develop 186 affordable apartments
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
MaineHousing awards $12.7M in tax credits to develop 186 affordable apartments across four communities
The state and federal tax credits will leverage $45.8 million in housing investment.
MaineHousing awards $12.7M in tax credits to develop 186 affordable apartments across four communities
The state and federal tax credits will leverage $45.8 million in housing investment.
The Maine State Housing Authority (MaineHousing) announced Thursday that it has awarded $12.7 million in state and federal tax credits to develop 186 affordable apartments across four communities.
According to MaineHousing, the tax credits will leverage more than $45.8 million in investment into the state's economy, sustaining construction jobs and creating or preserving much-needed affordable housing for families and older Mainers in Portland, Biddeford, Fairfield and Camden.
"Everyone deserves a safe, affordable place to call home, but New England and the nation face a severe housing crunch," Gov. Janet Mills said in a statement. "Because of investments like these, we’re one step closer to ensuring every Maine family has a place to call home."
MaineHousing has awarded tax credits to two developments in Portland. The Mayo Housing project received $2,838,138 in state low-income housing tax credits and $686,869 in federal low-income housing tax credits to develop 27 units for families. The Prosperity Place project received $1.2 million in federal tax credits to develop 50 units for families.
The Acadia project in Biddeford also received $1.2 million in federal tax credits to develop 45 affordable apartments for Mainers age 55 and older.
The Fairfield School Apartments project received $900,000 in federal tax credits and an additional $5,153,690 in historic preservation tax credits to develop 30 units for older Mainers at a historic school property. In August, Maine's Total Coverage reporter Jim Keithley toured the vacant school building in Fairfield that is being redeveloped by the Kennebec Valley Community Action Program.
In Camden, the Megunticook House received $750,000 in federal tax credits to develop 34 units for older Mainers.
MaineHousing said it selected the five developments from a pool of 17 that applied for funding in what was a very competitive tax-credit award process.
The 12 developments that were not awarded funding have been placed on a ranked waiting list and may receive funding if any of the approved projects are unable to complete financing. MaineHousing said the developments that had unsuccessful proposals may also reapply for future tax credit awards later this year.

title: Maine Public Advocate seeks records in CMP rate case following whistleblower allegations
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
PORTLAND, Maine (WMTW) - Maine’s Public Advocate is asking state regulators to review records related to allegations of misconduct involving Central Maine Power’s parent company, Avangrid, as part of CMP’s pending rate case.
The motion follows a whistleblower lawsuit filed by Andrew Jacobs, the former chief compliance officer at Avangrid.
In the complaint, Jacobs alleges he was directed to withhold information from federal auditors, downplay a 2025 bribery matter involving CMP and overstate the company’s compliance with federal requirements.
The Office of the Public Advocate says the allegations could have implications for CMP’s rate case and what customers ultimately pay.
The office is seeking access to records related to the claims as regulators consider the utility’s request to raise rates.
CMP says the incident involved approximately $39,000, including unauthorized credit card charges in 2025. The company maintains there will be no rate consequences for customers.
CMP also expressed disappointment that the Office of the Public Advocate did not contact the company before filing the motion.
“We investigated, we disclosed this to FERC, and we no longer work with this individual who was involved,” said Jon Breed, speaking on behalf of CMP.
Breed said the company will review the motion carefully and respond through the appropriate process.

title: Investigators determine Kittery house fire was arson
text:
Maine investigators determine Kittery house fire was arson
The Maine State Fire Marshal's Office is seeking information about a house fire in Kittery after investigators determined that it was intentionally set.
The fire at 155 Pepperrell Road happened the evening of Friday, Nov. 6.
The Kittery Fire Department called in the State Fire Marshal's Office to investigate, and the Kittery Police Department was also involved in the investigation.
The Fire Marshal's Office said investigators confirmed that the house fire was arson.
The people who live at the home, a Cape-style house with an accessory dwelling unit, and the property owner have been cooperative with investigators, according to officials.
The arson investigation remains active and ongoing. Investigators have since returned to the scene and the surrounding area to conduct additional investigative work and collect more evidence.
Authorities are asking anyone with information about the fire to call the State Fire Marshal's Office at 207-624-7076 or the Kittery Police Department at 207-439-1638. People can also share information anonymously by calling the Arson Tip Line at 1-888-870-6162.

title: Maine’s Teigan Pelletier excelling for playoff-bound Harvard football — but first, Yale
text:
We’re proud to make high school sports coverage free for everyone, because these moments matter. At Maine State Credit Union, we’re here for the people and places that make Maine strong. Let’s go! Learn more at mainestatecu.org. 
Teigan Pelletier appeared in just two games for Harvard as a freshman last season.
Now a sophomore, the Paris native has become a reliable target for the Crimson, and on Saturday he will play in his first Harvard-Yale game — one of college football’s most storied rivalries. The game is set for 3:30 p.m. at Fenway Park in Boston.
“It’s crazy,” said Pelletier. “It’s a historic matchup, a historic place. Obviously, I’m from Maine and a huge Boston Red Sox fan, so being at Fenway is just a surreal experience. I’m very excited to play, but (we’ve) got to try not to let the emotions get to us when we’re at the Green Monster.”
Pelletier has played in eight games this fall and is third on the team in receiving with 20 receptions for 287 yards and four touchdowns — a significant leap from last season. And he’ll get a chance to participate in the NCAA’s Football Championship Subdivision playoffs, because Harvard (8-1 overall, 5-1 Ivy League) has already clinched the Ivy League’s automatic berth.
“It’s definitely a lot different than last year because I got hurt right at the beginning of the season, so it’s definitely a change up from last year, but I definitely lean on the older guys,” Pelletier said. “Our tight end group, everybody’s a great guy. They’re helping me out with everything, really.”
One of Pelletier’s receptions this season drew more attention than others.
Against Colgate on Oct. 3, Pelletier caught quarterback Charlie Smith’s Hail Mary pass at the 6-yard line then pitched the ball to wide receiver Nathan Bailey, who ran in for the winning touchdown as time expired. The heads-up sequence, which gave Harvard a 20-17 victory, was the day’s No. 1 play on ESPN’s SportsCenter.
“We practice those type of drills all the time in practice, so it was just due from practice,” Pelletier said. “And I knew (Bailey) was going to be trailing and I heard him yelling my name, and he’s going, ‘Me, me, me.’ So I knew he was there. And then he caught the ball and scored.”
Nate Danforth, who was the defensive coordinator at Oxford Hills when Pelletier played football there before transferring after his junior year to St. Paul’s School in Concord, New Hampshire, said Pelletier’s accomplishments so far at Harvard are no surprise.
“You kind of see guys like (Pelletier) coming up through when they are young, you know they’re going to be something special at some point,” said Danforth, the current Oxford Hills head coach.
While Pelletier and Harvard are facing Yale on Saturday, earlier in the day Danforth and the Vikings will be playing for their first state championship since 2022, when Pelletier was a key player on both sides of the ball. Pelletier also was a key player on the Oxford Hills basketball team and won a state championship in the high jump.
Danforth said that he and the rest of the coaches on the Oxford Hills staff have enjoyed watching Pelletier’s development.
“I don’t think any of us are surprised that (Pelletier’s) able to play at that level and do things like that,” Danforth said. “He’s an incredibly hard worker … his competitiveness, his drive, he has that.”
Saturday will be the 142nd iteration of “The Game” between Harvard and Yale. Harvard has a four-game losing streak against its biggest rival, including a 45-28 loss last year. Regardless of this year’s outcome, the Crimson know they’ll have at least one more game in the NCAA playoffs.

title: Maine Turnpike communications center prepares for AI upgrade
text:
The Maine Turnpike is getting ready to install new computer software, designed to help its staff respond more quickly to emergencies on the highway, including wrong-way drivers.
The Maine Turnpike serves as the state’s transportation backbone, stretching 109 miles from Kittery to Augusta and carrying more than 80 million vehicles a year. Keeping that traffic moving is a task that falls to a crew of turnpike maintenance workers, a Maine State Police detail and safety patrol trucks. All are coordinated through the Turnpike’s Traffic Management and Communications Center.
It’s tucked in the corner of the Turnpike’s headquarters in Portland, usually staffed by just two people during the day and only one overnight. On a Friday afternoon before a long holiday weekend, three people were surrounded by computer screens, monitoring a video board with images of the Turnpike’s live webcams. They also kept an ear to two radio systems — one for state police and the other for Turnpike workers.
One of them reported an abandoned vehicle at the Rand Road interchange in Portland.
“It’s not in a good spot and I’m wondering if you have a trooper in the area that can come and make a decision on this, whether we want to get rid of it,” the worker said. By get rid of it, he meant summoning a tow truck.
A state trooper gave the go-ahead to Shira Andersen, the supervisor on duty, by phone. Until a wrecker arrived, a notice was posted on two electronic message boards along the highway to warn motorists, and alerts were also posted to the Maine Turnpike website and sent to the news media.
Natalie Halvorsen, the operator on duty, said it’s not unusual to have long stretches of quiet, followed by brief periods of intense activity.
“You’re picking up the phone, you’re talking on both radio channels,” she said. “It can be chaotic for the first 20 or 30 minutes, but once everybody’s dispatched to where they need to be, everything is how it’s supposed to be, it’s … over.”
But there are emergency situations, such as wrong-way drivers, that are hard to watch for under the current monitoring system, said Greg Stone, who is in charge of the communications center.
“So, as you can see, there’s all these cameras here, but everybody here is fairly busy, so, the chances of somebody actually looking at a screen at the right time to catch something like that … They’re great for verifying something, but they’re not necessarily great for a human being to detect it,” he said.
According to the Maine Department of Transportation, wrong-way drivers were blamed for 66 crashes in the last decade, resulting in 10 deaths.
Stone said a new AI-based system that’s due to be in service by early next year will be much better at detection.
“There’s a lot of integration with our existing hardware in the field: cameras, sensors, things like that,” he said.
Stone said when the new system spots a deviation in the traffic flow, it will immediately notify the communication center operators via text and audio alerts.
Turnpike officials say the new AI system, which will be operational in January, is intended to assist the control center staff, not replace them.

title: Seawall opens to thru traffic, repairs almost complete
text:
SOUTHWEST HARBOR — Repairs to the damaged stretch of road through Seawall, originally repaired by the surrounding community, are nearing completion after crews began new work in early October.
At press time, both lanes were open.
Back-to-back storms in January 2024 caused severe damage to Route 102A at Seawall, followed by another storm with a massive tide in March. The road was shut down until July 2024, when the community came together to repair a washed-out section of road that runs through Seawall in Southwest Harbor and Acadia National Park.
That repair, funded by the Department of Transportation, has served residents and visitors on Mount Desert Island to date with no issues.
That specific stretch of road is a vital piece of infrastructure connecting Southwest Harbor with Tremont and Bass Harbor.
According to Highway Department Foreman Scott Alley, a new culvert has been installed, and crews have since installed several larger gabion baskets for erosion control and paved the road above the culvert, extending the entirety of the Seawall crossing.
Alley said the work was going well and “crews would be coming back to finish paving, but the road would stay open.”
Town Manager Karen Reddersen agreed that the town was pleased with the work performed by local contractor RF Jordan.
The new road at Seawall is on Route 102A and begins 0.07 miles south of Beaver Lodge Lane and extends south 0.42 miles. According to Reddersen and Alley, crews will finish the project and stripes will be painted in the near future.

title: Part of Commercial Street in Portland reduced to one lane 24/7 for storm drain work
text:
Part of Commercial Street in Portland reduced to one lane 24/7 for storm drain upgrade work
Thursday marked the start of 24/7 alternating one-way traffic on a section of Commercial Street in Portland to facilitate ongoing storm drain construction.
Back on Oct. 26, the part of Commercial Street between Maple and Center streets was reduced to one lane between the hours of 9 a.m. and 3:30 p.m. on weekdays. But now, that stretch of Commercial Street is permanently reduced to one lane until the storm drain work is completed in the winter of 2027.
On-street parking has also been significantly reduced along this section of Commercial Street throughout the construction period.
The work is being completed as part of the Commercial Street/Portland Fish Pier Storm Drain Outfall Project.
City officials said the storm drain project is meant to help mitigate flooding issues the area sees, especially during storms.
Workers will be installing 1,000 feet of 42-inch storm drain piping beneath Commercial Street to replace the 18-inch pipes that are currently there. Work had already started on the Portland Fish Pier, where the city is constructing a new 42-inch separated storm drain outfall.
The city said the new system will include tidal backwater valves to reduce tidal backflow and improve performance during high tides. The upgraded storm drain is designed to handle a 25-year storm.
The project received a $3.6 million grant as part of the Maine Department of Transportation's Maine Infrastructure Adaptation Fund.
The city of Portland is asking drivers to avoid the area if possible to avoid traffic congestion.

title: Which Maine towns and cities have banned data centers?
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Since Gov. Janet Mills vetoed a temporary statewide ban on AI data centers in April, dozens of Maine communities have explored imposing restrictions of their own.
At least 30 towns and cities in Maine had taken action on data centers as of Nov. 19, and a few more are weighing it, according to news reports and public notices.
Three municipalities — North Berwick, Scarborough and Westbrook— have permanently banned data centers, and more than two dozen others have passed moratoriums. Those temporary bans are typically designed to give local officials time to weigh more permanent policies.
While some municipalities have passed bans due to proposed (or rumored) data centers, many others have done so as a precaution.
Mills vetoed the temporary statewide ban after lawmakers declined to include an amendment that would have allowed for a data center project at the former Androscoggin Mill in Jay. That proposal was put on pause this summer, but the effort resumed in November.
Data center projects have been proposed, or at least publicly explored, in several Maine communities, from Sanford to the ocean off Eastport. Some proposals have been withdrawn in the face of public opposition, such as one in Lewiston.
Following the Nov. 3 election — during which a slew of towns’ voters passed data center bans or moratoriums — elected officials have signaled support for revisiting a temporary statewide ban.
The following list of municipalities that have passed permanent bans or temporary moratoriums, or are considering action, is derived from reporting by journalists in newsrooms across Maine. It will be updated on a regular basis.
Did we miss your city or town? Send information to [email protected].
BANS
NORTH BERWICK
North Berwick voters approved a permanent ban on data centers in the Nov. 3 election.
The ban applies to facilities with an aggregate data center area of at least 25,000 square feet.
The Select Board initially explored a moratorium but in June opted to send the issue straight to voters instead.
Source: Portland Press Herald
SCARBOROUGH
The Scarborough Town Council passed a data center ban in November.
The ban distinguishes between standalone data centers and accessory spaces, such as server rooms, telecommunications closets and computer equipment rooms.
Officials had approved a 180-day moratorium in June as they worked on the ordinance changes.
Source: Portland Press Herald
WESTBROOK
The Westbrook City Council approved a ban on data centers in November.
The ban still allows data centers as an accessory use, like server rooms and IT rooms for hospitals and other large organizations.
In June, the council passed a 180-day data center moratorium as it drafted the ordinance changes.
Source: Portland Press Herald
MORATORIUMS
BANGOR
The Bangor City Council passed a 180-day moratorium in April and extended it in September.
Source: Bangor Daily News
BETHEL
Bethel residents approved a 180-day moratorium at a town meeting in October.
Source: The Bethel Citizen
BROWNFIELD
Brownfield voters passed a 180-day moratorium in the Nov. 3 election.
Source: Bangor Daily News
BUCKSPORT
The Bucksport Town Council approved a 180-day moratorium in October.
Source: The Ellsworth American
BUXTON
Buxton residents passed a 180-day moratorium, retroactive to Aug. 12, at a town meeting in October.
Source: Portland Press Herald
DIXFIELD
Dixfield residents passed a 180-day moratorium at a town meeting in September.
Source: Rumford Falls Times
ELLSWORTH
The Ellsworth City Council approved a 180-day moratorium in August.
Source: The Ellsworth American
FREEDOM
Freedom voters passed a 180-day moratorium in the Nov. 3 election.
Source: Midcoast Villager
FRYEBURG
Fryeburg residents passed a 180-day moratorium, retroactive to Aug. 25, at a town meeting in October.
Source: The Bridgton News
GORHAM
The Gorham Town Council approved a 180-day moratorium in June and directed the planning board in September to weigh a permanent ban.
The council extended the moratorium in November.
Sources: Portland Press Herald, News Center Maine
GRAY
The Gray Town Council passed a 180-day moratorium, retroactive to July 14, in August.
Source: Portland Press Herald
HALLOWELL
The Hallowell City Council passed a 180-day moratorium in November.
Source: Kennebec Journal
MERCER
Mercer passed a 180-day moratorium on large-scale data center development at an October town meeting.
Source: Maine Monitor
OLD TOWN
The Old Town City Council passed a 180-day moratorium, retroactive to Sept. 8, in October.
Source: Bangor Daily News
PARIS
Paris residents passed a 180-day moratorium at a town meeting in November.
Source: Advertiser Democrat
SABATTUS
Sabattus voters passed a moratorium in the Nov. 3 election.
Sources: Sun Journal, Town of Sabattus
SACO
The Saco City Council passed a 60-day moratorium in August. In late September, the council extended the moratorium to Nov. 28.
Source: Portland Press Herald
SANFORD
The Sanford City Council passed a 91-day moratorium in May, halting a proposed data center along the Mousam River.
In August, the council voted to extend the moratorium 180 days; it is set to expire Jan. 31.
In November, the planning board unanimously decided to hold off on recommending legislation restricting data centers and will instead hold a workshop to strengthen its language.
Source: Portland Press Herald
SOUTH BERWICK
The South Berwick Town Council passed a 180-day moratorium, retroactive to July 14, in October.
Source: Portland Press Herald
WELLS
Wells voters approved a 180-day moratorium in the Nov. 3 election. The moratorium is retroactive to mid-June and is set to expire Dec. 13.
Source: Portland Press Herald
WISCASSET
Wiscasset voters approved a six-month-long moratorium in the Nov. 3 election.
Source: Lincoln County News, Maine Morning Star
CONSIDERING ACTION
BIDDEFORD
The Biddeford Planning Board has recommended ordinance changes to the City Council that would ban large data centers.
The recommendation was unanimously supported by the planning board during its first read in September and again when it agreed to send it to the City Council in October.
Sources: Portland Press Herald, News Center Maine
BREWER
The Brewer Planning Board recommended data center regulations in November for the City Council to consider, which it is scheduled to do in December and January.
The city says the proposed regulations would increase the allowable size for data centers in some industrial zones while also addressing concerns about water usage, electricity costs, noise and environmental impacts.
Source: Bangor Daily News, City of Brewer

What ‘die with zero’ means, and who it is meant for
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
(InvestigateTV) — A money philosophy called “die with zero” is getting attention on social media. The idea is not really about burning through a bank account. Kate Ashford, lead writer with NerdWallet, said it is about intentional, joy-based spending after a solid financial foundation has been built.
Ashford described the concept this way.
“It sounds kind of dire, but it’s really this idea that if you’re hoarding your money to the end of your life maybe you should consider spending it down, over time, so that when you die, you don’t just have this pile of cash in the bank. You’ve used that money to spend on experiences,” Ashford said.
She said the approach is about making the most of your money while you are still alive. A strategy like this is meant to make sure money lasts after retirement while also putting it to use.
Ashford said the approach starts with a solid financial foundation.
“With this approach you have to make sure you have a solid financial foundation,” Ashford said.
She said the basics include “a healthy emergency fund, no high interest debt,” and having insurance needs covered.
Ashford said this is a plan for someone who already has a financial foundation in place. She recommends working with a professional to make sure spending decisions are sound and that too much money is not taken out at a time.

title: AVEC’s furnace program helped about 62 households, but 160 remain on waiting list
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
PRESQUE ISLE, Maine (WAGM) - AVEC Community Action said its Central Heating Improvement Program, known as CHIP, helped about 62 households with furnace replacements and repairs this season, but about 160 households are still on the waiting list.
Hundreds of thousands of dollars in funding helped families repair or replace their furnaces this year. AVEC said it still can’t help everyone on its waiting list.
Waiting list remains
Heidi Rackliffe, AVEC’s chief program officer, said about 160 households are still on the list and the program isn’t able to cover them all.
“There’s no way we’d be able to empty the list of individuals who need a repair and a replacement with the funding that we have, unfortunately,” Rackliffe said.
How to sign up
AVEC is still adding people to the waiting list and encourages those who need help to sign up.
To receive CHIP assistance, households must first be approved for heating assistance, known as HEAP.
Rackliffe said more people could be helped if additional funding becomes available.
More information about the program is available at avecmaine.org.

title: A third Ukrainian strike in 4 days halts rail traffic on Russia's Kerch Bridge to Crimea
text:
A third Ukrainian strike in 4 days halts rail traffic on Russia's Kerch Bridge to Crimea
A third Ukrainian aerial attack in four days on the key Kerch Bridge linking Russia and illegally annexed Crimea halted rail traffic across the span, a Russian official said Thursday, after earlier strikes shut down the road section of the landmark that is a symbol of Moscow's invasion.
Train traffic across the bridge stopped after the overnight strike while authorities assessed the damage, but it was to be restored starting from around 4 p.m. local time (1300 GMT) on Thursday, the Moscow-appointed head of Crimea, Sergei Aksyonov, said.
The Ukrainian strikes seemed calculated to embarrass Russian President Vladimir Putin as he met in China with President Xi Jinping and U.S. President Donald Trump, as well as demonstrate that Kyiv still holds cards in the war and undermine Russia's argument that its victory is inevitable.
Related video: Trump: Different approach on 3-way talks with Putin, Xi
The attack came hours before the start of talks in Berlin between U.S. envoys Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy alongside European leaders.
Russian strikes wound 10 and cause damage in half Ukraine's regions
The 19-kilometer (12-mile) Kerch Bridge is a key route for military and civilian supplies to Crimea, which Moscow seized in defiance of international law in 2014 and uses to support front-line troops. It is a potent reminder of Russia’s illegal annexation and has been a prime target for Ukraine.
A large section of the road deck and an arch collapsed in this week's attack that was the culmination of weeks of preparatory strikes over seven stages of the operation, according to Zelenskyy.
Ukrainian officials did not immediately comment on the latest reported strike.
The Russian Defense Ministry said Thursday that its air defenses intercepted 53 Ukrainian drones over 10 Russian regions during the night.
Ukrainian authorities said that Russia launched anti-ship missiles and 98 drones at Ukraine, with hits recorded at 18 locations, according to the statement.
At least 10 people were reported wounded as Russian strikes caused damage in 12 regions, Prime Minister Serhii Koretskyi said.
Russia’s bigger army hopes to exhaust Ukraine on the front line through sheer weight of numbers in terms of soldiers, armor and weapons. But Kyiv’s defenses are largely holding the Russians back, sapping Russian momentum with the help of drones that quickly choke off troop advances.
Russia has resorted to strategic bombing to wear down Ukraine’s resistance, placing special emphasis on knocking out power ahead of winter, while Kyiv’s domestically developed long-range drones and missiles have struck deep inside Russia, often targeting its oil refineries.
Kyiv fears Trump and Putin may try to decide Ukraine's fate
In China, Trump called Putin “my friend.” The American president’s relationship with Zelenskyy, meanwhile, has soured.
European leaders have tried to isolate Putin diplomatically and have heavily sanctioned the Russian economy.
Ukrainian officials fear their country’s fate could be determined by agreements between Trump and Putin, while European governments alarmed by Moscow’s aggression are trying to avoid being sidelined by Washington and Moscow.
The question of U.S. support for Ukraine, severely curtailed under Trump, could be raised by Democrats in Congress after their wins in midterm elections.
Britain’s Prince Harry offered a veiled criticism of the U.S. government’s policy toward Ukraine, saying in an interview released late Wednesday that he believes there is a “big separation” between the Trump administration’s stance and that of the American people.
Merz, Macron and Burnham to meet with US envoys and Zelenskyy
Kushner and Witkoff have led efforts to end nearly five years of war following Russia’s all-out invasion of its neighbor and recently have mediated new discussions, though the talks have yielded no major breakthrough.
Kushner said Thursday on X that Washington’s priority at Thursday's meeting in Berlin is to “further strengthen our close coordination with Ukraine and Europe, work toward a unified position on the key elements of a lasting peace, and to jointly prepare the agenda and proposed format for the next round of multilateral negotiations.”
The meeting will also explore how Ukraine’s European backers can fit into postwar security arrangements. Kyiv wants to ensure that Russia doesn’t invade again, while Moscow wants to keep the NATO military alliance away from its borders.
German Chancellor Friedrich Merz was due to welcome French President Emmanuel Macron and British Prime Minister Andy Burnham as well as other leaders to the meeting.
___
Hatton reported from Lisbon, Portugal.

title: Grand Theft Absence: Midcoast gamers play hooky to play GTA VI
text:
There was a time when classes at colleges and universities practically had to shut down with the arrival of a new “Harry Potter” book. In 2026, we have a new similar, if somewhat less smiled-upon phenomenon — Grand Theft Auto VI day.
That would be Nov. 19 to the uninitiated.
However, for some clever local youths, they were actually able to play their game a day early.
Oceanside High School senior Conner, 17, of Rockland has had the game uploaded to his Xbox for six months. Most of the game’s many fans downloaded it early on pre-order. He noted he was unofficially taking the day off from school on Thursday so he could spend more time with the game.
“There’s a trick on Xboxes where I set my location to New Zealand so that I could play it yesterday as well before it technically came out in America,” he said.
His coworker, Jack, 17, of Washington did the same thing.
Both of them work at Flagship Cinemas in Thomaston part-time where “GTA6!!!” has been marked on the office calendar for a while — along with the names of four employees planning to take that day off.
There have been jokes online about the sudden increase in people moving to New Zealand.
“There are so many people that just want to play and have been waiting so long, and they have more anticipation for it than any other game I’ve seen before,” he said.
It has actually been 13 years since the release of GTA V, one of the best-selling video games of all time with more than 235 million copies shipped. The latest edition has arrived to stellar reviews and sales figures, with industry analysts projecting sales topping $3 billion in its first year.
The long-running game franchise allows players to work for crime bosses, stealing cars and pulling heists, while causing general havoc in an open-world simulation where you go almost anywhere and do pretty much anything. It has been massively popular going back to earlier installments including “Vice City,” set in a 1980s Miami-like metropolis, and GTA III, set in the fictional Liberty City. Fans don’t talk about GTA IV. The new game returns to fictionalized Florida and its fabled Vice City.
“I was super excited, and it just felt like an extraordinary day where you just have that feeling of, I will finally be able to play it!” said Jack.
Local players report that the game did not disappoint. With a massive estimated $1 billion-plus budget, it delivers in terms of state-of-the-art visuals, high-end storytelling and A-list voice actors.
“It’s the best game I’ve ever played with just the amount of things you can do in it,” Conner said. “Every NPC (Non-Player Character) you talk to has its own voice lines. It’s like it’s its own person.”
Asked what he would say to parents who are concerned about the game’s employment of violence, sexual content and crime, he said: “I think if you know that it’s going to negatively affect your child, then probably have a conversation with them about it, and bring it up. But I also think that there are kids that are mature enough to be able to play it and know that it’s just a video game and like, just to leave it at that, it’s just a video game. Obviously, you’re not gonna go out into the real world and carjack someone or go rob a liquor store.”
He said that in this digital era, young people are exposed to a lot early, and even where their parents put in firewalls, they get it from other kids at school.
Oceanside High School was having a half-day for parent-teacher conferences on Thursday, but did not have an immediate answer for whether it was seeing an unusual uptick in absences. Camden Hills High School reported 70 absences on Thursday, which was about average according to staff, with 38 of them being male students.
The phenomenon is not reserved for teenagers. Online outlets are reporting that 1.5 million workers in America were expected to take time off from work, either by requesting it or calling in sick, to play the game. Some have even gone so far as to speculate it could lead to $1 billion in lost productivity.
Conner said the gaming itself does not interfere with his work or studies, but said the late nights sometimes take a toll. For now, we can chalk a couple days of gaming up to his version of senior skip day, knowing of course that he is not alone.
This story appears through a media partnership with Midcoast Villager.

title: A van Gogh with a complex past sells for a record $190 million at auction
text:
LONDON (AP) — A vibrant landscape painted by Vincent van Gogh weeks before his death has sold for $190.4 million at auction, a record for a work by the artist.
“Châtaigniers en fleurs” (Chestnut Trees in Flower) exceeded its $180 million estimate at a Sotheby’s auction in New York on Wednesday. The sale went ahead after an agreement between its current owners and the heirs of a Jewish family that sold it in Nazi-era Germany.
A day before the auction, Sotheby’s announced an agreement between the Blaquier-Arrieta family, which has owned the painting since 1975, and the descendants of Hedwig and Samuel Fischer, who sold it in 1936.
A lawyer for the Fischer heirs had asked for the sale to be postponed until Sotheby’s showed the painting had not been sold under duress.
The auction house said that “in recognition of the painting’s complex Nazi-era history and the suffering endured by the Fischer family during the Holocaust, the two families have reached a mutually satisfactory resolution.” It did not disclose details of the agreement.
The Fischer heirs said they were “grateful for the trusting and fair negotiation and collaboration with Sotheby’s and the Blaquier-Arrieta family, which make it possible to acknowledge the suffering of the Fischer family during the Nazi era.”
Van Gogh painted “Châtaigniers en fleurs” in a burst of creativity after his release from a psychiatric asylum in May 1890. He took his own life two months later.
The previous record for a van Gogh was $117.2 million paid for “Verger avec cyprès” (Orchard with Cypresses) at a Christie’s auction in 2022.
Paul Cézanne’s portrait “Arlequin” sold for $111 million in Wednesday’s sale of a dozen Impressionist and post-Impressionist works amassed by the late Argentine art collector Nelly Arrieta de Blaquier and her sugar magnate husband, Carlos Pedro Blaquier.
The 12 works sold for a total of $412 million.

title: Trump posthumously pardons MLB hits leader Pete Rose
text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — President Donald Trump on Thursday said he had posthumously pardoned Pete Rose more than two years after the baseball star’s death and a year after he was reinstated by Major League Baseball Commissioner Rob Manfred.
“I have just given a Complete and Total Pardon to the Late, Great Pete Rose, a true Baseball SUPERSTAR & LEGEND,” Trump posted on social media.
Rose, baseball’s career hits leader at 4,256, entered guilty pleas on April 20, 1990, to two counts of filing false tax returns, admitting he failed to report $354,968 during a four-year period. That was about eight months after Rose agreed to a permanent ban from baseball.
″I know I’m not a bad person, but I did make some mistakes and it’s in the eyes of the judge,″ Rose said that night during his weekly talk show on WCKY-AM in Cincinnati. ″All you can say is it’s up to the judge.″
The pardon comes after Manfred issued a sweeping decision last May that opened a pathway for Rose to be considered for baseball’s Hall of Fame. Manfred declared that individuals on MLB’s permanently ineligible list would have their statuses restored at death, a ruling that impacted 17 people, most notably Rose and Shoeless Joe Jackson.
Under a rule adopted by the Hall’s board of directors in 1991, anyone on the permanently ineligible list can’t be considered for election to the Hall. The earliest Rose or Jackson could now be inducted would be in 2028.
Rose agreed to his permanent ban in August 1989 after Major League Baseball investigator John M. Dowd concluded he bet numerous times on the Cincinnati Reds while playing on and managing his hometown team from 1985-87.
Facing a sentence of up to six years in prison and $500,000 in fines, Rose was sentenced on July 19, 1990, by U.S. District Judge S. Arthur Spiegel in Cincinnati to five months in prison. He also was fined $50,000 and ordered to perform 1,000 hours of community service as a gym teacher’s assistant with inner-city youths in Cincinnati as part of a one-year probation period. The first three months of the probation were to be spent at the halfway house.
Rose repaid the Internal Revenue Service $366,042.
“History and the tincture of time will decide his place among the all-time greats of baseball,” Spiegel said. “With regard to Pete Rose, the individual, he has broken the law, admitted his guilt, and stands ready to pay the penalty. Under our system of law and sense of fairness, when he has completed his sentence, he will have paid his debt to society and should be accepted by society as rehabilitated. Only time will tell whether he is to be restored to his position of honor for his accomplishment on the ball fields of America.”
Rose reported that Aug. 10 to the U.S. Penitentiary Marion Camp in Illinois, a minimum security facility, and was released Jan. 7, 1991. He entered Talbert House to start serving his probation and departed on April 5.
A 17-time All-Star during a playing career from 1963-86, Rose was the 1963 National League Rookie of the Year, 1973 MVP and 1975 World Series MVP. A three-time NL batting champion, he broke the prior hits record of 4,191 set by Ty Cobb from 1905-28.

Maine Health Officials Say Vaccinations are the Best Defense Against Respiratory Viruses
Maine CDC officials say the best way to reduce the risk of getting a respiratory virus is to get vaccinated.
While those vaccinations won't prevent a person from getting the flu or COVID-19, they will greatly reduce the length and severity of the illness.
There are several symptoms of both illnesses that Mainers are urged to watch for:
- Cough
- Fever or chills
- Headache
- Body aches
- Shortness of breath or difficulty breathing
- Fatigue
- Congestion or runny nose
- Nausea or vomiting
A sudden loss of taste or smell could signal a COVID-19 infection.
People should wash their hands often, cover coughs and sneezes, and stay home if they're sick.
Maine Pharmacies and Health Facilities Offer Flu, Covid-19, Pneumonia, and RSV Vaccinations
Maine residents can get vaccinations for flu, COVID-19, RSV, and pneumonia at most pharmacies or healthcare facilities.
Most vaccinations are covered by insurance.
For more information about respiratory illnesses and vaccinations, contact your primary care physician.

title: Soaking storms shift north to Florida's Space Coast and prompts water rescues of humans and horses
text:
Storms that brought record rains to South Florida this week shifted north to the Space Coast on Thursday, sending rivers over their banks and prompting water rescues of both humans and horses alike. In California, rain continued to pound the coast, filling streets with water, submerging cars and forcing hundreds of flight cancellations.
This is supposed to be Florida’s dry season that runs from October to May.
So far, it’s been quite the opposite.
“Never seen such a thing like this in Florida,” said Jazmin Foster, who has lived in her Melbourne home for eight years.
The storms have already dumped nearly 17 inches of rain over 48 hours in the Fort Lauderdale area, according to preliminary totals from the National Weather Service. Fort Lauderdale and West Palm Beach have already seen their wettest November on record, the National Weather Service said.
This week’s storms have been fueled by persistent high pressure over Virginia and a low-pressure system and an associated stationary front in the Gulf, which together have pushed a steady onshore flow across the Florida Peninsula, the weather service said.
Some South Florida school districts were closed for a second day Thursday. The heavy rains and flash flooding were expected to persist through Friday, possibly moving north toward coastal portions of the Carolinas and mid-Atlantic into the weekend, the weather service said.
Dozens of horses and other animals caught in floodwaters at equestrian center
On Thursday, the storms hit Brevard County directly. Some residents who have endured numerous hurricanes in their lifetimes said they saw airboats on their streets for the first time on Thursday being used to rescue residents.
In Palm Bay, the city conducted mandatory evacuations for some residents of Palm Bay Estates, a mobile home community for residents age 55 and older. Crews arrived by boat to assist residents, while the city strongly encouraged others in a voluntary evacuation area to relocate. Shelters were opened for residents forced from their homes.
Water inundated Foster’s home Thursday, a little more than two weeks after she endured a previous round of flooding. She said an insurance claim she filed for the earlier flood was denied.
“Now this time we have standing water in our yard, but not as much, but our road was flooded and sewers overflowing and more water coming in my two kids’ bedrooms again,” Foster told The Associated Press via social media. “Where is FEMA? Multiple people here in Brevard need help! I know other people are worse than we are!”
The St. Johns River near Cocoa rose above a record flood level set in 1953 and was forecast to stay at least 2 feet above flood stage through early next week, according to the weather service.
Nearly 200 Florida National Guard personnel with 50 high-water vehicles have been deployed to help with flood response efforts along the east coast, the state Division of Emergency Management said Thursday. They are among many local and state authorities responding, including about 235 officers with the Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission.
California endures more flooding
Some areas of Southern California saw 1 to 2 inches of rainfall within an hour Thursday, the weather service said. A flash flood warning was issued for southwestern Los Angeles County, including Malibu, Pacific Palisades and the Hollywood Hills.
More than 200 flights to and from Los Angeles International Airport were delayed Thursday, about 12% of the total air traffic, but there were only a handful of cancellations, according to Flightradar24.
Evacuation warnings for the Sunset, Hearst and Palisades burn scar areas in Los Angeles County remained in effect until Friday morning, due to heavy rains and possible debris flows. Authorities warned residents to prepare for possible evacuations, and firefighters would be visiting high-risk homes.
Along the southern and central California coast, the weather service forecast high surf, dangerous waves, rip currents, beach erosion and coastal flooding, with possible damage to some piers.
South of the Monterey Peninsula, heavy rains spurred rock and mud slides in Big Sur, forcing a more than 40-mile (64-kilometer) closure of Highway 1 along the Pacific Coast.
Photos posted by the California Highway Patrol show sections of the highway covered with debris. There were no immediate reports of injuries.
Flash flood watches were posted for the Timber and Plaskett burn areas in the Big Sur area along the coast and the Pickett burn area in Napa County through Thursday afternoon, with the potential for debris flows, the weather service said.
Watching the skies — and surf — for Thanksgiving week
A non-tropical low-pressure system expected to form Friday could become a subtropical or tropical storm along the southeastern U.S. coast, the National Hurricane Center in Miami said. The southeast and mid-Atlantic coasts should expect strong winds, dangerous surf and coastal flooding into early next week.
In Southern California, the weather service said extremely high tides of more than 8 feet (2.4 meters) were expected to continue through next week.
___
Associated Press writer Amy Taxin contributed to this report.

title: Build strength without stressing joints through water exercise
text:
(Aging Untold) — If your joints don’t love the treadmill, water exercises, from aqua aerobics to swimming laps, can be a game changer. There are options for every comfort level and every fitness level.
Why the pool is easier on the joints
Water exercises are a good fit for so many older adults because of the way water supports the body, Dr. Rhea Rogers, a board-certified physician, said.
“Water supports 90% of the body weight,” Rogers said. “People who want to still have that benefit of exercise can get cardiovascular endurance, help with prediabetes, insulin resistance and all that. You still want to be able to exercise, but it’s going to make it easier on your joints.”
For people with joint pain, stiffness or muscle stiffness, water exercise may be a better fit than land-based activities because of the pounding those activities involve, she said.
Know the risks before you get in
Gerontologist “Sam” Cradduck said low-impact doesn’t mean risk-free, especially for older adults.
“It doesn’t come without risk, especially for our aged community,” Cradduck said. “Your skin is thinner, so wear water shoes so you don’t end up with a sore on the bottom of your feet.”
Cradduck said ankle weights made for the water are also available.
Things to watch for:
Dehydration
“You can dehydrate in a swimming pool, which sounds weird,” Cradduck said.
Temperature
Rogers added that thermoregulation can be different for older adults.
“You have to watch also for the temperature and blood pressure, especially if you’re getting into the hot tub,” Cradduck said.
Lymphatic issues
“If you have a lymphatic issue, lymph nodes that aren’t working well or fluids that aren’t draining well, the higher temperatures are going to create problems there,” Cradduck said. “Some cancer survivors, if they’ve had lymph node involvement, have to watch for the higher temperatures.”
Slippery surfaces
“Watch the slipperiness of the wet feet, especially on the concrete coming out,” Cradduck said. “Falls happen.”
Muscle soreness
“Just because it’s low impact doesn’t mean it’s not moving muscle, so you could become sore from those workouts if you haven’t worked those muscles,” Cradduck said.
But don’t let muscle soreness detract you, she said.
“Don’t take the soreness to say, ‘Oh, I can’t ever do this again.’ That is your muscles responding and building,” Cradduck said.
You don’t have to know how to swim
Aging expert Amy O’Rourke said many people hear “pool” and assume swimming skills are required. She said that isn’t the case.
“I taught water aerobics, and I would say easily half of the students couldn’t swim,” O’Rourke said. “The range of motion that they experienced and the look on their face, they could finally get their leg all the way up. They could finally get their arms all the way up. They were joyful at the range of motion they could have.”
You don’t necessarily have to swim to be able to do it, she said.
“You can stand by the side of the pool and do leg lifts and get strength. You can do knee lifts and get strength,” O’Rourke said.
Rogers cautioned that anyone who does not know how to swim should stay in the shallow end of the pool.
Public pools have to be accessible, with accessible entrances and exits, Cradduck added.
Classes, community and cost
Aging well coach Katherine Ambrose said water exercise classes are designed to be fun and well-rounded.
“Someone has designed the class to be fun, but also be well-rounded and provide you a good workout,” she said. “Usually there’s music involved that’s been selected for your group, and the group itself is super fun.”
Rogers also pointed to social and mental health benefits, including laughter, less stress, better sleep and improved confidence.
On cost, O’Rourke said community pools and Ys are available in many places.
“It’s not like you have to have a lot of money and join a big fancy club to be able to get in the water,” O’Rourke said.
“If you can get Silver Sneakers, maybe through Medicare Advantage, then there might not be any cost at all,” Ambrose said. “That’s something that you could go to right away.”

5-year-old gets Disney-themed send-off before Make-A-Wish trip
A 5-year-old Wisconsin girl undergoing leukemia treatment celebrated her upcoming Make-A-Wish trip to Walt Disney World with a send-off party inspired by her favorite things.
5-year-old gets Disney-themed send-off before Make-A-Wish trip
A 5-year-old Wisconsin girl undergoing leukemia treatment celebrated her upcoming Make-A-Wish trip to Walt Disney World with a send-off party inspired by her favorite things.
A 5-year-old Wisconsin girl undergoing treatment for leukemia got a celebration inspired by her favorite things on Tuesday, as she and her family prepare for a Make-A-Wish trip to Walt Disney World.
Ava's wish trip is planned for early December. Badger Mutual Insurance Company and Make-A-Wish Wisconsin hosted the send-off party at Badger Mutual’s Milwaukee headquarters.
The celebration included appearances by Glinda and Elphaba from “Wicked,” along with Disney-ear decorating, bracelet-making, crafts and Culver’s.
"I came all the way from Oz for you tonight," Glinda said as she welcomed Ava.
Ava’s father, Antonio Green, said she has been talking about the trip and the things she hopes to do — including eating ice cream.
"Every other day it's always, yeah, I want to do this or all this or does Disney have this. I can't wait to eat ice cream,” Green said. "So, it's going to be a great time to go to see her just smiling and just enjoying the moment. So yeah, we're really looking forward to it."
Green described Ava as a sweet and resilient child, and said it is difficult to watch her go through treatment.
"She's such a sweet kid. To have to watch her go through this, it’s just tough as a parent," he said. "But she’s still got a lot — a lot of blessings."
The event was designed to celebrate Ava and her family and create memories before their trip. Make-A-Wish Wisconsin and Badger Mutual have partnered for more than 25 years, according to the company.

title: Maine Will Have The Earliest Sunset in The Nation Next Month
text:
The summer stuff has been put away and the winter flannels have made their way out of storage.
It's about this time every year that people from Maine really begin to plan for the forthcoming winter.
The nights will get colder and soon the weather forecasts will feature snowfall maps and wind chill advisories.
Another clear sign that winter is nearly upon us is the shortened amount of sunlight Maine receives.
For 2026, the earliest sunset of the year will actually arrive before winter is even official.
Aroostook County in Maine Will Have The Earliest Sunset in The Nation For 2026
According to data pulled together from the NOAA solar calendar, Aroostook County in Maine is set for the earliest sunset in the nation on December 10. The sun will drop below the horizon that day at 3:46pm.
If you compare that to another state along the eastern seaboard, it gets a little depressing. The earliest sunset in Florida for 2026 will happen in Miami on December at 5:31pm. That's nearly a two-hour difference in sunlight.
The earliest sunset of the year arrives 11 days before the winter solstice, which happens on December 21 this year.
Other Parts of Maine Will See A Little Bit More Sun
While The County will feel the pain with the earliest sunset in the nation, other parts of Maine will see a little more sunshine before it sets behind the horizon.
The earliest sunset for Portland, Maine, will be on December 9 at 4:03pm.
The earliest sunset for Augusta, Maine, in 2026 will happen on December 7 at 3:59pm.
The earliest sunset for Bangor, Maine, in 2026 will also be December 9 at 3:54pm.

title: Florida pastor convicted of US charges related to assassination of Haitian president
text:
MIAMI (AP) — A Florida pastor with dual Haitian-American citizenship was convicted Wednesday of U.S. charges arising from the 2021 assassination of Haitian President Jovenel Moïse, a killing that plunged the Caribbean nation into deep turmoil.
Christian Emmanuel Sanon was found guilty on all charges including conspiring to kill Moïse, capping a nearly eight-week trial in federal court in Miami. He had faced eight charges, the most serious being conspiracy to kidnap or kill a person outside the United States.
Sanon, who remains in federal custody, showed little reaction as the jury verdict was announced. He faces up to life in prison and is set to be sentenced next Feb. 10.
Prosecutors declined to comment after the verdict. But Sanon’s attorney, Zeljka Bozanic, said the defense team was disappointed and would file an appeal at the appropriate time.
Haiti has been without a president since the assassination
Haiti has not had a president since authorities said a squad of mostly retired Colombian soldiers killed Moïse and wounded his wife in a nighttime raid at their home on July 7, 2021. The poorest country in the Americas, Haiti has a history of dictatorship, political upheaval and foreign intervention that has long hindered democratic rule.
Federal prosecutors said at trial that South Florida was a hub for planning and financing the plot to oust Moïse and install a president of the conspirators’ choosing. The prosecutors said Sanon was their initial choice for Moïse’s replacement. They also said Sanon helped raise money for the conspiracy and arranged travel to Haiti and lodging there for himself and others.
Sanon had acknowledged in trial testimony that he was in communication at one point with people trying to replace Moïse, but said the group had moved on to another candidate long before the assassination. He denied any knowledge of plans to kill Moïse.
Born in Haiti, Sanon moved to the U.S. as a teenager. He testified that he has worked with churches in Haitian immigrant communities in Florida and the Midwest.
Prosecutors said South Florida was a hub for plotting against Haiti’s leader
Prosecutors said the scheme to kill Moïse included paying about two dozen foreign mercenaries with money obtained from U.S. government programs that were intended to help businesses during the COVID-19 pandemic, according to court records. U.S. prosecutors have charged more than 40 people with crimes related to the assassination and a dozen have been convicted, including five who are serving life sentences.
The plot to oust Moïse began taking final shape in April 2021, when Sanon met in South Florida with a former Haitian senator and several U.S. businesspeople, according to an indictment. The group agreed that Sanon, once in power, would award contracts to two Florida-based companies — Counter Terrorist Unit Federal Academy and Counter Terrorist Unit Security, collectively known as CTU — for infrastructure projects, security forces and military equipment, according to investigators.
CTU initially hired about 18 Colombian nationals with military training to provide security for Sanon, according to prosecutors. Conspirators also spent months obtaining weapons and body armor and attempting to build ties with Haitian gangs, officials said.
By June 2021, the conspirators realized Sanon had neither the constitutional qualifications nor sufficient popular support to become president. They shifted their backing to Wendelle Coq Thélot, a former Haitian Supreme Court judge who died in January 2025 while a fugitive.
Sanon was once scheduled to be tried with four other men
Sanon had been previously scheduled to be tried with four other men who were ultimately convicted last May of conspiracy in the assassination. But Sanon’s case was subsequently separated from theirs and delayed for health reasons.
At the earlier trial, Arcangel Pretel Ortiz, Antonio Intriago, Walter Veintemilla and James Solages were found guilty of conspiring to kill or kidnap the country’s elected leader and of providing material support for the plot. They were also convicted of violating the U.S. Neutrality Act and also face possible life sentences. They await sentencing.
Separately, in late September, 18 suspects arrested in the case were extradited from Haiti to the U.S.
Suspects who were in the Caribbean nation awaiting trial included 17 former Colombian soldiers and Joseph Badio, a former Haiti Ministry of Justice employee who was part of an anti-corruption unit.
Badio, considered a key suspect, was arrested in Haiti in October 2023 after more than two years on the run and is currently in U.S. custody. His Miami-based attorney, William Barzee, didn’t immediately respond to an email seeking comment from The Associated Press.
A general election in Haiti is scheduled next year for a new president. Candidates include the widow of Moïse, a respected economist, a well-known prosecutor accused of multiple summary executions and a former president accused of drug trafficking and sponsoring gangs.
