title: ‘I’m not sure what MAGA means’: Elon Musk backs away from Trump’s brand after GOP’s midterm defeats
text:
ATLANTA (AP) — Elon Musk was on the front row at Donald Trump’s second inauguration and has spent hundreds of millions of dollars trying to help the Republican president and his “Make America Great Again” allies win elections.
Now, after Republicans’ midterm thrashing by Democrats, the world’s richest man insists he’s not a MAGA acolyte after all and feels “pretty foolish” for spending so much money on the cause.
It’s the latest example of billionaire tech executives shifting their stances as Democrats prepare to take control of Congress and many more U.S. statehouses in January after they spent months promising a regulatory and oversight crackdown on artificial intelligence firms, their data center expansion and their interactions with the Trump administration.
“I mean, I’m not MAGA,” Musk told The New York Times on Wednesday during the newspaper’s DealBook Summit.
“I’m not sure what MAGA means,” added the Tesla and SpaceX CEO, who once sported a black MAGA hat in the Oval Office and coined the “Dark MAGA” label. “But I, I don’t think I’m, like, if, if that means sort of blind adherence to a set of policies by the Republican Party,” Musk continued, “then I certainly don’t have that. I think there are, there, there are positives and negatives in both parties.”
Trump takes Musk’s shift in stride
Trump, whose relationship with Musk has ranged from ally and trusted adviser to pariah, reacted Thursday with a seeming shrug.
“He’s a friend of mine,” Trump told NBC News in a telephone interview, similar to how the president described Russian President Vladimir Putin when they met earlier in the day in the Chinese tech hub of Shenzhen. “Elon is — Elon’s got very good intentions. I mean, he was with me the whole — he traveled with me.”
Musk, who has based himself and several of his companies in Texas, spent more than $400 million on Trump-aligned Republicans running in November. That included around $200 million backing Texas Senate nominee Ken Paxton, who lost to Democrat James Talarico.
Democrats scored sweeping victories after making Musk, other tech titans and the proliferation of artificial intelligence and AI data centers a campaign focus. They plan new scrutiny on the industry, including congressional investigations into tech firms’ dealings with Trump and his administration. That leaves Musk and others scrambling to rebrand themselves after spending years aligning closely with Trump and his fellow Republicans as they sought government contracts and favorable policies on everything from taxation to AI regulation.
Palantir co-founder and CEO Alex Karp, whose AI software company counts the Pentagon among its lucrative government clients, earlier this month raised eyebrows when he insisted to Politico that he’s always been a progressive.
“I’ve been a Democrat my whole life. I grew up in a far-left environment,” he said. “I know more about being a progressive than almost anybody on the planet, and I absolutely believe Palantir — all of our products are essentially progressive.”
Karp, a donor to Trump’s White House ballroom project who has adopted the president’s rhetoric to describe his own business as “anti-woke,” said he’s willing to support a Democrat for president in 2028.
At the Times’ event, Musk said if he had a do-over, he “probably” would have “spent less money” on the midterms.
“I feel pretty foolish about having spent so much money and not seeing much for it,” Musk told columnist Andrew Sorkin. “Or maybe it would’ve been much worse without that. But it certainly shows that American elections are not just about money.”
Democrats and Trump offer takes on Musk’s future
Musk sat alongside other Big Tech billionaires at Trump’s inauguration and led the president’s Department of Government Efficiency, a post that for months made him the most high-profile figure in the administration other than Trump himself.
Hours after Trump was sworn in on Jan. 20, 2025, Musk appeared at a Trump rally in Washington, where he enthusiastically embraced the president’s agenda and his supporters.
“This was no ordinary victory,” he said. “This was a fork in the road of human civilization. OK? There are elections that come and go. Some elections are important, some are not. But this one really mattered. ... It is thanks to you that the future of civilization is assured.”
Some Democrats were unimpressed with Musk’s change in tenor.
Responding to Musk’s turnabout on X, the social media platform that Musk owns, Sen. Ruben Gallego of Arizona was concise: “You are still getting a subpoena.”
Trump, his friendly remarks notwithstanding, offered his own prediction about Musk’s future.
“MAGA, to me, means something very specific,” the president said, without elaborating, “and when people veer from it, they don’t do very well.”

title: Will President Trump's agreement with Putin and Xi bring down gas prices?
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Will President Trump's agreement with Putin and Xi bring down gas prices?
President Donald Trump, Russian President Vladimir Putin and Chinese President Xi Jinping agreed Thursday to boost global fuel supplies following a historic trilateral summit in China, but it's unclear whether the agreement will bring Americans any additional relief at the gas pump.
The three leaders also agreed to pursue United Nations reforms and discuss ways to reduce nuclear risks as part of their Declaration Toward Peace.
The declaration specifically calls for increasing the production and supply of refined petroleum products, such as gasoline and diesel. However, it does not specify how much additional fuel the countries intend to produce, when those supplies could reach the market or how they plan to achieve those goals.
Patrick De Haan, head of petroleum analysis at GasBuddy, told Hearst Television that the three countries face significant challenges in bringing additional supplies to the global market.
The United States has limited capacity to quickly increase oil production and refining, while China, the world's largest oil importer, is unlikely to provide significant additional supplies. Russia, meanwhile, faces Western sanctions and repeated Ukrainian attacks on its oil refineries.
"I really don't foresee any trilateral agreement being able to add much more supply to the global market," De Haan said.
In a report last week, the International Energy Agency said global oil supplies were exceeding demand for the first time since the war in Iran began.
Trump had said he planned to discuss the wars in Iran and Ukraine during the summit, but neither conflict was mentioned in the declaration.
"And though there may be an agreement between these three countries, it still does not end the geopolitical tensions that inflame prices to begin with," De Haan said.
The declaration also calls for respecting the immunity of government officials and criticizes potential abuses of jurisdiction by the International Criminal Court. Putin faces an arrest warrant from the court over alleged war crimes in Ukraine.
What will gas cost this Thanksgiving?
Americans hitting the road for Thanksgiving can expect some relief at the pump, regardless of Thursday's agreement.
With more oil flowing through the Strait of Hormuz and a seasonal decline in demand, the national average has fallen from $4.50 per gallon on Sept. 24 to below $3.70 Thursday, according to GasBuddy.
De Haan expects prices to continue falling through Thanksgiving before stabilizing between $3.45 and $3.55 per gallon in late November or early December.
AAA projects nearly 73 million Americans will travel by car for Thanksgiving. Despite the recent declines, AAA says the national average remains more than 60 cents higher than this time last year.
Americans could also face the highest Thanksgiving Day gas prices on record. According to AAA, the previous record was $3.58 per gallon in 2022. AAA's national average stood at $3.72 Thursday, though the organization said prices could fall another 15 cents by Thanksgiving.
The war in Iran could also have lasting consequences for global energy markets.
In its annual World Energy Outlook, released Thursday, the International Energy Agency said disruptions to energy supplies through the Strait of Hormuz have resulted in the largest energy supply shock in history.

title: Pierce Gorneault Finishes Fall With Four Straight Wins
text:
The Fall Five and Five No. 2: Gorneault Runs Through a Championship Fall
By the time championship season rolled around, it was already pretty clear Pierce Gorneault was having a special fall.
Then came the Festival of Champions.
The Caribou sophomore finished seventh against one of the biggest and strongest fields he would see all season.
After that, nobody in Maine beat him again.
Gorneault won his next four races, taking Pendales, the PVC championship, the Class B North championship and finally the Class B state title.
That finish to the season puts Pierce at No. 2 in my five moments that defined the fall.
The streak started October 10 at Pendales, where Gorneault got back into the win column. A week later came the PVC Championships in Old Town, and that’s where the championship run really started to take shape.
Pierce won the Large School boys race in 16:26.22, more than a minute ahead of second place, and helped Caribou edge John Bapst for the team championship.
One week later, the Vikings headed to Belfast for the Class B North meet.
Pierce was even faster.
He crossed the finish line in 16:01.03 to win the individual Northern Maine championship, and Caribou added another title as a team.
At that point, Gorneault had won three straight races and had the PVC and regional championships checked off.
There was one big one left.
Finishing It at States
The Class B state championship was held at Cony High School in Augusta, and Pierce finished his run through Maine exactly the way he had spent the previous three weeks.
Out front.
He covered the 5K course in 16:26.85, finishing nearly 10 seconds ahead of Yarmouth’s Jackie Chalmers to become the Class B state champion.
Four straight races. Four wins. And the last three came with championships attached.
For me, there was also a pretty cool piece of history that came with it.
Thirty years earlier, Pierce’s father, PJ Gorneault, won a Maine state cross country championship of his own. This time PJ was there coaching his son as another Gorneault crossed the finish line as a state champion.
That’s a pretty special full-circle moment to have attached to an already remarkable season.
A Big Fall for Caribou
Pierce was the headline, but there was a lot more happening around him.
Caribou’s boys won both the PVC and Class B North team championships before finishing third at the state meet.
The girls had plenty to celebrate too. Emma Graves won the Class B North championship and then finished as the Class B state runner-up.
Caribou also left the state meet with both the boys and girls Class B Sportsmanship Awards.
So while Pierce put together one of the best individual seasons we saw anywhere in the County, it came during a pretty impressive fall for the entire Caribou cross country program.
His state championship also earned him a chance to compete at the New England Championships in Belfast, where he lined up against some of the best runners from across the region.
Cross country doesn’t always give you the kind of obvious dramatic moment you get from a last-second goal or a championship game. Sometimes the story builds a little differently. And he did it all as a sophomore.
That’s one heck of a fall, and it’s why Pierce Gorneault’s championship season is No. 2 in my five moments that defined the fall of 2026.

title: Skydance to combine Warner Bros. TV Group and Paramount Television Studios
text:
NEW YORK (AP) — Skydance will combine two of its key TV production units, Warner Bros. Television Group and Paramount Television Studios, bringing such shows as “The Pitt,” “Ted Lasso,” “Reacher” and “Landman” under the same roof.
The combined entity will be known as Warner Bros. Television Studios, with Channing Dungey and Matt Thunell serving as presidents. The merger of the studios will be completed in early 2027, according to a memo released Wednesday.
“Bringing together two of the industry’s most prolific television studios creates a formidable creative engine, uniting extraordinary talent, resources, acclaimed programming and iconic franchises with the global scale to compete at the highest level,” George Cheeks, co-chair and chief content officer of Skydance TV, said in the memo.
It’s the latest move since Skydance-owned Paramount last month closed its $81 billion takeover of Warner Bros. Discovery, ushering in a new Hollywood giant under the leadership of David Ellison.
The new Warner Bros. Television Studios will house more than 120 TV series, including HBO’s “Harry Potter and the Philosopher’s Stone,” Netflix’s “Emily in Paris” and CBS’ “Marshals.”
CBS Studios — another studio that produces shows such as the “NCIS” and “Fire Country” franchises — will continue to operate as a standalone entity under David Stapf.

title: Maine environmental board delays power line forest plan again
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
AUGUSTA — State environmental regulators on Thursday once again delayed a final decision on the 50,000-acre conservation plan for the New England Clean Energy Connect power line, sending it back to state staff for further revisions.
The Board of Environmental Protection continues to wrestle with the question of how to best mitigate the environmental impact of clearing a 150-foot-wide corridor through 54 miles of commercial forest from the Quebec border to The Forks Plantation.
“We’re going to put a bow on it and send it back,” said board Chairman Robert Duchesne.
NECEC Transmission LLC, which is owned by Central Maine Power parent company Avangrid, has argued its initial forest plan was an unprecedented landscape-scale conservation deal connecting over 400,000 acres of existing protected wilderness surrounding the corridor.
Environmental groups contesting the plan — the Appalachian Mountain Club, Natural Resources Council of Maine, Maine Audubon and Trout Unlimited — claim it allows commercial timber owner Weyerhaeuser to clear-cut set-aside land under a shifting logging schedule.
In September, the board sided with the environmental groups and ordered the state to come up with a new plan that would let more of the 50,000 acres of conservation area grow into mature forest, which has the greatest value for wildlife, and stay that way for a longer period.
But Thursday, board members said the state’s latest plan went too far by calling for a 10,000-acre no-cut sanctuary, a ban on harvesting forest stands more than 100 years old and changing the way that tree health is measured by valuing tree width and total wood over tree height.
The board voted 5-1 to return the plan to the department of Environmental Protect for revisions.
NECEC’s attorney, Lisa Gilbreath, told the board Thursday she did not know if her client and Weyerhaeuser could have complied with the state’s latest plan. She urged board members to go back to the original plan, which would eventually grow half of the conserved woods to maturity.
“They moved the goalposts,” Gilbreath said. The new plan “targets late successional old growth, not mature forest, substitutes preservation for conservation, and it gives up a bird in hand for a proposal no one has shown to be feasible. The appellants keep asking for more.”
The $950 million transmission line, built to carry 1,200 megawatts of Canadian hydropower to Massachusetts, went online in January 2026. Thursday’s vote to delay approval of a forest plan doesn’t stop the transmission of electricity, but it threatens to land the yearslong debate in court.
To offset habitat fragmentation and loss, state regulators issued orders mandating the NECEC permanently conserve 50,000 acres. Under the first state plan, NECEC proposed doing it with a working forest easement on 50,063 acres owned by Weyerhaeuser.
But that plan allowed Weyerhaeuser to continue commercial logging across the property — with the exception of 100-foot stream buffers — relying on a “shifting mosaic” schedule that gave the timber company until 2065 to ensure that half of that forest contained 50-foot tall trees.
That 40-year delay and reliance on tree height triggered the appeal. Expert testimony submitted to the board revealed that in Maine’s commercial timberlands, native trees can reach 50 feet tall in just 30 to 40 years.
Ecologists argued that 50-foot trees represent midaged “pole” stands rather than mature forests, lacking essential habitat features such as multilayered canopies, large denning hollows, standing dead snags and decaying forest floor logs needed by wildlife like the pine marten.
The small, bushy-tailed weasel known for climbing trees doubles as a so-called umbrella species in Maine. Protecting its large, unfragmented forest habitat also safeguards other forest wildlife, like fishers, snowshoe hares, red squirrels, black bears, deer and moose.

title: Head-on crash with speeding car kills father, leaves wife and daughters on ventilators, family says
text:
SAFFORD, Ariz. (KPHO/Gray News) — A father has lost his life and his wife and daughters are fighting for theirs following a head-on crash in southeastern Arizona over the weekend.
Family members identified the father as Aaron Johnston. They said he was in a car that collided with another vehicle on U.S. 191 in Safford.
Johnston was traveling with his wife, Sierra, and their daughters, Angelyc, 5, and Eryn, 3, who suffered severe injuries in the crash and have since been placed on ventilators.
Relatives said Eryn may not survive. Investigators said another adult died in the collision, but not many further details were released from the scene.
People close to the family said the Johnstons were heading home to Apache Junction after a day trip to Morenci, about a 50-minute drive northwest of Safford, watching big trucks operate.
Family and witnesses at the scene said a car was speeding and weaving through traffic on the two-lane highway before it hit the Johnstons’ vehicle head-on.
Loved ones said Johnston died on impact.
A GoFundMe has been set up for the Johnston family.

title: Holden police hold jail and bail event for 25 Days of Kindness
text:
HOLDEN, Maine (WABI) - Holden police arrested more than 20 local business owners in the afternoon, but the business owners did not break the law. They turned themselves in.
The Holden Police Department held its second jail and bail event to raise money for 25 Days of Kindness.
Local business owners put themselves behind bars to raise money for their “bail.”
The money donated will go into the 25 Days of Kindness fund. The fund helps community members across the state with things like heating oil and food insecurity.
Holden Police Chief Eddie Benjamin said raising the money is a lot of work, but helping the community is always worth it.

Last year, the event raised $22,000. Donations can be made year-round.

title: Bangor Drone Locates Man Who Fled A Rollover Crash On Hammond Street
text:
Bangor PD Nab Man On The Run, Find Him Lying In A Field With The Help Of A Drone
Since April of this year, the Bangor Police Department has incorporated a drone into their tool kit, using it for everything from tracking down missing people to looking for folks on the run.
It was about a month ago, when authorities in Bangor used their drone to locate a woman who became in the Bangor City Forest.
Read More: Maine Emergency Services Turn To Drones For Rescue
This week, the drone was used to find a man who had fled the scene of an accident, authorities say.
Just before 2 AM, the Bangor Police Department says is was called out to a crash on Hammond Street, when a person had rolled their vehicle over and subsequently run away from the area before law enforcement arrived.
Authorities they called in a K9 tracking dog, and established a perimeter around the area, but fearing the individual may be injured, time was of the essence, so a drone operator was also called in.
"Det. Joe Orcutt arrived on scene and was able to deploy the drone and conduct a search of the area. Det. Orcutt was able to locate a man in nearby field within minutes of deployment. The man was identified as Quinn Dernbach, 29, of Anson, who declined medical treatment repeatedly."
Bangor Police say that Dernbach showed signs of that he might be under the influence, and was arrested and taken into custody.
Read More: The Role Of Drones In Enhancing Public Safety In Maine
Dernbach faces charges of violating bail condition and operating under the influence.

title: Coastal storm threatens Maine early next week
text:
Coastal storm threatens Maine early next week
Tracking rain on Monday and a sharp midweek chill
Coastal storm threatens Maine early next week
Tracking rain on Monday and a sharp midweek chill
Enjoy a stretch of mild, dry weather to wrap up the workweek and kick off the weekend across Maine. High pressure will keep skies mostly sunny through early Sunday, with afternoon temperatures running well above average in the 50s to lower 60s through Friday before cooling slightly over the weekend. While this quiet pattern keeps conditions nice for outdoor plans, it also deepens ongoing rainfall deficits across the state.
Changes arrive Sunday night into Monday as a strong area of low pressure develops off the Southeast coast and tracks northward. While the exact path remains uncertain, coastal Maine is most likely to see a beneficial, soaking rain, with a growing chance for more than an inch. Inland rainfall totals will drop off quickly unless the coastal low links up with another disturbance approaching from the west, though the storm is moving fast enough that widespread flooding is not expected.
Gusty winds and coastal flooding remain the biggest wild cards, as both depend heavily on how close the storm tracks to the shoreline. The timing coincides with the start of higher astronomical tides, including a 10.8-foot tide in Portland on Monday afternoon. Because even a storm surge of just over a foot could push water levels toward minor flood thresholds during that single tide cycle, we will be monitoring the storm's track closely over the coming days.
Once the storm clears out, a surge of colder air will settle over Maine by the middle of next week, dropping daytime highs below normal. Because the provided forecast discussion only extends into midweek, it is still too early to pinpoint details for Thanksgiving, but another storm system will develop for the holiday.

title: Thanksgiving Bake Sale Nov. 21
Thanksgiving travel dips for the first time in three years
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Best and worst times to travel by car during Thanksgiving holiday
AAA says fewer people are hitting the road and skies this Thanksgiving, while cruises, buses and trains are on the rise.
Best and worst times to travel by car during Thanksgiving holiday
AAA says fewer people are hitting the road and skies this Thanksgiving, while cruises, buses and trains are on the rise.
Fewer people are expected to travel for the Thanksgiving holiday, but a new report from AAA shows there are still several times drivers should skip to avoid traffic.
The busiest days on the road will be Tuesday and Wednesday, as most travelers head out those days, according to INRIX transportation data cited in AAA's Thanksgiving travel forecast. Traffic is expected to worsen from 2 p.m. to 8 p.m. on Tuesday, Nov. 24, and from noon to 7 p.m. on Wednesday, Nov. 25.
As for the drive back, INRIX data said that from afternoon to evening on Sunday and Monday, travelers will see the heaviest traffic congestion. Drivers are advised to hit the road in the morning to avoid the traffic rush.
In which cities will traffic be the worst?
Peak congestion times are different in each metro area, with areas like Boston, Los Angeles, New York and Washington, D.C., expected to see double their normal traffic congestion.
How this year's Thanksgiving travel compares
Around 81.5 million Americans are projected to travel during Thanksgiving week, ending a three-year streak of record-high travel. According to AAA, 121,000 fewer travelers are making the trip this year, a 0.1% decline from the 81.6 million people who traveled in 2025.
The Thanksgiving holiday travel period spans seven days from Tuesday, Nov. 25, to Monday, Dec. 1. AAA's travel projection includes travel at least 50 miles from home by car, airplane, bus, train or cruise.
AAA said higher travel costs are driving the slight dip in traveler numbers. This year's forecast shows slightly fewer people are taking flights and road trips, while travelers taking cruises, buses and trains are on the rise.
In 2025, at least 73.28 million people were projected to travel by car, nearly 90% of Thanksgiving travelers. This year, that number is down to 72.93 million.
Air travel went down by 0.2% to 5.96 million travelers in 2026 compared with 6.07 million the year before.
The national average gas price reached $4.50 per gallon this year after the U.S. war with Iran disrupted global oil supplies. But it has trended downward to $3.81 in the week of Nov. 16, according to AAA.
Airfares also rose nearly 16% this year compared with 2025, as jet fuel prices increased. The average cost of domestic flights in the U.S. reached $445 in June, according to the latest data from the Bureau of Transportation Statistics. This is up nearly 16% from the same time last year.

title: Bangor police use drone to find driver who allegedly fled from crash

title: Solidarity Harvest returns to support Maine farms and families
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
BREWER, Maine (WABI) - A local staple in solidarity is back to support Maine farms and families across the state.
This year marks the 24th Solidarity Harvest, put on by Food AND Medicine. Each year, the organization partners with local farms to purchase organic vegetables and works with other organizations to provide bread, stuffing and sweets.
With the help of about 200 volunteers, the food is packed into baskets and given to unions, churches and other agencies to distribute across the state.
The effort began with 134 baskets 24 years ago. Now, Food AND Medicine assembles close to 1,700.
As the need rises, organizers say their mission is to support local food producers and provide solidarity, not charity, to Mainers in need.
“Over 20% of children in the state of Maine live in food insecure households. And our goal really here is to try and strengthen the network and the supports for everybody, but especially children, to get access to food,” said Jack McKay, director of Food AND Medicine.
Volunteer Liam Parent said the quality of locally sourced food makes a difference.
“And these are honestly better than what you get at the store. And it’s fresher too, because these come right from the farmers,” Parent said. “You don’t have to deal with any middle man. You don’t have to worry about any of the real, like, bad stuff. ‘Oh, what hands does it touch before it gets to your plate?’ Here, your farmers and local volunteers.”
Food AND Medicine is still looking for volunteers as it continues to pack baskets, specifically on Thursday, Friday and Monday.
The organization is also accepting financial donations and is $29,000 away from reaching its fundraising goal.
For more information on how to help, visit their website.

title: Bog woman decapitated 2,000 years ago, scientists find
text:
(CNN) - A 2,000-year-old mystery is unfolding in Northern Ireland.
Scientists say the remains of a young Iron Age woman discovered in a bog in 2023 reveal she likely died by decapitation. The body was remarkably preserved by the cool, acidic conditions of the wetlands, but her skull was missing.
Experts believe she was struck twice in the neck and may have been kneeling when she was killed.
The findings were presented Monday at Belfast’s Ulster Museum during a public event modeled after a coroner’s inquest.
Some researchers believe the killing may have been part of an ancient ritual or human sacrifice, but other experts caution there isn’t enough evidence to determine a motive.

title: Woman missing since 1994 identified in decades-old cold case
text:
GREENBRIER COUNTY, W.Va . (WDTV/Gray News) - Authorities have made a breakthrough in a decades-old cold case involving a Virginia woman who disappeared in 1994.
Investigators identified the woman as Elizabeth Jean Acton, who had been reported missing from Colonial Beach, Virginia.
The investigation began May 9, 2001, when a West Virginia Paving employee discovered skeletal remains near an interstate exit in Greenbrier County, West Virginia.
Investigators determined the remains belonged to a woman who was approximately 37 to 47 years old and about 5 feet tall. Her identity was unknown, and she became known as “Greenbrier County Jane Doe.”
Investigators learned that Acton was 41 when she was last seen on Aug. 24, 1994, in Colonial Beach.
The case was entered into the National Missing and Unidentified Persons System and the Combined DNA Index System, but no matches were found.
For more than two decades, state police continued to investigate and followed numerous tips and leads.
In September 2024, state police submitted the case to Marshall University for additional DNA testing. On Aug. 12, 2026, the West Virginia Office of the Chief Medical Examiner notified investigators that the remains had been identified as Acton.
West Virginia State Police and the Colonial Beach Police Department are working together to determine how Acton traveled from Virginia to the roadside dump near U.S. Route 60 and the Interstate 64 Alta exit in Greenbrier County.

title: Becky the basset hound leads rescuers to missing owner with dementia
text:
Dog leads rescuers to missing owner with dementia
Dog leads rescuers to missing owner with dementia
A 69-year-old man with dementia was rescued from a hike in northern New York after his dog made a solo journey to alert staff at the Whiteface Mountain ski lodge.
Around 9 p.m. on Nov. 12, Becky, a basset hound, showed up at Whiteface Mountain ski lodge without her owner, according to the New York Department of Environmental Conservation.
Staff recognized the dog and knew her owner had dementia, so they called state police.
A total of 12 forest rangers, four members of New York State Police, and a drone searched for the man for more than 12 hours on Whiteface.
They found the missing hiker the next morning at 10 a.m. without shoes or gloves.
He was suffering severe frostbite, so rangers decided to get him down with a hoist, then fly him to the hospital.
"If the dog had not shown up at Whiteface, it definitely would have been a different outcome. He may or may not have survived the rest of the day, and probably not another night," said Charlie Foutch, a forest ranger with the New York State Department of Environmental Conservation.

title: Pierce Gorneault Finishes Fall With Four Straight Wins
text:
The Fall Five and Five No. 2: Gorneault Runs Through a Championship Fall
By the time championship season rolled around, it was already pretty clear Pierce Gorneault was having a special fall.
Then came the Festival of Champions.
The Caribou sophomore finished seventh against one of the biggest and strongest fields he would see all season.
After that, nobody in Maine beat him again.
Gorneault won his next four races, taking Pendales, the PVC championship, the Class B North championship and finally the Class B state title.
That finish to the season puts Pierce at No. 2 in my five moments that defined the fall.
The streak started October 10 at Pendales, where Gorneault got back into the win column. A week later came the PVC Championships in Old Town, and that’s where the championship run really started to take shape.
Pierce won the Large School boys race in 16:26.22, more than a minute ahead of second place, and helped Caribou edge John Bapst for the team championship.
One week later, the Vikings headed to Belfast for the Class B North meet.
Pierce was even faster.
He crossed the finish line in 16:01.03 to win the individual Northern Maine championship, and Caribou added another title as a team.
At that point, Gorneault had won three straight races and had the PVC and regional championships checked off.
There was one big one left.
Finishing It at States
The Class B state championship was held at Cony High School in Augusta, and Pierce finished his run through Maine exactly the way he had spent the previous three weeks.
Out front.
He covered the 5K course in 16:26.85, finishing nearly 10 seconds ahead of Yarmouth’s Jackie Chalmers to become the Class B state champion.
Four straight races. Four wins. And the last three came with championships attached.
For me, there was also a pretty cool piece of history that came with it.
Thirty years earlier, Pierce’s father, PJ Gorneault, won a Maine state cross country championship of his own. This time PJ was there coaching his son as another Gorneault crossed the finish line as a state champion.
That’s a pretty special full-circle moment to have attached to an already remarkable season.
A Big Fall for Caribou
Pierce was the headline, but there was a lot more happening around him.
Caribou’s boys won both the PVC and Class B North team championships before finishing third at the state meet.
The girls had plenty to celebrate too. Emma Graves won the Class B North championship and then finished as the Class B state runner-up.
Caribou also left the state meet with both the boys and girls Class B Sportsmanship Awards.
So while Pierce put together one of the best individual seasons we saw anywhere in the County, it came during a pretty impressive fall for the entire Caribou cross country program.
His state championship also earned him a chance to compete at the New England Championships in Belfast, where he lined up against some of the best runners from across the region.
Cross country doesn’t always give you the kind of obvious dramatic moment you get from a last-second goal or a championship game. Sometimes the story builds a little differently. And he did it all as a sophomore.
That’s one heck of a fall, and it’s why Pierce Gorneault’s championship season is No. 2 in my five moments that defined the fall of 2026.

title: A place to call home: Bangor mother, daughter receive keys to Habitat for Humanity house
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
BANGOR, Maine (WABI) - Habitat for Humanity is celebrating 50 years of making homeownership accessible, and the Bangor affiliate celebrated Wednesday for accomplishing just that.
Bangor resident Angie Works is now a proud homeowner, as she and her five-year-old daughter, Hope, received the keys to their new Grove Street home from Habitat for Humanity of Greater Bangor.
“I was living in a one-bedroom apartment for the last few months after my divorce,” explained Works. “When I was looking for permanent housing, I just thought, ‘Well, you can’t get anything you don’t apply for, so...’”
Qualified applicants who earn 30% to 80% of the area’s median income can apply. After getting approved for an affordable mortgage, Habitat helps close the financial gap.
“They are the homeowners. They are purchasing this home and will have a mortgage payment,” Habitat for Humanity of Greater Bangor’s Executive Director Melissa Huston said. “It’s just that Habitat partners with them and helps bridge the gap between what they can afford and the appraised value of the home.”
For Works, Habitat for Humanity’s involvement was critical, saying “there would have been no home without Habitat.”
“This area, Maine in general, is pretty high with the real estate costs and not very high with the incomes. There is a big divide between people that can afford the homes and the people that need the homes,” Works described. “So, for me, being a single mom, not having two incomes in the house, it wasn’t going to be feasible for a long time. So, this really helped with that.”
She added that Hope is excited to decorate her own bedroom, already painted a unique shade of purple that Works surprised her with.
Works’ Grove Street home is the 31st house constructed by Habitat for Humanity of Greater Bangor.
For the past 11 houses, Habitat has partnered with students at Eastern Maine Community College to build the frame, install insulation and more before having it delivered to the lot for finishing touches.
“I think it just brings a great opportunity for people to learn how to build a house, especially in a trade like this,” said Kason White, an EMCC student who helped build Works’ home. “Here we are with a whole house behind us, and it’s just cool to be able to donate to the community and help and just make a house for someone to live in.”
White was joined by other EMCC students to see the house fully painted and complete, which was done by volunteers, partner contractors and the homeowner as part of “sweat equity” required for the property.
As rents rise and starter homes become harder to find, organizers say Habitat makes the dream of homeownership a reality.
“It’s understandable why for-profit developers aren’t spending their time and their energy on small starter homes because they really just can’t turn a profit on it. As a non-profit, that is not our mission,” Huston described. “Our mission is to partner with those that wouldn’t be able to realize the dream of homeownership.”
Works said what homeownership ultimately provides is stability for her and her daughter: “Being able to have a home and know where you’re going to be and that you can afford that home, the stability of that just takes a lot of weight off your shoulders, especially in this market.”
Works was able to complete about 10% of her sweat equity before the home was ready, so she will be one of many volunteers for the next Habitat for Humanity of Greater Bangor home.
Lucky for her, it’s planned to go right next door!

title: ‘Unknown’ illness causes nearly 150 aboard cruise ship to get sick with vomiting, diarrhea
text:
(Gray News) - Nearly 150 people aboard a Princess cruise ship are experiencing vomiting and diarrhea from an unknown illness.
Passengers reported the symptoms to the Center for Disease Control’s Vessel Sanitation Program on the fifth day of a 12-night trip throughout the Caribbean.
Although the cause of the sickness is currently unknown, Princess Cruise Lines has taken preventative measures to stop its potential spread, such as increased cleaning, isolating sick passengers and collecting specimens for testing.
Sick on board
Cruise ships that dock at any U.S. port are required to follow CDC reporting guidelines for any deaths or signs and symptoms of a “serious communicable disease of public health concern.”
Per these guidelines, an outbreak is defined as 3% or more passengers being impacted.
This incident is the 10th reported outbreak reported this year.
The industry funded Cruise Lines International Association reports that cases of gastrointestinal illness are much less common on cruises than in regular everyday life.
CLIA says that chances of GI sickness is 1 in 5,500 while cruising versus 1 in 15 on land.
How to protect yourself
Having fun is usually the first priority of most cruise passengers, and taking a few small steps can help people stay well during their trip.
Advent Health has published a list of “12 Tips to Stay Safe and Healthy on a Cruise.”
Some of the suggestions are:
- Wash hands frequently, especially after using the restroom, touching high traffic surfaces like door handles and stair railings, and before eating.
- Find where the onboard doctor or clinic is located on the ship before you board.
- Avoid overeating and drinking too much while on board.

title: States should never have elected presidents
text:
Douglas Rooks has been a Maine editor and columnist for 42 years. His biography of Gov. Ken Curtis, “Transformational,” is now available. He welcomes comment at [email protected].
With the landslide midterm election results, enough state legislatures controlled by Democrats are poised to join the National Popular Vote Compact, which would allow the 2028 presidential election to be determined by vote of the American people acting as a single body.
The positive effects of this electoral revolution will be immediately apparent. Various objections have been filed against the compact, chiefly that it would diminish the voice of “small states” such as Maine — though not by much.
They don’t ultimately matter for a simple reason. From the beginning, votes by all Americans should have counted equally.
In short, states should never have elected presidents. Just as we would never elect a governor by allowing counties to do it, or a mayor by expecting wards to “vote” for us, citizens should have elected presidents directly.
That they didn’t has little to do with perceived “elitism” among the Founders. Instead, it was simple mathematics. The notorious three-fifths clause accounting for slaves — who could never vote — would be impossible to implement without indirect election: hence, the “Electoral College.”
When slavery was abolished, the electoral vote system should have been, but it wasn’t. Memories of the 1824 election, the only one decided by the House of Representatives, were dim, and “minority presidents” chosen in 1876 and 1892 were unforeseen.
We got another scare in 1968, when it appeared likely that George Wallace, a defiant segregationist, would win enough Southern states to send the election to the House, where Wyoming and California would each have one vote. That didn’t happen; Richard Nixon won an electoral vote majority, but the following year a constitutional amendment to remove the elector clause gained broad support.
It passed the House overwhelmingly, with polls showing 85% of voters agreed. They weren’t allowed to ratify it, however, because Senate leaders — mostly segregationists who’d favored Wallace — filibustered, and it died.
Maine undertook a decidedly second-best experiment by dividing its vote by congressional district, emulated by precisely one other state, Nebraska. Then came the 21 st century and two more “minority presidents,” in 2000 and 2016.
In the first, George W. Bush was installed by the Supreme Court even though Florida wasn’t permitted to finish its recount. In the second, Donald Trump — who as a candidate supported the national popular vote — won the presidency despite receiving nearly 3 million votes fewer than his opponent.
As we all know, given today’s divisions it’s impossible to pass any constitutional amendment, so the National Popular Vote Compact was advanced as a democratic (small “d”) alternative.
There’s nothing inherently partisan about it. Republican chambers in Michigan and Arizona advanced it, but it soon became identified with the Democratic Party. So be it. The compact — which unites a constitutional provision requiring Congress to respect such compacts with a second directing states to instruct their electors — will do us all a great favor.
We struggle with a system where a handful of “swing states,” mostly Midwestern, can determine the outcome, and get all the attention from candidates. With the popular vote, Republicans in Maine and Democrats in Wyoming will have exactly the same influence as Democrats in California and Republicans in Alabama.
On election night, there will be only a single line after each candidate. It won’t matter how any state votes. A national vote will be unifying, and we need unity more than any time since the Civil War. The winner won’t be known immediately, thanks to mailed ballots, but we’ll have a good idea on election night. Never again will the Supreme Court decide an election, as in 2000 and the centennial year of 1876.
Response to popular vote election will likely be so positive a new constitutional amendment should pass by acclamation. Then we can attend to the equally serious problem of containing out-of-control campaign spending through an amendment overturning Supreme Court rulings equating money with speech.
Citizens United of 2010 is the usual villain, but the problem started in 1976, with Buckley v. Valeo, where the court shredded post-Watergate campaign reforms. Justices reasoned that limiting campaign spending violated the First Amendment — with the absurd result that billionaires get a billion times more “speech” than the rest of us.
The amendment would allow Congress and state legislatures to regulate campaign finance, and drastically reduce the pollution of the airwaves and internet that reached record levels in 2026. Just because the billionaires’ attempt to determine outcomes failed this time doesn’t mean it couldn’t work later.
No one step will restore confidence in elections, but the popular vote compact and campaign finance reform would certainly help. By huge majorities, Americans say they want and need relief. Soon, it could be within our grasp.

title: Prosecutor declines to charge a white police officer who fatally shot a Black man in Wisconsin
text:
MADISON, Wis. (AP) — The Madison police officer who shot and killed a 38-year-old Black man in July, sparking racial justice protests and renewed calls for police reform, will not face criminal charges, a prosecutor announced Thursday.
Kiel Baitinger-Peterson, a white officer with more than a decade of experience in law enforcement, fired the shots that killed Corey Ruiz on July 22. Baitinger-Peterson was one of four officers who responded to calls about someone checking out parked cars and an alleged burglary attempt, police said. They surrounded Ruiz, who was on a bicycle.
“I conclude it was reasonable for the officer to use deadly force when this person resisted officers, produced a knife, and was not affected by multiple attempts to use Tasers while officers attempted to take him into custody,” Dane County District Attorney Ismael Ozanne said in a statement announcing his decision.
The Wisconsin Department of Justice said immediately after the shooting that two officers attempted to use a Taser on Ruiz but weren’t successful. Ruiz “brandished a knife and injured” Baitinger-Peterson, the department said.
Civil rights attorney Ben Crump, who represents Ruiz’s family and had called for the officer to be charged, said in a statement that there was nothing in the videos that the district attorney showed them on Thursday to justify the shooting.
“The medical examiner told the family that if the officer had not fired that shot to his head, Corey would have survived,” Crump said. “It was clearly an excessive use of force. This police killing in Madison, Wisconsin, was unjustifiable, unreasonable, unnecessary, and unconstitutional.”
Ozanne said he reached his decision after reviewing evidence that included police reports, diagrams, surveillance videos, police squad car videos and citizen videos. Madison police officers do not wear body cameras.
“A person does not have to like and/or agree with the law, however I am sworn to apply the law to the facts at hand,” the prosecutor said. “The law applies equally to members of law enforcement and to those who are not.”
Baitinger-Peterson has not replied to an email seeking comment.
It was the third time since 2012 that Madison police had shot and killed someone in the same neighborhood. The killing sparked days of protests and forced the city to reckon with calls for police reform to address racial justice issues.
Baitinger-Peterson and the other three officers who interacted with Ruiz that day have been on paid administrative leave since the shooting.
While bystanders captured the confrontation on video, there is no body camera footage because Madison police officers don’t wear them. All Madison police officers could be equipped with body cameras by the end of 2027 thanks to a $350,000 donation from a local nonprofit that city officials announced in September.
The donation will help cover operational expenses, while other costs are being funded through grants and other means.

title: Thomas Markle, Meghan's father, is competent to face child sex abuse images case, expert says
text:
Thomas Markle, Meghan's father, is competent to face child sex abuse images case in California, expert says
An expert has determined that the 82-year-old estranged father of Meghan, the Duchess of Sussex, is mentally competent to face charges of keeping child sexual abuse material in storage in California, a judge said Thursday.
Thomas Markle's defense lawyer said they would not contest the finding by Dr. Amie Gerodimos. The exam was ordered after his arrest at a senior care center in Lakeland, Florida, on Nov. 6.
Investigators seized approximately 78 items from two storage units rented by Markle in the Los Angeles area, including slides, film negatives and books that contained suspected child sexual abuse images, according to the FBI.
Some images appear to depict him with children, the FBI said.
Markle is in custody in a jail while the case remains in federal court in Tampa. It will eventually shift to a similar court in Southern California.
Markle was initially released on bond but was arrested again when authorities accused him of cutting off his electronic ankle monitor on Nov. 10.
He had a stroke earlier this year while living in the Philippines and had to have his left leg amputated. That forced him to return to the U.S. and settle in Florida.
The Sun, a British tabloid newspaper, reported that Meghan’s half brother found child sexual abuse images while clearing out their father’s home in the Philippines. The discovery led to a search of the two U.S. storage units in California, which Markle had rented since 2008.
Meanwhile, in the Philippines, Markle is under investigation for possession and intent to distribute images. The Women and Children Protection Center, a branch of the Philippine National Police, filed a formal criminal complaint against Markle on Monday, police spokesperson Brig. Gen. Allen Rae Co said in a written statement.
The complaint was filed with the prosecutor’s office following an investigation into digital devices found at Markle’s former home in Cebu City, the statement said. The prosecutor’s office will assess the case for possible charges.
Markle did not attend his daughter Meghan’s 2018 wedding to Prince Harry at Windsor Castle. She said at the time he needed to tend to his health. Meghan is an American citizen who starred in the U.S. television drama “Suits.”
___
Associated Press reporter Ed White in Detroit contributed.

title: Is frozen food more nutritional than canned food?
text:
No.
Frozen foods initially retain more heat-sensitive vitamins, but neither preservation method is consistently more nutritious, according to a 2007 scientific review.
Canning uses heat, which can reduce vitamins B and C, but the airtight seal slows further nutrient losses during storage. Freezing causes fewer initial vitamin losses, but oxidation can reduce nutrients more rapidly during storage. Both methods preserve fiber and minerals.
The American Heart Association recommends checking for added salt in both canned and frozen vegetable products, as well as added sugar in canned and frozen fruit.
Modern canning dates to the early 1800s, after Napoleon offered a prize for a way to preserve food for his armies. The tin can debuted in 1810, nearly half a century before the first U.S. can opener.
Modern frozen food followed in the 1920s, when Clarence Birdseye developed quick-freezing methods inspired by Inuit fishermen in Labrador, Canada.
This fact brief is responsive to conversations such as this one.

- Journal of the Science of Food and Agriculture: Nutritional comparison of fresh, frozen, and canned fruits and vegetables II. Vitamin A and carotenoids, vitamin E, minerals and fiber

title: GTA VI is here. What non-gamers need to know
text:
Want to discuss 'Grand Theft Auto VI' with gaming friends? Here's what to know as the game drops
Have a gamer in your life or work? Wave goodbye for a while — and get literate on “GTA VI.”
That's “Grand Theft Auto VI,” the latest installment in the hyperviolent, open-world gaming world that's skewered American culture with fictionalized versions of New York, Los Angeles and is returning to its sun-baked version of Miami — Vice City.
The first new “GTA” game in 13 years — so long that the interval became a punchline — has the power to make millions of people vanish from their real lives ahead of the Thanksgiving holiday in the United States. With a massive rollout that includes huge billboards, a takeover of an NBA game and a soundtrack stacked with Grammy winners, “GTA VI” will affect the lives of tens of millions, including many nongamers.
Even for those who never pick up a controller, YouTube, memes and viral clips will extend the game's reach, its edgy content and its viral catchphrases — the ever-present “wasted,” for one — far beyond those planning midnight playing sessions or time off work.
“It's not just relationships on the line,” notes a mock boilerplate for a leave agreement to present to HR. “Every console generation has one game that erases its players from normal life for a while, and Grand Theft Auto VI is shaping up to do it at a scale nobody has really tested.”
Now version VI is arriving, and here we go again: The game started its march across the globe Thursday at midnight local time, kicking off in New Zealand and leaving North American gamers panting in anticipation.
It's an immersive narrative that carries players away
These days it's part of the culture, but the arrival of a “Grand Theft Auto” game didn't always capture such mainstream attention and adulation. Earlier editions drew pointed criticism for their violence — against police, women and innocent bystanders — and emphasis on casual sex, including with prostitutes.
Take-Two Interactive, the studio behind the “GTA” juggernaut, has layered its fictional worlds with social satire. One character in “GTA V,” for instance, prompted a lawsuit from actor Lindsay Lohan over perceived similarities. A New York court tossed the case.
Experts note that “GTA” games tend to have a long life span, with the 13-year hiatus this time giving plenty of time for “GTA” to seep into culture through social videos and memes. Expect an explosion of “GTA VI” videos in the days ahead as people discover new aspects of it.
The story of “GTA VI” is centered on a couple, and early reviews for the game have noted that it has a depth of relationship building that goes beyond the violent stickups and bank robberies.
“It’s an amazing piece of entertainment, but also culturally, just the way it brings a simulated world to life. And how they use music, and just the world that they build is really incredible. Again, it’s made by 4,700 people who worked for a decade to build this thing, so it is a monumental game in terms of the scale and scope of what it is,” said gaming journalist Geoff Keighley.
The “Grand Theft Auto” franchise has sold more than 470 million units globally, according to publisher Take-Two Interactive. “Grand Theft Auto V,” released in 2013, accounts for more than 230 million of those sales and generated $1 billion in retail sales in just three days. It will be awhile before “GTA VI” sales are available.
Related video below: Miami prepares for new GTA release
It focuses on a couple trying to succeed at crime
The main characters of the open-world game are a couple, Lucia and Jason, who are trying to improve their circumstances through crime.
Lucia has recently been released from prison while Jason, a former soldier who became involved with drug runners in the game's “Leonida Keys,” is looking for a different path. The game feels especially personal to Florida residents.
Early reviews of “GTA VI” praise its level of detail and choices that allow players to resolve certain some interactions without violence and for the way players have to carefully approach Jason and Lucia’s relationship.
Also, some players think it's fun just to “drive” around the game's virtual world. (Just more carefully in this edition, the New York Times notes in its review.)
You can view the trailers for the new version of “GTA VI” here.
It got to New Zealanders first — and the reviews are good
Adam Simmons, 50, fired up the game at midnight in New Zealand. He kept it on low volume to avoid waking his wife and daughters. Simmons, a director of photography who moved to New Zealand just five months ago from Portland, Oregon, was impressed.
“You really feel like you are in a world,” he said. “The places and how they’re put together feel right.”
He played for about an hour before heading to bed. Work is a priority, though he jokingly expects to be distracted by Vice City in the days ahead. “I have my own company that I have to run,” he said. “So I’m the boss, but also I’m just going to lose sales because a video game came out.”
It has gamers rearranging their lives to play, and some employers are OK with that
Some organizations have been planning for months how to accommodate the intense interest to play the game on launch day.
At least one U.S. Army unit offered a reenlistment bonus that included four days to play “GTA VI” at launch. Logitech, the maker of keyboards, mice and gaming peripherals, announced it was giving its 7,000 employees a paid day off to play games — “GTA” or any one of their choosing.
One German educational institution is offering a paid three-day course for people to play the game and apply what they’ve learned to community-building, collaboration and storytelling lessons.
Its music will probably reach your ears even if you don't play
One of the many ways the new “Grand Theft Auto” is permeating culture is through music.
Music has long been woven into the game’s experience, with fictional radio stations and carefully curated soundtracks accompanying players as they drive through the series’ cities.
For “GTA VI,” Rockstar Games commissioned an original adaptive score from Grammy-winning French electronic duo Justice. The music is designed to shift depending on where players are and what they are doing.
A 30-track “Grand Theft Auto VI: Original Score” is scheduled for release Dec. 11 and includes collaborations involving Tame Impala, SZA, King Gizzard & The Lizard Wizard and Gesaffelstein.
A music festival featuring “GTA VI” artists is planned for Miami this weekend, and some of the music is being played on SiriusXM stations.
That means the game’s music could soon be a part of people’s real-world drives around town. Sometimes, it seems, life does imitate art.
——-
Kellman reported from London. Associated Press Entertainment Writers Jonathan Landrum Jr. and Anthony McCartney contributed to this report from Los Angeles.

title: FIRST ALERT WEATHER: Sunshine and November Warmth Continue Through the Weekend, Colder Air Arrives Next Week
text:
PRESQUE ISLE, Maine (WAGM) - Good evening everyone and happy Wednesday. If you’re enjoying these warmer-than-average temperatures we’ve been experiencing across Northern Maine and Western New Brunswick, I’ve got some good news for you! Not only are those warmer temperatures sticking around through the weekend, but we’re also expecting to see more sunshine over the next several days. Unfortunately, that also means we’re continuing to go without any meaningful precipitation across the region, which isn’t helping our ongoing drought conditions. We’re still watching for an opportunity for some rainfall early next week, followed by a fairly significant drop in temperatures as we approach Thanksgiving.
Heading into the overnight hours tonight, I expect we’ll continue to see mostly cloudy skies across much of the region. Between the cloud cover and the continued westerly breeze, temperatures aren’t going to fall all that much overnight. Most communities will see temperatures settling into the mid to upper 30s, with a few locations remaining close to 40 degrees. I’m forecasting overnight lows of 39 degrees in both Caribou and Presque Isle, and 37 degrees in Houlton. To put that into perspective, our forecast low temperature in Caribou tonight is actually a degree warmer than our average high temperature for tomorrow! Winds will remain out of the west at around 5 to 10 mph, with some lingering gusts up to 25 mph this evening.
As we head into Thursday, I think we’re looking at one of the nicer days we’ve had in a while across the region, especially considering we’re in the second half of November. We’ll see more sunshine working its way into the region as high pressure continues to build in, with temperatures climbing into the upper 40s and lower to mid 50s. I’m forecasting a high of 53 degrees in both Caribou and Presque Isle, with 55 degrees in Houlton. That’s around 15 degrees above average for this time of year! Unlike what we experienced today, winds will be fairly light out of the southwest at around 5 to 10 mph. If you’ve still got some things you need to get done outside before winter arrives, tomorrow would be a great opportunity to do so.
We’ll continue to see plenty of sunshine heading into the day on Friday, with temperatures once again climbing into the lower to mid 50s across much of The County. Some of our communities in Western New Brunswick could even approach the upper 50s (mid-teens Celsius)! The biggest difference between Thursday and Friday will be the winds. We’ll see a bit more of a breeze developing on Friday, with west winds around 10 to 15 mph and gusts up to 25 mph. Outside of that, I don’t expect we’ll have much to complain about in terms of the weather.
Looking ahead to the weekend, there really isn’t much changing in our forecast. We’ll see a few more clouds around during the day on Saturday, but there should still be a decent amount of sunshine making its way through those clouds. Sunday is looking fairly sunny as well, with the next noticeable increase in cloud cover not expected until late Sunday night and into Monday. While this extended stretch of sunshine is certainly enjoyable, I do wish we had a little more precipitation in the forecast. The ridge of high pressure that’s been responsible for our quiet weather this week will continue to keep any significant weather systems away from the region through the weekend. Unfortunately, the longer we go without precipitation, the more concerned we become about our ongoing water resource drought. Even with the cooler temperatures this time of year, we still need a considerable amount of precipitation to help replenish our groundwater supplies.
Taking a look at our temperature trend over the next several days, you’ll notice that we do see a slight dip in temperatures on Saturday, with highs falling back into the upper 40s before rebounding into the lower to mid 50s on Sunday. The biggest change in our temperature trend comes between Monday and Tuesday, when afternoon highs could drop from around 50 degrees to just above the freezing mark. I’m continuing to monitor the development of a coastal low pressure system early next week, at the same time that a cold front will be making its way through the region. How those two features interact with one another will ultimately determine how much rainfall we end up seeing across Northern Maine. There are still some differences in our forecast guidance regarding the timing and track of that coastal system, but our chances for seeing some rainfall on Monday have increased a little compared to yesterday, especially across southern portions of The County. We could even see some snowflakes mixing in Monday night as colder air begins to work its way into the region. As much as we’d like to see some beneficial rainfall out of this system, I don’t expect it will provide any substantial drought relief. What we’re becoming increasingly confident in is the arrival of a colder air mass behind that system. Canadian high pressure will build into the region heading into the middle of next week, with afternoon temperatures potentially struggling to get out of the upper 20s and lower 30s. Overnight lows will also be falling back into the lower 20s, with the latest indications suggesting that this colder and drier pattern could stick around through Thanksgiving and Black Friday.
We’ve still got several days of warmer weather to enjoy before we get there, so I would certainly take advantage of it while we have it! For a closer look at the forecast, make sure to check out my First Alert Video Forecast attached to this article. Have a great evening everyone!

title: Build strength without stressing joints through water exercise
text:
(Aging Untold) — If your joints don’t love the treadmill, water exercises, from aqua aerobics to swimming laps, can be a game changer. There are options for every comfort level and every fitness level.
Why the pool is easier on the joints
Water exercises are a good fit for so many older adults because of the way water supports the body, Dr. Rhea Rogers, a board-certified physician, said.
“Water supports 90% of the body weight,” Rogers said. “People who want to still have that benefit of exercise can get cardiovascular endurance, help with prediabetes, insulin resistance and all that. You still want to be able to exercise, but it’s going to make it easier on your joints.”
For people with joint pain, stiffness or muscle stiffness, water exercise may be a better fit than land-based activities because of the pounding those activities involve, she said.
Know the risks before you get in
Gerontologist “Sam” Cradduck said low-impact doesn’t mean risk-free, especially for older adults.
“It doesn’t come without risk, especially for our aged community,” Cradduck said. “Your skin is thinner, so wear water shoes so you don’t end up with a sore on the bottom of your feet.”
Cradduck said ankle weights made for the water are also available.
Things to watch for:
Dehydration
“You can dehydrate in a swimming pool, which sounds weird,” Cradduck said.
Temperature
Rogers added that thermoregulation can be different for older adults.
“You have to watch also for the temperature and blood pressure, especially if you’re getting into the hot tub,” Cradduck said.
Lymphatic issues
“If you have a lymphatic issue, lymph nodes that aren’t working well or fluids that aren’t draining well, the higher temperatures are going to create problems there,” Cradduck said. “Some cancer survivors, if they’ve had lymph node involvement, have to watch for the higher temperatures.”
Slippery surfaces
“Watch the slipperiness of the wet feet, especially on the concrete coming out,” Cradduck said. “Falls happen.”
Muscle soreness
“Just because it’s low impact doesn’t mean it’s not moving muscle, so you could become sore from those workouts if you haven’t worked those muscles,” Cradduck said.
But don’t let muscle soreness detract you, she said.
“Don’t take the soreness to say, ‘Oh, I can’t ever do this again.’ That is your muscles responding and building,” Cradduck said.
You don’t have to know how to swim
Aging expert Amy O’Rourke said many people hear “pool” and assume swimming skills are required. She said that isn’t the case.
“I taught water aerobics, and I would say easily half of the students couldn’t swim,” O’Rourke said. “The range of motion that they experienced and the look on their face, they could finally get their leg all the way up. They could finally get their arms all the way up. They were joyful at the range of motion they could have.”
You don’t necessarily have to swim to be able to do it, she said.
“You can stand by the side of the pool and do leg lifts and get strength. You can do knee lifts and get strength,” O’Rourke said.
Rogers cautioned that anyone who does not know how to swim should stay in the shallow end of the pool.
Public pools have to be accessible, with accessible entrances and exits, Cradduck added.
Classes, community and cost
Aging well coach Katherine Ambrose said water exercise classes are designed to be fun and well-rounded.
“Someone has designed the class to be fun, but also be well-rounded and provide you a good workout,” she said. “Usually there’s music involved that’s been selected for your group, and the group itself is super fun.”
Rogers also pointed to social and mental health benefits, including laughter, less stress, better sleep and improved confidence.
On cost, O’Rourke said community pools and Ys are available in many places.
“It’s not like you have to have a lot of money and join a big fancy club to be able to get in the water,” O’Rourke said.
“If you can get Silver Sneakers, maybe through Medicare Advantage, then there might not be any cost at all,” Ambrose said. “That’s something that you could go to right away.”

title: Maine lawmakers might ease property taxes. Here’s what’s on the table.
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
A group that has spent more than a year searching for ways to ease Maine’s heavy property tax burden finalized its recommendations after a lengthy meeting Tuesday.
The 13-member Real Estate Property Tax Relief Task Force, led by Sen. Nicole Grohoski, D-Ellsworth, and Rep. Ann Matlack, D-St. George, will send more than a dozen suggested policy changes to the Legislature to consider.
The recommendations ranged from broad changes in some of the state’s largest tax relief programs to smaller changes designed to reduce municipal spending or increase revenue. Other ideas were passed along for further study.
“I have been consistently supporting looking under every rock and not exempting any rock from consideration as to where to look to help make the property tax situation better for those who are acutely affected, and I’m going to continue to do that,” Grohoski said at the meeting.
‘IMMEDIATE PROPERTY TAX RELIEF’
The most consequential recommendations were to expand the Property Tax Fairness Credit and Homestead Exemption, the state’s largest tax relief programs.
Updating them is “the best option for bringing immediate property tax relief,” according to the task force.
The Property Tax Fairness Credit provides lower-income residents a partial refund on property taxes or rent.
For the 2025 tax year, it can be worth up to $1,000, or $2,000 for those over 65, according to Maine Revenue Services. Single filers must make less than $63,750 to qualify, while heads of households and married people generally must earn less than $82,500 (or slightly more for larger families).
In 2024, the average credit was $845, according to the Progress and Poverty Institute, the nonprofit contracted to do research and data analysis for the task force.
The group recommended increasing eligibility by removing family size and age requirements. It also suggested the Legislature consider a two-tiered credit with 100% reimbursement for taxpayers who pay more than a certain percentage of their income on property tax or rent, and 50% for any remaining amount.
The task force also recommended doubling Maine’s homestead exemption.
That tool can reduce the value of a qualified homeowner’s primary residence by up to $25,000 for tax purposes, reducing their overall property tax bill. The task force recommends increasing that to $50,000.
The group also passed a handful of recommendations to increase awareness about these programs. Only about 72% of eligible households applied for the property tax fairness credit and only 75% of eligible households claimed the homestead exemption in 2024, according to the Progress and Poverty Institute.
While task force members unanimously supported bolstering the programs, they could not come to an agreement on how to pay for the changes.
A ‘CRITICAL’ PROGRAM
Another program that could see some changes is the Property Tax Deferral Program, which lets older adults or homeowners with disabilities defer their property taxes as a state-backed loan until they sell the home, move or pass away.
The state pays the property taxes for people who apply and qualify, but also has the authority to obtain a lien on the applicant’s home.
“For residents of this state whose home values have greatly appreciated, but who are income-poor and not able to remain current on rising tax bills, this program is a critical tool to help those individuals remain in their homes and communities,” the task force wrote in the draft report.
Despite this, it said uptake since the program’s passage in 2021 has been “uniformly and strikingly low.” Of the nearly 91,000 households that are eligible, only 235 are enrolled, according to the draft report. That’s a participation rate of 0.26%.
The group hopes to boost that rate by loosening or removing limits on acreage and liquid assets, changing the interest rates and allowing eligibility even if a homeowner has an existing municipal lien.
It also recommends that municipalities send out information about the program with each notice mailed to taxpayers who fall behind on their payments.
HIGH-VALUE SECOND HOMES
The task force was split on a recommendation that the Legislature consider what the Progress and Poverty Institute referred to as a “Taylor Swift tax,” or a tax on high-value second homes.
The nonprofit estimated that a 0.5% tax on the value of second homes above $1 million would generate about $50 million in revenue per year.
However, members were previously told the tax violates the Maine Constitution.
The group couched the recommendation, failing to say the Legislature should adopt the tax, rather that it should “consider” the idea as a source of property tax relief.
That suggestion passed 6-5, but its inclusion in the report could depend on the votes of two people who were absent Tuesday and have until the end of the week to weigh in.
The task force also passed several other recommendations that members hope will ultimately help chip away at the problem, like an inventory of municipalities charging impact fees, standardized audit and assessing requirements and a report on regionalization efforts among towns. It suggested finding more stable ways for towns and cities to bring in money outside of revenue sharing, including allowing them to charge tax-exempt properties for municipal services.
Maine nonprofits pushed back on the latter, arguing that they operate on slim margins without many new revenue opportunities.
However, a recommendation to allow municipalities to require the state to make payments in lieu of taxes on state-owned land failed.

title: Freeport music venue has weekend of events
text:
SATURDAY
Kat and the Kooltones are returning to Cadenza on Saturday after several previous, well-attended performances. Expect a soulful and delightful evening of jazz, American standards, pop and some other musical surprises thrown into the mix. Kathleen “Kat” McCatherin is a multi-instrumentalist, former voice and piano teacher, and has fronted numerous bands, written and arranged music, plays in pit orchestras, and celebrates music every day.
Join Kat and the Kooltones from 7-8:30 p.m. as they take you on a musical adventure through the decades, entertaining you with a diverse selection of songs from various eras. The group will linger with The American Songbook, move through the ’60s, Motown, Broadway and offer some surprises along the way. The Kooltones will bring joy to the heart and leave you inspired by their talent and musicality. Kat has a captivating, playful stage presence that will have you smiling, toe-tapping and maybe even joining those “audience participation” invitations.
