title: South Portland library reopens, progress made at City Hall following cyberattack
text:
South Portland library reopens, progress made at City Hall following cyberattack
The main branch of the South Portland Public Library reopened on Thursday, days after it closed due to a cybersecurity incident.
City officials said they were also making "good progress" toward reopening City Hall and the Assessor's Office, but they did not announce a reopening date.
The city's IT team shut down the network Saturday night after discovering a cybersecurity issue. Officials said earlier this week that the network outage that is disrupting some municipal services may involve cybercriminal activity.
The library quietly opened on Thursday afternoon, though some people learned about the opening after receiving a hold pickup notification. Those were a result of the staff getting everything that had been received this week (hundreds and hundreds of items) checked in. Library staff said the notices are legitimate and items that were requested were waiting at the desk.
Library staff said circulation services were working as expected and they had the full ability to check items in and out, renew items, place holds and to look up items in the catalog.
However, as of Thursday afternoon, the library was unable to offer public access to Wi-Fi, public-use computers or printing (the photocopier was available) and the library was without phone service.
The library was able to open thanks to the ability to set up a network - independent of the wider city network - to access systems.
The branch library on Wescott Rd. will remain closed until a similar network can be established there.
Other City Progress
City officials said that they expected there would continue to be impacts on services even after City Hall and the Assessor's Office reopen. Officials said service times may be slower than usual and some functions may still be unavailable.
City officials said on Wednesday that officials have confirmed that most city data was not compromised in a recent cybersecurity incident. However, officials said on Thursday they were still working to verify what specific city data may have been accessed in the systems.
The city postponed the property tax payment deadline to Monday, Nov. 23. Residents can still leave payments in secure drop boxes outside City Hall. The city is working on a solution for new vehicle registrations; renewals are available through the state's Rapid Renewal website.
Police, fire and EMS services are not affected.

title: Sanford reworking data center, sludge plant restrictions after residents criticize proposal as too weak
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
SANFORD — The planning board on Wednesday night heard several city residents’ feedback about a proposal that would restrict large-scale developments such as data centers and a proposed biosolid gasification plant.
No one spoke in favor of the proposal in its current form, saying that the language didn’t appear to establish any substantial restrictions and would pave the way for controversial projects instead of regulating them.
By the end of the meeting, the board voted unanimously to table a recommendation that the City Council adopt the language as is.
In response to the residents’ concerns, the board plans to hold a workshop early next year to discuss strengthening the language.
The proposed ordinance amendment was generated in response to two major projects that have elicited pushback from residents over the past year: the Aries Clean Technologies biosolid gasification plant, which would use thermal processing to remove forever chemicals from sludge; and the Sanford Woods Industrial and Technical Campus, which would include a data center on more than 1,000 acres near the Mousam River.
Residents have vocally opposed both projects, citing environmental and economic impacts that they feel would negatively impact the community. That opposition prompted moratoriums temporarily halting both projects, as well as the formation of a task force charged with crafting permanent guardrails.
The proposed language details the standards that a developer would have to meet before the city could approve such developments. But the residents who spoke Wednesday argued that the language placed barely any actual restrictions on the developments.
Eve Dumont-Wilson, co-founder of the Sanford Clean Air & Water Coalition, said the lack of restrictions in the proposed amendment would pave the way for the developments.
“While many discussions were had, the outcome of this task force is a permitting pathway — and not the protections this community asked for,” she said.
In written statements to the board, multiple residents said limits on water consumption, noise emission and electricity demand were either absent or too vague to be effectively enforced.
“These are both fairly complex topics,” said Jamie Cole, director of planning and development. “I think it would probably be wise if the planning board scheduled a work session and that we go through these with a fine-tooth comb to make sure, as the public has asked, that we get it right the first time.”
Other planning board members agreed that the proposed language needed more work to identify ambiguities and lay out stricter regulations.
“When I read through the ordinances, my concern is the ordinances are written in a way to show how these businesses were allowed, and yet not enough information about why not,” said board member Todd Rothstein.
City Manager Stephen Buck said the City Council is expected to extend the moratoriums to allow for more work to be done on the language. The council will likely to vote to extend the biosolid plant moratorium on Dec. 8, Buck said, and has until Jan. 31 to reextend the temporary data center ban.
The City Council is still scheduled to hold its own public hearing on the proposed ordinance amendment at its next meeting Tuesday.
As attendees of Wednesday’s meeting gathered to go home, their morale was high.
“The news that the City Council is intending to extend the moratorium is definitely really good news, and a relief,” said Jordan Matthews, a lead organizer with the Sanford Clean Air & Water Coalition.
A workshop date has not yet been announced, but planning board members suggested it take place in the new year. Cole said the the board will likely set a date at its first meeting in January.

title: ‘VisionQuest’ Creator Confirms Huge Fan Theory About Human Torch
text:
‘VisionQuest’ Creator Confirms the Original Human Torch Was In the MCU Invaders
The following post contains spoilers for VisionQuest.
In the annals of Marvel history, there is no one quite like the Vision. Android, artificial intelligence, villain, Avenger, and even a husband and father on occassion. Through the years, his story has grown more and more complicated. At one point, he was destroyed and replaced by a “younger” version of himself that also contained the personality of Iron Lad (AKA Kang as a teenager). Another late ’80s storyline even confirmed that his android body was built out of parts and pieces used to create the original Human Torch — the flaming robot who is actually very first Marvel hero, having appeared on the cover of 1939’s Marvel Comics #1.
Even by Marvel standards, this dude’s got a lot of baggage. And one of the most impressive parts about Marvel’s VisionQuest TV series is how it honors so much of that baggage, and brings it into the backstory of the Marvel Cinematic Universe version of Vision played by Paul Bettany. The show confirms Vision’s connection to the MCU’s equivalent of the Golden Age Human Torch, a character known as the Joule Individual Machine — or J.I.M. for short, a tribute to the comic-book Human Torch’s human alter ego, Jim Hammond.
VisionQuest didn’t fill in all the details of J.I.M’s early years, but in an interview with ScreenCrush, series creator Terry Matalas confirmed that, at least in his own head, the character’s MCU history syncs up even further with the Human Torch of 1930s and ’40s Marvel Comics.
That character eventually went on to fight in World War II on behalf of the United States. Along with Captain America and Namor, the trio formed the core of a group known as the Invaders. In Captain America: The First Avenger, the Marvel Cinematic Universe showed Steve Rogers fighting the Nazis alongside Bucky and a bunch of soldiers who are commonly known in Marvel comics as the Howling Commandos. But that film condensed most of World War II into a single montage, leaving plenty of room to add the Invaders into Cap’s backstory — just as Marvel Comics did when they retroactively inserted the Invaders into continuity in the late 1960s.
Malas told ScreenCrush that he believes — and wrote VisionQuest under the assumption that — the Invaders are a part of MCU history we simply haven’t seen yet, and that J.I.M. was a member of the group.
As he put it to us: “The idea is there’s a whole series that happened that we didn’t see, that’s about that father and son running around with the gang in World War II.”
“I think he was a part of the Invaders ... Y’know, in the comic books, he kills Hitler,” Matalas added.
You can watch our full interview with Matalas about VisionQuest below:
READ MORE: Every Marvel Cinematic Universe Movie, Ranked From Worst to Best
An Invaders TV series sounds incredible, although the budget needed for a period superhero story probably makes it quite unlikely. (The fact that Marvel seems to have stopped almost all of the production of live-action Disney+ series also raises the odds against it.) What seems more feasible is an Invaders cameo in something like the upcoming Avengers: Doomsday or Secret Wars. The actors playing the key Invaders, from Chris Evans to Sebastian Stan to Tenoch Huerta, are all involved in those movies. Why not show them fighting Nazis in a flashback or on some alternate Earth somewhere? That would be super fun.

title: A community solar project may be coming to Yarmouth, aimed at reducing costs for residents
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
A large community solar project may be coming to Yarmouth, with the developer promising benefits for residents looking to save on their electric bills.
The Yarmouth Planning Board heard a proposal on Wednesday for a 4-acre ground-mounted solar facility at 269 Sligo Road, also known locally as the “Pole Yard.” Central Maine Power previously treated and stored wooden poles on the 14-acre parcel, resulting in its status as a brownfield site.
In 2021, the Yarmouth Town Council issued a request for proposals and authorized town staff to pursue a community solar project with EDP Renewables, with the goal of reducing the town’s carbon footprint.
In the proposal presented Wednesday, EDP Renewables shared its plan for about 2,200 panels on Sligo Road, which company representative Chris Byers said would generate power for 300 to 400 homes.
If the project moves forward, the town will purchase the land from CMP for $1 and lease it to EDP Renewables for $30,000 annually, town staff said.
Byers, who is also a member of the North Yarmouth Planning Board, said the project would allow for anyone with a CMP electric bill to lower their costs and benefit from renewable energy without installing personal solar panels. The project would produce power for the electric grid, and individuals and businesses in CMP’s territory could subscribe to the project and then receive credits on their electric bill for the power their share produces.
Yarmouth subscribers will have specific advantages, said Yarmouth Sustainability Coordinator Meddy Smith. The town negotiated that residents will be able to save an estimated 15% on the value of the solar credit subscriptions for the project and will have a priority enrollment period for 90 days, after which anyone in Maine can subscribe to the project at regular cost.
“Town staff have been investing in this project for five or six years or so because of the community benefits,” said Smith. “This is one mechanism the town can support energy affordability.”
The Yarmouth Climate Action Board expressed strong support for the project and said it aligned with the town’s climate action plan.
“The project represents a practical, responsible, and locally beneficial investment in Yarmouth’s clean energy future,” the board said in a statement.
The proposal was made possible by changes to Yarmouth’s zoning ordinance approved by the Town Council in October 2025. The amendments made explicit provisions for solar panel installations in the town, a use not previously specified.
The planning board moved to erase this ambiguity after a proposal for a solar panel next to Cross Cemetery was met with widespread resident opposition, prompting the board to examine whether this proposal — or any large-scale solar project — was allowed under the existing zoning ordinance.
In the updated zoning ordinance, principal-use solar arrays are only allowed in commercial and industrial districts in Yarmouth unless the project is located on a brownfield site. The Pole Yard plot, zoned rural residential, is one of the only parcels available in town for a solar project of this scale.
During public comment, several residents of Sligo Road spoke against the project, saying they were disappointed to not hear about the project prior to notices sent two weeks ago, that it was too risky for the town to acquire a brownfield site, and the solar panels would disrupt the rural character of the area.
Meagan McKusick, whose property abuts the land where the solar array would be built, said the project was not worth the electric bill savings to Yarmouth residents.
“I don’t want to lose my front yard for $10 a month,” she said.
The planning board asked EDP Renewables for more information on how much the project will be visible on the road and for further coordination with the fire department. The developer requested the board grant exemptions for some site requirements, such as soil surveys, so as to not risk disturbing the deeper contaminated layers of the brownfield site.
The board will discuss the proposal again at a meeting not yet scheduled. Following local permitting, the project would be be certified through the Maine Department of Environmental Protection’s Voluntary Response Action Program, which is intended to regulate and encourage the redevelopment of contaminated properties within the state.
If all requirements are met, Byers estimated construction would take place in the spring and summer.
It’s not the first time Yarmouth has been interested in benefiting from a large shared solar project. In 2021, the town signed a 20-year agreement with ReVision Energy to get its municipal electricity from two solar arrays in Acton and Naples, offsetting about 92% of its energy bill. The deal is projected to save the town $3.2 million over the course of the contract.

title: Chase Bank announces cyberattack, says hackers may have obtained customers’ personal information
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
(Gray News) — Chase Bank said Thursday that some customers’ information was compromised during a cyberattack.
In a post on X, the bank said third parties that provide services to the firm were the target of a cyberattack.
Chase Bank said investigators found that the attackers accessed “certain marketing data held by those vendors, which may include some customer names and email addresses.”
The bank said there was no disruption to its services.
Any customers affected will be contacted directly by Chase Bank. The bank said it will offer support, including free credit monitoring.
The cyberattack is not believed to be connected to technical problems at multiple major banks earlier this week.
Thousands of customers reported difficulty accessing online accounts at several major U.S. banks and the money transfer service Zelle on Monday after a technical issue at JPMorgan Chase caused ripple effects throughout the financial system.
However, JPMorgan Chase said Monday that the technical problems were not the result of a cyberattack.
“JPMorgan Chase has experienced a temporary issue related to a software bug in an on-premises hardware system — it is not cyber-related,” said spokesman Joe Evangelisti.

17-year-old killed in Waldoboro hit-and-run; suspect charged with OUI of drugs
Police say the 53-year-old suspect has also been charged with manslaughter and leaving the scene of an accident resulting in death.
A Maine man is facing multiple charges, including operating under the influence of drugs, in connection with a hit-and-run crash in Waldoboro that killed a teenager.
Waldoboro Police Chief John Lash said the crash happened at about 3:15 p.m. Wednesday on Friendship Road.
Gifford Campbell, 53, of Waldoboro, was driving a black 2015 Nissan Titan pickup truck north on Friendship Road when his vehicle veered to the right and struck a 17-year-old pedestrian, according to investigators.
Witnesses told Maine's Total Coverage reporter Jim Keithley that the pedestrian, a teenage boy, was thrown onto the front lawn of a nearby home as a result of the collision.
The teen was transported to Miles Memorial Hospital in Damariscotta, where they were later pronounced dead. Lash said he is not sharing the victim's name at this time out of respect for the privacy of their family.
"I just ache for the loss of the family because kids aren't replaceable," said Waldoboro resident Misty Cole. "It's going to be a big shock."
Lash said Campbell did not stop after striking the teen with his truck and continued to drive. Campbell's truck, however, was stopped shortly thereafter near Sammi's Family Entertainment and he was arrested.
Campbell has been charged with manslaughter, OUI drugs resulting in death and leaving the scene of an accident resulting in death. He is being held at the Two Bridge Regional Jail and is scheduled to appear in court on Friday.
Lash said that members of the Waldoboro Fire Department, Waldoboro EMS, Lincoln County Sheriff's Office, Damariscotta Police Department and Maine State Police either responded to the scene or helped with the crash investigation.
People who live in the area said Friendship Road has a number of hills and blind spots, and that they see a number of vehicles that drive too fast.
"You wouldn't have seen him until you are almost on top of him," said Waldoboro resident Matt Nosh.
"I think it's awful," Cole said. "A lot of people try to walk the sides of the roads or ride their bicycles, and it's not safe for them."
A candlelight vigil for the crash victim is being held at 7 p.m. Thursday at the Nobleboro Little League Baseball Field off of Route 1, which is near the Pemaquid Pond boat ramp.

title: Climate Action Team Replaced With Sustainable Wiscasset Committee
Duffy: Ground stop could have been shorter if contractor spotted issue sooner
text:
(AP) - The nationwide ground stop on Friday could have ended sooner if the contractor that did the work linked to the disruptions at key air traffic control facilities had located the problem sooner, according to Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy.
Investigators are still working to determine exactly why the newly installed router at the center of everything started blasting out thousands of connection attempts not long after it was turned on as part of a project to replace a section of old copper wires with fiber optic lines in Arkansas.
Duffy appeared on the 2WAY streaming platform’s “The Morning Meeting” show Wednesday and said that L3Harris failed to identify and isolate the router issue that caused the ground stop quickly enough. That contributed to this being the longest ground stop since the Sept. 11, 2001, terrorist attacks because it lasted more than four hours.
“The monitoring of the network matters,” he said, adding that officials were working on remedying that problem. In the meantime, any new installations of these same routers have been paused, and technicians have disabled the function that was linked to Friday’s outage.
Experts continue testing the equipment linked to the problem to determine why this Juniper router behaved differently from any of the ones installed in 68 previous projects across the FAA network. The investigators are focused on whether the router was configured incorrectly by the experienced technician who did the work or whether it was faulty. The company that made the router has said it believes the “device functioned as it was configured by the installer.”
Friday’s problems are reminiscent of a 2009 outage
The circumstances of the technical problems that led to last week’s nationwide ground stop appear eerily similar to a 2009 outage caused by a technician doing the same kind of work installing new fiber optic lines.
The Transportation Department’s Inspector General said the 2009 disruption that led to 820 delayed flights was caused by a Harris technician setting up a router incorrectly. Harris later became L3Harris as part of a merger, but that company has been operating and maintaining the FAA network for decades.
Matthew Hampton, who was the former assistant inspector general for aviation at that time, said that the FAA has long had weak oversight of the contractors it relies on.
“Poor contractor oversight has been a problem at the FAA in both developing systems and deploying them, there’s a whole history of that,” Hampton said.
Aviation safety expert Jeff Guzzetti, who worked in the Inspector General’s office for several years, said that inadequate oversight of contractors was a problem during the FAA’s last attempt at overhauling their systems called NextGen.
Normally, the FAA is quite good at dealing with unexpected challenges and adjusting quickly by shifting air traffic control responsibilities to a nearby facility when one location is having a problem or slowing traffic temporarily. But Guzzetti said that wasn’t possible this time because the entire network was affected Friday, including both the primary and backup systems.
“The FAA is really good at adapting, improvising and overcoming events. But if the whole system is down, it makes it very challenging,” said Guzzetti, who also investigated crashes for both the FAA and National Transportation Safety Board.
L3Harris hasn’t commented on the ground stop since issuing a statement Saturday pledging to support the FAA’s investigation into what happened. The company declined to say more on Wednesday.
FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford said at a different event hosted by The Hill on Wednesday morning that he understands that his agency is ultimately responsible for what happened even if L3Harris was the one doing the work.
“I am the chief accountability officer. I take full responsibility for it,” Bedford said. “I wish people would lay off the secretary. He’s got a lot of work to do, but I’m the guy they hired to get this done. So, blame me.”
It’s not clear how much more money Congress will approve for the overhaul
The FAA nearly doubled its funding request to Congress to $50 billion after Friday’s ground stop to pay for the rest of the overhaul of the nation’s air traffic control system. Last year, the agency received $12.5 billion to get started on the project. Bedford said he understands why members of Congress might be having “some indigestion associated with that.”
Several key lawmakers said Tuesday that Congress is unlikely to approve that full amount right now — especially when the FAA hasn’t spent all the money that was approved last year. Duffy has said that a big part of why some of the money hasn’t been spent yet is that the new radars and other systems that will be installed are still being built, so he hasn’t been able to buy them yet.
Only about $10 billion of the $50 billion request would go to air traffic control technology. The rest of the money would go to other projects, including upgrades to runways, airport towers and aging air traffic control centers that were built in the 1960s.
More problems are possible while upgrading the outdated FAA system
Chris Sununu, who is president of the Airlines for America trade group, praised Bedford for keeping the airlines informed during the ground stop. Sununu said Bedford asked to set up a conference call with all the airline CEOs and operations leaders within about half an hour of the ground stop starting and briefed them on what he knew so far. Several additional calls were held throughout the ground stop.
“To be honest, he stayed on the phone effectively with all the CEOs all night long,” Sununu said. “We did, I think, three or four calls over the period of the next few hours, brought in those operational folks. And so as they learned more, as they understood more of what was happening.”
Sununu said the FAA has a difficult job in trying to overhaul “what is really the most robust telecom system on the planet while you’re using it 24 hours a day and ensuring the safety of everyone who is part of it.” And he said this might not be the last technical problem that happens during the project because the work the FAA is doing is akin to trying to get your iPhone to talk to your flip phone.
“Can we say, ‘oh, you know, this is really the last time we’re going to have a bump like this?’, No, no. Because the technologies we’re replacing and that we’re asking to talk to each other are literally multigenerational,” he said.
____
Associated Press writers Ben Wieder, David Collins and Sudhin Thanawala contributed to this report.

title: South Portland man pleads not guilty in Belfast school bus crash
text:
BELFAST, Maine (WABI) - A South Portland man pleaded not guilty to four charges stemming from a 2025 crash involving a school bus in Belfast.
Kyle Young, 41, made his first court appearance by Zoom Wednesday afternoon. He is being held on $1,000 bail and, if released, has been ordered not to drive, among other conditions.
A Waldo County grand jury indicted Young last week on charges of aggravated criminal OUI, reckless conduct with a dangerous weapon, endangering the welfare of a child, and driving to endanger.
The crash
Prosecutors say Young was high on drugs when he crashed into an RSU 71 school bus in June 2025.
About two dozen students were on the bus. Two students, Young and his then-4-year-old child, who was in the car with him, were hospitalized.
The state said delays involving the lab and the investigation contributed to the time it took to bring charges.
Bail arguments
Young’s attorney asked for $1,000 unsecured bail, saying Young had no cash and wanted to return to his job. The attorney said Young has been sober for nine months and had stable employment before his arrest.
The state asked for $1,000 secured bail. Prosecutors acknowledged it was a low request for the charges, but cited the length of time between the alleged incident and the charges.
Young has one prior OUI on his record. He also was convicted of a felony drug charge in November 2025 and sentenced to 30 days in jail.

title: Pete Rose posthumously pardoned by Trump after baseball's career hits leader was reinstated by MLB
text:
Pete Rose posthumously pardoned by Trump after baseball's career hits leader was reinstated by MLB
President Donald Trump on Thursday said he had posthumously pardoned Pete Rose more than two years after the baseball star's death and a year after he was reinstated by Major League Baseball Commissioner Rob Manfred.
"I have just given a Complete and Total Pardon to the Late, Great Pete Rose, a true Baseball SUPERSTAR & LEGEND," Trump posted on social media.
Rose, baseball's career hits leader at 4,256, entered guilty pleas on April 20, 1990, to two counts of filing false tax returns, admitting he failed to report $354,968 during a four-year period. That was about eight months after Rose agreed to a permanent ban from baseball.
"I know I'm not a bad person, but I did make some mistakes and it's in the eyes of the judge," Rose said that night during his weekly talk show on WCKY-AM in Cincinnati. "All you can say is it's up to the judge."
The pardon comes after Manfred issued a sweeping decision last May that opened a pathway for Rose to be considered for baseball's Hall of Fame. Manfred declared that individuals on MLB's permanently ineligible list would have their statuses restored at death, a ruling that impacted 17 people, most notably Rose and Shoeless Joe Jackson.
Under a rule adopted by the Hall's board of directors in 1991, anyone on the permanently ineligible list can't be considered for election to the Hall. The earliest Rose or Jackson could now be inducted would be in 2028.
Rose agreed to his permanent ban in August 1989 after Major League Baseball investigator John M. Dowd concluded he bet numerous times on the Cincinnati Reds while playing on and managing his hometown team from 1985-87.
Facing a sentence of up to six years in prison and $500,000 in fines, Rose was sentenced on July 19, 1990, by U.S. District Judge S. Arthur Spiegel in Cincinnati to five months in prison. He also was fined $50,000 and ordered to perform 1,000 hours of community service as a gym teacher's assistant with inner-city youths in Cincinnati as part of a one-year probation period. The first three months of the probation were to be spent at the halfway house.
Rose repaid the Internal Revenue Service $366,042.
"History and the tincture of time will decide his place among the all-time greats of baseball," Spiegel said. "With regard to Pete Rose, the individual, he has broken the law, admitted his guilt, and stands ready to pay the penalty. Under our system of law and sense of fairness, when he has completed his sentence, he will have paid his debt to society and should be accepted by society as rehabilitated. Only time will tell whether he is to be restored to his position of honor for his accomplishment on the ball fields of America."
Rose reported that Aug. 10 to the U.S. Penitentiary Marion Camp in Illinois, a minimum security facility, and was released Jan. 7, 1991. He entered Talbert House to start serving his probation and departed on April 5.
A 17-time All-Star during a playing career from 1963-86, Rose was the 1963 National League Rookie of the Year, 1973 MVP and 1975 World Series MVP. A three-time NL batting champion, he broke the prior hits record of 4,191 set by Ty Cobb from 1905-28.
___
AP Baseball Writer Jay Cohen contributed to this report.

title: Jared Golden calls Maine’s DC lobster lobbyist a ‘waste of taxpayer dollars’
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
The Bangor Daily News was the first to report this story. What you’re reading here would likely not be made public without the efforts of professional journalists asking questions, interviewing sources and obtaining documents.
The Maine Department of Marine Resources has paid a Washington lobbyist at least $360,000 since 2019 to work on lobster fishery issues, a sum that outgoing U.S. Rep. Jared Golden called wasteful amid a dispute on a key bill.
The department and the Maine Lobstermen’s Association strongly disagree. They say Capitol Hill Policy Group and its managing principal, Todd Bertoson, have rallied members of Congress and federal agencies around policies favoring Maine and helped blunt increasingly stringent federal whale protections that could have decimated the state’s lobster industry.
The divide comes at a critical moment for one of Maine’s most important industries. Gov.-elect Hannah Pingree is about to take over for Gov. Janet Mills facing a $1 billion budget gap. Incoming Democratic leadership on Capitol Hill is expected to place lawmakers less friendly to the industry in committee positions.
Golden’s bill extending a pause on whale regulations through 2035 is in doubt after DMR recently told lawmakers it was no longer essential. He said he only learned of Bertoson’s work for the state earlier this year even though both have worked on the issue since 2019.
“I was shocked to learn that a state agency is paying a lobbyist in Washington, D.C., particularly when we have a very tight knit delegation that’s very accessible to the governor and state agencies,” he said in an interview. “It seems like just a giant waste of taxpayer dollars.”
The department has paid Bertoson’s firm between $20,000 and $80,000 per year from 2019 through 2025, according to the federal lobbying database OpenLobby. The $360,000 total ranks 16th among Maine spenders on federal lobbying, and Bertoson is the state government’s only disclosed lobbyist.
The hiring of Washington lobbyists is more common in bigger states with more complex congressional delegations and issues. Maine has paid Washington lobbyists in briefer stretches before.
In 2005, Gov. John Baldacci’s administration hired the PMA Group to make the case for Brunswick Naval Air Station and Portsmouth Naval Shipyard as the Pentagon moved to shed bases, The Sun Journal reported. Under former Gov. Paul LePage, a lobbyist worked on agricultural issues for the state from 2012 to 2014, according to Open Secrets.
Dave Sullivan, general vice president for the Eastern Territory of the International Association of Machinists, which represents lobstermen and fishery workers, said he’s heard few if any details from state officials on Bertoson’s efforts.
“We would call it a waste of money because we’ve never had reports or an update from DMR or the governor on what this lobbyist has done for the industry,” he said.
Bertoson declined to comment. The offices of U.S. Sens. Susan Collins and Angus King and U.S. Rep. Chellie Pingree did not respond to requests for comment.
Bertoson is a former aide to the late Alaska Sen. Ted Stevens and a former staff director of the Senate Commerce Committee. Since 2018, he has appeared in nearly 600 federal lobbying filings for 33 clients, according to OpenLobby.
Many are seafood interests, including the Groundfish Forum, Alaska Bering Sea Crabbers and the National Seafood Marketing Coalition. Others include the Alaska Native corporation Calista Corp., the Lummi Nation, the Makah Tribe, the American Chemistry Council and T-Mobile.
Jeff Nichols, a DMR spokesperson, called Bertoson one of the top fisheries lobbyists in Washington. He noted that Bertoson was on the Commerce Committee’s fisheries staff during the drafting and the 2007 reauthorization of the Magnuson-Stevens Fishery Conservation and Management Act.
The department did not rely on Washington lobbyists before 2019, Nichols said. It hired Bertoson that year because of “escalating regulatory battles over North Atlantic right whale protections that threatened Maine’s lobster industry,” he said in a statement.
Bertoson was “instrumental” in the 2022 pause, Nichols said. Golden’s bill would extend that seven years. The lobbyist’s work has often focused on outreach to members of Congress across the country, along with policy guidance, strategy and support.
A spokesperson for Mills said the governor supported the hire “to advocate for Maine’s interests and to help the state navigate a complex federal issue that directly impacts Maine’s economy and culture.”
“His work has been excellent and very, very necessary to achieve the pause secured in 2022,” Patrice McCarron, president of the Maine Lobstermen’s Association, said. “He’s very professional, very knowledgeable. He’s boots on the ground in D.C., an important piece of keeping that process going and not falling behind on advocacy.”
BDN writer Michael Shepherd contributed to this report.

Robbins Lumber cited for five serious safety violations after deadly mill fire
Robbins Lumber has been cited by OSHA for five serious safety violations and faces $54,691 in proposed penalties after the deadly May 15 explosion and fire at its Searsmont mill, according to the U.S. Department of Labor.

Robbins Lumber has been cited for five serious safety violations and faces $54,691 in proposed penalties after the deadly May 15 explosion and fire at its Searsmont mill, according to the U.S. Department of Labor.
A spokesperson for the Department of Labor says the company has 15 business days from receiving the citations to comply, request an informal conference with the Occupational Safety and Health Administration's area director or contest the findings before an independent review commission.
The Department of Labor did not disclose the specifics of the citations.
OSHA opened an inspection into the mill on the day of the deadly explosion and fire. The incident killed two firefighters and injured mill co-owner Alden Robbins, who later died from those injuries. Ten others were also left with burn injuries.
The Maine State Fire Marshal's Office ruled the fire to be accidental and said it likely started in the unloader mechanism at the base of a silo. Investigators believe that the explosion was caused by suspended particulate material rapidly igniting inside the silo.
A prior OSHA citation
Robbins Lumber faced several fires and an OSHA citation even before the May 15 disaster.
8 Investigates found at least three fires connected to the mill in recent years, as well as a 2025 OSHA citation for failing to follow preventative safety procedures and failing to conduct an annual inspection of its energy-control procedures.
Robbins Lumber did not immediately respond to our requests for comment.

title: Appeals court grants Trump request to halt order restoring Venezuelan TPS
text:
A federal appeals court has agreed to keep deportation protections frozen for hundreds of thousands of Venezuelan migrants, shortly after the Trump administration filed an emergency appeal to the Supreme Court.
The order handed down late Wednesday means the administration remains free to detain and deport Venezuelans who had previously been granted temporary protected status. Federal attorneys have said some 1,800 are in detention, and about 330 are subject to deportation proceedings.
The Supreme Court previously intervened to allow the administration to temporarily end the program for Venezuelans.
Congress created the TPS program in 1990 to protect migrants from deportation to countries experiencing natural disasters or civil unrest. The designation is granted in periods of up to 18 months.
The Trump administration argues that TPS is a temporary program and that Venezuela no longer meets the requirements for its renewal.
During President Donald Trump’s second term, the Department of Homeland Security has terminated TPS for more than 1 million people from 13 countries, including Venezuela, Haiti, Honduras, Nicaragua, Afghanistan and Syria.
However, in a shift in policy in recent months, the administration has maintained protections for nearly 200,000 Salvadorans and more than 100,000 people from Ukraine and Sudan.
TPS was first granted to Venezuelans in March 2021, under Democratic President Joe Biden. The designation was expanded in September 2023 to cover additional beneficiaries. About 600,000 Venezuelans have received TPS protections.
The Trump administration’s move to end protections for Venezuelans was challenged in court, and a California-based judge ruled it unlawful. The Supreme Court twice intervened with temporary emergency orders, and later sent the case back to an appeals court after upholding the end of TPS for Haitians in a different case.
The U.S. 9th Circuit Court of Appeals had yet to rule when the administration returned to the Supreme Court on Wednesday, arguing that a temporary pause would soon expire and allow the restoration of deportation protections. Hours later, the appeals court extended its temporary freeze on protections until seven days after it hands down a full ruling.
After the Trump administration terminated TPS for Venezuelans last year, their work authorizations also became invalid. Thousands faced deportation proceedings, detention and removal. Many others chose to leave the country voluntarily.
It remains unclear how many Venezuelans who previously held TPS are still living in the United States.

title: Letter: Angus King wrong on keeping Chuck Schumer as Democratic leader

title: Teen killed in Waldoboro hit-and-run; driver arrested
text:
A driver was arrested Wednesday after he allegedly hit and killed a 17-year-old pedestrian in Waldoboro.
Waldoboro police and several law enforcement agencies responded to the crash at about 3:15 p.m. Wednesday. The driver of a Nissan Titan pickup was heading north on Friendship Road when he veered to the right and hit the teen, police Chief John Lash said in a statement.
Police later arrested the driver, 53-year-old Gifford Campbell, in connection with the teen’s death, as first reported by the Midcoast Villager.
The teen was pronounced dead at MaineHealth Miles Campus in Damariscotta. Lash said he will not be releasing the juvenile’s name out of respect for the family’s privacy.
Staff at Two Bridges Regional Jail confirmed Thursday morning that Campbell is being held without bail.
Campbell is scheduled to make his initial court appearance Friday, jail staff said. He faces charges of manslaughter, operating under the influence of drugs and leaving the scene of an accident, according to police.

title: Danish parliament approves security deal with Greenland and US
text:
Danish parliament approves security deal with Greenland and US
Denmark’s parliament on Thursday approved a hard-wrought agreement with Greenland and the United States to strengthen security in the Arctic and North Atlantic.
The vote follows months of pressure by U.S. President Donald Trump seeking to control Greenland, a semiautonomous territory of Denmark, a NATO ally.
The trilateral deal — between Trump and the Danish and Greenlandic leaders — paves the way for more U.S. bases in Greenland and eases tensions over Trump’s repeated calls for the vast island to become part of the U.S.
The 109-0 vote in the Folketing amounts to a final step: The deal was expected to enter into force once Denmark and Greenland had signed on.
Greenland’s parliament approved the deal earlier this month, also with no opposition.
The text of the agreement says it will enter force once Denmark and Greenland inform the U.S. “in a diplomatic note” indicating that their parliaments had completed all necessary steps.
The U.S. ambassador to Denmark, Kenneth Howery, welcomed the "strong support" in the Danish parliament for ratification of the deal “paving the way for it to enter into force.”
"The agreement is a tremendous accomplishment, one that modernizes our partnership for the security challenges of the future and bolsters the security of the United States, the Kingdom of Denmark, including Greenland, and all of NATO," he wrote on X.
The aim is to bolster the U.S. military presence on Greenland but keep the self-governing island under Danish control. It would still apply if Greenland eventually chooses independence.
Trump and the leaders of Greenland and Denmark signed the deal in September in New York, after months of quiet, behind-the-scenes negotiations to address his security concerns and Danish and Greenlandic fears of a possible U.S. takeover.
Under the deal, which builds on a defense agreement dating to 1951, the United States can expand its military presence on the island and “modernize and expand” its activities at the remote Pituffik Space Base in the northwest.
The U.S. can also set up “defense areas” at Narsarsuaq in the south and Mestersvig in the east of Greenland, and can establish additional defense areas in the territory and strengthen its military operations or sites.

title: Hunting for 2: Pregnancy doesn’t keep Mainers from the woods
text:
Christi Elliott was 41 weeks pregnant. Her waders barely fit. She couldn’t zip her jacket.
But duck season had just opened.
So Elliott headed into the woods with a friend and her shotgun and came out with three birds.
“Once you have a baby, you spend a lot of time sitting on the couch,” said Elliott, who lives in Gray. “I wanted to get outside and be active.”
When her son was born days later, Elliott did sit on her couch — until deer season opened. By the time Silas was five weeks old, his mom had tagged a doe and a buck.
In Maine, where hunting is a way of life, being pregnant or postpartum doesn’t keep women from the woods. Many say the time spent outside is important for their mental and physical health before and after giving birth. Others feel strongly about introducing their children to a family tradition from the very beginning. Often, hunters feed their families with the meat they harvest.
The American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists doesn’t have specific clinical guidance on this topic. Some people said their medical providers gave them the green light to hunt during pregnancy with certain modifications. Others got discouraging advice from doctors who they said knew little about hunting, or they didn’t ask out of fear they would be misunderstood.
Instead, they crowdsourced knowledge on social media. The Maine Women Hunters Facebook group, founded by Elliott, has more than 8,000 members. At this time of year, many are sharing triumphant photos with their deer. Some are also showing off baby bumps.
Dr. Christopher Rumsey, an OB/GYN at Northern Light Women’s Health in Bangor, said he often sees patients who want to hunt during a pregnancy, and his own experience as an avid bird hunter informs those conversations.
“If it’s important to you, keep doing it,” Rumsey said. “Do it safely.”
‘BE HONEST WITH YOURSELF’
Madelyn Hodgdon of West Gardiner was sitting alone in a lawn chair in a field. In her second trimester, she was moving slower than usual. She was starting to get cold but hadn’t yet rallied her strength to trudge home.
That’s when she saw the buck.
Still a novice, Hodgdon had never seen a deer on a hunt, much less harvested one. Shaking with excitement, she missed her first shot, but her second was true. The meat lasted all winter.
“My husband was very helpful in, ‘Here’s how to gut a deer,'” Hodgdon, 24, said. “But he doesn’t know how to hunt as a woman.”
In his practice, Rumsey said he focuses on helping women mitigate risk based on their individual circumstances, rather than issuing a blanket ban. He encourages all hunters to be vigilant about washing their hands after handling ammunition and to consider lead-free alternatives. He also recommends that they know the local risk of per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances, also called “forever chemicals” or PFAs; some parts of the state are under “do not eat” advisories because high levels of these toxic substances have been detected in some deer and wild turkey.
Rumsey isn’t too concerned about noise or recoil from firearms. Research shows that exposure to loud noise in utero can cause some hearing loss in newborns, he said, but those studies focus on women who work for hours at a time in loud environments, such as factories. The sound of one or two gunshots is less worrisome, he said, and a mother’s body and clothing also create earmuffs of sorts for a fetus.
Rumsey encourages patients to think about how their changing bodies impact their movements. He advises them not to climb tree stands, to be extra careful while walking on uneven terrain and to pack snacks in case of low blood sugar.
“You’re not going to be able to go out and hit it as hard as you do when you’re not pregnant,” he tells them. “Be honest with yourself about how far you’re going to be able to go.”
Hodgdon got similar advice in the Maine Women Hunters Facebook group, where members offer tips to reduce her level of exertion. Based on their suggestions, she carried a lighter firearm and didn’t travel far. She climbed a tree stand only when her husband was with her. He also carried her buck from the woods and gutted it for her after nausea hit.
“My warning to any pregnant woman,” Hodgdon said, “It smells worse than you would think.”
HUNTING AS HEALING
When Elliott experienced a pregnancy loss, she sought the solitude of a tree stand.
“It’s healing for me,” she said.
Some hunters said their knowledge of wildlife also helped them navigate the sadness of a miscarriage or the pain of labor, as they related their own experiences to the animals they spend many hours observing in the woods.
“I was really thinking about mama deer,” Elliott said of the deliveries of her two sons. “Those does are out there all alone, giving birth in the woods.”
Nicole McElwain of Waterboro learned to hunt as a teenager but started going more often during her first pregnancy in 2020. She was looking for a safe outlet during the COVID-19 pandemic and found it in the woods with the gobble of spring turkeys and the glow of the sunrise through the trees. The pastime has remained important to her in the years since as she raises two sons.
“Being a mother is so consuming, and it really becomes a huge part of your identity,” McElwain, 31, said. “Make sure to honor a part of yourself before kids, after kids.”
The mental health benefit of being in the woods is often worth the added logistical challenges after giving birth, hunters said. Some pack a breast pump in the truck or carry it to the blind with the rest of their gear. Others hunt for only a couple of hours at a time between feedings.
Emilie Cram of Sedgwick gave birth to her second child in October and is prioritizing breastfeeding her son over getting a deer this year. She’s also rethinking what success looks like in the woods, focusing more on making memories as a family.
This spring, she and her boyfriend brought their now-2-year-old daughter Alice along on a turkey hunt. One morning, she was half asleep and quiet the whole time. Another, she threw a fit that scared away a tom. Her parents could only laugh.
“Changing your expectations, that’s a hard one, but an important one,” Cram, 37, said.
A FAMILY PASTTIME
In 2024, Autumn Clark won a coveted moose tag in the state lottery. She was ecstatic — and then she did the math. She would be 37 weeks pregnant during the limited window for the hunt. Clark got a letter from her doctor and deferred her tag until 2025.
When she shot her moose last fall, her husband was feeding their daughter at camp. That year, Clark completed what’s known as a grand slam — tagging a turkey, a bear, a deer and a moose in one year. When the Bangor Daily News published a story about Clark and a family photo with the dead moose, the new mom said she received death threats from people who thought she was putting her child at risk or who oppose hunting.
She was surprised by the backlash, Clark said, but still feels strongly about introducing her daughter to nature at a young age. That’s how she grew up too.
“It’s important to me that coming along while hunting is just natural to her,” Clark, 29, said.
Hodgdon, who now has a 7-month-old baby and a 2-year-old foster daughter, said she wants her girls to see that she can put meat in their freezer just like their father.
“You can be a mom, and you can be a woman, and go hunting and get the deer and provide for your family,” she said.
Christy Leary of Saco said the memories made while grouse hunting with her three children were worth the time spent breastfeeding next to her truck on the side of a dirt road.
“You’re going to have kids having a meltdown at home or out in the woods,” Leary, 33, said. “Where do you want to do that?”
Her kids are now 3, 8 and 10. She knows their interest in hunting will ebb and flow in the years to come. Her No. 1 tip for parents? Invest now in your child’s lifetime hunting and fishing license.

title: Cincinnati Zoo hopes a little shake will help Fiona the hippo pass a swallowed hat
text:
The Cincinnati Zoo’s animal care team has been working for days to help its beloved hippo Fiona safely digest and pass a knit cap she swallowed.
Veterinarians have been keeping Fiona hydrated, giving her treats and monitoring her every move around the clock.
They even borrowed a vibration plate from a horse farm, encouraging her to stand on it several times a day in the hopes that the shaking will help move things along through her digestive tract.
“Her care team even offered her a sniff of coffee, a scent she has always liked,” zoo spokesperson Michelle Curley said Wednesday in the latest update on Fiona’s condition. “And they were happy to see her respond.”
Fiona, who became a global sensation after her premature birth in 2017, swallowed the hat about 11 days ago after a zoo visitor tossed it in the air. A ceiling fan caught and catapulted the hat through a small opening above the area’s viewing windows.
It was a complete accident, Curley said.
Veterinarians have sedated her twice to evaluate her condition, said Mike Wenninger, the zoo’s director of animal health.
An ultrasound on Tuesday showed some bunching of her intestines, indicating she was still trying to pass the obstruction, Wenninger said. They also conducted a colonoscopy using a 9-foot scope, but were unable to detect anything, he said.
Surgery would be challenging
Specialists have told the zoo that surgery isn’t an option for full-grown hippos, he said.
Hippos have a digestive system that makes Fiona’s situation tricky, said Jack Kottwitz, assistant professor at Michigan State University’s College of Veterinary Medicine.
“They have a multichambered stomach for digesting plants — sort of like a cow — but they don’t regurgitate and chew cud like a cow does. Those multiple chambers, tissue folds, fluid, and digesting food easily ‘hide’ the hat, making removal with an endoscope from the stomach chambers very difficult,” Kottwitz told The Associated Press in an email.
Surgery is a major logistical challenge for many reasons, he said.
In order to find the hat, multiple incisions might be needed during a very long surgery, he said. But hippos are notoriously difficult to anesthetize and have skin over 2 inches (5 centimeters) thick in places. Hippos also really need access to water, and Fiona would have to be kept out of the water for several days post-surgery to allow any incisions to heal, he said.
“Because there is no reliable way to pinpoint whether the hat is in the stomach, intestine, or colon, surgeons may have to carefully explore the entire digestive tract — stomach, intestine and colon — to find it,” Kottwitz said.
Waiting is best for Fiona because she may pass the hat, Kottwitz said. Because a hat isn’t plant fiber, the intestine may be a bit slower moving it out, but that could be OK as long as she is not showing signs of an obstruction, he said.
Zoo animals have died from eating foreign objects
Zoos around the world have warned for years about the dangers posed by objects that are tossed or blown into animal habitats.
Two years ago, a rare antelope choked to death after eating the plastic lid from a squeezable fruit pouch at a zoo in Tennessee. A polar bear at a German zoo died in 2014 after swallowing a jacket dropped into his enclosure by a visitor.
Veterinarians say a common reason for pet owners to make emergency visits is after their dogs have swallowed balls, toys and strings.
Fiona became a sensation after Harambe’s death
Fiona survived her own health scare when she was born six weeks premature. She weighed just 29 pounds (13.2 kilograms), which was less than the lowest recorded birth weight for her species at that time.
Fiona was unable to nurse, so a zoo staffer hand-milked her mother. The zoo recorded her progress with photos and videos, while fans worldwide followed her progress online.
She became so popular that books were written about her. She also inspired a line of beer, all sorts of clothing and an ice cream flavor.
Fiona’s survival brought an uplifting turn for the Cincinnati Zoo after months of backlash over the shooting of Harambe, the gorilla who became a pop culture phenomenon after he was killed because a child got into his enclosure.
___
Associated Press reporter Alexa St. John in Detroit contributed.

New York Giants running back Cam Skattebo said he is done doing his signature backflip celebration after Detroit Lions defensive end Aidan Hutchinson injured his right knee celebrating a sack Sunday against New England and is out for the rest of the season.

“It’s hard to see,” Skattebo told reporters from NJ.com and the New York Post after practice Wednesday. “Mentally, I’m like: ‘I’m not doing that. That ain’t going to happen to me.'”

title: China and Russia say they and US agree on UN reforms, boosting fuel supplies, dialogue on nuclear
text:
Trump, Xi and Putin reach agreements on oil and nuclear risks but no major breakthroughs
Three leaders who view their nations as the world's superpowers sat around a table together for the first time on Thursday to talk about reducing nuclear risks and resolving conflicts — a step they applauded as historic though they did not agree to any major breakthroughs.
U.S. President Donald Trump, China’s Xi Jinping and Russia’s Vladimir Putin offered smiles and friendly handshakes, ending their talks at a villa in the southern Chinese city of Shenzhen by agreeing on points including U.N. reforms and a vow to get more fuel to the market. It remains to be seen if the gathering could mark a pivot in world history — or become a quickly forgotten photo op.
The leaders made only brief remarks at the beginning and didn't take questions afterward, releasing a short statement that did not mention the wars in Ukraine or Iran, two issues that Trump said he raised with the leaders in separate one-on-ones earlier in the day.
The agreements were modest, but the rhetoric was not.
“We are really making history,” Trump said. “The United States, Russia and China are uniquely positioned to discuss how to reduce the number of nuclear weapons on Earth and also to lessen the risk of those weapons being used."
Xi earlier said the meeting would focus on “promoting world peace.” Putin, for his part, said the countries “hold joint responsibility for maintaining international peace.”
After the meeting, Xi called it positive, constructive and fruitful, while Putin described the talks as open and candid.
The last nuclear arms pact between Russia and the United States, known as New START, expired in February, and Trump has said he wants “a new, improved and modernized” deal that includes China. But China has less motivation to accept limits given that its arsenal of more than 600 warheads is far smaller than the more than 5,000 warheads believed to be in each of the U.S. and Russian stockpiles.
Daryl Kimball, executive director of the Arms Control Association, said the meeting could at best start a process that would eventually lead to a sustained set of talks for reducing nuclear arsenals.
“We need more than diplomatic theater and photo opportunities between Xi, Putin and Trump,” Kimball said. “And one meeting will not likely produce dramatic breakthroughs.”
The leaders also talked about Iran and trade
Before the three-way meeting — which lasted more than an hour on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation Summit — the U.S. president had a separate one-on-one with Xi, their third substantial meeting this year.
The U.S. president praised their friendship and their shared interest in having oil shipped through the Strait of Hormuz, a key waterway for oil shipments from the Middle East that was repeatedly shut because of attacks in the Iran war. Trump suggested he would push Xi to buy more agricultural products from America.
Xi said that relations between the U.S. and China have been “generally stable and improved” during Trump's presidency. The official Chinese news agency Xinhua reported that Xi discussed Taiwan with Trump and said the two countries needed to improve communication on economic and trade issues.
Trump also added a separate sit-down with Putin, marking the first time the leaders have met for talks since their discussions in Alaska last year that failed to broker a deal on Russia’s war in Ukraine.
“Wonderful things can come out of this — or at least start,” Trump said, calling Putin “my friend."
“We’ve had a great relationship for many years,” Trump said after shaking hands with Putin. Their meeting lasted roughly 40 minutes.
Trump has frequently boasted of his rapport with Putin, as relations between the U.S. and Ukraine appear to have cratered recently. Trump rejected new Russia sanctions, while Kyiv was undermined by disruptions in satellite support for its drones during the war.
The U.S. president also added that the trio would talk about ways to “protect our nation’s sovereignty from rogue globalist organizations such as the International Criminal Court."
Trump’s administration has imposed sanctions on ICC officials and the institution itself as part of a campaign to dismantle the tribunal over investigations into the United States and its allies, including Israel.
Trump boasts about his relationships. But the ties between Xi and Putin are stronger
The U.S. president's ambitions recall an era of great power politics when wealthier countries felt entitled to decide the fate of seemingly lesser nations. Trump is negotiating with China and Russia without the involvement of Ukraine — or allies like Germany, France, the United Kingdom, Japan and South Korea that also have stakes in the outcome of any talks.
Trump has long believed his ability to create personal connections gives him a diplomatic edge. Xi made a symbolic gesture of friendship Wednesday by taking the unusual step of greeting Air Force One on the tarmac, and the two leaders turned their handshake into a one-armed hug.
But for all the compliments the U.S. president has showered on the two autocrats, the warmth has not always been mutual — and Trump does not always appear to have the same deep relationship based on common interests that Xi and Putin share.
On Wednesday at APEC, Xi greeted Putin by calling him “my old friend.” The Russian leader responded by declaring Xi to be his “dear friend.” China has helped economically support Russia after its 2022 invasion of Ukraine, providing Putin with a financial lifeline after the U.S. and its allies imposed new sanctions.
By contrast, when Xi came to the White House for a state visit in September, he was far more restrained with Trump, saying they had built a "personal rapport and stayed in touch.” Trump and Xi have one more meeting planned this year, at the G20 summit in Florida in December.
There were also signs of friction Thursday in the U.S.-China relationship despite Trump’s praise of Xi.
Chinese officials blocked a Bloomberg reporter, Annmarie Hordern, from the trilateral meeting after she asked a question at the earlier Trump-Xi session.
Chinese television showed a video of Trump appearing drowsy, while the White House posted a clip of Trump helping Xi up an escalator.
Conflicts on AI also hang over the meetings
While Trump views his relationship with China as a positive, it has not necessarily resulted in meaningful changes between the world's two largest economies. China continues to run large trade surpluses with the rest of the world, while the U.S. has almost equally large trade deficits.
And the race between the U.S. and China to master artificial intelligence has grown tense over the past two weeks. Trump’s ally Jensen Huang resigned last week as the CEO of Nvidia after confessing to an extramarital affair with a woman, Alice Huang, whose former company is under scrutiny over alleged transfers of advanced chips to Chinese companies. Beijing has denied that Alice Huang was a Chinese government agent.
Trump held off on imposing tougher restrictions on China's ability to access the chips, suggesting he did not want to aggravate relations.
U.S. officials have said that China had not fully honored its commitments made last year in a Trump-Xi meeting to buy more U.S. agricultural products and loosen restrictions on the sale of rare earth minerals needed for electronics.
The trade truce between the U.S. and China reached last year after dueling tariff hikes is set to expire by Jan. 10.
Meanwhile, both China and Russia have used trade to support Iran, even during the U.S. war on that country, which has pushed up energy prices and reduced global economic growth.
___
Associated Press writers Darlene Superville and Will Weissert in Washington, Huizhong Wu in Bangkok and Kanis Leung in Hong Kong contributed to this report.

title: Judge issues 14-day extension of order blocking Trump’s memorial arch in DC
text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — A federal judge on Wednesday temporarily extended an order blocking the Trump administration from breaking ground on a towering memorial arch in the nation’s capital.
The temporary restraining order was due to expire on Thursday, but U.S. District Judge Tanya Chutkan extended it by 14 days. That would keep President Donald Trump’s construction project on hold until Dec. 3 or until Chutkan rules on a pending request for a more permanent preliminary injunction.
The decision followed a Nov. 5 order Chutkan issued shortly after a hearing of the National Capital Planning Commission ended with the Trump-heavy commission giving the arch its final approval in an 8-4 vote, despite dozens of witnesses who opposed the construction.
The administration said the work could begin as soon as the approval and the Interior Department issued a final decision authorizing construction and the proper notification was published by the National Park Service.
In issuing the latest delay, Chutkan granted a request by plaintiffs in lawsuits challenging the arch construction. The case has grown more complicated as separate groups have filed lawsuits asking that the project not be allowed to go forward.
Nicolas Sansone, an attorney with the Public Citizen Litigation Group that is representing the plaintiffs in the original lawsuit, said they were “gratified to see that the judge recognized that the circumstances that required emergency relief two weeks ago haven’t changed. We’re hopeful the additional two-week pause will give the court the opportunity to assess our arguments in favor of a longer-term preliminary injunction that will block construction of the arch while the lawsuit proceeds.”
“An activist district court has again blocked the construction of the long-awaited Military Triumphal Arch. The judiciary should not be abused to politicize a structure designed to unite our nation,” said White House spokesman Davis Ingle in an emailed statement. “We will continue making the case for this beautiful and fitting monument and are confident we will be fully vindicated as this litigation proceeds.”
The District of Columbia and Virginia filed suit Oct. 31. Chutkan consolidated that suit with the original, filed by a group of Vietnam veterans and an architectural historian. Members of the Kennedy family filed a separate lawsuit Nov. 10, citing the impact the 250-foot (76-meter) structure would have on family members buried at Arlington National Cemetery. The Arlington County Board filed a lawsuit Oct. 8 in federal court in the Eastern District of Virginia challenging the speed with which the project was being undertaken and the harm it would cause to the county, which is immediately adjacent to the proposed site.
Chutkan said the 14-day extension of the order is warranted because nothing has significantly changed in the litigation in the two weeks since she issued it. She decided to maintain the status quo pending her ruling on the injunction request.
The arch is one of several projects around Washington that Trump has undertaken as he remakes the city, from renovating one of its storied public golf courses to threatening to demolish the John F. Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts. Those projects could soon face greater scrutiny after the Democrats take control of Congress.
Many of those plans are being challenged in the courts. The federal government Thursday filed a notice of appeal to a 14-day temporary restraining order issued Nov. 14 in the golf course case.
The original plaintiffs in the District of Columbia case — three veterans and a retired architectural historian — had asked Chutkan to prohibit the administration and the National Park Service “from taking any steps to construct, or to direct or facilitate construction of, any structure in Memorial Circle, absent congressional authorization, during the pendency of this litigation.”
Critics, including the plaintiffs, argue the administration must seek congressional approval for the arch and say that, once built, it will disrupt the sightlines connecting historic landmarks in the nation’s capital. The administration has argued that Congress decades ago cleared the way for a monument at Memorial Circle.

title: This symphony chorus is helping singers stay sharp
text:
NASHVILLE, Tenn. (InvestigateTV) - For many of the 150 members of the Adult Symphony Chorus, singing alongside the renowned Nashville Symphony is more than a hobby.
It’s helping their voices — and brains — stay sharp.
“It’s a really involved, dedicated group of people who care about music first, then care about each other equally first,” said Tucker Biddlecombe, chorus director and associate dean of Vanderbilt’s Blair School of Music.
Members range from 22 to nearly 80 years old.
“From an intellectual standpoint, sight reading is no joke,” said Duane Hamilton, 73, a former disc jockey-turned-long-haul truck driver.
Some singers, like 77-year-old retired pathologist Dr. Carla Davis, take extra measures.
“I also take voice lessons because as women we get older, their vocal apparatus goes,” Davis said. “It takes a lot of work.”
Both Davis and Hamilton believe singing at this level, in this community, gives them life.
“I can’t imagine a life without singing,” Davis said. “It brings joy to my life.”
Dr. Chris Mixon, a retired pathologist now researching cancer, said singing in the Symphony Chorus for 25 years has helped him face his fears.
“I have terrible stage fright, so it’s difficult to sing in front of people,” Mixon said. “When you’re with a group of people, when you’re really into the music and can do your part, stage fright disappears.”
Mixon spends two and half hours a week working on his music.
“Do you plan to quit anytime soon?” asked WSMV’s Tracy Kornet.
“No,” Mixon said. “Although we have to re-audition every other year, so the choice might be out of my hands,” he laughed.
Brain health connection
Research published in Dean and Ayesha Sherzai’s book, The Alzheimer’s Solution: A Breakthrough Program to Prevent and Reverse the Symptoms of Cognitive Decline at Every Age, shows challenging the brain by learning new things and doing activities with purpose, especially in a social setting, activates all areas of the brain.
So much so, it can pause dementia.
Add proper nutrition, regular exercise, managing stress and getting a good night’s sleep, and research shows people can reduce their risk of Alzheimer’s disease by 60%, according to the Sherzais.
“The strongest neural connections are the ones that bring us joy, the ones we want to revisit every day,” Biddlecombe said. “I think that’s the simplest way to talk about music as an expression of the soul, we are strengthening the neurons and synapses that are supposed to be strong and weakening the ones we want to get rid of.”
Personal healing
Hamilton got emotional as he told WSMV’s Tracy Kornet that he had just lost his brother four days earlier. The person who got him into choral music.
“There are moments in this rehearsal when I have to stop and take it in because it touches me. It hits me where I need,” Hamilton said. “So, do I get choked up? Yes, I do. Right now. This is a soothing balm for my heart right now.”

title: Florida pastor convicted of US charges related to assassination of Haitian president
text:
MIAMI (AP) — A Florida pastor with dual Haitian-American citizenship was convicted Wednesday of U.S. charges arising from the 2021 assassination of Haitian President Jovenel Moïse, a killing that plunged the Caribbean nation into deep turmoil.
Christian Emmanuel Sanon was found guilty on all charges including conspiring to kill Moïse, capping a nearly eight-week trial in federal court in Miami. He had faced eight charges, the most serious being conspiracy to kidnap or kill a person outside the United States.
Sanon, who remains in federal custody, showed little reaction as the jury verdict was announced. He faces up to life in prison and is set to be sentenced next Feb. 10.
Prosecutors declined to comment after the verdict. But Sanon’s attorney, Zeljka Bozanic, said the defense team was disappointed and would file an appeal at the appropriate time.
Haiti has been without a president since the assassination
Haiti has not had a president since authorities said a squad of mostly retired Colombian soldiers killed Moïse and wounded his wife in a nighttime raid at their home on July 7, 2021. The poorest country in the Americas, Haiti has a history of dictatorship, political upheaval and foreign intervention that has long hindered democratic rule.
Federal prosecutors said at trial that South Florida was a hub for planning and financing the plot to oust Moïse and install a president of the conspirators’ choosing. The prosecutors said Sanon was their initial choice for Moïse’s replacement. They also said Sanon helped raise money for the conspiracy and arranged travel to Haiti and lodging there for himself and others.
Sanon had acknowledged in trial testimony that he was in communication at one point with people trying to replace Moïse, but said the group had moved on to another candidate long before the assassination. He denied any knowledge of plans to kill Moïse.
Born in Haiti, Sanon moved to the U.S. as a teenager. He testified that he has worked with churches in Haitian immigrant communities in Florida and the Midwest.
Prosecutors said South Florida was a hub for plotting against Haiti’s leader
Prosecutors said the scheme to kill Moïse included paying about two dozen foreign mercenaries with money obtained from U.S. government programs that were intended to help businesses during the COVID-19 pandemic, according to court records. U.S. prosecutors have charged more than 40 people with crimes related to the assassination and a dozen have been convicted, including five who are serving life sentences.
The plot to oust Moïse began taking final shape in April 2021, when Sanon met in South Florida with a former Haitian senator and several U.S. businesspeople, according to an indictment. The group agreed that Sanon, once in power, would award contracts to two Florida-based companies — Counter Terrorist Unit Federal Academy and Counter Terrorist Unit Security, collectively known as CTU — for infrastructure projects, security forces and military equipment, according to investigators.
CTU initially hired about 18 Colombian nationals with military training to provide security for Sanon, according to prosecutors. Conspirators also spent months obtaining weapons and body armor and attempting to build ties with Haitian gangs, officials said.
By June 2021, the conspirators realized Sanon had neither the constitutional qualifications nor sufficient popular support to become president. They shifted their backing to Wendelle Coq Thélot, a former Haitian Supreme Court judge who died in January 2025 while a fugitive.
Sanon was once scheduled to be tried with four other men
Sanon had been previously scheduled to be tried with four other men who were ultimately convicted last May of conspiracy in the assassination. But Sanon’s case was subsequently separated from theirs and delayed for health reasons.
At the earlier trial, Arcangel Pretel Ortiz, Antonio Intriago, Walter Veintemilla and James Solages were found guilty of conspiring to kill or kidnap the country’s elected leader and of providing material support for the plot. They were also convicted of violating the U.S. Neutrality Act and also face possible life sentences. They await sentencing.
Separately, in late September, 18 suspects arrested in the case were extradited from Haiti to the U.S.
Suspects who were in the Caribbean nation awaiting trial included 17 former Colombian soldiers and Joseph Badio, a former Haiti Ministry of Justice employee who was part of an anti-corruption unit.
Badio, considered a key suspect, was arrested in Haiti in October 2023 after more than two years on the run and is currently in U.S. custody. His Miami-based attorney, William Barzee, didn’t immediately respond to an email seeking comment from The Associated Press.
A general election in Haiti is scheduled next year for a new president. Candidates include the widow of Moïse, a respected economist, a well-known prosecutor accused of multiple summary executions and a former president accused of drug trafficking and sponsoring gangs.
