title: Gray town councilor censured for ‘unprofessional’ communications with residents
text:
Former Gray Town Council Chair Michael Johnson resigned Tuesday, a week after his fellow councilors censured him in a 4-0 vote for “unprofessional” communications with residents.
Johnson used expletive-laden insults to criticize residents in email exchanges, which were read out loud at a special town meeting on Nov. 10. He resigned from his seat during a council meeting Tuesday.
Council Chair Vincent Palange said he was “deeply disappointed” and that recent public statements and electronic communications by Johnson have fallen well short of council standards.
Johnson was out of town and not at the Nov. 10 meeting. Palange said he spoke with Johnson the week before the censure vote, and said Johnson told him he didn’t want to attend.
During public comments ahead of the censure vote, Mary Johnson, Michael Johnson’s mother, said her son had devoted countless hours to serving the town, and, while acknowledging that he sometimes gets “too passionate” about his work, criticized the council for holding a special meeting while he was out of town. Mary Johnson claimed the censure vote was a “tool of public shaming” meant to isolate dissenting votes, and criticized the council for not giving a notice in person about the meeting.
Councilor Anne Gass compared Johnson’s comments to the vulgar rhetoric of President Donald Trump, and said that, during her first five years on the council, the council worked to create a positive climate in terms of communications with residents. She said the council previously had a public meeting during which other councilors spoke with Johnson about his behavior, and urged her fellow councilors to consider their own behavior and make sure they are complying with council rules.
Gass also read aloud some of Johnson’s communications, which included referring to a resident as “the biggest piece of (expletive) (he has) ever dealt with.”
Resident Fran Monroe recounted an interaction she had with Johnson in which she asked him to resign on account of his alleged tendency to leave meetings early, and alleged that, in the subsequent email exchange, Johnson sent her emails with “foul and abusive language.”
In a Nov. 3 Facebook post, Johnson acknowledged that he had missed or prematurely left three meetings in recent months, including one that saw a Maine School Administrative District 15 vacancy filled. He claimed Monroe’s comments about him missing meetings were hypocritical, as both of them had missed in-person meetings due to health issues, and acknowledged telling her to “(expletive) off” in a heated exchange regarding his son’s role on the school board.
At the Nov. 17 council meeting, Johnson acknowledged that the language he used was vulgar, but claimed he was pushed to a breaking point after he and his family were repeatedly harassed over his son’s service on the Gray-New Gloucester school board. He also criticized the council’s handling of the matter, particularly when they read excerpts of his communications publicly.
At the meeting, Johnson said he spoke with his attorney, who identified several questions the council needed to answer, and said the censure was “procedurally improper” and should be vacated.
However, in an interview Thursday, Johnson indicated he does not intend to pursue legal action at this time, saying that “stirring the pot does not help anyone.”
Editor’s note: This story was updated on Nov. 20 to include information about Michael Johnson’s resignation.

title: Asian American women feel the impact of Nvidia CEO affair scandal and 'spy' accusations
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
The reveal earlier this month that billionaire Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang had extramarital affairs sent shock waves through the tech world, particularly with Asian Americans who revered him as a once-in-a-generation talent. But what has hit hard for Asian American women is the discourse around the allegation that Alice Huang, a Chinese businesswoman at the center of the scandal, was possibly a spy.
Almost immediately, videos and memes reviving tired tropes fetishizing Asian women hit social media.
“So few Asian women in general make it to the news for positive things. This is just going to continue to perpetuate negative stereotypes or biases for Asian women,” said Misa Chien, founder of a network for Asian American women leaders called The Authentic Asian. Whether or not the allegation is true, “just the news will definitely influence people’s opinions of women who have broken the ceiling or are trying to.”
Asian American women working in tech, civil rights advocacy and academia have felt a sense of dread that this ordeal will diminish how their peers are viewed and treated in their workplaces. It’s a reminder that no accomplishments will completely dispel centuries-old stereotypes.
Jensen Huang has since resigned. However, the U.S. Justice Department has not found sufficient evidence that Alice Huang, who is not related to Jensen Huang, was a spy.
“I don’t know if that’s been determined yet,” President Donald Trump told reporters this week.
Asian women struggle to be taken seriously as leaders
Among the social media posts being spread was a collage of photos showing CEOs with Asian female partners. Author May-lee Chai, who has written about the treatment of Asian women throughout history, called it “disgusting.”
Depicting them like trophy wives “implicates these spouses like they’re somehow similar to this suspected spy,” said Chai, a creative writing professor at San Francisco State University.
The speed at which people glommed onto the Asian female spy narrative was shocking to April Moh, chief marketing officer for a financial technology company and board member of Stand with Asian Americans, a legal civil rights organization specializing in combating workplace anti-Asian discrimination. The chatter has also led to women sharing stories of uncomfortable interactions.
“I have women in technology who tell me that they get really weird looks and they get questioned about laptop security by their colleagues when they’re visiting China,” Moh said. “I have another person telling me that she has been jokingly asked, ‘So, are you a spy?’ by people who think that’s a joke now. It’s not funny to her or me.”
Many clients of Stand with Asian Americans are Asian women who have proved their competence yet are still accused of being fraudulent or deceitful, said Rachel Lee, the organization’s president and general counsel.
“It is deeply disturbing to see this not just unique to the Nvidia Jensen Huang case, but as a part of a long-standing dangerous narrative that Asians are perpetual foreigners, untrustworthy, disloyal,” Lee said.
On top of their integrity being questioned, Asian workers also deal with misconceptions that they cannot lead. The annual Social Tracking of Asian Americans in the United States Index from The Asian American Foundation found at least half of U.S. adults characterized Asian Americans in the workplace as “respectful” or “reliable.” Only 1 in 10 viewed them as “assertive.”
“The No. 1 theme in onboarding interviews all last week were ‘I’m mistaken for the secretary, I don’t look like the typical face of leadership,” said Chien, talking about new members of her Asian leaders network.
Stereotypes around Asian women go back centuries
Years before Chinese laborers were fully banned from entering the U.S. under the 1882 Chinese Exclusion Act, the federal government targeted immigrant Asian women. In 1875, Congress passed the Page Act to control immigration from “any Oriental country.” It included a specific prohibition of women coming for prostitution.
“Chinese women were deemed — and East Asian women in general — as being untrustworthy,” Chai said. “It was presumed that they would be coming for illicit means as prostitutes to the United States and that would cause harm to white men.”
By the early 20th century, the Asian woman as a seductress, spy or “dragon lady” started becoming an archetype on Hollywood screens, she added.
The headlines had Chien reflecting on when she played a spy in a building security ad in Hong Kong 20 years ago. She was instructed to wear three bras to resemble Angelina Jolie’s figure. She wrote an Instagram post to point out “how the media enjoys putting Asian women in that kind of role” and urged women to not let people’s assumptions keep them from success.
“So many followers messaged me saying ‘thank you so much for speaking up,’” Chien said.
Real harm can come from stereotypes
Suspicion toward Chinese people in the U.S. has dramatically heightened geopolitical tensions. Over two dozen states in the last few years have proposed or enacted “alien land laws” to prevent Chinese nationals from buying property. The number of international students enrolling in American universities has fallen. And the first Trump administration created a plan known as the ” China Initiative ” to crack down on espionage by profiling Chinese professors.
Critics say that initiative contributed to the 2024 suicide of Jane Ying Wu. A neuroscientist at Northwestern University who had lived in the U.S. for 40 years, the 60-year-old came under federal investigation in 2019. She was never charged with anything.
“This type of pernicious stereotype can actually destroy lives,” Chai said. “It’s not in any way an accurate portrait of an entire race and ethnicity.”
Jokes rooted in stereotypes under the guise of being complimentary also do not help Asian female workers, Lee added.
“Whether it’s a compliment or not, a trope is a trope,” she said. “I don’t care if it comes out of the mouth of the U.S. president.”
Ideally, Lee said more companies should allow for education and training around the harm and history of stereotypes. She encourages any woman who has had uncomfortable interactions to reach out to advocacy groups such as Stand with Asian Americans if she has nobody to turn to at work. At Stand with Asian Americans, people do not need to have a legal case of discrimination or harassment to receive assistance including education on their rights and mental health support.
Individuals also have the right to draw boundaries and make clear what’s not OK to say, Lee added. It’s in employers’ best interest to make sure no federal laws against discrimination and harassment are being violated.
“It’s a win-win to have that conversation,” Lee said.

title: Jury finds man guilty of murder in 2024 Bayside shooting
text:
PORTLAND — A jury has found a man guilty of murder in the shooting of another man in the Bayside neighborhood two years ago.
Omar Abdelkader, 23, had testified that he shot Edgar Cando in self defense during a fight. A prosecutor said he fired the shots as Cando was walking away, citing surveillance videos that the jury watched multiple times throughout the trial.
The jury reached its verdict after two hours of deliberation. Abdelkader will be sentenced at a later date.
Abdelkader and Cando, who was 31, had engaged in three fistfights on Oct. 28, 2024, before the shooting. Their interactions were recorded by cameras from nearby businesses, and the videos have been replayed multiple times for the jury — slowed down, zoomed in, frame-by-frame and rewound. That includes the pair’s last fight, with video showing there were a handful of other people nearby at the time.
Video shows Cando swept Abdelkader off his feet in their last fight, then hit Abdelkader in the face and started to walk away.
“It was after that altercation, after he is on the ground and Edgar is walking away from that fight — that is the moment that matters,” Assistant Attorney General Kate Bozeman said during closing arguments Thursday. “That is where the duty to retreat applies.”
Footage shows the moment Abdelkader stood up, broke free from a friend’s grip and started running to where Cando was standing. A prosecutor said during the trial that, at that point, Cando was more than 40 feet from Abdelkader.
Abdelkader shot Cando three times.
To acquit Abdelkader for self defense, the jury had to consider whether he reasonably believed Cando was about to use deadly force against him, and whether Abdelkader believed using his gun was necessary. The jury would also have had to agree that Abdelkader didn’t provoke the deadly force, and that he didn’t believe he could retreat safely.
Bozeman argued before the verdict that Abdelkader had “ample opportunities to get away safely” from the fights.
Cando and Abdelkader began fighting that afternoon, Bozeman said during closing arguments, likely because Cando was standing up for a friend who got into a physical fight with Abdelkader over a bicycle. Three fistfights ensued, video shows. In the first, Cando hit Abdelkader in the chin. In the second, Abdelkader’s friend hit Cando in the back of the head.
Defense attorney Tina Nadeau argued that, despite the video evidence, her client’s case was not so straightforward. She said the cameras couldn’t capture what Abdelkader felt during the last fight.
After Cando knocked him down, Nadeau said, her client’s nose was displaced, and he was losing so much blood that he thought he had been stabbed. Because of his difficulty breathing, she said, Abdelkader believed he was having a seizure that would have made it impossible to defend himself if Cando struck again.
Abdelkader testified previously that when he got up from being knocked down, he believed Cando was still standing over him. Video shows Cando was already walking away.
“When we are in a crisis, we’re not experiencing distance and time the same way we do here,” Nadeau said. “Forty-four feet is nothing when someone is motivated, as he believed Edgar was, to finish the job.”
Jurors rewatched footage of the third fight, and the shooting, before they were given the case. Bozeman brought the courtroom’s TV screen close to the jury box, and replayed the clip from start to finish, pointing out the moment Abdelkader fell, got up, and ran for what she said was 12 seconds to reach and shoot Cando.
“He’s thinking that he just got embarrassed, he just got disrespected,” Bozeman said of Abdelkader. “This is nothing but intentional and knowing murder.”

title: Ravens to bench star player for making disparaging comments about Baltimore
text:
Ravens to deactivate CB Humphrey for Carolina game after 'criminals' comment about Baltimore
The Ravens are deactivating cornerback Marlon Humphrey for this weekend's game at Carolina after the veteran said on a podcast that "criminals" are among the things Baltimore is best at making.
Coach Jesse Minter announced the move Thursday and said Humphrey was sent home and would not practice.
"I would say this: He's very remorseful. I think he really understands that words mean a lot, especially to people in this city," Minter said. "When you say something like that, it's not a reflection of our team and our organization and how we want to operate."
Humphrey apologized for the comments Wednesday, and Baltimore mayor Brandon Scott said a verbal apology was "not enough."
"They're best at making criminals," Humphrey said on the podcast. "Yeah no, that's obviously going to get cut out."
Minter said Wednesday he loved the city. A day later, he made the announcement that Humphrey was being removed for the rest of the week. He said it would be a one-game deactivation.
"Having to be a leader when the team needs you the most is my job. This is a team thing in my opinion," Minter said. "He's going to deal with a lot of stuff from this. This is about the team and putting us in the best position to be successful — going down there for one reason, to play well and win the football game."

title: Cincinnati Zoo says Fiona the hippo has died, days after ingesting a visitor’s hat
text:
CINCINNATI (AP) — Fiona, the hippo whose premature birth and fight for survival at the Cincinnati Zoo turned her into a global sensation nearly a decade ago, died Thursday from complications after swallowing a knit hat that was accidentally flung into her enclosure. She was 9 years old.
“It is with extreme sadness that we share with you the devastating news that Fiona did not make it after multiple attempts from our amazing vets and keeper team to help her through what ended up being a medical emergency,” the zoo said in a statement.
EN ESPAÑOL | Muere Fiona la hipopótamo tras ingerir un gorro en Zoológico de Cincinnati
The zoo said Monday that it was providing Fiona with round-the-clock care after she swallowed the hat more than a week ago. Specialists had advised that surgery wasn’t an option for a full-grown hippo like Fiona.
Before she died, veterinarians had been keeping Fiona hydrated, giving her treats and monitoring her every move, the zoo said. They borrowed a vibration plate from a horse farm, encouraging her to stand on it several times a day in the hopes that the shaking would help move the hat through her digestive tract.
“Despite multiple attempts to move the hat out of her system, it was ultimately too much to overcome,” the zoo said.
Within an hour of the announcement, visitors began leaving flowers and cards by a hippo statue outside the zoo. “Forever our Fiona,” one note read.
Fans mourn Fiona
Fiona captivated people worldwide after her premature birth in 2017. Her presence was felt all around the zoo, which was scheduled to stay open late Thursday for the first night of its Festival of Lights.
Amy Haacke, a special educator from Dayton, said outside the Cincinnati Zoo that she’s been a “huge fan” of Fiona since she was born because she likes underdogs. Haacke said she uses the Fiona book series in her classroom and owns three Fiona shirts.
“We were coming here anyway, but it kind of means a lot to be here,” Haacke said Thursday. “We were here when she was first born and, I guess, now we’re here when she’s gone.”
Yolanda Gould, who works more than 80 miles (130 kilometers) away in Covington, said she and others in her office left early to travel to the zoo after learning about Fiona’s death. She said outside the zoo that she was feeling “a little devastated” after following Fiona since she was born.
Cincinnati Mayor Aftab Pureval said on social media that Fiona was “a symbol of perseverance and joy” in the city. Ohio Gov. Mike DeWine called her “a true icon.” The Cincinnati Bengals also expressed condolences, dubbing Fiona “the queen of the Queen City.”
In a joint post with U.S. Vice President JD Vance on Instagram, second lady Usha Vance shared a photo of one of their children face-to-face with Fiona through a glass wall of her enclosure. The family has a home in Cincinnati.
“We are so sad to hear the news about Fiona,” she said in the caption. “Our family loved visiting her at the Cincinnati Zoo.”
Fiona was under close care
Fiona swallowed the hat about 11 days ago after a zoo visitor tossed it in the air. A ceiling fan caught and deflected the hat into the hippo enclosure through a small opening above the area’s viewing windows.
It was an accident, zoo spokesperson Michelle Curley said.
Before Fiona died, Mike Wenninger, the zoo’s director of animal health, said veterinarians had sedated her twice to evaluate her condition.
An ultrasound on Tuesday showed some bunching of her intestines, Wenninger said. They also conducted a colonoscopy using a 9-foot (2.7-meter) scope but were unable to detect anything, he said.
The Association of Zoos and Aquariums, the accrediting body for facilities, said in a statement Thursday that the Cincinnati Zoo provided “extraordinary 24/7 care for Fiona throughout this heartbreaking event.”
Surgery would have been challenging
Surgery would have been a major logistical challenge — multiple incisions would have been needed during a very long surgery, as hippos are notoriously difficult to anesthetize and have thick skin, said Jack Kottwitz, assistant professor at Michigan State University’s College of Veterinary Medicine.
The hat and its blend of fibers posed a particular danger despite its relatively small size.
Experts said hippos have a multichambered stomach for digesting plants, and the system makes for a very large gastrointestinal tract through which anything would have to travel.
Jan Hawkins, doctor of veterinary medicine at North Carolina State University, said Fiona’s situation was difficult because it would have been hard to tell where in her body the hat was.
“You can’t do the normal imaging and things that you can do in some of the smaller animals, or even horses,” Hawkins said.
Zoos around the world have warned for years about the dangers posed by objects that are tossed or blown into animal habitats. Two years ago, a rare antelope choked to death after eating the plastic lid from a squeezable fruit pouch at a zoo in Tennessee. A polar bear at a German zoo died in 2014 after swallowing a jacket dropped into his enclosure by a visitor.
Fiona became a sensation after Harambe’s death
Fiona survived her first health scare when she was born six weeks premature. She weighed just 29 pounds (13.2 kilograms), which was less than the lowest recorded birth weight for her species at that time.
She was unable to nurse, so a zoo staffer hand-milked her mother. The zoo recorded her progress with photos and videos, while fans worldwide followed her progress online.
Her story marked an uplifting turn for the Cincinnati Zoo after months of backlash over the shooting of Harambe, the gorilla who became a pop culture phenomenon after he was killed because a child got into his enclosure.
The zoo’s hippo family expanded in 2022 with the birth of Fiona’s baby brother, Fritz.
Fiona’s father, Henry, was euthanized months after her birth as his health badly declined. He had lived 36 years, slightly beyond the average life expectancy for a Nile hippopotamus in captivity.

title: Visa, Mastercard, and JPMorgan Chase customer data reportedly compromised in cyberattack
text:
Visa, Mastercard, and JPMorgan Chase customer data reportedly compromised in cyberattack
Data from thousands of Visa, Mastercard and JP Morgan Chase customers was leaked Thursday by a ransomware group, according to several reports.
It’s the latest in a string of tech incidents that have unnerved customers across the U.S. over the past two weeks.
Related video above | Trump admin takes questions on recent tech outages
Though the scope and source of the information remain unclear, The Wall Street Journal reports that thousands of customers’ data was involved. The incident has not disrupted payment services and is not linked to banking problems from earlier this week.
JPMorgan Chase said Thursday that attackers targeted third-party service providers and may have accessed marketing data, including some customer names and email addresses.
The bank said the incident was not connected to service disruptions customers experienced earlier in the week. JPMorgan Chase did not disclose when the cyberattack occurred or name the third-party providers that were targeted.
“Where appropriate, we will contact affected customers directly and offer support, including complimentary credit monitoring,” a JPMorgan Chase statement said.
Visa also confirmed a security incident involving a third-party provider in the Asia-Pacific region. Its own systems were not affected, and there was no indication that payment data, including card numbers, had been compromised, The Wall Street Journal reported Thursday.
A Mastercard spokesperson said hackers accessed a limited amount of information belonging to some cardholders enrolled in a particular benefits program.
The spokesperson said Mastercard contained the exposure and that its payment network and customers’ ability to use their cards were unaffected.
The news comes after several days of technology outages across the U.S. disrupted air travel, email and hotel bookings, and compromised classified internal communications at the National Security Agency.

title: Blind reader says Elin Hilderbrand’s novels helped her heal
text:
Nantucket novelist Elin Hilderbrand meets fan who says books became her lifeline
Elin Hilderbrand met a blind fan in Boston who says the author’s novels helped her cope after a violent attack.
Nantucket novelist Elin Hilderbrand meets fan who says books became her lifeline
Elin Hilderbrand met a blind fan in Boston who says the author’s novels helped her cope after a violent attack.
Elin Hilderbrand, a best-selling author known for her Nantucket-based novels, recently met Janet Houle Blanchard, a fan whose life was profoundly impacted by Hilderbrand's books, at her Boston apartment.  
Hilderbrand has written books including "28 Summers," "The Five-Star Weekend," "The Perfect Couple" and "The Hotel Nantucket."
Blanchard, who was left blind after a brutal attack five years ago, shared how Hilderbrand’s novels became a source of solace and escape.
"Before the incident, I never read a book," Blanchard said. "I've read them all."
The author spoke with Hearst sister station WCVB and reflected on the impact her work has had on readers.
"People tell me, you know, I'm never probably going to win the Pulitzer Prize. And I'm probably not going to win the Booker or the National Book Award. But what I've been able to do with my books is — I've allowed people who are overcoming challenges to escape," she said.
Blanchard recounted the traumatic events that changed her life. She and her daughter were walking their dog when a car struck them in Haverhill.
"Just as I looked at my daughter to tell her something, I could see out of the corner of my eye a car, a car coming right at us," she said. "He hit me."
Her daughter ran for help as the attacker assaulted Blanchard on the ground.
"They told me he had a box cutter. I don't remember. The first thing he does is stab my eyes," she said.
Despite the trauma, Blanchard found comfort in listening to Hilderbrand’s novels.
"It means so much to me that they — you know — these works mean something to you and that they give you some comfort," Hilderbrand told her.
Blanchard described the books as a lifeline. "I try to go to bed. I'm like, I'm going to read a little more," she said.
Hilderbrand expressed her gratitude for the connection. "I'm so, so humbled. Really humbled and honored," she said.
Blanchard hopes advancements in technology will one day restore her vision. On her bucket list is a trip to Nantucket to visit the places she has come to know through Hilderbrand’s novels.
Editor's Note: Janet Houle Blanchard is a childhood friend of WCVB anchor Maria Stephanos, who reported this story.

title: Inside the all-civilian 'Traitors': 80,000 applicants and a hands-off castle
text:
Inside the all-civilian 'Traitors': 80,000 applicants and a hands-off castle
'The Traitors: New Blood' has been renewed for a second season
Inside the all-civilian 'Traitors': 80,000 applicants and a hands-off castle
'The Traitors: New Blood' has been renewed for a second season
NBC is sending more civilians to the Scottish castle: "The Traitors: New Blood" has been renewed for a second season, set to air in 2027, with Alan Cumming back as host.
The show has been a hit, with the two-episode premiere averaging 6 million viewers across NBC and Peacock over three days, including repeats, according to NBCUniversal, which called it NBC's top new unscripted premiere in six years among adults 18-49. NBC announced the renewal ahead of Thursday's season one finale.
Related video above: Pattinson as Bond image released
"The Traitors" is set in a castle in Scotland where a few secret Traitors "murder" the other players, called Faithfuls, one by one, while the Faithfuls vote to banish suspected Traitors. Players also compete in various challenges to increase the ultimate cash prize. Heading into the finale, marketing manager Katie Fites and ironworker Shane Beatty were the two remaining Traitors against six Faithfuls, including teacher Clyde Moser and nurse Abbey Benjamin.
The celebrity version has won the Emmy for outstanding reality competition program two years running, upending a category long dominated by "The Amazing Race" and "RuPaul's Drag Race." It also generates a steady stream of memes and social chatter.
"New Blood" airs on NBC, unlike the celebrity version, which streams on Peacock. Producers made slight adjustments for a family-friendly 8 p.m. slot. Players arrived by steam engine, which executive producer Sam Rees-Jones said "has feelings of joining the Hogwarts Express." The language stayed clean, with no cursing. The aim, he said, was "that family feel" and a "multi-generational viewing experience."
A bet on civilians
It's "the same game," Rees-Jones said, "but different people, different dynamics, no preconceived notions. Everyone's starting on a level playing field."
Picking the right contestants was important, he added, and there were more than 80,000 applicants. Selections included Arisa Thomas, a dog groomer from Los Angeles; attorney Michael Foote from New York; and Abby Lee, an astrophysicist from Minnesota.
"We wanted to pull from different walks of life, from different places, with different ages. We wanted the viewers to be able to maybe see a bit of themselves in some of the cast, that felt important," Rees-Jones said.
The success of "The Traitors" helped cast a wide net. Most contestants knew what to expect. Joe Vanella, a funeral director from New York, described pulling up to the castle as Cumming made his entrance.
"Imagine somebody picking you up and dropping you into your favorite show," he said. "It's an indescribable feeling."
A hands-off approach
Rees-Jones said the players had no trouble adjusting to the cameras, in part because production works hard to make them forget they're being filmed. Roundtable discussions have hidden cameras, and no producers are in the room.
"I say it to all the cast before they join: 'If no one starts talking at the roundtable, that's on you,'" he said. "There's times when there are long silences, and we just sit back and wait for someone to talk."
Producers don't instruct players on what to talk about, he said.
"It's a game first for these players and the TV show second," he said, adding that the producers "basically hand over the castle to them."
Before filming begins, Rees-Jones said, production decides the order of missions, when the twists will happen and who Cumming will tap to be Traitors in the first episode. Once cameras roll, he said, the plan doesn't change. That held even early in this season, when the Faithfuls went a stretch without banishing a Traitor.
Some moments surprised even him in the control room, such as a player using a pardon to save another from banishment and Vanella's choice to reveal to a fellow contestant he was a Traitor before her "murder."
"It's the most stressful show to make because you don't have control," said Rees-Jones.
Higher stakes, harder choices
Vanella and Tomica Adams, a pilot from Boston, are both banished Traitors. They said money made the game feel different for civilians.
"A lot of the celebrities, whether they win $250,000 or not, they're going home to the same life," Vanella said. "Whoever gets it this time, it's going to change things."
"That weighed on the turret," where the Traitors go to plot their next moves, said Vanella. He said it was harder to eliminate people, knowing their stories.
Adams said lying is hard for anyone with a conscience.
"If you're a liar, you're a liar," she said. Her approach was to stay in character: "You got to be faithfully a Traitor as long as possible."
She also found the long filming days draining.
"You're embedded in treachery," she said.
What's next for 'The Traitors'
Season 5 of the original, celebrity-laden "The Traitors" premieres Jan. 14 on Peacock. Rees-Jones said it's in post-production and has an "eclectic" cast that includes actor Kristin Chenoweth, two-time Olympic gold medalist Chloe Kim, and former star of ABC's "The Bachelor" Joey Graziadei.

title: ‘Pure anger’: Therapist fired over video that appears to show her hit 7-year-old with autism
text:
ATLANTA (ANF/Gray News) - An Atlanta therapist who works with children on the autism spectrum has been fired after doorbell camera video appears to show her hitting a 7-year-old client.
Lakita Walker and Rameriz Pass say the incident was caught on their neighbor’s Ring camera Tuesday. The video allegedly shows their 7-year-old son’s therapist yanking then hitting him.
“I was distraught. I was heartbroken because I see this all the time, and I couldn’t believe it happened to me,” Walker said.
“It’s like pure anger,” Pass said. “But after that happened, it’s like a kick in the face almost. It hurts.”
Walker and Pass say their son has autism and is nonverbal. He has received in-home applied behavior analysis (ABA) therapy from a licensed therapist with Centria Autism Life Skills Autism Academy since he was 3 years old. The therapy consists of life skills, playing, behavioral management and academics.
The parents say this therapist had only been with him for a month.
“It’s your worst nightmare when you have a nonverbal child dealing with autism. It’s like the last thing you want is someone to mistreat him,” Pass said.
“People think you could trust someone because you hear that they’re trained... That doesn’t mean you can trust them,” Walker said.
The incident happened during the victim’s outside playtime. His parents say he and the therapist were walking around their building when their son ran toward the neighbors’ Ring camera.
“She was too comfortable with what she did in broad daylight in front of my neighbor’s house,” Walker said. “If he looks like he’s been slanged around like a rag doll to me, she’s definitely an adult. She’s more than twice the size. He’s not even 70 pounds.”
Walker says she called police immediately, and they came and took a report. Atlanta police confirmed they are investigating.
“I do feel like she should have been arrested on scene because she struck him twice,” Walker said.
The mother says she then called the therapist’s supervisor with Centria Autism.
“She was shocked. She apologized. She called her boss. They just called and apologized. It was nothing else really said about it,” Walker said.
A spokesperson with Centria Autism provided the following statement to Atlanta News First:
“The individual is no longer employed by Centria, and we remain committed to supporting the child and family affected by this incident. The actions of this individual are unacceptable and do not reflect the values, standards, or expectations of Centria Autism. The safety and well-being of the children and families we serve has always been, and will continue to be, our highest priority.”
The victim’s parents say the therapist being fired is a step in the right direction. The incident has left the whole family traumatized.
“I’m overprotective. Overly protective, and I feel like I let my guard down. It’s already hard for me to trust, and I trusted the company... I trusted what they told me, and they failed. They failed us tremendously,” Walker said.
“The trust is just broken. And when the trust is broken, and my son can’t tell me when he’s being mistreated. So, it’s like, ‘How could I trust anyone right now?’” Pass said.
The parents say they will be talking with their son’s school to get him extra help there. A family member who is a board-certified behavioral analyst has also offered to step in and help.

title: BRHS French students connect with peers and film at International Francophone Film Festival
text:
In October, Boothbay Region High School (BRHS) students in the upper-level French language class and the French Speaking Cultures class attended the International Francophone Film Festival at the Portland Museum of Art (PMA). The festival was organized by the Alliance Française du Maine (AFDUME) and brought BRHS students together with French language students from six other schools in the region.
Before the festival began, students viewed the Winslow Homer exhibit on temporary display at the museum and explored art and artifacts from Maine’s indigenous and historically French-speaking regions. They then attended a pre-screening talk by AFDUME Executive Director Lisa Scali.
The centerpiece of the day was a special screening of the award-winning French film “La Venue de l’Avenir” (2025). Filmed in Normandy and Paris, the film tells a visually stunning story of how discovering family relationships can connect the past and the future.
“Hearing French spoken by filmmakers, museum guides, and students from other schools showed my students that the language is alive well beyond our classroom,” said Kristen Anthony, French teacher at BRHS. “They left more confident and more curious.”
The trip was made possible by a grant from Education Boothbay.
“Education Boothbay is proud to support experiences like this one, where students learn in the world and not just in a classroom,” said Bruce Harris, Education Boothbay Board Chair. “A day at the Portland Museum of Art with peers from across the region is exactly the kind of enrichment our community wants for its students.”
BRHS plans to attend the festival again next year.
Education Boothbay supports enrichment opportunities for students in the Boothbay Region schools through grants and community partnerships. Its first-ever campaign, Our Children, Our Community, is raising $1.2 million from 2026 to 2028 to support place-based learning, STEAM, and teacher innovation and student enrichment. To learn more, visit www.educationboothbay.org.

title: Niece escapes after car drives into river, leaving aunt and 13-year-old cousin dead
text:
ANCHORAGE, Alaska (KTUU/Gray News) - The bodies of a mother and daughter were pulled from a vehicle found in the Thorne River this week.
According to Alaska State Troopers, the mother and daughter went missing last week after the car they were in went off the roadway and crashed into the river.
Alaskan authorities said the river’s depth and strong current initially made it unsafe to attempt recovery efforts following the crash, but crews were able to continue rescue efforts this Wednesday when they pulled the vehicle from the water.
The mother was identified as 34-year-old Kelly Jenkins, along with her daughter, 13-year-old Kayleigh Favor.
A third passenger, Jenkins’ niece, was also in the car at the time of the crash and was able to escape to safety.
The area where the car entered the water was said to be at least 20 feet deep with a fast-moving current.
Alaska troopers thanked the multiple agencies and community members who helped them in the rescue efforts.

title: Russian nuclear-capable bombers leave Vietnam as Putin meets world leaders in China
text:
Russian nuclear-capable bombers leave Vietnam as Putin meets world leaders in China
Two Russian nuclear-capable strategic bombers left Vietnam on Thursday morning, in an apparent display of Moscow’s military reach across Asia even as Russian President Vladimir Putin met world leaders in China.
The two Tu-95 nuclear-capable strategic bombers, along with two support aircraft, were at an airport in the central Vietnamese city of Da Nang on Wednesday.
The meeting with U.S. President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping gave Putin a chance to portray Russia as one of the preeminent global powers. The bombers flew to Vietnam shortly before the summit. As Putin arrived in China, Russian television cameras focused on an officer accompanying him who carried a briefcase used to authorize the use of nuclear weapons.
Related video: What happened during the historic trilateral summit between Trump, Xi , and Putin?
After the bombers left Vietnam, Taiwan’s Defense Ministry said Thursday afternoon that it tracked two Russian Tu-95 military aircraft flying past the island’s eastern coast after approaching from the south.
The bombers also alarmed U.S. allies Japan and South Korea when they flew from Russia to Vietnam earlier in the week.
Japan protested to Moscow on Tuesday after the two Russian aircraft entered Japan’s airspace. Defense Minister Shinjiro Koizumi told reporters that the aircraft violated Japanese airspace for about five minutes early Tuesday near Fukuoka, long enough for Japan to scramble fighter jets and send warnings.
“The violation of the Japanese airspace by the Russian aircraft is not only a serious violation of our country’s sovereignty, but also a threat to our safety,” Koizumi said.
South Korea’s military said several Russian military aircraft temporarily entered its air defense identification zone over waters between the Korean Peninsula and Japan on Monday, though they did not violate South Korean airspace.
“Moscow’s message to Asia is that Russia remains a global great power that can project military force into every region of the world. Putin’s chest thumping is meant to assert Russia’s parity with the US and China" ahead of his meeting with Trump and Xi, said Ian Storey, principal fellow at Singapore’s ISEAS – Yusof Ishak Institute.
The move is also “Hanoi’s none-too-subtle reminder to Beijing that two months after China opened an air base in neighbouring Laos, Vietnam still has close strategic ties with Russia,” Storey said.
The last known use of a Vietnamese airport by Russian military aircraft was in 2014, when Russian refueling planes landed at Cam Ranh to support long-range bombers flying over the South China Sea, according to Vietnam’s state-controlled media.
Vietnam and Russia have had diplomatic relations since 1950. Evidence of the long-running relationship and its influence can be seen in Vietnamese cities like the capital, Hanoi, where Soviet-style apartment blocks are commonplace, although now dwarfed by skyscrapers.
A statue of Vladimir Lenin, the founder of the Soviet Union, stands in a park where kids skateboard every evening. Many in the Communist Party’s top leadership in Vietnam studied in Soviet universities.
Since the early 2000s, Russia has accounted for the bulk of Vietnam’s arms imports. This has been declining over the years due to Vietnamese attempts to diversify its supplies.

title: Children at Framework Church pack 54 shoeboxes for Operation Christmas Child
text:
PRESQUE ISLE, Maine (WAGM) - Children at Framework Church packed 54 shoeboxes for Operation Christmas Child during the church’s first packing party, said Kaleb Sperrey, the church’s children’s ministry director.
Five families attended the event. The goal was to fill 50 boxes. The group packed 54 in less than an hour.
Children choose toys for children overseas
Tables of toys filled the room as children picked out items for other children they don’t know. The children who will receive the boxes live overseas.
“All the kids had a great time picking out what they would want to put in the shoebox for a kid they may not even meet or even know,” Sperrey said.
Madison Davis, 10, was one of the children filling boxes. She showed a reporter what was inside the shoebox she filled, everything from art supplies and a stuffed animal to a hairbrush. That box will be sent to another girl in the same age group as Davis.
Box total reaches 73
The 54 boxes packed at the event are in addition to boxes the church had already collected.
“54 is on top of what we’ve already collected, so for a total of 73 so far,” Sperrey said. “The majority of the boxes came from the packing party.”
Children write notes for each box
Most of the event was spent writing notes to go into each gift box.
“Many of them said Jesus loves you and that Jesus has a purpose for you and that they would like to meet them one day,” Sperrey said.
Plans for next year and drop-off deadline
Sperrey said he plans to hold the packing party again next year.
“And so hopefully next year will be bigger and better,” he said.
The boxes will be sent Monday. Each box will go to a child and contain toys and a note from a child who wrote it.
People can drop off a box at a participating church until 2 p.m. Monday. More information on how to get involved is available at samaritanspurse.org.

title: A cyberattack using artificial intelligence targeted the EU in October, official says
text:
A cyberattack using artificial intelligence targeted the EU in October, official says
A cyberattack using software powered by artificial intelligence targeted the European Union in October, an official in Brussels said on Thursday, with some of the bloc's digital tools still remaining offline.
The official did not elaborate on the cyberattack, or say who could have been behind it. It was the first time the 27-member bloc reported a cyberattack using an AI tool.
Related video: "The safeguards did not work": Four major AI chatbots helped plan terror attacks in hours
“AI-assisted tools can be used and especially misused to detect vulnerabilities," said Thomas Regnier, spokesperson for the European Commission, the executive body of the EU.
"Indeed we can confirm that this was done with AI tools," he added. "We have seen many global cyber attacks recently, and of course no one is immune to this.”
Regnier said the EU first detected the incident on Oct. 22 and that authorities launched an investigation while also imposing “preventative measures."
“We temporarily took down several applications, and most of them have since then been restored," he said.
The investigation is ongoing and so far "we have not detected any evidence of a data breach affecting commission staff as a whole,” he said.

title: Maine Public Advocate seeks records in CMP rate case following whistleblower allegations
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
PORTLAND, Maine (WMTW) - Maine’s Public Advocate is asking state regulators to review records related to allegations of misconduct involving Central Maine Power’s parent company, Avangrid, as part of CMP’s pending rate case.
The motion follows a whistleblower lawsuit filed by Andrew Jacobs, the former chief compliance officer at Avangrid.
In the complaint, Jacobs alleges he was directed to withhold information from federal auditors, downplay a 2025 bribery matter involving CMP and overstate the company’s compliance with federal requirements.
The Office of the Public Advocate says the allegations could have implications for CMP’s rate case and what customers ultimately pay.
The office is seeking access to records related to the claims as regulators consider the utility’s request to raise rates.
CMP says the incident involved approximately $39,000, including unauthorized credit card charges in 2025. The company maintains there will be no rate consequences for customers.
CMP also expressed disappointment that the Office of the Public Advocate did not contact the company before filing the motion.
“We investigated, we disclosed this to FERC, and we no longer work with this individual who was involved,” said Jon Breed, speaking on behalf of CMP.
Breed said the company will review the motion carefully and respond through the appropriate process.

title: Skydance to combine Warner Bros. TV Group and Paramount Television Studios
text:
NEW YORK (AP) — Skydance will combine two of its key TV production units, Warner Bros. Television Group and Paramount Television Studios, bringing such shows as “The Pitt,” “Ted Lasso,” “Reacher” and “Landman” under the same roof.
The combined entity will be known as Warner Bros. Television Studios, with Channing Dungey and Matt Thunell serving as presidents. The merger of the studios will be completed in early 2027, according to a memo released Wednesday.
“Bringing together two of the industry’s most prolific television studios creates a formidable creative engine, uniting extraordinary talent, resources, acclaimed programming and iconic franchises with the global scale to compete at the highest level,” George Cheeks, co-chair and chief content officer of Skydance TV, said in the memo.
It’s the latest move since Skydance-owned Paramount last month closed its $81 billion takeover of Warner Bros. Discovery, ushering in a new Hollywood giant under the leadership of David Ellison.
The new Warner Bros. Television Studios will house more than 120 TV series, including HBO’s “Harry Potter and the Philosopher’s Stone,” Netflix’s “Emily in Paris” and CBS’ “Marshals.”
CBS Studios — another studio that produces shows such as the “NCIS” and “Fire Country” franchises — will continue to operate as a standalone entity under David Stapf.

title: Turner Fire-Rescue adds ambulance with design dedicated to suicide prevention
text:
Turner Fire-Rescue adds ambulance with design dedicated to suicide prevention, mental health awareness
The Turner Fire-Rescue Department is hoping to raise awareness for mental health and suicide prevention by introducing a new ambulance with a design dedicated to the cause.
The ambulance prominently features the colors of purple and teal, the primary and most widely recognized colors for suicide prevention awareness.
The 988 number for the Suicide and Crisis Lifeline is also featured on the new ambulance.
Turner Fire-Rescue Chief Lisa Bennett said the ambulance is dedicated to the first responders who have died of suicide and to anyone who is struggling.
"The hope that I have with this is that if somebody does see it, and somebody is struggling, that they see the 988 on the side of it, that they know that there are people here to help, that we do care, and that they will call that number," Bennett said.
Bennett said the ambulance with the suicide prevention design will be on the streets for the next five years.

title: Aging Untold: How to make it work when parents move in with adult children
text:
(Aging Untold) — On this episode of Aging Untold, we explore how aging parents moving into their adult children’s homes can successfully share space, set healthy boundaries and protect family relationships under one roof.
Plus, we look at how low-impact water workouts can build strength and endurance without stressing your joints.
Then, we meet a Michigan man who defied the odds to walk again after surviving a traumatic brain injury.
Multigenerational living can bring comfort along with adjustments.
When a parent moves in with an adult child, a grown child may feel their space is changing. A parent may feel they are losing independence, aging expert Amy O’Rourke said.
She said she likes the idea of a “town hall meeting” each week to check in on how everyone is doing.
Water exercises can be a game changer for people with joint pain or muscle stiffness, and there are options for every comfort and fitness level.
“People who want to still have that benefit of exercise can get cardiovascular endurance, help with prediabetes, insulin resistance and all that. You still want to be able to exercise, but it’s going to make it easier on your joints,” Dr. Rhea Rogers, a board-certified physician, said.
The Aging Untold experts are explaining the benefits, the risks and where to begin without spending a lot of money.
Adults who contract the measles can get seriously sick.
There is an antibody test, known as a titer test, that can show whether a person is likely protected.
The test measures immunoglobulin G (IgG) antibodies, which indicate past exposure to or vaccination against a virus like measles.
Jim Lowden was driving a motor home when a truck traveling the other way blew a tire, went over the median and struck him head-on.
“Eight weeks of my life are gone,” Lowden said. “I don’t remember anything at all.”
The injuries Lowden sustained included a traumatic brain injury, a brain bleed, a fractured skull, broken bones, broken ribs and a punctured lung.
He has lived at an inpatient transitional rehabilitation center since the crash and walks with a cane.
Lowden calls himself the luckiest man alive.

title: Mental competency at issue in US criminal case against Meghan Markle’s father
text:
TAMPA, Fla. (AP) — A judge scheduled a mental competency hearing Thursday for the 82-year-old estranged father of Meghan, the Duchess of Sussex, two weeks after he was arrested in Florida and charged with storing child sexual abuse material in California.
Thomas Markle was released after his arrest at a senior care center but was ordered to jail four days later, on Nov. 10, when authorities accused him of cutting off his electronic ankle monitor. A judge also ordered him to be examined by a mental health professional.
A hearing was set for Thursday afternoon in federal court in Tampa, Florida. Prosecutors declined to comment Wednesday. Markle’s lawyer did not reply to an email seeking comment.
Markle’s arrest in Lakeland, Florida, followed the seizure of approximately 78 items from storage units in the Los Angeles area, including slides, film negatives and books that contained suspected child sexual abuse images, the FBI said in a court filing.
Some images appear to depict him with children, the FBI said.
Markle had a stroke earlier this year while living in the Philippines and had to have his left leg amputated. That forced him to return to the U.S. and settle in Florida.
The Sun, a British tabloid newspaper, reported that Meghan’s half brother found child sexual abuse images while clearing out their father’s home in the Philippines. The discovery led to a search of the two U.S. storage units in California, which Markle had rented since 2008.
Meanwhile, in the Philippines, Markle is under investigation for possession and intent to distribute images. The Women and Children Protection Center, a branch of the Philippine National Police, filed a formal criminal complaint against Markle on Monday, police spokesperson Brig. Gen. Allen Rae Co said in a written statement.
The complaint was filed with the prosecutor’s office following an investigation into digital devices found at Markle’s former home in Cebu City, the statement said. The prosecutor’s office will assess the case for possible charges.
Markle did not attend his daughter Meghan’s 2018 wedding to Prince Harry at Windsor Castle. She said at the time he needed to tend to his health. Meghan is an American citizen who starred in the U.S. television drama “Suits.”

title: Suspects charged in brazen train heist ring that netted $22 million in cargo from major retailers
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Suspects charged in brazen train heist ring that netted $22 million in cargo from major retailers
More than a dozen people were charged Thursday with allegedly orchestrating a massive train heist operation to steal over $22 million in cargo — from popular shoes to power tools — from major retailers.
A federal indictment unsealed on Thursday paints a picture of an organized group that targeted more than three dozen trains carrying Nike sneakers, Crocs footwear, power tools and other consumer goods that were imported into the United States through Los Angeles and Long Beach, which are home to the busiest ports in the country.
Trains that shuttle goods to stores and customers around the country have become a prominent target for large-scale theft in recent years, especially at large ports in the U.S. that receive hundreds of millions of dollars of shipments every day. The relatively low-tech robberies have demanded attention from the world's largest retailers, including the likes of Amazon.
The men would disable the trains at a planned location by busting the brakes, the indictment alleged, at which point the goods would be offloaded onto trucks. The goods were then peddled to an unnamed company that would resell the stolen merchandise for profit.
“The scale of the theft is staggering,” said First Assistant United States Attorney Bill Essayli. He said that anyone who tries to steal the merchandise in the future will be prosecuted.
In group chats, the men shared numerous photos and videos of themselves busting into the hulking train cars, and posing with wads of cash and stolen merchandise. They also shared AI photos of themselves captioned “Los Trenes,” which means the trains in Spanish, beneath glamorized photos of men throwing boxes of shoes off trains into nearby cars while police helicopters descended overhead.
The 13 men were indicted for conspiracy and theft of interstate railroad cargo. Two were also charged with violence against railroad carriers.
If convicted, the men could face anywhere from five to 20 years in federal prison.

title: Anthropic begins trading in the biggest IPO on record despite the many fears surrounding AI
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
NEW YORK (AP) — The artificial intelligence giant Anthropic rose sharply Thursday after making the biggest public stock offering ever, at one point surpassing $2 trillion in value, despite anxiety about an AI bubble and fear that the technology threatens lives and livelihoods.
Its shares shot higher as trading began and held on to much of those gains to close up 17% at $97.17. The initial offering overtook SpaceX as the largest IPO in history.
Anthropic’s initial offer of $82 per share was surprisingly high given the investor worries that ratcheted up even more recently following the stunning ouster of AI’s chief promoter, the CEO of Nvidia, in a possible Chinese spying scandal. Anthropic had earlier set a lower price range between $70 and $78 per share.
“It’s a big win for the tech sector after a white-knuckle time with Nvidia,” said Dan Ives, a financial analyst at Yorkville Ives & Co. “The pricing shows strong demand among investors.”
For his part, Anthropic’s CEO tried to dampen worry about AI’s threat to society.
“If we can show it’s possible to make the right choices on safety and still build an incredibly successful company, others in our industry will be inspired to do the same,” Dario Amodei said.
The San Francisco-based maker of the Claude AI tool offered 980 million shares to the public, which at the $83 per share price translated into proceeds of $81 billion.
IPO offers a way to raise money without going deeper into debt
In addition to recent market jitters, Anthropic’s debut sale had to overcome fears of a potential regulatory crackdown next year by the Democratic-led Congress and growing anti-AI sentiment among the public. Anthropic rival OpenAI decided to postpone its initial offering until next year.
The company, trading under the ticker symbol ANT, also faces big financial challenges ahead.
Anthropic already has taken on $6.2 billion in debt, which it acknowledges in financial filings is “substantial.” Adding to the strain, the company is unprofitable, at least under standard accounting rules, suggesting that its resources to pay interest and principal are limited.
While the company showed ample cash in its last financial report, it would have likely run through it quickly given its outsize spending plans. In the same financial report, the company said it had signed leases and other deals requiring it to spend $900 billion on computing power and infrastructure in the coming years, including $70 billion in the next 12 months.
Such massive spending by AI companies, comparable to the Gilded Age splurge on railroads, has scared lenders, helping to push borrowing rates high recently.
With the IPO, though, Anthropic will now have enormous resources to accelerate its expansion without taking on more debt. In addition to the cash from public investors, the company also planned to sell $26 billion in shares in a private sale Thursday to bring the total raised to $107 billion — an impressive haul for a business not yet six years old.
The offering will also allow its employees to sell vested stock, making many of them millionaires overnight — and adding billions of dollars to the fortunes of CEO Dario Amodei and his sister, Anthropic President Daniela Amodei.
AI industry faces concerns about data centers, a possible bubble and regulations
Anthropic is locked in a fight for dominance with OpenAI. But both companies have plenty of other competitors, including Google, startups in the U.S. and China and SpaceX, which has an AI business.
Anthropic, OpenAI and SpaceX’s AI division have all lost more money than they’ve made because of the huge costs associated with building AI. That has fueled growing concerns about a bubble forming in the sector.
Dario Amodei cautioned in September that the AI industry should slow its fast-moving development to give safety measures time to catch up. Without such a slowdown, Amodei warned, AI could be capable of letting loose a swarm of agents that could take over the internet within months.
Amid mounting fears, the regulatory environment could change for Anthropic once the new Congress is in session. Newly elected Democrats are vowing to crack down on the industry as a backlash unfolds against data centers. And two big states offering incentives for data centers, Texas and Georgia, just elected Democratic governors who have vowed to stop new construction.
In his comments Thursday, Amodei also touted a range of positive uses for AI, noting that Claude already is helping scientists do quicker research and that the technology could help accelerate that progress in the future.
“Human intelligence has already made diseases like plague, smallpox and polio history for most of the world,” he said, “but progress in other diseases has been too slow for so many patients and their families.”
He also pointed to Claude’s use across companies, nonprofits and government services. “I’m extremely optimistic about what we can do together in the future,” he said.
Adding to the pressure to go public was the possibility that demand for AI shares could drop or even collapse. Investors have become anxious about the massive financing needs of the sector, and several tech companies have pulled IPO plans recently.
Market valuation for AI companies is going to be “up and down for many years to come, but more up than down,” said Rich Lesser, the global chair and former CEO of Boston Consulting Group.
“Exactly what the flow of that will be, it’s very hard to predict,” Lesser said Tuesday in an interview with The Associated Press at the Semafor Silicon Valley & the World forum. “There’s no question what Anthropic and OpenAI and Google and a number of the other players in this industry have done is pretty remarkable.”
___
Ortutay reported from Oakland, California. Associated Press business writers Kaitlyn Huamani in Los Angeles and Michelle Chapman in New York contributed.

title: 'This is really special': Dolly Parton's niece wears dress made for late singer to 2026 CMA Awards
text:
'This is really special': Dolly Parton's niece wears dress made for late singer to 2026 CMA Awards
Dolly Parton was honored at the 2026 CMA Awards Wednesday night, with her niece remembering her aunt in a special way.
Danielle Parton, 50, arrived at the 60th awards show carpet sporting a white and gold dress, telling reporters it was originally made for the late country singer.
"The dress that I'm gonna be wearing, this is really special," she said. "It was actually made for Dolly for 'Light of a Clear Blue Morning,' and the song was just nominated for a Grammy. She has tried it on. She obviously didn't get to wear it for the purpose it was designed for, and so I'm gonna get to wear it to honor her. Isn't that precious?"
Video: Family remembers Dolly Parton’s lasting gift to dying fan
Danielle said the Grammy-winning singer was supposed to wear the gown in honor of her track "Light of a Clear Blue Morning," which earned a 2027 Grammy nomination for best country duo/group performance and also features Lainey Wilson, Queen Latifah, Reba McEntire and Parton's goddaughter, Miley Cyrus.
In October, the country icon's estate named Danielle as its new brand ambassador.
Danielle said she was "so grateful to help care for a legacy," which means "so much" to not only her family, but also to many of Dolly's fans, in a heartfelt Instagram Reel.
She reassured fans that she would "never try and speak for Dolly," but instead help tell the world the incredible stories "behind the global icon."
Vince Gill and Lainey Wilson paid tribute to the late star at the start of the show, singing her 1974 hit, "I Will Always Love You."
Dolly died on Aug. 25 at the age of 80 following a brief fight with cancer.

title: Troy Jackson liked what he heard in a chat with Chuck Schumer’s challenger
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
U.S. Sen.-elect Troy Jackson had a productive conversation this week with Sen. Chris Van Hollen, the Maryland Democrat challenging longtime Democratic leader Sen. Chuck Schumer of New York.
But Maine’s incoming freshman hasn’t committed to backing Van Hollen.
“It was a very good conversation,” Jackson said Thursday in his first interview with the Bangor Daily News after upsetting five-term Republican Sen. Susan Collins. “I appreciated where he was going and his vision for the caucus.”
Jackson is among at least 10 current and incoming senators either backing Van Hollen or calling for new leadership. Sixteen have lined up behind Schumer, including Jackson’s colleague and Maine’s soon-to-be senior senator, independent Sen. Angus King.
The leadership race is the first test of how Democrats will use the 56-44 majority they’re poised to take in January after flipping nine seats, Maine’s among them. But Jackson, a former state Senate president who campaigned on making life more affordable, said the bigger question for him and his fellow freshmen is what that majority actually delivers.
Speaking from Orono after a few days home in Allagash following orientation in Washington, Jackson said kitchen table issues have dominated his early conversations with other incoming senators.
“Honestly, the discussions I’ve had with other new members were more about priorities getting done than who the leader was,” he said. “It’s one thing to believe strongly in core values, but then to have eight other people that feel almost the same coming in is a tremendous opportunity.”
Most of those priorities boil down to affordability. Getting out of the Iran war, ending tariffs and making health care more affordable after Trump administration cuts to Medicaid are “pertinent right out of the gate,” Jackson said.
“We’ve got to go after making people’s lives better financially,” he said. “It’s way too damn tough right now.”
The former logger said he’s received significant input from business owners, the labor community and others. He aims to help bolster Maine’s lobster and agriculture industries in particular.
Pressing the administration on Iran and tariffs could help drive down fuel prices for farmers and fishermen, as well as processing costs for the forestry industry, he said.
That range of issues is a key reason he’s sought seats on a host of committees, including the Appropriations panel currently chaired by Collins, a rare spot for a freshman. He recently told WMTW he also put in for the Health, Education, Labor and Pensions Committee, which Collins also is on, along with panels on commerce, banking, agriculture and veterans affairs.
Before committee assignments are made, the “big thing that has to drop is the leader” position, Jackson said. He expects to learn more by the first or second week of December, and he has already talked to Schumer about the process.
“I was talking with Schumer early on and he said that’s a discussion that has to happen between the majority leader and minority leader, in terms of how many members are on committees,” he said.

Maine designates 25 new federal opportunity zones to attract investment

Maine designates 25 new federal opportunity zones to attract investment
Gov. Janet Mills visited Lewiston Wednesday to highlight 25 new federal opportunity zone designations aimed at attracting investment to economically distressed communities across Maine
Gov. Janet Mills visited Lewiston Wednesday to highlight 25 new federal opportunity zone designations aimed at attracting investment to economically distressed communities across Maine.
The designations include a development site in Lewiston that is expected to bring more than 400 new apartments, along with space for small businesses.
Opportunity zones are designated areas where investors can receive tax incentives in exchange for investing in local projects, with the goal of encouraging economic development.
The 25 areas were recommended by the Mills administration and approved by the U.S. Department of the Treasury earlier this month.
"These new federal opportunity zone designations will be another incentive for developers to invest in our state, in addition to the historic state investments that we've made over the past eight years to expand businesses and spur housing development," Mills said.
The designations cover nine Maine counties and take effect in January. They will remain in place through 2037.

title: Trump wants the Supreme Court to let his EPA cancel billions in Biden-era climate grants
text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — The Trump administration is appealing to the Supreme Court in its push to cut $16 billion in grants for a climate program, the largest grant cancellation case ever and one that could affect Republican President Donald Trump’s push to defund the priorities of prior administrations.
The justices have not said whether they will take the case.
If they do, it could resolve a fight over grants that the Environmental Protection Agency rescinded in 2025. Democratic President Joe Biden’s administration awarded the money under a 2022 law to finance clean energy projects and accelerate the transition from fossil fuels. Trump has targeted other grants, such as those considered to be supporting diversity, equity and inclusion. A favorable outcome at the high court could help his administration defeat other grant lawsuits, according to the government’s filing this month.
At issue is the Greenhouse Gas Reduction Fund, commonly referred to as a “green bank.” Climate United Fund and other nonprofits were picked to operate the program authorized by the 2022 Inflation Reduction Act. If the justices decline to take the case, the groups could regain access to their money because a federal appeals court already ruled in their favor.
The EPA canceled the nonprofits’ grants soon after the start of Trump’s second term in January 2025, with EPA Administrator Lee Zeldin accusing the groups of mismanagement and potential fraud.
The nonprofits’ lawsuit argues that the EPA broke the law and violated the Constitution. It demands access to their grant money so they can run the program. The administration says it is immune from legal and constitutional claims and contends the groups filed their case in the wrong court.
If the justices eventually side with the EPA, it could “have far-reaching implications for the government’s ability to reshape grant programs and to terminate grants that do not advance a particular administration’s policy priorities,” said Romany Webb, deputy director of the Sabin Center for Climate Change Law at Columbia University who has supported Climate United’s arguments.
The EPA says the $16 billion at stake is the largest grant cancellation case ever and is another reason it warrants Supreme Court review.
The courts have so far tried to thwart the administration’s priorities, the EPA wrote in its petition to the Supreme Court.
The EPA and Climate United declined to comment.
Federal appeals court sided with the nonprofits
In August, a divided federal appeals court in Washington sided with the nonprofits and said the administration improperly terminated the grants. The release of any money was paused to give the Supreme Court a chance to weigh in.
The justices ruled for the administration recently in decisions over canceled National Institutes of Health grants and teacher training grants.
The administration has built its arguments around the Tucker Act, which gives the Court of Federal Claims exclusive authority over contract disputes. The claims court can award money, but not direct the government to take certain actions in the way federal courts can.
The nonprofits argued the way the EPA canceled the grants did not upend a contract with the federal government, but was done illegally and undercut spending on entire programs Congress had required, a constitutional violation. The government argues the matter is a contract dispute.
The administration’s broad use of contract cancellations to enact policies is a novel approach, according to Bob Wagman, president of the Court of Federal Claims Bar Association and a partner at the firm White & Case.
“I would hate to think that the only programs that could be supported have a four-year life,” he said, mentioning cancer research as an example of a grant program that would need longer than a single administration to pay off. “It is just not good for the country.”
Government rushed to cancel grants and criticize the nonprofits
Zeldin last year told Fox News that he suspected the green bank “was a clear-cut case of waste and abuse.”
U.S. District Judge Tanya Chutkan said that when the government was asked for evidence of fraud, the EPA did not provide it and shifted its position to more general concerns about the level of oversight over the program. Chutkan said the government cannot terminate the contracts in violation of the law and that the groups should have access to some of their frozen money, which is held in an account at Citibank.
The administration has been adamant that nothing requires them to make these grants to these groups.
Passage of the Inflation Reduction Act created the green bank. Trump’s tax and spending bill passed last year rescinded part of the law that established the bank and the money that had not already been obligated to its recipients. The EPA has said that those changes mean it should not have to release any money to the groups.
___
Associated Press writer Jennifer McDermott in Providence, R.I., contributed to this report.

title: Seventh graders create e-bike to help paralyzed friend join outdoor fun
text:
Seventh graders create e-bike to help paralyzed friend join outdoor fun
Students at Christian Academy of Louisville, Kentucky, were tasked with creating inventions to make the world a better place for their seventh-grade science project.
Jolanda Blandford, a seventh-grade teacher at the school, said the goal was to help others while teaching students physical skills like coding and engineering.
"It just brings so much joy to my heart to see them be able to use their talents to make somebody else's world a little bit better," Blandford said.
Among the projects were innovations to assist first responders in reaching crash scenes faster and devices for people with hearing or vision impairments.
The projects were then judged by professional engineers from Ford, Norton, and other local businesses.
One group created a robot called the "Fit Bot," designed to help people exercise.
"We learned that it's really hard to build a robot," Luke Schultz said.
"The most fun thing was learning how to work as a team and learning from our mistakes," Henry Schmied added.
Another team created the "Paralyzed Dirt Destroyer," an e-bike built for their friend Malcom, who is paralyzed from the waist down due to bone cancer.
"He's been wanting to do outdoor activities with me and my friends, like ride bikes and stuff. But he doesn't have anything that he could do this with. So we made this to give him an opportunity to just have fun with us," Bayard Donaldson said.
The students used parts from their garages to build the e-bike, learning new skills along the way.
"While we were building this, we learned how to weld and laser cut and wire stuff, which was really fun," Ford Manley said.
The boys said they are grateful for the opportunity to help their friend and others who could benefit from the bike.
"It made me realize that helping other people is way better than just helping yourself," Jack Lowe said.
The group plans to give Malcom his new e-bike on Christmas.

title: ‘Unknown’ illness causes nearly 150 aboard cruise ship to get sick with vomiting, diarrhea
text:
(Gray News) - Nearly 150 people aboard a Princess cruise ship are experiencing vomiting and diarrhea from an unknown illness.
Passengers reported the symptoms to the Center for Disease Control’s Vessel Sanitation Program on the fifth day of a 12-night trip throughout the Caribbean.
Although the cause of the sickness is currently unknown, Princess Cruise Lines has taken preventative measures to stop its potential spread, such as increased cleaning, isolating sick passengers and collecting specimens for testing.
Sick on board
Cruise ships that dock at any U.S. port are required to follow CDC reporting guidelines for any deaths or signs and symptoms of a “serious communicable disease of public health concern.”
Per these guidelines, an outbreak is defined as 3% or more passengers being impacted.
This incident is the 10th reported outbreak reported this year.
The industry funded Cruise Lines International Association reports that cases of gastrointestinal illness are much less common on cruises than in regular everyday life.
CLIA says that chances of GI sickness is 1 in 5,500 while cruising versus 1 in 15 on land.
How to protect yourself
Having fun is usually the first priority of most cruise passengers, and taking a few small steps can help people stay well during their trip.
Advent Health has published a list of “12 Tips to Stay Safe and Healthy on a Cruise.”
Some of the suggestions are:
- Wash hands frequently, especially after using the restroom, touching high traffic surfaces like door handles and stair railings, and before eating.
- Find where the onboard doctor or clinic is located on the ship before you board.
- Avoid overeating and drinking too much while on board.
