title: Iowa residents brace for a lead dust cloud as Army plans to detonate 5 tons of bomb-making chemicals
text:
DES MOINES, Iowa (AP) — Plans by the U.S. Army to detonate about 5 tons of bomb-making chemicals that have become unusable and might explode if moved have residents in southeast Iowa worried that a cloud of lead dust could cause environmental contamination and health problems.
The detonation at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant is set for Friday, and officials recommend that residents of a neighborhood in nearby Middletown begin vacating the area that morning. If they can’t leave their homes, they should stay inside and keep windows and doors closed.
“The detonation will result in an air plume with some lead-containing particles which will disperse in the air and deposit on the ground,” an advisory states. “Lead is toxic to humans and animals. The goal of this advisory is to provide the public with actionable information out of an abundance of caution to minimize lead exposure.”
Officials also have released maps showing the potential for lead dust to drift north toward other communities. Some schools in the path of the plume have canceled classes.
Nearly 400 people live in Middletown, but there are thousands more in the track of the plume.
The vibrations from the two blasts will be quick but could break old windows in town. The resulting dust is expected to linger for no more than one hour, depending on wind speed, officials said.
While the Army recommends washing cars and cleaning windowsills and outdoor surfaces, residents have taken to social media to voice concern and question whether that will be enough.
Surrounding communities get late notice
Middletown residents learned in March that the Army needed to dispose of several dozen barrels containing lead azide, after the ammunition plant paused operations as part of a review and the degraded material was discovered.
“The safety of our people and our neighbors is non‑negotiable,” Lt. Col. Daniel Nosse, commander of the plant, said at the time, acknowledging the volatility of the chemical compound used in munitions production.
The Army shared more details during a public meeting in Middletown in October, advising that a detonation was planned for an unspecified date in November. The Environmental Protection Agency on Nov. 13 approved an emergency permit, paving the way for Friday’s detonation.
That permit required the Army to track the potential air and dust dispersion and notify the public five days in advance, prompting Sunday’s notification to communities as far as 100 miles (160 kilometers) away.
Less than 20 miles (32 kilometers) northeast in Mediapolis, city officials were approached about allowing soil, water and air testing late last month. But they only learned of their potential exposure from the planned detonation Sunday, when the map put them dead-center in the dust exposure area.
Mediapolis Community School District announced Tuesday that the “uncontrollable variables” prompted the decision to close school Friday, with no events or sports practices. The public library also is set to close, and the local fire department will hose down playgrounds that could be covered in lead particles.
The EPA will have a command center in Mediapolis to sample the air, soil and water during and after the detonation, according to city officials. But the city will do its own testing as well to try to assure concerned residents.
“This is probably a first for me. I believe it’s a first for a lot of our citizens,” said Deputy City Clerk Amy Stucker. “The biggest issue we’re having is the lack of information.”
Even Iowa Gov. Kim Reynolds’ office was first briefed Monday on the public advisory, her office said.
News of the planned blasts also caught the attention of environmental and public health officials in Illinois. They urged the U.S. military to conduct comprehensive sampling in that state following the detonations.
Long-term storage leaves lead azide vulnerable
The barrels of lead azide had been stored at the ammunition plant for more than 20 years in earthen-covered containers, sitting in a bath of ethanol and water to keep the material stable, said Justine Barati, public affairs specialist at the Army Sustainment Command.
During a routine check earlier this year, they found that some of the water had evaporated, causing the lead azide to crystallize. That makes it more sensitive to friction and shock, thus “creating a highly unstable and dangerous situation,” according to an emergency permit approved last week by the EPA.
Moving or relocating it posed an unacceptable risk of accidental detonation, officials said. Barati said that possibility increases in cold weather.
“We’re really concerned about the weather situation,” Barati said on moving forward with Friday’s detonation. “We’re really concerned that it will detonate on its own.”
The Army said it put together a panel of experts in munitions chemistry, engineering and environmental safety to come up with the detonation plan.
The barrels are surrounded above, below and on all sides with concrete, which is buried under soil. Sand barriers are stacked two stories high around the soil.
During the detonation, the soil will be sprayed with water and the air will be misted to try to keep the majority of lead on Army property, Barati said.
Young children are a particular concern for potential exposure
Patrick O’Shaughnessy, a professor at the University of Iowa’s Department of Occupational and Environmental Health, said it is encouraging to see that the Army and the EPA are doing all they can to minimize the dust, but it’s still unknown how much will end up in the atmosphere and on surfaces.
Lead is a neurological toxicant that can decrease brain activity and development, especially in young children, O’Shaughnessy said. He is particularly concerned for toddlers who are at the age of putting everything in their mouth.
According to EPA documents, alternatives such as neutralizing and decomposing the contents of the drums using other chemicals were considered. But officials said any plan that involved handling the drums would increase the probability of accidental, fatal detonation.
___
Hill reported from Las Vegas and Montoya Bryan from Albuquerque, New Mexico.

title: Record number of women elected to 120th Congress
text:
WASHINGTON (Gray DC) - At least 162 women will serve when the 120th Congress is sworn in Jan. 3, 2027, the most ever. However, women will still only make up about 30% of all lawmakers.
Nebraska Congresswoman-elect Denise Powell, a Democrat, is one of those incoming members. “It’s unreal,” Powell said.
Powell is one of 41 new women who will be part of the 138 women in the next House of Representatives. That number breaks the 2024 record of 127.
“It’s absolutely thrilling,” said Patti Russo, executive director of The Campaign School at Yale (TCSYale).
Russo runs the school, a nonpartisan, issue-neutral training program that seeks to increase the number of women in elected and appointed office.
“It’s not going to be the same old thing, right? It’s going to be very different. In the House and the Senate, women bring their life experience to leadership. We know that. So as a result of that, what I’m hoping to see is more collaboration,” Russo said.
Incoming and returning women lawmakers said their life experience will help them advance legislation next year.
Rep. Teresa Leger Fernandez, a Democrat and chair of the Democratic Women’s Caucus, said they plan to bring forward bills on pay.
“We are going to actually exercise our power to bring forward bills that actually make sure that women have, that they get paid what they deserve. And then that pay is enough to pay for childcare, eldercare, housing, health care,” Leger Fernandez said.
Powell said women are often disproportionately affected by policies.
“We understand that women are often disproportionately impacted by a lot of the policies that we see from Congress to your school board,” she explained. “So this is such a good opportunity to make some really good change for our families.”
The House will have 118 Democratic and 20 Republican women. Russo said she believes more women in Congress means more bipartisanship.
“We are much more collaborative in our leadership style,” said Russo. “I don’t care who gets the credit. Just get it done. You know, I don’t have to have my name on everything. I don’t have to be front and center, just get it done… We’re not going to agree on everything, but we have to be able to find one or two or three priorities that are going to improve the quality of life for Americans in our country.”

title: New Tuttle Road Bridge in Cumberland open to traffic
text:
New Tuttle Road Bridge in Cumberland open to traffic, MaineDOT says
The bridge carries Tuttle Road over Interstate 295, U.S. Route 1 and state-owned railroad tracks.
New Tuttle Road Bridge in Cumberland open to traffic, MaineDOT says
The bridge carries Tuttle Road over Interstate 295, U.S. Route 1 and state-owned railroad tracks.
The Maine Department of Transportation (MaineDOT) has opened the new Tuttle Road Bridge to traffic in both directions, clearing the way for demolition of the old bridge.
The contractor for the bridge replacement project, Reed & Reed of Woolwich, said the new bridge opened to traffic at 3:30 p.m. Wednesday.
The new bridge was built alongside and to the north of the existing bridge, which was built in 1959 and underwent preservation work in 1990.
The replacement bridge still carries Tuttle Road over Interstate 295, U.S. Route 1 and state-owned railroad tracks, maintaining the connection between Middle Road and Foreside Road.
Drivers continued to use the existing bridge during most of the new bridge's construction, reducing the need for an extended closure. MaineDOT said now that the new bridge is in use, crews will begin demolishing the old bridge over the winter.
The new bridge includes two 11-foot travel lanes and 5-foot shoulders, and will include a 6-foot sidewalk. MaineDOT reminded drivers that the bridge opening does not mark the end of the bridge replacement project, and asked them to use caution around crews and equipment.
Remaining work on the new bridge, including sidewalk construction, final paving of the roadway approaches and other finishing work, will happen in the spring and summer of 2027.
Reed & Reed received a contract worth approximately $12.9 million for the bridge replacement project, according to MaineDOT.

By the way, if you see an asterisk (*) that is an up-to-the-minute update as I type this.
This week and next week in these columns, I want to tell you the story of some of these businesses and the experience they are having supporting this event. The organizations who support this event are incredible, and their participation deserves to be recognized each and every year. Many businesses will have festive crews of employees setting up their tree spaces, as this is a premier team building activity and some have already begun.

They make a whole evening of it, and honestly Hammond Lumber Co. employees are here daily for all six days of the festival.
Central Maine Power is a great supporter of the chamber, and is one of our stage and entertainment sponsors. Its support allows us to pay entertainers to add to those artists who are donating their time, which brings daily entertainment that is well worth the $2 suggested donation for entry, with children 12 and younger admitted free.
*Bill Dodge Auto Group just confirmed a sponsorship — after a very late ask in the last 24 hours by Cory the Elf. They will be another Stage & Entertainment Sponsor this year.
*Two more wreaths just came in.
*The kitchen has an island.
*Also just got an email for a new tree sponsor — we have 30-plus trees!
The Merrymeeting Tree Fest is happening this weekend and next weekend at the Brunswick Landing Y (24 Venture Ave., on Brunswick Landing) and, as I said, is a fundraiser for the Bath Brunswick Topsham Regional Chamber and the Brunswick Landing Y. The dates and times are:

title: Bog woman decapitated 2,000 years ago, scientists find
text:
(CNN) - A 2,000-year-old mystery is unfolding in Northern Ireland.
Scientists say the remains of a young Iron Age woman discovered in a bog in 2023 reveal she likely died by decapitation. The body was remarkably preserved by the cool, acidic conditions of the wetlands, but her skull was missing.
Experts believe she was struck twice in the neck and may have been kneeling when she was killed.
The findings were presented Monday at Belfast’s Ulster Museum during a public event modeled after a coroner’s inquest.
Some researchers believe the killing may have been part of an ancient ritual or human sacrifice, but other experts caution there isn’t enough evidence to determine a motive.

title: US Army delays detonation of bomb-making chemicals in Iowa after safety concerns raised
text:
DES MOINES, Iowa (AP) — The U.S. Army decided to delay Friday’s detonation of several tons of bomb-making chemicals in southeast Iowa after an outpouring of public concern that a cloud of lead dust could cause environmental contamination and health problems.
The plan is now to carry it out on Monday.
Iowa Gov. Kim Reynolds, who was among those who called for the detonation to be delayed as the clock ticked down Thursday, spoke directly with Acting Secretary of the Army Adam Telle, her office said. Environmental groups filed a lawsuit earlier in the day, seeking emergency court action to halt the plan.
Planning for the detonation at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant began after staff earlier this year found several dozen barrels containing lead azide that had degraded, “creating a highly unstable and dangerous situation,” according to an emergency permit approved last week by the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency. Moving or relocating it posed an unacceptable risk of accidental detonation, a possibility that increases in cold weather.
“This will delay the detonation until the latest possible moment prior to a forecasted temperature drop, which would risk further destabilization of the material,” Telle said in a post on X announcing the push to Monday.
The Army had shared details during a public meeting in Middletown in October, but a public advisory Sunday was the first time other communities — some as far away as 100 miles (160 kilometers) — became aware of the potential impact. Nearly 400 people live in Middletown — about 160 miles (257 kilometers) southeast of Des Moines — but thousands more in surrounding areas could be affected by detonated material that could disperse in the air and land on the ground.
“Public communication is essential to public trust,” Telle said.
Businesses and schools adjusted Friday schedules
Vibrations from the two planned blasts were expected to be quick, but they could break old windows in the Middletown area. That led officials to recommend some residents in Middletown vacate the area.
Iowans in the region were told to stay inside; keep windows and doors closed; bring pets and livestock indoors; and clean cars, windowsills and outdoor surfaces afterward.
“The detonation will result in an air plume with some lead-containing particles which will disperse in the air and deposit on the ground,” an advisory states. “Lead is toxic to humans and animals.”
Many schools throughout the region had already announced closures Friday and would now have to decide how to proceed on Monday.
Lucy Giehl, her husband and two dogs live just about 4 miles (6.4 kilometers) north of the ammunition plant. She first learned of the detonation on Sunday and was still trying to figure out where she’d go during the detonation.
But Giehl, 64, also wondered what happens when she gets home after. She voiced frustration about the lack of information about how to mitigate the risks. Her questions remained Thursday even after the delay.
“What are they going to do during those three days to help people be better prepared?” Giehl asked, asking whether she needs to wear gloves to wipe down surfaces or to keep her dogs from drinking water in their pond. “There’s just so many details that I feel like haven’t been addressed with the public.”
Environmental groups are still pursuing legal action
Environmental groups sued Thursday in an effort to stop the detonation, arguing that the EPA failed to require the Army to consider safer alternatives and that the Army failed to give adequate notice of its plans.
The detonation should be canceled outright, not merely delayed, said Wally Taylor, legal chair for the Sierra Club, one of the groups involved in the lawsuit.
“We don’t want the explosion to take place at all,” Taylor said Thursday after the announcement. “There are ways to do it without all the air quality problems and potential health problems.”
According to EPA and Army documents, alternatives such as neutralizing and decomposing the drums’ contents with other chemicals were considered. But officials said handling the drums would increase the probability of an accidental, fatal detonation.
The Army also says taking no action could lead to an accidental detonation that would result in “the sudden, uncontrolled release of vaporized lead, particulate matter, and toxic combustion gases.” Without planning based on weather patterns, that could cause “severe health impacts,” according to the Army’s environmental assessment.
The Army said a panel of experts in munitions chemistry, engineering and environmental safety prepared the detonation plan.
Experts urged residents to take precautions
Patrick O’Shaughnessy, a professor at the University of Iowa’s Department of Occupational and Environmental Health, said it’s still unknown how much contamination will end up in the atmosphere and on surfaces.
Lead is a neurological toxicant that can harm the brain, nervous system and other organs.
With high doses over a short period, people can be subject to lead poisoning and begin to feel sick, said Andrew Whelton, an environmental engineering professor at Purdue University who has helped communities recover from chemical disasters.
Long-term exposure to low doses can lead to neurological development problems, especially in young children, O’Shaughnessy added.
Iowa State’s Des Moines County Extension field office was busy fielding calls Thursday from concerned residents who have been “deathly afraid” for their health and their animals, said staff member Morgan Hoenig.
“We ran out of soil test kits yesterday,” she said.
___
Hill reported from Las Vegas and Montoya Bryan from Albuquerque, New Mexico.

title: Local author releases book honoring beloved Brunswick volunteer
text:
Local author Steven Levy has published a series of stories titled “My Buddy Paul” honoring his longtime friend Paul D’Alessandro’s support of Mid Coast Hunger Prevention Program. D’Alessandro, his wife, Judy Montgomery, and their rescue dog, Sparrow, were killed in a tragic car accident in Lewiston in 2021.
D’Alessandro joined MCHPP as a volunteer in 2014 and spent hundreds of Monday hours cooking at the organization’s soup kitchen, helping ensure healthy and delicious meals were available to all community members, no questions asked. As the go-to pasta maker, D’Alessandro brought positivity, joy and often a song to his work in the kitchen.
D’Alessandro and Montgomery also volunteered with MCHPP’s Merrymeeting Gleaners to harvest and pick up excess and less-than-perfect crops from local farmers and farmers markets. This local produce was then earmarked for meal-making in MCHPP’s Community Kitchen or distributed directly to program participants.
“Paul and I walked through Brunswick most Saturday mornings, sharing stories and youthful reminisces. He always had to hurry home to join Judy for their gleaning trips,” Levy said in a prepared release.
“My Buddy Paul” recounts many of these humorous recollections and shares tales of walking, hiking and paddling through Maine, which typically ended badly.
“I started writing about my adventures with Paul during the COVID lockdown, but he never got to see this special collection,” Levy said. “I know he and Judy would be honored by the community’s generosity.”
“We were deeply saddened by Paul and Judy’s passing five years ago, and are heartened that Steven is honoring his friendship in such a meaningful way by publishing this collection of stories,” said Hannah Chatalbash, MCHPP’s executive director. “Paul and Judy’s joy for life and service was always obvious, and their smiles contagious. This book is a wonderful way to continue to spread that joy.”
All proceeds from the sale of “My Buddy Paul” will be donated to Mid Coast Hunger Prevention Program. Books may be ordered through the author’s website at stevenclevyauthor.com.
Levy was born, raised and educated in Worcester, Massachusetts, in a suburban residential neighborhood settled primarily by Jewish World War II veterans and their families. He learned the art of storytelling over breakfast at the feet of soft goods salesmen at Worcester’s Broadway Restaurant on Water Street. Fortunately, he never had to pay for his meals. He was voted third funniest boy in his high school graduating class. He still feels robbed.
He has worked in dozens of occupations over the past 50 years, from machine tool rigger to agricultural economist; from association executive to farm grant writer. He helped write the reauthorization of the Safe Drinking Water Act and dabbled as a professional clown. He and his wife Stephanie raised a family of two and he has been sitting on the porch of their Sears Craftsman house for the past 10 years, talking to people who walked by, whether they wanted to or not, feeding dogs, and writing stories and anecdotes about friends and family. He hopes sharing these stories will finally get them out of his system, but many doubt it.
Mid Coast Hunger Prevention Program strengthens the community by providing food today while advancing lasting solutions to food insecurity through education, collaboration and advocacy. The organization envisions a compassionate, connected community rooted in nourishment for all. Services include prepared meals, grocery distribution on site, at local schools and to various satellite locations. The MCHPP food pantry at 12 Tenney Way, Brunswick, is open to the public from noon to 6 p.m. on Tuesdays, noon to 3 p.m. Wednesdays and Fridays, and 1-4 p.m. Saturdays; the Soup Kitchen makes freshly made-to-go meals available on site or through partner distributions six days per week. In 2026, MCHPP welcomed over 22,000 food pantry visits and distributed 1.39 million meals. More information on MCHPP’s services can be found at mchpp.org/find-food.

title: Perfect Fall Days Are Here—Enjoy the Sunshine and Mild Weather
text:
BANGOR, Maine (WABI) - High pressure continues to gradually work its way towards the East Coast... dominating our forecast and providing us with some beautiful fall weather.
We’ll see more sunshine returning to the forecast today with skies expected to average partly to mostly sunny (leaning towards mostly sunny for most locales). The mild weather continues with highs in the mid to upper 50s across the north and upper 50s to low 60s elsewhere. We’ll be under clear skies tonight with low temperatures dropping to the 30s.
Friday looks awesome with partly to mostly sunny skies and high temperatures again topping off in the mid-50s to low 60s from north to south. This beautiful fall weather continues into the weekend with sunshine Saturday and highs in the 50s. We’ll see a bit more cloudiness Sunday leading to a mix of sun and clouds with highs in the 50s to around 60°.
Our next best chance of any rainfall will arrive Sunday night into Monday as low pressure approaches from the south. There is still some uncertainty with how far north the storm makes it but the overall trend in the model data has been to bring the storm further north... closer to New England... leading to a better chance for rain Sunday night into Monday at least for some parts of the state. Right now... it looks like the best chance for steadier rain will fall over areas along and to the south and east of I-95 with a lesser chance for areas to the north and west of the interstate. Coverage... as well as rainfall totals... will be dependent on the exact track of the system. A track closer to New England would lead to more widespread and heavier rainfall and a track further south would mean lighter/lesser rain. Stay tuned for updates. It looks like that colder weather will stick around through the remainder of next week.

BELFAST, Maine (WABI) - A South Portland man pleaded not guilty to four charges stemming from a 2025 crash involving a school bus in Belfast.
Kyle Young, 41, made his first court appearance by Zoom Wednesday afternoon. He is being held on $1,000 bail and, if released, has been ordered not to drive, among other conditions.

The crash
Prosecutors say Young was high on drugs when he crashed into an RSU 71 school bus in June 2025.
About two dozen students were on the bus. Two students, Young and his then-4-year-old child, who was in the car with him, were hospitalized.
The state said delays involving the lab and the investigation contributed to the time it took to bring charges.
Bail arguments
Young’s attorney asked for $1,000 unsecured bail, saying Young had no cash and wanted to return to his job. The attorney said Young has been sober for nine months and had stable employment before his arrest.
The state asked for $1,000 secured bail. Prosecutors acknowledged it was a low request for the charges, but cited the length of time between the alleged incident and the charges.

title: South Portland elementary students may not have to swap schools
text:
South Portland elementary school districts could remain mostly the same next year.
The school board may vote on Monday, Nov. 23, on a plan for redistricting the city’s four elementary schools. Among the questions the board will have to answer is whether the schools will be reconfigured by grade level or left alone.
Reconfiguring schools by grade level was an option on the table during budget negotiations this spring.
After more than a dozen public meetings, the reconfiguration committee narrowly recommended continuing with a slightly modified version of the status quo. If the board approves this model, students will continue to attend kindergarten through fourth grade at the same school, generally based upon where they live.
The district would eventually plan to transition students who live in Turners Island to Frank I. Brown Elementary School because it makes logistical sense, Assistant Superintendent Johanna Prince said.
Superintendent Angela Atkinson Duina, in a memo to the school board, said that while the city might have an appetite for a unified elementary school or organizing by grade level in the future, making that change would require more time and energy to execute.
“That may be a possibility in the far-off future but it is not achievable right now,” she said.
Caretakers and staff members need stability right now, she said, after staffing reductions and the closure of James O. Kaler Elementary School at the end of the last school year. She recommended that the board revisit school boundaries more regularly; the last change was at least 15 years ago.
Some board members, however, want to take a proactive approach now.
“The district has been a prisoner of the moment for years,” School Board member Tyler Smith said. “This is just making short-term decisions to avoid short-term pain in a way that does not solve our long-term problems.”
Students have significantly different educational experiences depending on the elementary school they attend, according to the findings of a committee formed several years ago to look into achievement disparities between elementary schools.
The committee found that diverse schools benefit all students by increasing tolerance, positive racial attitudes and learning outcomes. When economically disadvantaged students learn alongside their more privileged peers, the schools overall have higher test scores and college enrollment, and fewer dropouts, the committee found.
School Board Chair Rosemarie De Angelis sees grade band reconfiguration as an opportunity for teachers to work together across specialized teams and for students to form friendships with peers from different backgrounds.
“I want my grandkids to go to a school that looks like the world,” she said. She was the only board member to vote against delaying the process, worried that slowing things down would increase the chances that the district wouldn’t take action.
Atkinson Duina said that the district can still address inequities in the district even if it does not reconfigure elementary schools right now.
The district will develop a proposal for consolidating early childhood special education services, form a committee to look into differential funding options for elementary schools with high populations of economically disadvantaged students, and commission an audit of special education offerings in the district.
If the school board moves forward with minimal changes, there will be no major changes to transportation routes or costs, or transitions for students and staff members, according to Prince. There might be some reshuffling because of waivers and special education needs, she said.
If the school district reconfigured the elementaries, students would be organized by grade level bands along the east and west sides of the city. Waldo T. Skillin and Dora L. Small Elementary Schools would house kindergarten through second grade and Helena H. Dyer and Brown Elementary Schools would be the third and fourth grade campuses.
This reshuffling would relocate 411 students, including 56 who just moved from Kaler, and would involve longer bus rides.

title: Anthropic's IPO caps an explosive growth period for the AI startup, filled with contradictions
text:
A mere five years before breaking the record for the biggest public stock offering ever, Anthropic began as a Silicon Valley startup when its founders broke away from OpenAI with their own ideas about how to develop artificial intelligence.
Today, the company that dedicated itself to prioritizing safety, building the Claude chatbot along the way, has been one of the loudest voices raising warnings about how the same technology could bring catastrophe.
It’s one of the contradictions that mark the brief, colorful history of Anthropic, which emerged Thursday from its first day of trading on Wall Street with a market value of $1.75 trillion.
The company, which still pledges to prioritize humanity’s benefit, now faces pressure from shareholders to wring profits from the technology its most senior leaders have described as posing existential threats.
Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei described the push and pull between safety and AI advancement as one of the “central tensions at the heart of the company” on Thursday.
In an interview with CNBC, he described the rapid pace of AI advancements — due in large part to advanced models helping to build the next, improved version of themselves — as akin to building something that lets a driver go 200 miles per hour when they had previously been driving at 60. His company, he said, is working to develop it safely.
“What we’ve done with pacing is essentially said, ‘Look, you know, we could drive at 200 miles an hour. Maybe let’s only drive at 90 miles an hour, spend time figuring out how to do that safely,’” he said. “And the rest of that surplus, we spend building the model in the right way.”
Warning of potential calamity, the company forges ahead
The company’s seven founders — Amodei, 43, his sister and Anthropic’s president Daniela Amodei, 39, and five other former OpenAI employees — left the rival company in pursuit of building one that more clearly prioritized safety in artificial intelligence development.
Anthropic publicly has been committed to safety and transparency around their AI models, but insiders have sounded alarm bells in recent months.
An Anthropic researcher resigned from the company in September, criticizing the safety practices of both Anthropic and OpenAI. Jacob Coxon, whose message spurred industry-wide conversations about the speed of AI’s growth, wrote that both Anthropic and OpenAI are “gambling with our lives.” He warned that some working on AI development believe it could threaten human life by the end of the decade.
Dario Amodei responded with an essay calling for an industry-wide slowdown on the technology’s development. He enumerated detailed plans for slowing development and ushering in coordination across different companies and countries, and championed the idea of having independent evaluators embedded within Anthropic and other labs.
But the results from at least one of those independent evaluations underscored Coxon’s concerns. A recent report from the nonprofit Model Evaluation and Threat Research found Anthropic is developing its systems around twice as quickly as it was a year ago, largely because of the help of AI itself.
Amodei said Thursday in comments at the Nasdaq opening bell that the company’s “most difficult safety work lies ahead of us.”
“And to state it unequivocally, we will pace the training and deployment of AI systems, taking as long as is necessary to have confidence that they are safe and will remain under human control,” he said.
A company pledging to benefit humanity has enriched its founders
Anthropic is a public benefit corporation, meaning it has a legal obligation to balance shareholder interests with the public good. But these types of companies are rarely public, and of the few that are, they are significantly smaller than Anthropic, so the company is entering uncharted territory.
The company has said it is working towards a future where “AI’s benefits are shared by everyone,” but the initial public offering has created a concentration of extreme wealth for its founders, employees and other investors.
Before the IPO, the two Amodei siblings each had a net worth of just over $14 billion, according to Forbes. By Thursday afternoon, Dario Amodei’s net worth was $22.7 billion and Daniela Amodei’s was $22.8 billion.
The Amodeis and the other co-founders have said they are committed to pledging 80% of their equity to philanthropy, although that commitment is voluntary. The company has an equity donation match program that allows employees to pledge equity, which Anthropic matches. Anthropic has also pledged at least 5% of its stock to a “public benefit” fund.
Speaking to CNBC Thursday, Daniela Amodei said the concept of a public benefit corporation “spoke” to the co-founders when they were initially creating the company.
“We’re really trying to do something that we do think can have this incredible economic value and impact, but we want it to be baked into essentially our structure that we also have to balance that against building things that are good for people,” she said.
Anthropic offers itself as a solution for AI doomsday fears
In a filing with the Securities and Exchange Commission last month, Anthropic devoted an unusually lengthy 93 pages to the risk factors they must spell out for investors. Among the concerns were that advanced AI systems could pose “catastrophic or existential risks to humanity.”
Some argue Anthropic has outlined the ways its technology and that of its competitors could have devastating consequences in the name of sheer transparency. But critics have questioned the emphasis the company has placed on these dystopian-like potentials while positioning itself as the logical solution given its safety-minded focus.
A “Saturday Night Live” sketch in September made this contradiction a punchline. Cast member Jane Wickline played Dario Amodei, saying: “Sam Altman, myself, all the major AI players, we have talked about this extensively, and we are all on the same page here: We do not condone what we are doing.”
The faux interview on “SNL” concluded with a line that seems to have resonated with skeptics, showing up on a protest sign outside of Anthropic’s San Francisco headquarters on Thursday: “I urge you to urge me to stop.”
___
Associated Press business writer Wyatte Grantham-Philips contributed.

title: Aging Untold: How to make it work when parents move in with adult children
text:
(Aging Untold) — On this episode of Aging Untold, we explore how aging parents moving into their adult children’s homes can successfully share space, set healthy boundaries and protect family relationships under one roof.
Plus, we look at how low-impact water workouts can build strength and endurance without stressing your joints.
Then, we meet a Michigan man who defied the odds to walk again after surviving a traumatic brain injury.
Multigenerational living can bring comfort along with adjustments.
When a parent moves in with an adult child, a grown child may feel their space is changing. A parent may feel they are losing independence, aging expert Amy O’Rourke said.
She said she likes the idea of a “town hall meeting” each week to check in on how everyone is doing.
Water exercises can be a game changer for people with joint pain or muscle stiffness, and there are options for every comfort and fitness level.
“People who want to still have that benefit of exercise can get cardiovascular endurance, help with prediabetes, insulin resistance and all that. You still want to be able to exercise, but it’s going to make it easier on your joints,” Dr. Rhea Rogers, a board-certified physician, said.
The Aging Untold experts are explaining the benefits, the risks and where to begin without spending a lot of money.
Adults who contract the measles can get seriously sick.
There is an antibody test, known as a titer test, that can show whether a person is likely protected.
The test measures immunoglobulin G (IgG) antibodies, which indicate past exposure to or vaccination against a virus like measles.
Jim Lowden was driving a motor home when a truck traveling the other way blew a tire, went over the median and struck him head-on.
“Eight weeks of my life are gone,” Lowden said. “I don’t remember anything at all.”
The injuries Lowden sustained included a traumatic brain injury, a brain bleed, a fractured skull, broken bones, broken ribs and a punctured lung.
He has lived at an inpatient transitional rehabilitation center since the crash and walks with a cane.
Lowden calls himself the luckiest man alive.

title: Bangor PD's Armored Vehicle Breaks Through Ohio Street Windows And Door At 5 AM Warrant
text:
Dramatic Video Of Bangor PD Using Armored Response Vehicle While Executing Early Morning Search Warrant On Ohio Street
A dramatic video has emerged of the Bangor Police Department utilizing a unique vehicle to break out doors and windows at an apartment building on Ohio Street Thursday morning.
According to one witness in the neighborhood, an armored vehicle full of officers with weapons drawn pulled up to the scene and closed down both sides of Ohio Street just after 5 AM. They then brought in a specialized truck equipped with a long-armed ramming rod of sorts and parked it in front of one of the apartments.
Read More: 1 Dead, 2 Hurt After Vehicle Hits Pedestrians At Maine Walmart
The vehicle was positioned near 143 Ohio Street as authorities used a bullhorn to direct residents to comply.
The voice over the loudspeaker stated:
"Occupants of 143 Ohio Street, this is the Bangor Police Department. We have a search warrant. Exit the building through the front door with your hands up and nothing in your hands. Do it now."
Moments later, when no one complies, the vehicle can be seen breaking through one window on the front of the building, then the front door, and finally another window before those inside eventually exited the premises.
Katy England, with the Bangor Police Department, says the vehicle used to break through the windows and doors is Bangor PD's Armored Response Vehicle.
Read More: Brewer, Maine Police Arrest Suspect Fleeing Chamberlain Street Drug Bust
She says it's usually utilized in situations that have the potential to become high risk.
"In this case, it assisted in executing a search warrant at that location. The investigation is ongoing and we don't have further details we can release at this time. "
We will update this story when more information becomes available.

title: Former property owner sues Houlton for seizing his home over unpaid taxes
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
The former owner of a downtown Houlton house that the town seized earlier this year over unpaid taxes has gone to court to challenge the town’s foreclosure of his home.
Albert Carmichael, 54, said he paid more than $2,500 in past, present and advance taxes on 26 Mill St. in late May, five months after the town foreclosed on the property. He said he believes the town is rejecting his efforts to get his house back because of a history of police calls and code enforcement issues at the property when he and his family lived there.
In a Nov. 5 emergency filing in Aroostook County Superior Court in Houlton, Carmichael sued the town for breach of contract, wrongful conversion and unjust enrichment for allegedly retaining his tax payments but stripping him of his property rights and ownership.
But the Houlton Town Council never approved any proposed agreement to return the property to Carmichael, according to the town’s records.
Carmichael had been in contact with the town attorney in June about his taxes. Believing they had reached an agreement to have the property deeded back to him, he told the Bangor Daily News he was taken aback when on Sept. 14 the town gave him 30 days to vacate the premises.
“I didn’t agree to this,” he said. “Why would I, my stuff was paid and I had no other place for me and my 16-year-old son to live.”
In public comments before the Town Council this month and in repeated correspondence with the BDN, Carmichael said he believes the town is using his prior disputes with the town and neighbors against him in not returning the property.
It started with the police chief and a neighbor, Carmichael said.
Town officials declined to comment on the seizure of Carmichael’s property, or on Carmichael’s accusation that it is connected to its history of law and code enforcement issues.
In four and a half years the property generated 93 calls to the Houlton Police Department for service, including domestic issues, family fights, overdose, theft, noise, animal complaints and littering, according to police call reports that Houlton Police Chief Tim DeLuca shared with the BDN.
Deluca declined to comment on Carmichael’s situation, but said when calls for service impact neighborhoods, the Houlton Police Department works within the law and collaborates with code enforcement to ensure lawful compliance.
Amber Jones, the new town manager, who has been on the job since Sept. 28, said Carmichael made several erroneous statements in his public comments, but declined to identify the errors. The most important aspect of the situation, she said, is “the 5 years of anguish he caused his neighbor.”
“We are working with [the neighbor] because the former residents of 26 Mill St. made no legally viable attempts to get rid of their garbage,” Jones said. “This has had a major impact on the neighbor among other disturbing and disruptive behaviors she endured.”
The neighbor, Rosa McNally, said that Jones is the first and only town manager to genuinely listen, investigate and work toward a solution.
“It is deeply angering that five years of code enforcement inaction harmed my health, safety and property value — no one should have to live in squalor because of their neighbors’ choices,” she said.
Carmichael cites three documents related to the matter in claiming he and the town worked out an agreement for him to get his house back: the letter from the town attorney and two receipts for tax payments totalling $2,501, copies of which he filed with his court complaint and provided to the BDN.
On June 4, the town’s attorney, Dan Nelson, wrote to Carmichael acknowledging tax payments for 2023, 2024 and 2025, as well as a $1,309 overpayment. In the June letter, Nelson proposed a plan to release the property back to Carmichael, who agreed to the terms in writing, according to documents filed in Aroostook County Superior Court.
In the proposed June agreement, copied to the town tax collector, Nelson detailed specific actions necessary to have the property deed reversed, including paying $550 for 2026 taxes, fixing code violations related to trash and premises, and paying a $400 release fee and $40 to record the deed, court documents show.
“I have $1,300 credit, so take it and pay taxes up to [2026] and whatever else for the other fees. Is there any way I could use what’s left to get a dumpster delivery?” Carmichael responded via email to Nelson the same day.
Still, the proposed agreement was never approved by the council.
“There is nothing that can stop the automatic foreclosure except for payment in full prior to the date of foreclosure. Tax law in Maine is very cut and dry,” Emily Mills, the town’s tax collector told the Bangor Daily News this week, without commenting on Carmichael’s specific situation. “Our administrative time has been exhausted on this topic.”
Carmichael maintains the town is still retaining the funds he paid, but Mills said they issued a refund check in full.
In his lawsuit, Carmichael asked the court to immediately apply the funds to the liens placed by the town on the property, to convey the cleared deed back to him and issue an injunction halting any further actions or sale.
“Unfortunately, even when taxes are paid in full after the foreclosure date, the town is not required to deed the property back to the former owner,” Mills said.
On Nov. 6, Carmichael also filed an emergency motion in court to have his lawsuit court fees waived. Justice Patrick Larson denied the motion. The window is closing for Carmichael to pay the court fees. If they remain unpaid, his lawsuit will be dismissed, according to the court clerk.
Town officials said the property remains foreclosed, but there are no immediate plans to sell it.
Carmichael said he is currently living in an off-grid and unheated camper on Garrison Lane.

title: Maine Cancer Foundation celebrates 50th anniversary
text:
'Incredible to see the growth': Maine Cancer Foundation celebrates 50th anniversary
The Maine Cancer Foundation (MCF) is celebrating 50 years of statewide work to reduce cancer's impact in the state.
On Wednesday, the foundation hosted a dinner honoring past and present board members who make the work possible.
According to MCF, cancer rates in Maine are significantly higher than the national average and are the worst in New England.
Though cancer rates have declined nearly 13% from an all-time high in 2000, MCF officials said more work needs to be done in Maine.
The foundation focuses on several things, including fostering cancer prevention, as well as improving patient outcomes.
"It's incredible to see the growth," said MCF executive director Ray Ruby. "What the organization wanted to do is raise funds, to stay here in Maine, to help the people of Maine, and that has evolved over the years in many different ways. So we've had many missions over the years in different ways, but we're always serving the state."
If you wish to donate to MCF or find other ways to support the foundation, information is available on mainecancer.org.

title: A year ago, Scarborough voters approved a $139M school building project. Here’s where it stands now.
text:
SCARBOROUGH — One year ago, Scarborough voters approved a $139 million school overhaul project that has been years in the making. Since then, the school district and town have continued to make progress on the project, working on floor plans, permitting and design development.
On Tuesday night, the town hosted a forum to update the community on the state of the project. Here’s what Lisa Sawin, of the architectural engineering firm Harriman, and Superintendent Diana Nadeau said:
PROJECT OVERVIEW
In 2023, voters rejected a $160 million project that would have consolidated three primary schools, moved sixth graders to Wentworth School and renovated Scarborough Middle School.
Following the referendum’s failure, about 70 community members formed the School Building Advisory Committee and spent over a year to find another solution that addressed taxpayers’ cost concerns and met infrastructure needs.
The project that voters approved in 2025 will demolish and rebuild Eight Corners Primary School, and construct additions to Pleasant Hill and Blue Point primary schools, which currently have portable classrooms. Wentworth will have a small addition to add new classrooms, and Scarborough Middle School will be renovated and have a two-story addition to meet capacity needs for current enrollment.
Most of the schools have undersized nurse offices, so many of those will be renovated and expanded. There will be air conditioning and better insulation at most of the schools, too.
Staff at many of the schools said they want to prioritize outdoor play and learning spaces and breakout and pull-over spaces.
Of the five schools being renovated or expanded, three have already gone before the Scarborough Planning Board. Pleasant Hill and Eight Corners will go before the planning board in December.
The project is currently $2.8 million under budget. The next steps are determining the approach to bidding and advertising for bidding. Construction is expected to begin in 2027.
EIGHT CORNERS PRIMARY SCHOOL
A new building will replace the current school on the same site to accommodate 380 students and eliminate the need for portables. There will be a separate cafeteria and gym, separate bus and parent drop-offs, an emergency lane around the whole school and a courtyard in the middle of the building.
The construction will occur in two phases. First, students will remain in the original building while half of the new building is constructed. Then, in the summer of 2028, they will move to the new one while the old building is demolished and replaced with the second half of the new building.
Students will be able to occupy both sides of the building in the 2029-30 school year.
BLUE POINT PRIMARY SCHOOL
At Blue Point, the project will renovate the current building and build two additions to accommodate 232 students in total and remove the portables. One of the additions will be a cafeteria so the cafeteria will no longer be in the same space as the gym, and the other will have new classrooms. There will be a separate bus and parent drop-off.
The cafeteria and classroom additions will be built in during the 2027-28 school year. Then, students will move to the new wing so the old building can be renovated. The project will be completed for the 2029-30 school year.
PLEASANT HILL PRIMARY SCHOOL
Pleasant Hill will keep its existing building — with some renovations — and will get a large addition and more parking. The play area will be relocated to make room for the new addition, and there will be an emergency lane all around the building.
There will be a courtyard in the middle of the building, the library will be renovated, and the addition will have kindergarten classes, special education spaces and a cafeteria.
The construction will also occur in two phases, and the project will be completed by the 2029-30 school year. The portables will be removed and there will be room for 224 students.
WENTWORTH SCHOOL
Wentworth School will see the smallest change of the five schools. A small addition will be built to include three new classrooms and accommodate the enrollment expected in 2031. The total school capacity will be 936 students. Construction will be done by the 2027-28 school year.
SCARBOROUGH MIDDLE SCHOOL
The new additions at Scarborough Middle School will eliminate the need for portables, provide more space for music and art programming, expand the cafeteria and improve safety and security.
Currently, because the cafeteria is too small for all the students, the school has six lunch times ranging from 10:30 a.m. to 1:30 p.m. Typically, schools have three lunches.
There will be a small addition near the school’s entrance for administrative offices and a large two-story addition with classrooms and band, music and chorus rooms.

title: Bangor Drone Locates Man Who Fled A Rollover Crash On Hammond Street
text:
Bangor PD Nab Man On The Run, Find Him Lying In A Field With The Help Of A Drone
Since April of this year, the Bangor Police Department has incorporated a drone into their tool kit, using it for everything from tracking down missing people to looking for folks on the run.
It was about a month ago, when authorities in Bangor used their drone to locate a woman who became in the Bangor City Forest.
Read More: Maine Emergency Services Turn To Drones For Rescue
This week, the drone was used to find a man who had fled the scene of an accident, authorities say.
Just before 2 AM, the Bangor Police Department says is was called out to a crash on Hammond Street, when a person had rolled their vehicle over and subsequently run away from the area before law enforcement arrived.
Authorities they called in a K9 tracking dog, and established a perimeter around the area, but fearing the individual may be injured, time was of the essence, so a drone operator was also called in.
"Det. Joe Orcutt arrived on scene and was able to deploy the drone and conduct a search of the area. Det. Orcutt was able to locate a man in nearby field within minutes of deployment. The man was identified as Quinn Dernbach, 29, of Anson, who declined medical treatment repeatedly."
Bangor Police say that Dernbach showed signs of that he might be under the influence, and was arrested and taken into custody.
Read More: The Role Of Drones In Enhancing Public Safety In Maine
Dernbach faces charges of violating bail condition and operating under the influence.

title: Portland recount experience restores faith in voting
text:
I participated, as a volunteer for candidate Jake Viola, in the recount of ballots for the Portland District 4 race between Viola and Councilor Anna Bullett. The city clerk, Abbey Lombard, backed by staff including Paige Marcello and Hanna Daniel and many others, including Annie James, paralegal, and corporation counsel Michael Goldman, ran the all-day counting of votes — by volunteers for both candidates — with skill, kindness and accuracy.
The ultimate difference of 12 votes in Councilor Bullett’s favor did not change. That result convinced us all we can trust the new tabulators supplied by the Maine secretary of state. We are well served by these civil servants and by many engaged volunteers.
Every time a voter fills in the little circles on our paper ballot they create a physical record of their choice in an election. I will not look at the ballot again so casually. Especially in such a close race, trust in the system makes it possible to accept the results and move on.
My thanks to residents for voting, to city workers for supervising the elections so capably, and to everyone who cares about making government work in our beautiful city of Portland.
Nancy English 
Portland

title: FCC expected to allow state prisons to jam contraband cellphone signals with Thursday vote
text:
COLUMBIA, S.C. (AP) — The Federal Communications Commission is poised to grant permission to state prisons across the United States to jam the signals of cell phones smuggled to inmates, devices that authorities say represent the No. 1 security threat in the nation’s correctional facilities.
Inmates have used contraband cell phones — smuggled inside hollowed-out footballs, whisked in by corrupt employees and sometimes even dropped by drone — to run drug rings, coordinate prison riots and even order acts of violence like assassination attempts on prison guards, according to officials.
For decades, officials have unsuccessfully pushed for permission to jam the signals with technology already allowed in federal facilities but that, thanks to a nearly century-old communications law, would require FCC permission.
That’s set to change on Thursday, according to FCC Chairman Brendan Carr, who traveled to South Carolina this week to stand with state law enforcement and prisons officials who have long sought the permission.
U.S. Attorney Bryan Stirling, who led South Carolina’s Corrections Department for more than a decade, led an effort from many of his counterparts across the country to gain use of the technology. South Carolina Attorney General Alan Wilson, elected this month as the state’s next governor, marshaled his fellow prosecutors across the country urging Congress, unsuccessfully, to change the law.
FCC chair says it’s ‘ready to take action’
Standing alongside Stirling, Wilson and other South Carolina officials before a display of hundreds of confiscated cell phones and massive drones used to ferry the contraband over prison fencing, Carr said Wednesday that his agency is ready to take action against what he described as a scourge of which many might not understand the danger.
“People really don’t understand the threat that these pose,” Carr said, noting that 25,000 cell phones were confiscated in the nation’s state and local prisons each year. “We’re going to put a new tool in the hands of law enforcement, and it’s going to make a dramatic difference.”
One of the starkest examples of the illegal phones’ danger, Carr said, is the case of Robert Johnson, a South Carolina Corrections officer nearly killed at his home in a 2010 rain of bullets in a hit officials said had been orchestrated by a prisoner using a contraband cell phone.
After nearly three dozen surgeries and now in “pain 24/7,” Johnson — who has testified in previous FCC hearings over jamming requests and often spoken out on the issue — said Wednesday that he refers to the phones as “weapons of mass destruction” because of the potential dangers for which they can be used.
“No one should have to go through what I went through,” Johnson said. “But I also believe that the Lord chose my wife and I to go through this because someone had to carry the banner, and he chose us to do it.”
South Carolina tested the tech in 2008
South Carolina has been the testing ground for state prison cell phone jamming. In 2008, the FCC allowed the state to conduct a one-time test of a jamming system at a maximum-security prison, where a briefcase-sized device emitted a frequency that immediately shut down cell phones around an auditorium; outside, cell service was uninterrupted.
Another test took place at a different state prison in 2019, the first time federal officials collaborated with a state prison for such a test. A year earlier, seven South Carolina inmates died in the worst U.S. prison riot in 25 years, a gang fight officials said was orchestrated in part using illegal cell phones.
The FCC has shown willingness to work on eradicating prison cell phones, holding a 2016 field hearing in South Carolina and hosting meetings with members of Congress, prisons officials and stakeholders from the wireless industry.
Since becoming FCC chairman, Carr has signaled that the agency was ready to move on jamming, announcing the upcoming vote last month in an appearance with U.S. Sen. Tom Cotton, R-Ark., who has led multiple pushes to change federal legislation to allow state use of the technology.
Groups that advocate for inmates’ rights have opposed the move, arguing that the high rates inmates must pay to use official prison phones have pushed them toward using contraband cell phones just to stay in touch with family. The telecommunications industry has long argued against it, too, saying that jamming technology risks interfering with legitimate communications.
On Wednesday, Carr said that he felt the industry was softening on jamming, in part due to recognition of the problem’s size as well as agencies’ experiments with targeted technologies.
“We aren’t considering jamming outside this unique context,” Carr said. “Maybe people aren’t cheering it on from industry, but the opposition has receded substantially.”
___
Meg Kinnard can be reached at http://x.com/MegKinnardAP

title: Gorgeous Fall Conditions Last Through The Weekend!
text:
BANGOR, Maine (WABI) - Dry, sunny weather and above-average temperatures will carry us through much of the weekend. A coastal storm may bring beneficial rain to Maine late in the weekend into Monday, followed by a sharp drop in temperatures early next week.
Tonight will remain mild for late November, with lows above freezing in the mid-30s to lower 40s.
Friday and the weekend: More sunshine
Friday will bring plenty of sunshine, with highs once again in the 50s and lower 60s. A dry cold front will pass through Friday evening into early Saturday, trimming temperatures by a few degrees for the weekend.
Even so, highs are expected to remain above average in the 50s. Saturday looks especially nice, with lots of sunshine. Clouds will increase Sunday ahead of our next approaching system.
Sunday into Monday: Watching a possible coastal storm
An area of low pressure is expected to move northeast along the East Coast. The storm will have characteristics of a nor’easter and its track and strength remain uncertain. Those details will determine how much rain reaches Maine.
Rainfall possibilities:
- Stronger storm, farther north: Widespread, beneficial rain is possible, with totals potentially exceeding 1 to 2 inches across much of the region.
- Weaker storm, farther south: Less rain would be expected overall, with the best chance near and southeast of the interstate and Downeast. Those areas could still receive more than an inch.
Monday night into Tuesday: Much colder air arrives
A cold front is expected to move through Monday night into early Tuesday, clearing the storm out and bringing much colder air. Falling temperatures could lead to a flash freeze early Tuesday morning if surfaces are still wet.
From Tuesday onward, highs will generally be in the 30s, with a few lower 40s possible. Overnight lows will fall into the teens and 20s.
Thanksgiving outlook: Another system to watch
We’re also keeping an eye on another possible storm around Thanksgiving. Some forecast models keep the system away from our area, while others bring it into the Northeast with a chance for a wintry mix. It’s still too early to know which scenario will unfold.

title: Penobscot County commissioners approve $41.6 million budget in 2-1 vote
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
BANGOR, Maine (WABI) - Penobscot County commissioners voted 2-1 Wednesday to approve the 2027 budget as recommended by the county’s budget committee.
Commissioner Dan Tremble cast the lone vote against the $41.6 million budget, which is about $6 million higher than last year’s. Commissioner Dave Marshall voted in favor.
The amount the county needs to raise through taxation, after other revenues are accounted for, is expected to increase by approximately 23%. That does not necessarily mean every taxpayer’s bill will rise by 23%; the impact will vary among municipalities and properties.
The increase follows a 15.6% rise in the amount the county needed to raise through taxation for 2026, according to the county’s budget calculation sheet.
Public comment
The vote followed more than an hour of public comment during Wednesday morning’s meeting. Most speakers urged commissioners to reject the budget, citing concerns about potential tax increases.
Brewer Mayor Michele LaBree Daniels said the county’s increases are affecting municipal spending.
“We keep eating these funds and we keep losing things. We were supposed to buy a fire truck last year. We did not do that because of the severity of the county increase,” Daniels said. “So, it’s stopping municipalities from actually doing the things they need to do because we have to keep Penobscot County in their budget.”
Marshall said the approved budget would help stabilize county finances.
“The budget that we have done today, in my opinion, is adequate to keep the county to stop hemorrhaging funds, to stabilize it somewhat. Stabilize, allow us to regroup, refocus. We know what we have to do,” Marshall said.
Jail costs
County officials have identified the cost of operating the jail as a major driver of the increase.
Penobscot County voters rejected a referendum on Election Day that would have allowed a new jail to be built outside the county seat of Bangor.

title: With Nobody on the Nov. 3 Ballot, Gov. Mills May Appoint the County’s Next Treasurer

title: Here’s who’s eligible for money in the $32 million class-action GoodRx settlement
text:
(Gray News) - GoodRx has agreed to a $32 million settlement in a class-action lawsuit that alleged the company disclosed customers’ personal and health information.
The lawsuit alleged GoodRx, a telehealth and prescription coupon company, disclosed customers’ personal and health information to advertising and analytics companies, including Criteo, between at least 2017 and 2020.
Both GoodRx and Criteo denied these allegations but agreed to a $32 million settlement. Now, some GoodRx users may be eligible to receive a payment.
Filing a claim
Settlement class members include those who used a website, app or service made available by or through GoodRx before April 20, 2024, according to the settlement’s website.
Settlement class members have until Dec. 29 to file a claim either by mail or online. You also have until the same date to exclude yourself from the settlement.
If you’re not sure whether you’re included in the settlement class, you can email info@goodrxprivacysettlement.com or call 1-877-888-9232 for more information.
The amount of each payment will depend on the number of claims approved.
A final hearing on the settlement is scheduled for Feb. 11, 2027.

title: GTA 6 economic hit? Experts say buzzy math is bunk
text:
Test-driving the math: Will Grand Theft Auto 6 have gamers skipping work and hurting the US economy?
Are you a gamer who’s planning to suddenly be struck by a stomach bug on Nov. 19? Or did you request paid time off that day?
This story was originally published on PolitiFact.com.
Viral online claims say you would be one of 1.5 million Americans planning to skip work the same day you can test-drive the much-anticipated Grand Theft Auto 6, Rockstar Games’ first new installment of the popular video game series since 2013.
The game, which had 17 million preorders as of Nov. 18 and is expected to earn upwards of $3 billion, is set in a fictionalized version of Florida known as Vice City. Rockstar creators traveled to Miami and other state locales while researching for the game, media reports show.
Social media posts and news reports have repeated the 1.5 million figure, and said the game’s release day could cost the U.S. economy $1 billion in lost productivity.
But is either number accurate? Not likely, experts say.
Nicholas Bloom, a Stanford University economics professor, estimated that perhaps 5% of full-time U.S. workers play Grand Theft Auto and only a fraction of those would take the day off, rather than just wait until after work or another day.
“I really don’t believe these numbers unless it’s backed up by a population-representative survey,” Bloom said. “It seems more like social media clickbait.”
Where the claim originated
We found no official survey or published study that shows either 1.5 million workers planning time off or $1 billion in lost productivity.
The earliest reference we found to the $1 billion figure is in a July 2025 article on Spanish broadcaster Cadena SER’s website. That article cited José García-Montalvo, a Pompeu Fabra University in Barcelona economics professor, but does not attribute either figure to him. He spoke about the profile of gamers who might stay home to play the new game, mainly men ages 18 to 30.
The article’s first paragraph references $1 billion in lost productivity, but does not give a source for that calculation or say how it was calculated. It does not mention 1.5 million workers calling in sick.
Many social media posts and news reports are citing those figures or an International Business Times story that referenced the interview, but the Times has published conflicting information about those numbers and their attribution. Two International Business Times articles said neither the 1.5 million nor $1 billion figures should be attributed to Garcia-Montalvo from the Cadena SER interview, while others credited him with the math.
PolitiFact reached out to Garcia-Montalvo but did not receive a response.
Estimates vary on GTA 6 days off
Several surveys show that workers are planning time off around the game’s release.
BambooHR says about 18% of U.S. workers planned to request paid time off on Nov. 19, 13% higher than equivalent days in past years. It based the calculations on a dataset that includes more than 3.4 million active workers and a survey of 1,500 salaried workers.
PCMag said a survey it commissioned showed 8% of adult gamers planned to take PTO or adjust their work or school schedules to play the game. It said that amounts to about 12.5 million people.
A GameSquare survey of 1,000 people identified as gamers said 10% were planning to take the day off and another 30% were considering it.
How many workers are normally absent?
The thought of 1.5 million workers taking the day off sounds like a lot, but it’s dwarfed by the number of U.S. workers who typically miss work.
The Bureau of Labor Statistics estimated a daily 3.2% absence rate among 121 million full-time salaried workers in 2025. About 2.2% of those absences were because of illness or injury.
That comes out to 3.9 million people absent per day, more than twice what the viral claims say will skip work for GTA 6.
There’s no way to know whether the supposed 1.5 million would be in addition to those normally absent; presumably there would be some overlap. And if people use sick days or PTO, those are days employers were planning to pay absent workers anyway.
Nicholas Huntington-Klein, a Seattle University associate economics professor, said the 1.5 million absent workers estimate seems “quite high.”
If it were accurate, he said, “The big question would be this: are they taking off work on Nov. 19 instead of on some other day? If so then the overall economic impact would be pretty near 0.”
Huntington-Klein guessed the $1 billion calculation likely came from multiplying 1.5 million by the typical workday of eight hours and an estimate of productivity per hour. According to Our World in Data, a global data research nonprofit, the U.S. in 2023 produced about $83.5 an hour.
“All of this hinges very heavily on the idea that these are lost days. It’s much more likely that some huge share of the people skipping work on GTA day will be taking that day off instead of on some other day,” he said.
This story was originally published on PolitiFact.com.
It is republished here as part of a reporting and fact-checking partnership between PolitiFact and Hearst Television.

title: A construction worker is missing in Maine
text:
Editor’s note: Alex Goncalves Dourado has been found safe.
A construction worker is missing in Maine.
Alex Goncalves Dourado has been working for the past few weeks for an unknown construction company in the Bethel area, according to the Oxford County Sheriff’s Office.
Dourado told his family recently that he wasn’t feeling well, the sheriff’s office said Wednesday.
He doesn’t have his own phone, and his family has attempted unsuccessfully to reach him.
Anyone with information about Dourado’s whereabouts can call Oxford County dispatchers at 207-743-9554.

title: Cause of death released for man who fell from Six Flags Over Georgia roller coaster
text:
ATLANTA (ANF/Gray News) — The cause of death for the man who fell from a Six Flags Over Georgia roller coaster in October has been released.
Hassan Kariem, 42, died of blunt force injuries, according to the report. The autopsy, which was performed on Oct. 13, one day after Kariem’s death, revealed the man’s traumatic injuries, including skull and bone fractures and lacerations on several organs.
Kariem’s death was listed as accidental, according to the report.
Kariem, who was sitting next to his niece on the Goliath, hit four other people when he was ejected from the roller coaster, injuring them. The riders had to be helped from the ground and the park was evacuated.
The investigation into the accident is ongoing, and the Goliath roller coaster is still closed.
Six Flags Over Georgia said it plans to add seat belts in addition to the existing lap restraints.
Several other roller coasters similar to Goliath have been closed at other Six Flags parks.

title: NSB donates $3K to New Beginnings in Lewiston
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
LEWISTON, ME – For more than 45 years, New Beginnings has been there for Maine youth experiencing homelessness, family crisis, and instability. As the organization says, “when a young person has nowhere safe to go, we meet them where they are.”
New Beginnings operates a 24-hour youth shelter named Marian’s Place on 491 Main Street in Lewiston, offers additional supportive housing, and sponsors a street outreach team to help youth in need throughout Maine find safety. The staff provides a warm welcome to youth (ages 10-21), encouragement for family mediation, and case management. The organization helps develop life skills through education and employment support and provides prevention services to curb the risk of homelessness.
Norway Savings Bank is proud to be a longtime supporter of the Lewiston-based nonprofit and is pleased to donate $3,000 to the organization, part of nearly $40,000 in contributions over the past decade.
“Norway Savings Bank’s ongoing investment helps ensure that 24 hours per day and 365 days a year, young people can find a friendly face, kind words, a hot meal, and a warm, safe place to sleep when they have nowhere else to go,” said Chris Bicknell, Executive Director of New Beginnings. “We’re thankful for this help in supporting youth in meeting urgent needs and helping them improve their long-term prospects.”
“The impact of New Beginnings is transformative. It’s so much more than a shelter. They work closely with youth to improve their health and life skills and pursue employment, education, and independence. It really is remarkable,” said Darci Hamm, President of NSB. “NSB is honored to be able to play a small part in helping New Beginnings steer at-risk youth from homelessness towards becoming healthy and flourishing adults.”
New Beginnings has a 24-hour helpline for anyone in need of assistance at 207-795-4070. To learn more about the organization, including the many ways in which you can help New Beginnings with its mission, visit www.newbeginmaine.org.

title: Body camera video shows arrest of mother after toddler nearly dies from fentanyl overdose
text:
CHANDLER, Ariz. (KPHO/Gray News) — Police in Arizona have released body camera video showing the arrest of a mother after her toddler nearly overdosed on fentanyl this summer.
Police said the boy’s grandmother called 911 at about 4:45 p.m. on June 27 from a home in Chandler.
Officer Zach Hardman was the first to arrive.
A woman who identified herself as the boy’s grandmother handed him the toddler.
“He was just so limp. He was breathing, but it was getting worse at the time,” Hardman said in a video shared by Chandler police.
According to court documents, the 17-month-old child was pale and limp, his eyes had rolled back, and he was breathing abnormally.
Hardman gave the boy Narcan, a medication used to reverse opioid overdoses.
“Once I administered that Narcan, his trend definitely started to get better,” Hardman said.
The boy was taken to a hospital and recovered from the reported overdose.
Police said the toddler’s mother, 28-year-old Alexis Sipple, had left the home before officers arrived.
Home surveillance video showed the mother leaving, and court documents said she appeared to be trying to evade police by attempting to take an Uber out of the neighborhood.
Officers found Sipple hiding next to a trash can in a neighbor’s backyard. Body camera video showed officers telling her to stand up. Sipple can be heard asking, “Is he OK?”
Officers then handcuffed her and placed her in a police vehicle.
Sipple was arrested on a felony child abuse charge.
“When you put your child in danger like that, you deserve to face justice,” Hardman said.
During a search, detectives noted finding drug paraphernalia in the bedroom Sipple shared with her two children.
Court documents said officers found aluminum foil and a black straw between the mattress and box spring, as well as two bottles of methadone.
Sipple pleaded guilty to felony child abuse.
On Oct. 13, Sipple was sentenced to one year in jail and 10 years of probation, with credit for time served and early release granted for an inpatient substance abuse treatment program, court documents stated.
Court records also showed Sipple had three prior felony convictions.
“My main goal is to better myself for my children, to go to treatment, and go back into college so I can pursue my dreams,” Sipple said during sentencing. “I have definitely learned my lesson.”
Hardman said he has children around the same age as the toddler involved.
“I have children that age, so it hit home a little bit more for me,” he said. “So, I was just so relieved that he was going to be OK. It just means a lot to be able to be there, to be able to provide care and aid to this kid.”
