title: Belfast Maskers’ ‘Keely & Du’ finds new urgency in a post-Roe world
text:
Keely is determined to end her pregnancy because she was violently raped by her ex-husband and is not ready for motherhood. Du and Walter are members of an anti-abortion religious cult that kidnaps women outside clinics and holds them prisoner, forcing the women to give birth. Keely is one of their prisoners.
The Belfast Maskers beautifully bring this provocative play, “Keely & Du,” to life this weekend at the Basil Burwell Community Theater, the company’s home in the former Unitarian Universalist Church. The Maskers first performed the play in 2000 in their former space on the waterfront.
Some may find the script full of cliches and its abortion debate dated. But the U.S. Supreme Court’s overturning of Roe v. Wade four years ago, which left abortion laws to the states, has given the play’s questions about who controls a pregnancy a new urgency, and the performances are raw and moving.
“Keely & Du” was written in the early 1990s by Jane Martin, a pseudonym for a playwright whose true identity has never been confirmed. It was a finalist for the 1994 Pulitzer Prize for Drama and won the 1993 American Theatre Critics Association Award for Best New Play.
Director Cassidy R. Small wrote in her program notes that the productions that have stayed with her most dealt with the hardest topics. “Life is hard, and it’s messy, and people make choices that other people don’t agree with or that even actively hurt others; where else is it better to explore those terrible and messy topics than a show?” she wrote.
And explore them she does, with a fine cast. There’s nothing subtle about “Keely & Du,” and there is no middle ground. Walter offers Keely what he calls a choice: She can give the baby up for adoption or raise it as a single mother. Keely vehemently refuses, as Du, a retired nurse who lost a daughter and raised three sons, tries to convince the young woman there are rewards to motherhood.
The heart of this play is the relationship between Keely and Du and how they grow close even though neither woman gives ground on her stance on abortion. Ahnna-Balai Beane and Amanda Chung as Keely and Du, respectively, work beautifully together and create three-dimensional characters who grow to care for each other despite their differences.
Beane’s Keely is all desperate anger. Her outrage over being raped, then kidnapped, spills out of her like a pot boiling over.
Chung’s Du is a kind and caring woman incapable of understanding how Keely could terminate her pregnancy, despite the violent conception. She comes to view the young woman as a surrogate daughter and, in the end, sacrifices herself to save Keely. Chung creates a sympathetic and likable character despite Du’s actions. That is an enormous accomplishment for an actress who returned to the stage in this show after a 20-year absence.
Peter Conant is pitch-perfect as Walter, a sanctimonious, self-righteous preacher who leads the cult. He is focused only on the “unborn babies” and is unmoved by Keely’s insistence that she could not love a child conceived in violence. Taylor Sherritt is convincing as the seemingly reformed Cole, Keely’s ex-husband and rapist, who begs and pleads with Keely to take him back so they can be a family. Sherritt’s performance is so nuanced that it’s impossible to tell if he’s truly a changed man.
“Keely & Du” is made up of many short scenes, and this production is dragged down by slow transitions between them, a perpetual problem the Maskers have not been able to remedy. The show runs about two hours without an intermission, and tighter transitions could have cut 10 to 15 minutes from the running time.
The Belfast Maskers’ production of “Keely & Du” will be performed at 7 p.m. Friday and Saturday and at 2 p.m. Sunday at the Basil Burwell Community Theater, 17 Court St., Belfast. For more information, visit belfastmaskers.com.

title: No turkey? No problem: Bangor seniors get a helping hand with Thanksgiving dinner
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
BANGOR, Maine (WABI) - Turkey is at the top of many grocery lists this week, but some local seniors will be enjoying a different kind of bird for Thanksgiving.
Bangor’s First Assembly Church created First Hope 30 years ago to help ease food costs for senior citizens.
For $27, recipients get about $70 worth of groceries delivered every month.
With Thanksgiving around the corner, the 60 November baskets include holiday staples like cranberry sauce and cookie dough. But many seniors live alone and told organizers that they didn’t want a whole turkey to themselves.
Hearing that, First Hope opted to provide whole chickens instead of turkeys.
To support the mission, Penquis donated small chickens to all 22 residents of Miller Square on Harlow, a Bangor older adult housing complex, who use First Hope.
“This building alone, there’s a lot of people that can’t get out to get anything, so they depend on anybody here or their families to bring their stuff into. So, it’s really a great deal,” said Patty Baker, a resident of Miller Square.
For people who can’t easily get to a food pantry, First Hope deliveries help make a Thanksgiving dinner more accessible.
“When this started 30 years ago, it started because gas and oil was high. Gas and oil is high again,” explained Beth Weston, coordinator for First Hope. “For us now, because we’re bringing it to the people, we feel like we’re meeting a need that nobody else is as far as delivering packages.”
First Hope delivers groceries on the fourth Saturday of every month.
If you’d like to get involved or hear more about the services, you can reach Weston by phone at 207-992-7473 or by email bmwbirds1@yahoo.com
Miller Square on Harlow will be hosting a craft fair Saturday. It will run from 9 a.m. to 3 p.m. and features raffles and handmade items for purchase.

title: Pitcher-turned-actor Lance Broadway dies at age 43 at Dallas apartment complex
text:
Pitcher-turned-actor Lance Broadway dies at age 43 at Dallas apartment complex
Lance Broadway, a major league pitcher who became an actor following his baseball career, has died. He was 43.
His cause of death was not immediately clear. The report posted Thursday by the Dallas County Medical Examiner’s Office said Broadway died Tuesday in a stairwell at an apartment complex near Love Field Airport.
Dallas Police did not immediately respond to an open records request for reports involving Broadway's death.
Broadway pitched in college at Dallas Baptist and Texas Christian. He was taken in the first round of the 2005 draft by the Chicago White Sox and appeared in a total of 27 games for them and the New York Mets from 2007-09.
He made his movie debut in “Olympus Has Fallen” in 2013 and appeared in several television series.

title: Record amount raised at gala for Ronald McDonald House Maine
text:
Record amount of $240K raised for Ronald McDonald House Maine
Ronald McDonald House Maine hosted its 26th annual gala in Portland on Friday night, raising a record amount of money for families with children receiving medical treatment.
Organizers announced on Thursday that the event, hosted by WMTW's Jon Chrisos and Meghan Torjussen, raised $240,000 for Ronald McDonald House Maine programs. That is a 47% increase over the total from last year.
"Whether you donated to our auction, attended the Gala, or sponsored the event, thank you. Your support allows us to provide free accommodations, meals, and support to thousands of Maine families each year during the most challenging times in their lives," Ronald McDonald House Maine said in a statement on Thursday.
Ronald McDonald House Maine provides families with a place to stay near the hospital while their children receive treatment. It's a home away during some of the most challenging times for families. Families are not charged to stay at the houses, making fundraising and donations an important part of the organization's work.
WMTW is the official broadcast partner of Ronald McDonald House Maine.

title: Kittery voters could approve a water district debt limit in December. What’s that mean?
text:
Kittery residents will vote in December on whether to approve a debt limit increase for the town’s water district, which is preparing to make significant infrastructure improvements.
The referendum comes amid a nearly four-month severe water restriction for Kittery Water District customers.
If voters approve the change on Dec. 30, the debt limit will be set at $75 million. The limit won’t immediately change services, and the district isn’t required to borrow that amount to complete planned capital improvements, Superintendent Matthew Berube said.
Instead, the limit is a guide that’ll help the district make “sound infrastructure investments,” Berube said, and comply with its charter, which is part of state law. (Depending on how its charter is written, a district may be required to establish limits if it needs to take out loans for improvements.)
Under Kittery Water’s previous charter — which Berube described as “open-ended” — there was no language to establish a specific borrowing limit.
The charter was rewritten in 2021 to require a limit when town officials realized the water district needed to begin planning improvements that include: replacing aging water mains, which have had a handful of severe leaks in recent months; expanding its treatment facility; and maintaining a stable water supply.
Now that the district has determined the improvements that should be made, it can set a specific borrowing limit.
The decision to finance the improvements allows the district to spread the cost of the projects over several years instead of immediately raising customers’ rates.
Conversely, nearby York Water District doesn’t have a debt limit because its charter doesn’t require it. Instead, it pays for improvements through rates and bonds, Superintendent Don Neumann said.
“It does not mean I am asking for any loans anytime soon for that or incurring that type of debt,” Berube said. “I’m trying to establish a large enough debt limit so that I’m not trying to do this every year or every couple years for the folks.”
The town of Kittery and its water district are separate entities, but state law requires the majority of local voters to approve. The vote is happening in December because funds need to be secured before a handful of projects can start throughout the next few years.
“I know people are not liking the timing of it, but the timing of it is us reacting to not having a debt limit and needing to get these loans passed,” Berube said.
HOW IS THE LIMIT CALCULATED?
Work on those projects is expected to be completed over the next 10 years, with an expected base of $46 million in capital needs such as water main replacements, sourcing and distribution improvements, and preparation for future projects — though the district hasn’t identified any that would exceed the borrowing limit.
Portsmouth Naval Shipyard, which uses more than half the district’s water supply, also recently began work on its $654 million P1080 project, including a treatment plant upgrade that could cost $90 million to $100 million. The water district plans to contribute $4.2 million — acquired through its own loan from the state revolving fund — for parts of the project not covered by the Navy.
Berube added that the district’s share will provide extra assurance that everyone gets the most out of PNSY’s improvements.
The remaining $29 million of the proposed new limit would account for planning, construction contingencies and inflation. It also comes with a 2% cushion and covers $9.2 million in existing bonds, both for work that’s completed and some that hasn’t begun.
Not every project will require borrowing. Some may also be funded through grants, reserves and other available funds.
HOW WILL APPROVING THE LIMIT IMPACT CUSTOMERS?
Berube said the limit won’t immediately impact water rates. But they’ll naturally increase over time because of the cost of maintaining some of the planned improvements, like the larger treatment plant.
“As things become more efficient, replacement costs — long-term replacement costs — probably will increase just due to inflationary pressures,” Berube said.
In October, roughly two months after enacting severe water usage restrictions for residents, Berube said the district’s source ponds are dangerously low for this time of year. On Nov. 6, the district announced that any new housing developments are temporarily barred from hooking up to the district’s water supply. These restrictions have been imposed as Maine remains mired in a monthslong drought that has shown little sign of positive progress.
The improvements are meant to mitigate recurring issues like leaks and low supply, which the district says will help prevent similar restrictions in the future.
If the referendum is rejected, the district would have fewer opportunities to finance the remaining improvements because of the charter requirements, and would need to rely on increased rates and other sources to complete work.
The district will hold a public hearing Dec. 16 at Kittery Town Hall ahead of the Dec. 30 vote.

title: I’m the new crime and justice reporter for the Bangor Daily News
text:
Hi, my name is Sabrina Martin, and I’m the Bangor Daily News’ new crime and justice reporter.
In this new role, I will prioritize stories that serve the Bangor community by holding people in power accountable to the public. I’ll follow criminal and civil court cases, law enforcement trends and any public safety story that could affect Mainers.
I was previously the BDN’s Ellsworth and Acadia reporter, covering a range of topics that mattered to Hancock County residents, from the most important City Council decisions to the latest changes at Acadia National Park under the Trump administration.
Before joining the BDN, I lived in Washington, D.C., and worked as the investigative reporter at the Alexandria Times. There, I covered a group of alleged gang members indicted on murder charges and the city’s parks and recreation department, which was accused of lying to OSHA officials, among other stories.
I graduated from Northwestern University’s Medill School of Journalism and spent two years working for a Chicago-based social services agency after college.
I was born and raised in a Maryland suburb of D.C.
I spend much of my free time worrying about my puppy, Lucas.
I look forward to serving the Bangor community with fair and accurate coverage of all things crime and justice. I welcome any and all tips or questions. You can reach me at smartin@bangordailynews.com and 301-922-2222.

title: Tractor-trailer hauling french fries crashes after Maine driver spilled hot coffee on his lap
text:
A tractor-trailer hauling french fries rolled over Wednesday night when the driver spilled hot coffee on his lap.
The 63-year-old Brunswick man was driving the 2024 Western Star south on Interstate 95 in Herseytown Township about 11:54 p.m. when he spilled hot coffee on his lap and then lost control of the truck, according to Maj. Aaron Turcotte, a spokesperson for the Maine Department of Public Safety.
The tractor-trailer rolled over into the median, Turcotte said Thursday morning.
The driver wasn’t injured.
Work to remove the tractor-trailer from the median began about 8 a.m. Thursday. That was expected to cause a lane closure for several hours.
Herseytown Township is northeast of Millinocket in Penobscot County.

title: Uplift LA announces 35 nominees for 2026 Finest Under 40 Awards

text:
LEWISTON AUBURN, ME – Uplift LA is recognizing 35 outstanding young professionals across 10 categories as part of its 10th year of the Finest Under 40 awards program. Community members have through November 16 to cast their votes and help recognize the next generation of leaders making a difference throughout Androscoggin County.
Finest Under 40 celebrates professionals under the age of 40 who live, work or play in Androscoggin County. The program recognizes individuals who are making an impact through their professional achievements, community involvement and contributions to the region.
This year’s nominees will be evaluated through a combination of community voting and selection committee scoring. Community votes will account for 30% of each nominee’s overall score, while a selection committee will review nominees based on three additional criteria:
Community Vote: 30%
Professional Achievement: 30%
Community Involvement: 20%
Impact and Results: 20%
“The future of our community is being shaped by the nominees that are all inspiring us with their drive, commitment, and hard work. Finest Under 40 is such an incredible opportunity for the rising professionals in our region to be honored and shown that their dedication is making a true impact,” said Sarah Keady, Uplift LA Chair Elect.
Community voting closed November 16.
“There is no better way to uplift our rising professionals than recognizing and celebrating the great work they do, day in and day out! The smiles go farther than we realize!” said Mikayla Plourde, Uplift LA Chair.
The 2026 Finest Under 40 honorees will be announced during the Awards Celebration on Friday, November 20, at 6 p.m. at the Hilton Garden Inn Auburn Riverwatch. The celebration will bring together nominees, colleagues, friends, family and community members to recognize the accomplishments and contributions of this year’s honorees.
Tickets are available to the public, and everyone is welcome to attend and celebrate these outstanding individuals. More information and ticket registration are available at upliftlamaine.com/finest-under-40/.

title: InvestigateTV+: Banning nitrous oxide retail sales
text:
(InvestigateTV) — A fight to ban recreational use of nitrous oxide heads to the nation’s capital. InvestigateTV+ explores the dangers and we introduce you to two moms who say their battle stems from personal pain.
Plus, we reveal how drone technology is transforming the process of matching patients with organ donors.
Then, how one woman’s idea to give back to her community evolves into a network of moms helping other moms.
High Stakes
Nitrous oxide, a product known as “laughing gas”, is used for legitimate purposes in dental and medical offices as well as culinary and industrial settings.
But InvestigateTV and Gray affiliate stations across the country have been documenting deaths and injuries involving people who have used it as a recreational drug by inhaling the gas.
Could drones help transport organs?
Federal data shows that the most common wait time for an organ transplant is between one and two years. Some people can remain on the list for five or more years.
In Missouri, a first-of-its-kind project aims to cut down on the time between identifying and confirming whether a potential donor is an exact match.
Mid-America Transplant is now using drones to transport donor blood samples.
Singing to stay sharp
For many of the 150 members of the Adult Symphony Chorus, singing alongside the renowned Nashville Symphony is more than a hobby.
It’s helping their voices — and brains — stay sharp.
Helping single mom with new car
It’s not like an episode of Oprah, but for single moms like Caroline Reed, it feels pretty close.
She was gifted with a white car topped with a big red bow, all thanks to Amanda Todd and her village.
To understand the gift is to learn about the journey.

title: 'I’m not MAGA': Elon Musk backs away from Trump's brand
text:
'I’m not MAGA': Elon Musk backs away from Trump's brand after Republicans' midterm election washout
Elon Musk was in the front row at Donald Trump's second inauguration and has spent hundreds of millions of dollars trying to help the Republican president and his “Make America Great Again” allies win elections.
Now, after Republicans' midterm thrashing by Democrats, the world's richest man insists he's not a MAGA acolyte after all and feels “pretty foolish” for spending so much money on the cause.
“I mean, I’m not MAGA,” Musk told The New York Times on Wednesday during the newspaper's DealBook Summit.
“I’m not sure what MAGA means,” Musk continued, “but I, I don’t think I’m, like, if, if that means sort of blind adherence to a set of policies by the Republican Party, then I certainly don’t have that. I think there are, there, there are positives and negatives in both parties.”
Musk, who has based himself and several of his companies in Texas, spent more than $400 million on Trump-aligned Republicans running in November. That included more than $150 million backing Texas Senate nominee Ken Paxton, who lost to Democrat James Talarico — Democrats' first statewide victory there in more than 30 years.
Musk said if he had a do-over, he “probably” would have “spent less money” on the midterms.
“I feel pretty foolish about having spent so much money and not seeing much for it,” Musk told columnist Andrew Sorkin. “Or maybe it would’ve been much worse without that. But it certainly shows that American elections are not just about money.”
That's all a stark contrast to how Musk has behaved for the last several years.
He sat alongside other Big Tech titans at Trump's inauguration and led the president's Department of Government Efficiency, a post that for months made him the most high-profile figure in the administration other than Trump himself.
Hours after Trump was sworn in on Jan. 20, 2025, Musk appeared at a Trump rally in Washington, where he enthusiastically embraced the president's agenda and his supporters.
“This was no ordinary victory,” he said. “This was a fork in the road of human civilization. OK? There are elections that come and go. Some elections are important, some are not. But this one really mattered. I just want to say thank you for making it happen. Thank you. My heart goes out to you. It is thanks to you that the future of civilization is assured.”

title: Investigators reclassify 1975 disappearance of Washington, Maine man as homicide
text:
WASHINGTON, Maine (WABI) - The Maine State Police Major Crimes Unit and the Attorney General’s Office said the 1975 disappearance of Ludger Belanger, who vanished during a deer hunt, has been recategorized as a homicide. Investigators said the person they believe is responsible has died.
Disappeared after being dropped off
Belanger, then 25, disappeared after being dropped off to go deer hunting in the woods near his home on Route 105 in Washington.
His wife, Linda Perkins, said he was going out for an hour or two. He never returned home.
New technology and the investigation
Officials said new technology helped investigators uncover leads, evidence and a person of interest in the 51-year-old case.
During the investigation, detectives traveled to multiple towns and states to conduct interviews and search wooded areas, bodies of water and wells. Belanger’s body has not been found.
Case remains open
Officials said the case remains open to pursue leads to the location of Belanger’s body so his family might bring him home.
State police said people can submit tips by calling 207-624-7076, extension 9.

title: Then and now: A look at the cost of living when the last 'Grand Theft Auto' game was released
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Then and now: A look at the cost of living when the last 'Grand Theft Auto' game was released
"Grand Theft Auto VI" was officially released to the world on Thursday, Nov. 19, a whopping 13 years after the last mainline entry in the "Grand Theft Auto" video game series was released.
It's an uncommonly long development period for one of the world's most profitable intellectual properties. The new game has already pulled in $1.7 billion, and it's not even widely available in the U.S. yet.
The world has changed a lot since "Grand Theft Auto V" was released in 2013, and the internet has been ablaze in recent days with social media posts of pictures comparing the state of affairs in 2013 to now.
But what does that change look like when it comes to the cost of living?
In 2013, when gamers were first cruising the streets of Los Santos, Rockstar Games' fictional interpretation of Los Angeles, it cost them $3.63 per gallon to fuel up on regular unleaded.
This year, it'll set them back an average of $4.45 a gallon to drive around Vice City, Rockstar's approximation of Miami. And they'll want to be conscious of that, as fueling up is an actual game mechanic in the latest entry in the series.
The housing market was also very different in 2013. According to the U.S. Census Bureau, the median price of a single-family home when "GTA V" was released in September 2013 was $269,800. In comparison, the median price of a house in 2026 is about $393,000, according to the Federal Reserve Bank.
According to information from the Bureau of Labor Statistics, a dozen eggs cost $1.91 in 2013 versus $2.32 this year. A gallon of milk used to cost $3.46 but now averages $4.10, and a pound of ground beef — once priced at $3.40 — will now set you back $6.76.
In general, prices are now about 45% higher than they were in 2013. One dollar in 2013 is about the equivalent of $1.45 today.
The Bureau of Labor Statistics says that something that cost $100 in 2013 costs about $144.88 today. The inflation rate in 2013 was 1.5%, and total inflation from 2013 to October 2026 was 45%.
The cost of the game itself has also increased. When "Grand Theft Auto V" was released in 2013, the cost of the standard edition of the game was $49.99. Now, the standard edition of its sequel will go for $79.99, with an "ultimate" edition marketed at $99.99.

title: High school valedictorians to get custom Nike Air Force 1s thanks to Sen.-elect Scott Colom
text:
(AP) - Nike is gifting high school valedictorians across the country with a pair of custom sneakers after Mississippi’s incoming senator appealed to the company on social media.
Scott Colom, who is poised to become the state’s first Black U.S. senator since Reconstruction, called on the sneaker giant to honor his historic election by giving every high school valedictorian in his state a pair of custom Air Force 1s -- his favorite style. The sneakers cost between $90 and $180 on the company’s web site.
“It would encourage MS students to hit the books the rest of the year! #justdoit,” the Democrat suggested Monday on X, referencing Nike’s famous slogan.
The company accepted the challenge and took it one step further.
“The athlete mindset makes things possible, including this idea,” Oregon-based Nike responded Tuesday on X. “@scott_colom, we’ll do you one better… For this year, 2026/2027 high school valedictorians from across the U.S., let’s go!”
Nike said more details would be forthcoming, but Colom has already suggested the custom sneaker should give a nod to Hiram Revels, a fellow Mississippian who was the first African American to serve in Congress when he took office in 1870.
“I’m so proud of @Nike for stepping up to motivate students across the country in this historic moment. This is the #justdoit mentality that makes your company great,” he wrote on X on Tuesday. “Please consider honoring Hiram Revels in the design.”
Colom, a 43-year-old local prosecutor, narrowly defeated Republican Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith in this month’s midterm elections.
When he takes office in January, he’ll become the state’s third Black senator, following Revels and Blanche Kelso Bruce, who was the only formerly enslaved person to serve in the U.S. Senate when he took office in 1875.
Colom’s victory marked a major shift in the Magnolia State, which has the nation’s largest proportional share of Black people but for decades has largely been controlled by white conservatives. The last time Mississippi chose a new Democratic senator was 1947; the winner was a staunch segregationist.

title: Trump administration urges judge to lift order blocking Kennedy Center's two-year closure
text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — President Donald Trump’s administration on Thursday urged a federal judge to lift a court order blocking its plans to close the Kennedy Center for two years of renovation work on the cultural and arts venue.
U.S. District Judge Christopher Cooper didn’t immediately rule from the bench after hearing arguments on the government’s request to dissolve the preliminary injunction that he issued in May. In that order, Cooper ruled that the Kennedy Center board’s vote to close the facility was “ill-informed and seemingly preordained” with no regard for its legal obligations.
A Democratic member of Congress sued to challenge Trump’s takeover of the Kennedy Center — a key piece of the Republican president’s campaign to leave his personal stamp on some of the most iconic landmarks in the nation’s capital.
In August and September, the center’s board voted twice to close its main building for two years to complete the planned repairs. Government lawyers said in a court filing that the center has become “dangerously dilapidated and decrepit,” with a ceiling partially collapsing in early September.
Justice Department attorney William Jankowski argued that the court’s review of the board’s decision must be “very, very deferential.”
“Plaintiff does not dispute the need for construction at the Kennedy Center,” Jankowski told the judge. “The board’s decisions here were reasonable, and they must stand.”
At the close of Thursday’s hearing, Cooper — who was nominated to the bench by Democratic President Barack Obama — didn’t specify how soon he would rule.
Cooper asked an attorney for the plaintiff, Rep. Joyce Beatty of Ohio, how keeping the injunction in place indefinitely would benefit the center and the public.
Beatty’s attorney Nathaniel Zelinsky warned the judge that lifting the order now would “embolden future breaches and misbehavior” by the administration. He urged Cooper to appoint an independent monitor to protect the center if he does dissolve the injunction.
“There’s a monumental breach of fiduciary duty that is ongoing,” Zelinsky said.
The judge asked what authority he has to appoint a monitor to oversee the center’s operations.
“It’s pretty standard trust law,” Zelinsky replied.
Beatty, an ex officio member of the Kennedy Center board, sued last December to prevent the addition of Trump’s name to the center. Beatty subsequently challenged the closing plans, too.
In May, when Cooper initially blocked the administration from closing the center for renovations, he also ruled that Trump’s name was illegally added to the building.
Beatty’s attorneys urged the judge to keep the injunction in place. The center’s closure plan is a “Band-Aid” designed to cover up officials’ mismanagement and to please Trump, they argued in a court filing.
Last year, Congress appropriated roughly $257 million for maintenance on the main building at the center’s request. Performing the work in phases, with partial closures spaced out over four years, would allow the center to remain open to patrons, Beatty’s lawyers argued.
A center official who consulted with Trump concluded that a total closure over two years would be the “most cost-effective and efficient path” to addressing the center’s infrastructure needs, government lawyers counter.

title: Judge issues 14-day extension of order blocking Trump’s memorial arch in DC
text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — A federal judge on Wednesday temporarily extended an order blocking the Trump administration from breaking ground on a towering memorial arch in the nation’s capital.
The temporary restraining order was due to expire on Thursday, but U.S. District Judge Tanya Chutkan extended it by 14 days. That would keep President Donald Trump’s construction project on hold until Dec. 3 or until Chutkan rules on a pending request for a more permanent preliminary injunction.
The decision followed a Nov. 5 order Chutkan issued shortly after a hearing of the National Capital Planning Commission ended with the Trump-heavy commission giving the arch its final approval in an 8-4 vote, despite dozens of witnesses who opposed the construction.
The administration said the work could begin as soon as the approval and the Interior Department issued a final decision authorizing construction and the proper notification was published by the National Park Service.
In issuing the latest delay, Chutkan granted a request by plaintiffs in lawsuits challenging the arch construction. The case has grown more complicated as separate groups have filed lawsuits asking that the project not be allowed to go forward.
Nicolas Sansone, an attorney with the Public Citizen Litigation Group that is representing the plaintiffs in the original lawsuit, said they were “gratified to see that the judge recognized that the circumstances that required emergency relief two weeks ago haven’t changed. We’re hopeful the additional two-week pause will give the court the opportunity to assess our arguments in favor of a longer-term preliminary injunction that will block construction of the arch while the lawsuit proceeds.”
“An activist district court has again blocked the construction of the long-awaited Military Triumphal Arch. The judiciary should not be abused to politicize a structure designed to unite our nation,” said White House spokesman Davis Ingle in an emailed statement. “We will continue making the case for this beautiful and fitting monument and are confident we will be fully vindicated as this litigation proceeds.”
The District of Columbia and Virginia filed suit Oct. 31. Chutkan consolidated that suit with the original, filed by a group of Vietnam veterans and an architectural historian. Members of the Kennedy family filed a separate lawsuit Nov. 10, citing the impact the 250-foot (76-meter) structure would have on family members buried at Arlington National Cemetery. The Arlington County Board filed a lawsuit Oct. 8 in federal court in the Eastern District of Virginia challenging the speed with which the project was being undertaken and the harm it would cause to the county, which is immediately adjacent to the proposed site.
Chutkan said the 14-day extension of the order is warranted because nothing has significantly changed in the litigation in the two weeks since she issued it. She decided to maintain the status quo pending her ruling on the injunction request.
The arch is one of several projects around Washington that Trump has undertaken as he remakes the city, from renovating one of its storied public golf courses to threatening to demolish the John F. Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts. Those projects could soon face greater scrutiny after the Democrats take control of Congress.
Many of those plans are being challenged in the courts. The federal government Thursday filed a notice of appeal to a 14-day temporary restraining order issued Nov. 14 in the golf course case.
The original plaintiffs in the District of Columbia case — three veterans and a retired architectural historian — had asked Chutkan to prohibit the administration and the National Park Service “from taking any steps to construct, or to direct or facilitate construction of, any structure in Memorial Circle, absent congressional authorization, during the pendency of this litigation.”
Critics, including the plaintiffs, argue the administration must seek congressional approval for the arch and say that, once built, it will disrupt the sightlines connecting historic landmarks in the nation’s capital. The administration has argued that Congress decades ago cleared the way for a monument at Memorial Circle.

title: Jackson 5 star Marlon Jackson reveals Stage 4 prostate cancer diagnosis
text:
Jackson 5 star Marlon Jackson reveals Stage 4 prostate cancer diagnosis
Marlon Jackson, a member of the Jackson 5 and the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame, has revealed that he has stage 4 prostate cancer.
The 69-year-old singer revealed this week that he’s been battling prostate cancer for four years.
But Jackson said his diagnosis has not slowed him down. "I'm great. I'm good. Bad grass don't die. So, I'm going to be around for a long time," Jackson said on an episode of the “Farah Shammas Podcast.”
Related video above | New prostate cancer screening recommendations
“I’ve had my prostate gland removed and I’ve had radiation treatment and everything is fine. Everything is great,” Jackson said.
Stage 4 prostate cancer means it has spread to nearby lymph nodes or organs, or to distant parts of the body, according to the National Cancer Institute.
Marlon Jackson was the Jackson 5’s second-youngest member, about a year and a half older than Michael, and the sixth of the Jackson family’s 10 children.
His twin Brandon died soon after birth.
Marlon Jackson formed the group the Jackson 5 with his brothers Jackie, Tito, Jermaine and Michael, performing during its rise to fame at Motown in the late 1960s. The Jackson 5 became one of the era’s most successful pop acts, scoring early hits including “I Want You Back” and “ABC.”
When the brothers left Motown in 1975, they continued recording and performing as the Jacksons, with Marlon among the members. Marlon Jackson also released a solo album, "Baby Tonight," in 1987.

title: Duffy: Ground stop could have been shorter if contractor spotted issue sooner
text:
(AP) - The nationwide ground stop on Friday could have ended sooner if the contractor that did the work linked to the disruptions at key air traffic control facilities had located the problem sooner, according to Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy.
Investigators are still working to determine exactly why the newly installed router at the center of everything started blasting out thousands of connection attempts not long after it was turned on as part of a project to replace a section of old copper wires with fiber optic lines in Arkansas.
Duffy appeared on the 2WAY streaming platform’s “The Morning Meeting” show Wednesday and said that L3Harris failed to identify and isolate the router issue that caused the ground stop quickly enough. That contributed to this being the longest ground stop since the Sept. 11, 2001, terrorist attacks because it lasted more than four hours.
“The monitoring of the network matters,” he said, adding that officials were working on remedying that problem. In the meantime, any new installations of these same routers have been paused, and technicians have disabled the function that was linked to Friday’s outage.
Experts continue testing the equipment linked to the problem to determine why this Juniper router behaved differently from any of the ones installed in 68 previous projects across the FAA network. The investigators are focused on whether the router was configured incorrectly by the experienced technician who did the work or whether it was faulty. The company that made the router has said it believes the “device functioned as it was configured by the installer.”
Friday’s problems are reminiscent of a 2009 outage
The circumstances of the technical problems that led to last week’s nationwide ground stop appear eerily similar to a 2009 outage caused by a technician doing the same kind of work installing new fiber optic lines.
The Transportation Department’s Inspector General said the 2009 disruption that led to 820 delayed flights was caused by a Harris technician setting up a router incorrectly. Harris later became L3Harris as part of a merger, but that company has been operating and maintaining the FAA network for decades.
Matthew Hampton, who was the former assistant inspector general for aviation at that time, said that the FAA has long had weak oversight of the contractors it relies on.
“Poor contractor oversight has been a problem at the FAA in both developing systems and deploying them, there’s a whole history of that,” Hampton said.
Aviation safety expert Jeff Guzzetti, who worked in the Inspector General’s office for several years, said that inadequate oversight of contractors was a problem during the FAA’s last attempt at overhauling their systems called NextGen.
Normally, the FAA is quite good at dealing with unexpected challenges and adjusting quickly by shifting air traffic control responsibilities to a nearby facility when one location is having a problem or slowing traffic temporarily. But Guzzetti said that wasn’t possible this time because the entire network was affected Friday, including both the primary and backup systems.
“The FAA is really good at adapting, improvising and overcoming events. But if the whole system is down, it makes it very challenging,” said Guzzetti, who also investigated crashes for both the FAA and National Transportation Safety Board.
L3Harris hasn’t commented on the ground stop since issuing a statement Saturday pledging to support the FAA’s investigation into what happened. The company declined to say more on Wednesday.
FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford said at a different event hosted by The Hill on Wednesday morning that he understands that his agency is ultimately responsible for what happened even if L3Harris was the one doing the work.
“I am the chief accountability officer. I take full responsibility for it,” Bedford said. “I wish people would lay off the secretary. He’s got a lot of work to do, but I’m the guy they hired to get this done. So, blame me.”
It’s not clear how much more money Congress will approve for the overhaul
The FAA nearly doubled its funding request to Congress to $50 billion after Friday’s ground stop to pay for the rest of the overhaul of the nation’s air traffic control system. Last year, the agency received $12.5 billion to get started on the project. Bedford said he understands why members of Congress might be having “some indigestion associated with that.”
Several key lawmakers said Tuesday that Congress is unlikely to approve that full amount right now — especially when the FAA hasn’t spent all the money that was approved last year. Duffy has said that a big part of why some of the money hasn’t been spent yet is that the new radars and other systems that will be installed are still being built, so he hasn’t been able to buy them yet.
Only about $10 billion of the $50 billion request would go to air traffic control technology. The rest of the money would go to other projects, including upgrades to runways, airport towers and aging air traffic control centers that were built in the 1960s.
More problems are possible while upgrading the outdated FAA system
Chris Sununu, who is president of the Airlines for America trade group, praised Bedford for keeping the airlines informed during the ground stop. Sununu said Bedford asked to set up a conference call with all the airline CEOs and operations leaders within about half an hour of the ground stop starting and briefed them on what he knew so far. Several additional calls were held throughout the ground stop.
“To be honest, he stayed on the phone effectively with all the CEOs all night long,” Sununu said. “We did, I think, three or four calls over the period of the next few hours, brought in those operational folks. And so as they learned more, as they understood more of what was happening.”
Sununu said the FAA has a difficult job in trying to overhaul “what is really the most robust telecom system on the planet while you’re using it 24 hours a day and ensuring the safety of everyone who is part of it.” And he said this might not be the last technical problem that happens during the project because the work the FAA is doing is akin to trying to get your iPhone to talk to your flip phone.
“Can we say, ‘oh, you know, this is really the last time we’re going to have a bump like this?’, No, no. Because the technologies we’re replacing and that we’re asking to talk to each other are literally multigenerational,” he said.
____
Associated Press writers Ben Wieder, David Collins and Sudhin Thanawala contributed to this report.

title: China and Russia say they and US agree on UN reforms, boosting fuel supplies, dialogue on nuclear
text:
SHENZHEN, China (AP) — For U.S. President Donald Trump, the meeting with the leaders of two other nuclear powers -- China’s Xi Jinping and Russia’s Vladimir Putin -- was supposed to be a diplomatic triumph: It would serve as proof that Trump could negotiate with two of America’s toughest rivals.
Before the trio met Thursday in a villa in the Chinese tech hub of Shenzhen, the U.S. president sought to flatter both Xi and Putin as his friends. The wars in Ukraine and Iran were on the agenda, as was reducing the dangers posed by their nuclear arsenals.
But after roughly 70 minutes behind closed doors, they agreed to a far narrower agenda. They would like to reform the United Nations, refine more fossil fuels and curb the reach of the International Criminal Court.
What was billed as a historic trilateral meeting in the end looked like a fleeting photo op. Trump quickly left the villa and boarded Air Force One without saying a word to reporters about his time with Xi and Putin. Still, he hailed the visit as “Highly Consequential” on social media as he made his way back to Washington and announced he would hold a press conference on Friday at the White House.
Following the Shenzhen talks, Trump dialed into a meeting in Berlin between U.S. envoys Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy alongside more than 40 European leaders who are supporting Ukraine’s war effort. Trump told the Berlin gathering that he spoke to Xi and Putin about finding a peaceful end to the Ukraine war, Witkoff said.
The agreements stemming from the trilateral meeting were modest, but the rhetoric that came at the start of it was not.
“We are really making history,” Trump said. “The United States, Russia and China are uniquely positioned to discuss how to reduce the number of nuclear weapons on Earth and also to lessen the risk of those weapons being used.”
After the meeting, Xi called it positive, constructive and fruitful, while Putin described the trilateral talks as open and candid, calling the format “useful and substantive.”
“It is a serious collaborative work,” he said in response to a question about whether the image of the meeting itself mattered more than the substance.
The last nuclear arms pact between Russia and the United States, known as New START, expired in February, and Trump has said he wants “a new, improved and modernized” deal that includes China. But China has less motivation to accept limits given that its arsenal of more than 600 warheads is far smaller than the more than 5,000 warheads believed to be in each of the U.S. and Russian stockpiles.
Daryl Kimball, executive director of the Arms Control Association, said the meeting could at best start a process that would eventually lead to a sustained set of talks for reducing nuclear arsenals.
“We need more than diplomatic theater and photo opportunities between Xi, Putin and Trump,” Kimball said. “And one meeting will not likely produce dramatic breakthroughs.”
The leaders also talked about Iran and trade
The U.S. president earlier had a separate one-on-one with Xi, their third substantial meeting this year.
Trump said they had a shared interest in having oil flow through the Strait of Hormuz, a key waterway for oil shipments from the Middle East that was repeatedly shut because of attacks in the Iran war. Trump suggested he would push Xi to buy more agricultural products from America.
Xi said that relations between the U.S. and China have been “generally stable and improved” during Trump’s presidency. The official Chinese news agency Xinhua reported that Xi discussed Taiwan with Trump and said the two countries needed to improve communication on economic and trade issues.
Trump also added to his calendar a separate sit-down with Putin, marking the first time the leaders have met for talks since their discussions in Alaska last year that failed to broker a deal on Russia’s war in Ukraine.
“Wonderful things can come out of this — or at least start,” Trump said, calling Putin “my friend.”
Trump has frequently boasted of his rapport with Putin, as relations between the U.S. and Ukraine appear to have cratered recently. Trump rejected new Russia sanctions, while Kyiv was undermined by disruptions in satellite support for its drones during the war.
After their trilateral meeting, the three leaders took aim at the International Criminal Court for overstepping its jurisdiction, saying government officials should enjoy immunity from its prosecutions. Putin is wanted by the court, and Trump’s administration has imposed sanctions on ICC officials and the institution itself as part of a campaign to dismantle the tribunal over investigations into the United States and its allies, including Israel.
Trump boasts about his relationships, but the ties between Xi and Putin are stronger
The U.S. president’s ambitions going into the meeting recalled an era of great power politics when wealthier countries felt entitled to decide the fate of seemingly lesser nations. Trump was negotiating with China and Russia without the involvement of Ukraine — or allies like Germany, France, the United Kingdom, Japan and South Korea that also have stakes in the outcome of any talks.
Trump has long believed his ability to create personal connections gives him a diplomatic edge. Xi made a symbolic gesture of friendship Wednesday by taking the unusual step of greeting Air Force One on the tarmac, and the two leaders turned their handshake into a one-armed hug.
But for all the compliments the U.S. president has showered on the two autocrats, he did not always appear to have the same deep relationship based on common interests that Xi and Putin share.
On Wednesday at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit, Xi greeted Putin by calling him “my old friend.” The Russian leader responded by declaring Xi to be his “dear friend.” China has helped economically support Russia after its 2022 invasion of Ukraine, providing Putin with a financial lifeline after the U.S. and its allies imposed new sanctions.
By contrast, when Xi went to the White House for a state visit in September, he was far more restrained with Trump, saying they had built a “personal rapport and stayed in touch.” Trump and Xi have one more meeting planned this year, at the G20 summit in Florida in December.
There were also signs of friction Thursday in the U.S.-China relationship despite Trump’s praise of Xi.
Chinese officials blocked a Bloomberg reporter from the trilateral meeting after she asked a question at the earlier Trump-Xi session. And Chinese television showed a video of Trump appearing drowsy, while the White House posted a clip of Trump helping Xi up an escalator.

title: Could drones help transport organs? Here’s how it might work
text:
ST. LOUIS, Mo. (InvestigateTV) - In 2025, the U.S. saw more organ transplants than ever before with nearly 50,000 transplants. The number of living donors who signed up grew slightly that year too.
Despite this progress, people are still waiting months or even years for the procedure that saves and enhances lives.
Federal data shows that the most common wait time for an organ transplant is between one and two years. Some people can remain on the list for five or more years.
In Missouri, a first-of-its-kind project aims to cut down on the time between identifying and confirming whether a potential donor is an exact match.
Mid-America Transplant is now using drones to transport donor blood samples.
Missouri opened the nation’s first dedicated healthcare drone corridor in April 2026.
The drone path begins near Springfield, Missouri, where blood samples from potential organ and tissue donors will be loaded onto the drone.
After flying around 94 miles, a technician will swap in a fresh battery before the drone completes the 66-mile flight to the St. Louis-area drop point at the Boles Fire Protection District, where the samples will be tested at Mid-America Transplant’s laboratory.
The route follows a defined flight path along existing railway systems several miles north of Interstate 44. The drone flies between 300 and 350 feet above ground level during daylight hours.
Kevin Lee, President and CEO at Mid-America Transplant, said the company expects to cut the travel time down by a third.
Mid-America Transplant said that retrieving a donor blood sample from Springfield previously took more than three hours using ground transport. The drone transport takes less than two hours and costs one-tenth as much.
“Mid-America Transplant has always embraced innovation to enhance donation and transplantation, and this drone corridor represents an exciting step forward,” Lee said. “In our work, every second counts, and faster, more reliable transport of lab samples helps us honor each donor’s gift to its fullest potential.”
If a drone has a malfunction, Lee said it has “multiple redundant systems within them.”
“So, if they have an engine failure, there are backups built into the drone so that it can safely land at a predetermined location by the drone operator. then we will deploy a coordinator to recover that lab sample immediately,” he said.
Right now, the company is only transporting blood samples, but the long-term vision is for the drones to transport kidneys.

title: Maine’s outdoor recreation economy climbs to record $4B
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Maine’s outdoor recreation industry reached a new high in 2025, generating $4 billion in value-added activity, up from $3.9 billion in 2024, according to data released this week by the U.S. Department of Commerce Bureau of Economic Analysis.
The figure marked the highest level recorded since the agency began measuring the sector in 2012.
In 2025, the industry supported more than 32,600 jobs, up from more than 32,000 jobs in 2024. Employees in those jobs earned $1.8 billion in compensation.
Outdoor recreation manufacturing contributed $357 million, up 1.5% from $349 million in 2024.
The industry’s share of gross domestic product fell slightly, accounting for 3.9% in 2025, down from 4% in 2024.
“From heritage names known around the world to startups building the next generation of outdoor gear, Maine’s homegrown outdoor brands are a big part of what makes this economy work,” said Jenny Kordick, executive director of Maine Outdoor Brands.
“Alongside them [are] the guides, outfitters, ski areas and sporting camps that get people outdoors support jobs and communities in every corner of the state. Keeping that momentum takes investment in public access, trails and outdoor infrastructure, and in the Maine businesses that make getting outside possible.”
Top activities
Boating and fishing continued to be the most popular activities, contributing $407 million to the state’s GDP, up from $390 million in 2024.
“Despite boat sales slowly softening since 2020, the recreational boating sector remains a strong contributor to Maine’s economy,” said Stacey Keefer, executive director of the Maine Marine Trades Association. “Many boatyards and marinas currently have waitlists for space and seek to hire more skilled technicians. Additionally, our custom yacht builders work to remain competitive in the global market.”
Recreational vehicle use came in second, with an impact of $269 million. Other top contributors included guided tours and outfitted travel; golf, court and snow activities; and hunting, shooting and trapping.
The numbers illustrate that Maine’s outdoor recreation economy is built on more than one activity or season, said Jeff McCabe, director of the Maine Office of Outdoor Recreation.
“By continuing to invest in outdoor access, infrastructure and workforce development, we can build on this momentum and ensure outdoor recreation remains a vital contributor to Maine’s economy and communities for generations to come,” said McCabe.
Nationally, the outdoor recreation economy generated $1.3 trillion in gross economic output in 2025, and represented 2.3% of U.S. GDP and more than five million jobs.

title: NFL Week 11 schedule, predictions and more
text:
NFL Week 11 schedule, predictions and more
NFL Week 11 schedule, predictions and more
With a solid road win on Monday Night Football, the Los Angeles Chargers earned their first win of the season — the last NFL team to record a victory in the 2026 season.
Video above: How the marching band kept Baltimore's football dreams alive
While it's likely too little too late for the Chargers (and the Miami Dolphins and Tennessee Titans), there are nearly 30 other teams still with playoff hopes.

All game times are in Eastern Standard Time.
Thursday, Nov. 19
Indianapolis Colts (3-7) vs. Houston Texans (3-6), 8:15 p.m.
Houston enters as a huge home favorite and should take care of business easily. While both teams have struggled mightily this season, the Texans' defense gives them the upper hand. The unit is second in the NFL with 33 sacks.

Sunday, Nov. 22
Miami Dolphins (1-8) vs. Buffalo Bills (8-1), 1 p.m.
The Dolphins don't stand a chance against the high-powered offense of Buffalo. As good as Josh Allen has been, leading the offense to an average of 386.7 yards per game, the rushing attack has been what the Bills need to create a balanced attack as the team averages 152.7 yards on the ground per game.
Prediction: Bills 48, Dolphins 14
Baltimore Ravens (4-6) vs. Carolina Panthers (4-5), 1 p.m.
Can the Ravens bounce back from quite an embarrassing loss to the Chargers last week? It was a short week without much time to dwell on it, and maybe playing away from Baltimore with a short week to prepare will allow them to flush it and focus on the Panthers.

New Orleans Saints (3-6) vs. Chicago Bears (7-2), 1 p.m.
The Bears have won four in a row, and they haven't trailed in any of those games. That dominant stretch should continue at home as heavy favorites against the Saints. New Orleans is still reeling after losing on a last-second field goal to the Panthers last week.
Prediction: Bears 38, Saints 17
Tennessee Titans (1-8) vs. Dallas Cowboys (4-6), 1 p.m.
Dak Prescott is primed for a big game as the Cowboys are third in the league in passing, with 265.5 yards per game. The Titans defense can't keep up with the Dallas offense. Tampa Bay Buccaneers (3-6) vs. Detroit Lions (7-2), 1 p.m.
The Lions are becoming one of the NFL's most balanced teams. Jahmyr Gibbs, Amon-Ra St. Brown and Jared Goff lead the offense, while defensive tackle Alim McNeill, linebacker Jack Campbell, and defensive backs Brian Branch and D.J. Reed will handle stopping Tampa Bay's inconsistent offense, while Aidan Hutchinson is out with a season-ending injury.
Prediction: Lions 28, Buccaneers 10
Arizona Cardinals (3-7) vs. Kansas City Chiefs (7-2), 1 p.m.
Kansas City might win this one by three scores. The Chiefs lost two in a row a month ago, but have bounced back with dominant wins in consecutive weeks. Patrick Mahomes has thrown 10 touchdown passes in his last three games, all without throwing an interception.
Prediction: Chiefs 34, Cardinals 16
Pittsburgh Steelers (6-3) vs. Philadelphia Eagles (2-7), 1 p.m.
Aaron Rodgers had one of the worst games of his career last week against the Bengals. Another poor outing will put a damper on his last professional season, while Steelers Nation will be calling for Mason Rudolph and Will Howard to get some playing time. The Eagles have nothing to lose, and with that, momentum is on their side following a bye week to get back on track after seven-straight losses.
Prediction: Eagles 22, Steelers 17
New York Jets (2-8) vs. Los Angeles Chargers (1-8), 4:05 p.m.
The Chargers might be able to pull off back-to-back wins. It will be ugly and tough to watch, but the Chargers are a gritty team that finally got one to roll their way against the Ravens. Meanwhile, it's been over a month since the Jets won, and they continue to suffer injuries that hold them down on both sides of the ball.
Prediction: Chargers 24, Jets 10

Jacksonville is dealing with injuries, including center Robert Hainsey, who was ruled out with a knee injury. It shouldn't slow down an offense that is coming off its best performance. Trevor Lawrence completed 25 of 35 passes for 352 yards, three touchdowns and one interception and the Jaguars finished with more than 450 yards of total offense. With the Giants reeling from a heartbreaking loss, the homestanding crowd won't be enough to reel them to victory here in Week 11.
Prediction: Rams 22, Cardinals 14
Las Vegas Raiders (4-6) vs. Denver Broncos (7-2), 4:25 p.m.
Fernando Mendoza played well in his first professional start, but it wasn't enough to get a win. He'll have to wait at least another week to record that initial victory because it won't happen against the Broncos. Las Vegas leading receiver, Brock Bowers, is out with an injury, making matters even worse for the Raiders.

This game takes place in Mexico City — the sixth regular-season game in the country's capital and largest city. They're getting a dandy as two of the league's best teams are set to square off. Kirk Cousins is creeping up the passing leaderboard as he is now fifth in the NFL with 2,547 passing yards. Prediction: Vikings 27, 49ers 17
Monday, Nov. 23
Cincinnati Bengals (7-2) vs. Washington Commanders (3-5-1), 8:15 p.m.
Cincinnati can pick up a second-straight primetime victory. Joe Burrow is second in the NFL with 2,795 passing yards and will surpass No. 1 Jordan Love after a win against the Commanders.
Prediction: Bengals 47, Commanders 17

title: From pop stars to poets to politicians, hundreds gather for joyful tribute to Gloria Steinem
text:
From pop stars to poets to politicians, hundreds gather for joyful tribute to Gloria Steinem
Cyndi Lauper sang "Girls Just Want to Have Fun.” Cynthia Erivo gave a stirring rendition of “Imagine.” And Gloria Steinem's memorial celebration ended with the audience on its feet singing “We Are Family,” in tribute to the trailblazing activist and most visible symbol of American feminism.
Luminaries from political figures to pop stars to poets gathered Wednesday for a joyful and music-filled memorial, which was just as Steinem, who died in September at 92, had wanted it, her friends told the crowd of 1,000 at the Park Avenue Armory. There were no fewer than three former first ladies — Michelle Obama, Jill Biden and Hillary Clinton. The former secretary of state delivered a speech in which she described her friend's huge impact on women's rights in America.
Related video above: Gloria Steinem was proud of championing women in 1984
“Gloria gave us 92 years of light,” Clinton said, "and all the tools, memories, inspiration and hope that we need to keep that light burning."
The late afternoon celebration mirrored the spirit of Steinem’s famed talking circles, which she hosted at her Upper East Side home for more than 50 years: a vibrant mix of people from near and far, reflecting Steinem’s extensive travels and eclectic tastes in art and music.
Clinton referred to the talking circles as she began her remarks. “How does it feel to be in a giant talking circle?” she asked the crowd, standing in front of a sign declaring “It’s Steinemite!”
“It's as if we were all in Gloria's living room,” she said.
Steinem's associates said the celebration was designed to be joyful and not mournful.
“Gloria wanted a true celebration filled with laughter and friends across generations,” said Jill Heller, director of programs at Gloria's Foundation, which is working to preserve Steinem's home as a center to further her work. The presenters “reflect how expansive a life Gloria lived but also just the spirit of community, celebration and hopefulness that she wanted for this moment,” Heller said.
Close friend Amy Richards, a chief organizer of the event, said Steinem “definitely wanted people to have a good time. She hoped that new people will meet each other and there will be laughter.”
Steinem became an activist after an early career as a journalist. She has said she might have remained a journalist had editors been willing to let her write about social issues of importance, like the nascent women’s movement — but they weren’t interested. It was at a meeting where women spoke out about illegal abortions that she decided to change paths.
“That speak-out was the beginning of activism for me,” Steinem told The Associated Press in 2022. “Either our control over our own bodies is equal, regardless of sex or race, or we’re not living in a democracy.”
Steinem went on to co-found Ms. Magazine and the National Women’s Political Caucus. She traveled constantly, to campuses and rallies and protests, despite an early fear of public speaking. And when she was at home in New York, her living room was a constant gathering place, where groups and movements were born as women gathered from across the country and around the globe.
Steinem, a prolific author, died just weeks before the release of her final memoir, “An Unexpected Life.”
“As I write this, I’m both older than I ever imagined I would become and happier than I ever imagined I could be,” she wrote in the introduction. “I’ve been rewarded with friends who are my chosen family. I have trusted friends in other countries, and we strive to be safe and free, and share hopes for a peaceful democracy in the world.”
Steinem added that she planned to live to 100.

title: Heat pumps aren’t magic. Here’s how to make them work for your Maine home
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Heat pumps have become a familiar sight on Maine homes, offering efficient heating in winter and air conditioning in summer. But can they keep a home comfortable when temperatures plunge?
Robert Cyr, founder and president of DIRFY Generators, which also installs heat pumps, says today’s cold-climate models have come a long way.
“The new generation has evolved,” Cyr said, explaining that some models operate efficiently down to -22 degrees Fahrenheit and continue heating at lower temperatures, though with reduced efficiency.
During last winter’s extreme cold, when temperatures reportedly reached those temperatures, Cyr said none of his customers reported being cold. Some said they were warmer than when using their furnaces.
But even impressive technology isn’t magic. Heat pumps must be properly sized and installed to deliver the comfort and savings homeowners expect.
The right system for the right home
The first thing Cyr asks customers is how they plan to use a heat pump. Some want to replace their heating system; others need supplemental heat for one room, heating during spring and fall, or simply air conditioning in summer.
Those goals call for different equipment. Cyr says skepticism about heat pumps often comes from stories of homes that stayed cold because systems were improperly sized, selected or installed.
Before recommending equipment, DIRFY evaluates insulation, windows, ceilings and the layout of the home. Placement matters, too: An indoor unit in the wrong location may not distribute heat effectively.
An undersized system may struggle to keep up, while an oversized unit can cycle on and off too often, reducing efficiency. Cyr says incorrectly matched outdoor units may also ice up.
When comparing estimates, homeowners should ask why a contractor recommends a particular system and placement, not just compare prices. Warranty terms matter as well. Cyr says DIRFY offers 12-year coverage for parts, labor and travel, while other warranties may cover fewer costs or shorter periods.
Don’t forget about hot water
Cyr also encourages homeowners to consider heat pump water heaters, particularly if an oil- or propane-fired boiler supplies their hot water.
In some homes, the furnace or boiler must operate throughout the summer solely to provide hot water, consuming fuel even when no space heating is needed. During the winter, the system may also fire up to replenish hot water after the home has already reached its desired temperature.
A heat pump water heater transfers heat into a storage tank rather than generating it directly. Depending on existing equipment, energy costs and the household’s overall need for hot water, it can also reduce expenses.
More comfort, less expense
Heat pumps use electricity, so homeowners may see higher electric bills even as spending on oil or propane falls. Cyr recommends comparing total household energy costs rather than one utility bill.
Results vary with energy prices, a home’s condition and how the equipment is used, but for one Maine couple, that calculation helped make heat pumps an appealing investment. Their propane system heated only one of their two bedrooms. After DIRFY installed heat pumps, both bedrooms had heat, and the couple gained air conditioning for summer.
“We are retired and on a fixed income,” they wrote in a testimonial, explaining that financing with no down payment made the heat pump installation possible. They later financed a heat pump water heater as well.
The couple estimated they would save about $110 per month with the heat pumps and another $97 with the water heater, after accounting for financing payments and electricity costs. “It was like getting paid $2,500 a year to install these [systems],” they wrote. “We are recommending to everyone we know to contact DIRFY Generators so that they can increase their spending money.”
The results may seem like magic, but the formula is practical: the right equipment, properly sized and installed for the home’s needs. That’s what makes the difference between a heat pump that simply works and one that works well.

title: Susan Smith denied parole again 32 years after drowning her sons in a South Carolina lake
text:
COLUMBIA, S.C. (WCSC/Gray News) — Susan Smith was denied parole for a second time, 32 years after she drowned her sons in a lake in South Carolina.
Smith, who is now 55, strapped her 14-month-old son, Alex, and her 3-year-old son, Michael, into her car and let it roll into John D. Long Lake in October 1994.
Smith told investigators that a Black man had carjacked her and taken the children. For nine days, Smith made several tearful pleas asking that Michael and Alex be returned safely before confessing to drowning her sons.
The car was found at the bottom of the lake with the boys still inside.
A jury convicted Smith on July 22, 1995, and she was sentenced to life in prison with the possibility of parole after 30 years.
Prosecutors have long argued that Smith killed her sons because she believed they were the reason the wealthy son of the owner of the business where she worked broke off their affair, according to the Associated Press.
During her trial, Smith and her attorneys said her mental health was to blame.
She was denied parole for the first time in November 2024. At that parole hearing, she said God had forgiven her and cried, saying that what she did was horrible and she would give anything to bring her sons back.
Smith can ask for parole again in 2028.
During Thursday’s parole hearing, Smith said her sons were innocent children who did not deserve to die. She said she has so much remorse for killing them and asked the board to give her a chance to get out of prison and do good for the world.
“I know that David didn’t get to see Michael and Alex grow up. You didn’t get to see him ride a bike or go to school. And I’m really, really sorry for that, and I would go back and change all of that if I could, I would, OK? I’m not the same person I was 32 years ago,” she said.
The boys’ father, David Smith, and original prosecutors oppose her release.
“She took away one of the greatest gifts God gives us – life. She did that deliberately. It wasn’t an accident, it wasn’t a mistake. She did it deliberately,” he said in testimony Thursday.

China and Russia say they and US agree on UN reforms, boosting fuel supplies, dialogue on nuclear
text:
SHENZHEN, China (AP) — For U.S. President Donald Trump, the meeting with the leaders of two other nuclear powers -- China’s Xi Jinping and Russia’s Vladimir Putin -- was supposed to be a diplomatic triumph: It would serve as proof that Trump could negotiate with two of America’s toughest rivals.
Before the trio met Thursday in a villa in the Chinese tech hub of Shenzhen, the U.S. president sought to flatter both Xi and Putin as his friends. The wars in Ukraine and Iran were on the agenda, as was reducing the dangers posed by their nuclear arsenals.
But after roughly 70 minutes behind closed doors, they agreed to a far narrower agenda. They would like to reform the United Nations, refine more fossil fuels and curb the reach of the International Criminal Court.
What was billed as a historic trilateral meeting in the end looked like a fleeting photo op. Trump quickly left the villa and boarded Air Force One without saying a word to reporters about his time with Xi and Putin. Still, he hailed the visit as “Highly Consequential” on social media as he made his way back to Washington and announced he would hold a press conference on Friday at the White House.
Following the Shenzhen talks, Trump dialed into a meeting in Berlin between U.S. envoys Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy alongside more than 40 European leaders who are supporting Ukraine’s war effort. Trump told the Berlin gathering that he spoke to Xi and Putin about finding a peaceful end to the Ukraine war, Witkoff said.
The agreements stemming from the trilateral meeting were modest, but the rhetoric that came at the start of it was not.
“We are really making history,” Trump said. “The United States, Russia and China are uniquely positioned to discuss how to reduce the number of nuclear weapons on Earth and also to lessen the risk of those weapons being used.”
After the meeting, Xi called it positive, constructive and fruitful, while Putin described the trilateral talks as open and candid, calling the format “useful and substantive.”
“It is a serious collaborative work,” he said in response to a question about whether the image of the meeting itself mattered more than the substance.
The last nuclear arms pact between Russia and the United States, known as New START, expired in February, and Trump has said he wants “a new, improved and modernized” deal that includes China. But China has less motivation to accept limits given that its arsenal of more than 600 warheads is far smaller than the more than 5,000 warheads believed to be in each of the U.S. and Russian stockpiles.
Daryl Kimball, executive director of the Arms Control Association, said the meeting could at best start a process that would eventually lead to a sustained set of talks for reducing nuclear arsenals.
“We need more than diplomatic theater and photo opportunities between Xi, Putin and Trump,” Kimball said. “And one meeting will not likely produce dramatic breakthroughs.”
The leaders also talked about Iran and trade
The U.S. president earlier had a separate one-on-one with Xi, their third substantial meeting this year.
Trump said they had a shared interest in having oil flow through the Strait of Hormuz, a key waterway for oil shipments from the Middle East that was repeatedly shut because of attacks in the Iran war. Trump suggested he would push Xi to buy more agricultural products from America.
Xi said that relations between the U.S. and China have been “generally stable and improved” during Trump’s presidency. The official Chinese news agency Xinhua reported that Xi discussed Taiwan with Trump and said the two countries needed to improve communication on economic and trade issues.
Trump also added to his calendar a separate sit-down with Putin, marking the first time the leaders have met for talks since their discussions in Alaska last year that failed to broker a deal on Russia’s war in Ukraine.
“Wonderful things can come out of this — or at least start,” Trump said, calling Putin “my friend.”
Trump has frequently boasted of his rapport with Putin, as relations between the U.S. and Ukraine appear to have cratered recently. Trump rejected new Russia sanctions, while Kyiv was undermined by disruptions in satellite support for its drones during the war.
After their trilateral meeting, the three leaders took aim at the International Criminal Court for overstepping its jurisdiction, saying government officials should enjoy immunity from its prosecutions. Putin is wanted by the court, and Trump’s administration has imposed sanctions on ICC officials and the institution itself as part of a campaign to dismantle the tribunal over investigations into the United States and its allies, including Israel.
Trump boasts about his relationships, but the ties between Xi and Putin are stronger
The U.S. president’s ambitions going into the meeting recalled an era of great power politics when wealthier countries felt entitled to decide the fate of seemingly lesser nations. Trump was negotiating with China and Russia without the involvement of Ukraine — or allies like Germany, France, the United Kingdom, Japan and South Korea that also have stakes in the outcome of any talks.
Trump has long believed his ability to create personal connections gives him a diplomatic edge. Xi made a symbolic gesture of friendship Wednesday by taking the unusual step of greeting Air Force One on the tarmac, and the two leaders turned their handshake into a one-armed hug.
But for all the compliments the U.S. president has showered on the two autocrats, he did not always appear to have the same deep relationship based on common interests that Xi and Putin share.
On Wednesday at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit, Xi greeted Putin by calling him “my old friend.” The Russian leader responded by declaring Xi to be his “dear friend.” China has helped economically support Russia after its 2022 invasion of Ukraine, providing Putin with a financial lifeline after the U.S. and its allies imposed new sanctions.
By contrast, when Xi went to the White House for a state visit in September, he was far more restrained with Trump, saying they had built a “personal rapport and stayed in touch.” Trump and Xi have one more meeting planned this year, at the G20 summit in Florida in December.
There were also signs of friction Thursday in the U.S.-China relationship despite Trump’s praise of Xi.
Chinese officials blocked a Bloomberg reporter from the trilateral meeting after she asked a question at the earlier Trump-Xi session. And Chinese television showed a video of Trump appearing drowsy, while the White House posted a clip of Trump helping Xi up an escalator.
___

text:
One person has died and another is in critical condition after they were hit by a driver while loading groceries at the Thomaston Walmart on Wednesday.
Thomaston police say they are still investigating the cause of the crash and whether the driver will be charged.
The driver was turning into a lane in the parking lot when they accelerated, crashing into two people who were putting items in the trunk of a parked car, police Cpl. Jarrod Leonardi said Thursday. Both were taken to the hospital with serious injuries.
Police said in a news release Thursday that Leita Wyman, 80, of Friendship, died after the crash. The other pedestrian remains in critical condition at MaineHealth Pen Bay Hospital in Rockport, according to police.
A third person was left with non-life-threatening injuries after the parked car was pushed into another vehicle.
The driver was not injured, Leonardi said.
