title: Letter: Ed Muskie would have rejected federal permitting reform bill
text:
Letters submitted by BDN readers are verified by BDN Opinion Page staff. Send your letters to letters@bangordailynews.com
If Maine’s legendary environmental champion, Sen. Ed Muskie, were still serving in Congress, would he vote for the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act (BAAJA)? I think the answer is no.
Muskie understood that economic prosperity and environmental protection aren’t competing goals. As the principal architect of the Clean Air Act and a driving force behind the Clean Water Act, he helped establish a simple but powerful principle: America’s natural resources should be protected for future generations, not sacrificed for short-term economic gains.
BAAJA, however, would dramatically weaken the Clean Water Act by severely limiting state and tribal rights to protect their own local waters. It would also weaken the National Environmental Policy Act and the Endangered Species Act, limiting opportunities for public input and reducing safeguards for wildlife and public health.
Muskie was a bipartisan legislator who believed in finding practical solutions, but he also understood that environmental laws must have teeth. He would likely support making permitting more efficient, but not at the expense of the protections he spent his career building.
It’s possible to build the infrastructure we need without damaging the waterbodies we love. Clean energy and grid investments must preserve safeguards for clean water, wildlife, and the communities affected by development.
Maine should expect better than a bill that trades away environmental safeguards in the name of expediency. I believe Ed Muskie would agree.
Ivy Frignoca
Portland

title: Cause of death released for man who fell from Six Flags Over Georgia roller coaster
text:
ATLANTA (ANF/Gray News) — The cause of death for the man who fell from a Six Flags Over Georgia roller coaster in October has been released.
Hassan Kariem, 42, died of blunt force injuries, according to the report. The autopsy, which was performed on Oct. 13, one day after Kariem’s death, revealed the man’s traumatic injuries, including skull and bone fractures and lacerations on several organs.
Kariem’s death was listed as accidental, according to the report.
Kariem, who was sitting next to his niece on the Goliath, hit four other people when he was ejected from the roller coaster, injuring them. The riders had to be helped from the ground and the park was evacuated.
The investigation into the accident is ongoing, and the Goliath roller coaster is still closed.
Six Flags Over Georgia said it plans to add seat belts in addition to the existing lap restraints.
Several other roller coasters similar to Goliath have been closed at other Six Flags parks.

title: The most dangerous mistake you can make with your slow cooker, according to experts
text:
Why you should never put frozen meat in a slow cooker, according to experts
Turns out, "set-it-and-forget-it" has its limits.
Why you should never put frozen meat in a slow cooker, according to experts
Turns out, "set-it-and-forget-it" has its limits.
With busy schedules and limited time each day, slow cookers are key to getting dinner on the table. They can take simple ingredients and transform them into a complete, ready-to-eat meal. Because the slow cooker does all the work for you, you may think that it can also handle defrosting meat.
Related video above: When to thaw your turkey: It might be sooner than you think
But think again. The idea seems convenient in theory, but in practice, it raises some serious food safety concerns. We consulted health experts to learn more about adding frozen meat to a slow cooker. So next time you plan a hands-off dinner, you can make sure your food is delicious and safe to eat.
Is It Ever Safe To Put Frozen Meat In The Slow Cooker?
Getty ImagesRusN
Sorry to be the bearer of bad news: You should never put frozen meat directly into your slow cooker. “I am all for cutting out unnecessary steps in cooking, but using frozen meat in your slow cooker is not one of them,” says Melissa Koch, RD, MEd.
Raw meat can carry harmful bacteria that cause foodborne illness. Freezing stops them from multiplying, but doesn't necessarily kill them. And because slow cookers heat food gradually, frozen meat can spend too long in what food safety experts call the “temperature danger zone.”
“The danger zone refers to a temperature range of 40°F (4°C) to 140°F (60°C) over two or more hours when harmful bacteria grow or multiply at a fast rate,” Koch explains. It can take hours for food in a slow cooker to move above the danger zone—and starting with frozen meat delays that process even further.
“The appliance heats food slowly, and starting with frozen meat means the internal temperature may sit in the ‘danger zone’ for too long,” says chef and dietitian Sharniquia White. “This gives bacteria like Salmonella or E. coli more opportunity to multiply before the food reaches a safe cooking temperature.”
What Are The Risks Of Cooking Frozen Meat In A Slow Cooker?
Getty ImagesGrace Cary
What happens after eating food that has sat in the danger zone? The consequences vary based on your immune system, the extent of the contamination, and the strains of bacteria present. But none are pleasant, and some may even send you to the hospital.
“Symptoms of food-borne illness can include nausea, vomiting, stomach cramps, and fever,” Koch says. “You can experience the effects of food-borne illness within a few minutes to days after consuming a load of harmful pathogens or bacteria.”
Cooking frozen meat on the “low” setting of your slow cooker increases the time it spends in the danger zone, but the risk is present regardless. “The 'high' setting reduces the amount of time food spends at unsafe temperatures, but still doesn’t fully eliminate the risk when starting with frozen meat,” says White.
The ingredients you're using can also increase your risk. “Larger, denser cuts (like roasts or whole poultry) take longer to thaw and heat evenly, so they pose a greater risk of staying at unsafe temperatures for extended periods,” White explains.
Smaller pieces may thaw faster, but that doesn't necessarily make them safe to cook from frozen. White explains that ground meat is “particularly risky” because of the way it's processed, so it should be cooked thoroughly.
“I feed three young children at my home, so in my opinion, I wouldn't chance cooking frozen meat, no matter the size, in a slow cooker,” Koch says.
How Can You Minimize The Risks?
PHOTO: LUCY SCHAEFFER
The answer is simple: thaw your meat before turning on your slow cooker. But your ideal method depends on how much time you have.
The safest, easiest, and least involved thawing method is to put your frozen meat in the fridge. The cold temperature of your refrigerator lets your food defrost gently without entering the danger zone.
Our editors recommend placing the meat on a plate or baking sheet to collect any juices and avoid contaminating other food in your fridge. This process can take anywhere from a couple of hours to a couple of days, depending on the cut of meat. “This requires some thought and effort, but in the long run it's worth your safety,” Koch says.
No time for that? No problem. You can thaw meat faster by submerging it in cold water in a leakproof bag, changing the water every 30 minutes, or defrosting it in the microwave, though the latter can compromise the meat's texture. Both methods require cooking the meat immediately afterward. “Once thawed, meat should go directly into the slow cooker,” White explains.
It all takes a little extra effort and planning, but it's worth it to avoid getting sick from your slow cooker dinner.

title: Former Sen. Ben Sasse’s memoir on surviving cancer, co-written with his daughter, is set for March 9
text:
NEW YORK (AP) — Nearly a year after doctors told him he had four months or less to live, former Sen. Ben Sasse has completed a memoir about confronting mortality and sorting out life’s priorities.
On March 9, the Hachette Book Group imprint Center Street will publish Sasse’s “Redeem the Time: The Strange Gift of Dying and the Lost Art of Living,” co-authored with daughter Alex Sasse. In a statement shared Thursday with The Associated Press, the Republican from Nebraska said that he and his daughter worked on the book in hospital hallways.
“To my surprise and my friends’ chagrin, I’m not dead … yet,” Sasse, 54, said.
“The reality is that we’re all dying — each one of us is on the clock, whether we acknowledge it or not. The ‘gift of dying’ is that it shatters our insane delusions of self-control. We didn’t write a boring cancer memoir — there’s nothing unique about my death — but reflections on time, habits, workaholism, and family.”
Sasse, who announced in December 2025 that he had been diagnosed with Stage 4 pancreatic cancer, has spoken often about his condition and how it has shaped his outlook. Center Street is calling “Redeem the Time” a “poignant book that reflects on many of these themes — our need for family and embodied communities in an era of digital rootlessness, our hearts’ need to worship amid a culture of consumerism, our inclination to turn work into workaholism, and our need to grapple with death and finitude early.”
Sasse’s previous books, written years earlier, include “Them: Why We Hate Each Other — and How to Heal” and “The Vanishing American Adult.” He also briefly served as the president of the University of Florida.

title: NASA's Voyager 1 phones home from an awe-inspiring one light-day away
text:
CAPE CANAVERAL, Fla. (AP) — NASA’s Voyager 1 has phoned home from one light-day away, humanity’s first emissary to cross this monumental threshold way out in interstellar space.
Flight controllers received the spacecraft’s call Thursday, exactly 24 hours after it was sent. That’s how long it took for the radio signal to traverse the more than 16 billion miles (26 billion kilometers) at the speed of light.
“Traveling a light-day is a singular feat for a spacecraft, but Voyager is so much more than a distant traveler,” NASA’s Joe Westlake, the heliophysics division director, said in a statement.
It marked another day in the history books for Voyager 1, which launched in 1977. It swept past Jupiter in 1979 and Saturn in 1980, snapped the most distant photo ever taken of our “Pale Blue Dot” in 1990, became the most distant human-made object in 1998, and crossed from the sun’s sphere of influence into the vast void between stars in 2012.
NASA could not confirm this newest distance record until the signal reached the control team at California’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory. But that didn’t stop the space agency from wishing everyone a “Happy Voyager light-day … day!” via social media the day before.
“Voyager 1 crossing the light-day threshold is yet another historic feat on an extraordinary voyage of discovery,” JPL director Dave Gallagher said in a statement.
Voyager 1 and its twin, Voyager 2, are NASA’s longest-operating space missions, still churning out data despite powering down most of their instruments to keep exploring.
Voyager 2 actually beat its twin into space by two weeks. But its route to Jupiter and Saturn plus Uranus and Neptune was slower and longer, and it did not reach interstellar space until 2018. It won’t reach the one-light-day mark until 2035.
Both spacecraft are doing well for their 49 years of age, plowing through space at 38,000 mph (61,000 kph) with plutonium for power. Picture-taking ended long ago, but they typically send back bits of precious data almost every day on their never-before-explored environment.
No science or engineering data have been received from Voyager 1 since Saturday, according to NASA. However, the carrier signal that normally conveys that data kept coming and, along with flight path calculations, allowed the team to confirm the light-day milestone. Controllers are trying to figure out why the flow of science and engineering data stopped.
Each carries a so-called Golden Record brimming with the sounds of Earth. The project was led by the late Cornell University astronomer Carl Sagan, who also coined the phrase “Pale Blue Dot” for Voyager 1’s farewell glimpse of Earth.
NASA expects the gold-plated phonographic records — time capsules for anyone or anything that might encounter them — to last more than 1 billion years.

title: Woman says she found maggots crawling on her LongHorn Steakhouse meal, lawsuit says
text:
TRUSSVILLE, Ala. (WBRC/Gray News) - An Alabama woman is suing LongHorn Steakhouse, claiming she found maggots on broccoli she ordered from the restaurant.
Alexandria Eatman said she picked up a to-go lunch for herself and coworkers from the Trussville restaurant around noon on Oct. 27. That’s when she and a coworker noticed something crawling on her food.
“We noticed I had maggots crawling on my broccoli,” Eatman said.
Her attorney, Antonio Spurling, said she had eaten much of her meal before noticing what was on the broccoli.
Eatman said she returned to the restaurant, where a manager told her someone would reach out. She said no one contacted her that day.
The next morning, Eatman said, she became ill and went to a hospital, where she spent about half a day receiving medicine and fluids.
“I had a lot of nausea, diarrhea. I was very weak for days. It just took a lot out of me,” she said. “I wasn’t able to work.”
Spurling said her illness is documented.
Eatman said she posted pictures of the meal on Facebook, and a corporate representative contacted her the next day. She said the representative apologized, told her there was a problem with the broccoli supplier and offered her a $100 gift card.
“I think I was very disappointed after they only decided, like, we’ll give you a $100 gift card,” Eatman said. She then began looking for an attorney.
A manager at the Trussville location declined to comment when contacted by WBRC.
Longhorn restaurant operator Darden Restaurants released the following statement to WBRC:
“What was shown in the image was moth larvae. Unfortunately, it can occasionally be present in fresh broccoli. We take food safety seriously and we immediately discarded all broccoli as soon as we became aware.”
Eatman is suing LongHorn Steakhouse, Darden Restaurants and RARE Hospitality International. The lawsuit, filed Nov. 5 in Jefferson County Circuit Court, alleges negligence in handling food and seeks compensatory and punitive damages. It does not specify an amount.
The latest inspection report on the department’s website, from March 2026, gave the restaurant a score of 90 and noted food temperature and handwashing violations. The inspection took place months before the incident Eatman described.

title: Maine Community Foundation testifies in front of the legislature regarding Lewiston shooting funds
text:
AUGUSTA, Maine (WMTW) - Three years ago, the Maine Community Foundation held a press conference explaining its plans to raise money after the Lewiston mass shootings. Victims have been saying for months that the foundation’s plan was not clear to them and they thought they would get 100% of the proceeds, instead of some of it going to nonprofits.
“We launched the Lewiston-Auburn response fund with two components. One to support victims and families and the other focused on broader community needs,” Maine Community Foundation President Deborah Ellwood said during a November 2023 press conference launching the fund.
Victims of the Lewiston mass shooting have been pushing back against the Maine Community Foundation for months now, as they believed all the money raised was to be distributed to victims.
$4.7 million of it was, but $1.9 million was given to area nonprofits that were providing support for those impacted by the shooting.
Wednesday morning, at the Government Oversight Committee hearing, foundation officials said it was clearly spelled out that there were two separate funds on the website where someone would donate, but there was different communication sent directly to victims, including a document that said 100% of the money raised would go to the victims.
“Why there were instances on the victim and survivor side of the communications that it was imprecise, that it did not clarify between the existence of those two funds,” Rep. Adam Lee, D-Auburn, asked Ellwood.
“What difference do you think that would make?” she responded, which caused scoffing in the room.
“What difference would it make? It makes a difference that people from a shooting were lied to. They were told 100% of this fund was for them, and that is not what happened,” Amy Sussman said. Sussman is the aunt of Maxx Hathaway, who was killed in the shooting.
The foundation faced pointed questions and some criticism, for about an hour, before the victims got the apology that they have been asking for.
“This is an error, wouldn’t you say?” Sen. Craig Hickman, D-Kennebec, asked Ellwood.
“Yes. I think it was confusing for victims for sure,” she responded.
“Do you have anything else to say to them?” Hickman followed up.
“Yes. I’m sorry that they felt confused. And by this particular piece of documentation,” Ellwood said.
The Government Oversight Committee invited the Maine Community Foundation to speak, but it doesn’t actually have jurisdiction over the foundation because it’s a nonprofit, not a government entity.

title: Class D state football championship set for rematch
text:
WINTHROP, WINSLOW, Maine (WABI) - The Class D State Football Championship is a rematch from last season.
The Winthrop Ramblers are hoping to repeat against Winslow after they beat the Black Raiders, 41-14, to claim the Gold Ball in 2025.
Winthrop beat Freeport, 13-3, in the South title game.
“It was a lot, building up from last year, losing a lot of seniors. We definitely did a lot of stuff to get us a lot better, like getting younger guys in, and working more. Taking that one loss early in the season really lit a fire underneath us to just keep going and doing what we’ve done the rest of the year,” said Carter Rand, senior running back, linebacker.
“It’s going to be strong efforts on both sides of the ball to win this game because Winslow is a very good team, and we’re going to have to give it all,” said Ross Fichthorn, senior running back, linebacker.
A state title on Saturday would make seven in the Ramblers’ trophy case.
Winslow is back in the Class D state title game after winning the North, 36-20 over John Bapst.
The Black Raiders spoke about what it would mean to complete their revenge tour against the Ramblers.
“This week, we’ve been grinding. We all remember what happened last year. It wasn’t a good feeling,” said Noah Harding, junior tight end, defensive tackle.
“They beat us bad, so we want to return it. We always wanted that. We always had that feeling that they were going to make it back. We always thought we were going to make it back,” said Ben Thomas, senior right guard, defensive tackle.
Winslow is going for its 13th state title.

title: Bangor PD's Armored Vehicle Breaks Through Ohio Street Windows And Door At 5 AM Warrant
text:
Dramatic Video Of Bangor PD Using Armored Response Vehicle While Executing Early Morning Search Warrant On Ohio Street
A dramatic video has emerged of the Bangor Police Department utilizing a unique vehicle to break out doors and windows at an apartment building on Ohio Street Thursday morning.
According to one witness in the neighborhood, an armored vehicle full of officers with weapons drawn pulled up to the scene and closed down both sides of Ohio Street just after 5 AM. They then brought in a specialized truck equipped with a long-armed ramming rod of sorts and parked it in front of one of the apartments.
Read More: 1 Dead, 2 Hurt After Vehicle Hits Pedestrians At Maine Walmart
The vehicle was positioned near 143 Ohio Street as authorities used a bullhorn to direct residents to comply.
The voice over the loudspeaker stated:
"Occupants of 143 Ohio Street, this is the Bangor Police Department. We have a search warrant. Exit the building through the front door with your hands up and nothing in your hands. Do it now."
Moments later, when no one complies, the vehicle can be seen breaking through one window on the front of the building, then the front door, and finally another window before those inside eventually exited the premises.
Katy England, with the Bangor Police Department, says the vehicle used to break through the windows and doors is Bangor PD's Armored Response Vehicle.

She says it's usually utilized in situations that have the potential to become high risk.
"In this case, it assisted in executing a search warrant at that location. The investigation is ongoing and we don't have further details we can release at this time. "

We're keeping a close eye on a potential coastal storm that could bring rain and gusty winds to Maine and New Hampshire on Monday. Forecast models are increasingly confident that a storm will develop off the Southeast coast and track north toward New England. However, uncertainty remains about its exact track, which will determine how much rain we receive and whether strong winds become a concern. title: Local police join boxing class supporting people with Parkinson’s in Brewer
text:

Rock Steady Boxing in Brewer hosted the departments as part of Holden PD’s 25 Days of Kindness program.
A $500 check was also presented to Rock Steady Boxing to help fund sponsors, equipment, and pay for space.
Holden police officer Mike Hegarty says he’s been volunteering at Rock Steady Boxing for three years and has helped members fight their symptoms.

“It’s been life changing. These people are my friends, my family. You’re walking with them every step of the way. I’ve learned a lot about boxing, more than I ever thought I knew before. So, it’s a lot of fun. There’s a lot of laughing,” said Hegarty.
“It’s exactly my goal in my life is to be able to continue to offer these classes, to be able to make sure people who’ve been diagnosed with Parkinson’s always have a place to go. To fight back against this disease, they deserve that,” said Lahaye.

title: Holiday shopping could top $1 trillion. Here's what's trending and how to save
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Holiday shopping could top $1 trillion. Here's what's trending and how to save
Price history tools may help shoppers spot the best deals.
Holiday shopping could top $1 trillion. Here's what's trending and how to save
Price history tools may help shoppers spot the best deals.
Holiday shopping is expected to top $1 trillion this year, according to the National Retail Federation, even as more than half of shoppers say the economy is influencing their spending plans.
"I think we're all feeling a little strapped right now," said Brie Schwartz, Good Housekeeping's director of editorial commerce. "But that said, spending is predicted to be going up this year, probably because people are waiting until there's a really good deal."
What's trending
Electronics, toys, TVs, apparel and computers are set to see some of the season's steepest discounts, according to research from Adobe Analytics, which tracks online spending during the holidays.
Schwartz says mattresses may be worth waiting on, since she expects better deals around Presidents' Day.
Beyond gifts, shoppers are also eyeing "boring buys" this holiday sales season. These are everyday essentials that can help stretch a few extra dollars.
"The dishwashers get all the attention, but the bottom line is you can save on laundry detergent," Schwartz said.
Before you shop, make a plan, set your budget and do your research by checking price history to make sure a deal is really the best price.
Price history tools
Amazon has a built-in price-tracking tool. Click the price history button located right next to the item's price on eligible product pages.
You can also ask for the price history with Amazon's Alexa for Shopping tool in the mobile app or on desktop.
For more Amazon price history, CamelCamelCamel or Keepa are also options.
For Walmart products, Camelmart uses Walmart's API to show price history charts and track price drops.
Compare deals
While researching, Schwartz said she uses AI to help find deals.
Here's her example prompt:
"Research the best current deals on X recommended or tested by [insert publisher, like Good Housekeeping], using today's date. Include the following retailers [insert retailers]. Find the lowest documented price EVER for each exact model and prioritize the actual historical selling price, not the retailer's advertised percentage off."
AI can help find options, but always verify yourself by checking the retailer's final price and price history.
Avoid impulse buys
Adobe says mobile devices will account for 57.4% of online holiday spending this season, and 63% on Thanksgiving day alone.
These impulse purchases can feel small in the moment but can add up fast over time. Learn four ways to curb impulse buying through our previous story here.
Extended return deadlines
Even after you buy, keep an eye on the price. Some retailers may lower the price of an item you've already purchased. If so, you may be able to return it and buy it again at the lower price.
"Most retailers right now have extended their return deadlines until after January, so you have ample time to really think about it," Schwartz said.

title: Grieving parents call for kratom crackdown
text:
WASHINGTON (Gray DC) - Rebecca Strang’s life turned upside down a few months ago.
“I’m here today as a mother who lost Robert to kratom 58 days ago,” Strang said.
She’s in Washington advocating for a kratom crackdown, and describes her new reality.
“The worst day of my life has suddenly become my life’s work,” Strang said.
What the DEA says about kratom
According to the DEA, the leaf-derived powder creates stimulant effects in low doses and sedative effects in high doses. The DEA said it can quickly develop into psychological and physical dependence.
Industry criticism
Dean Francis criticized the kratom industry.
“The greed of a nefarious industry that exploits loopholes in our dietary supplement laws to masquerade a highly addictive and deadly drug as a plant based herbal supplement,” Francis said.
Francis said the industry lures vulnerable groups, including young people and veterans, with promises of an energy boost. He said the industry then addicts them for profit.
Regulation status
The USDA has not issued guardrails or guidelines on kratom. The agency does warn against using it for medical purposes.
The Department of Health and Human Services has taken only initial steps toward regulation.
Support from Congress
The group’s call for a crackdown is supported by Iowa Sen. Chuck Grassley.
“We know that kratom is an opioid that kills people, and we have to have strong enforcement of that,” Grassley said.
Strang said she will continue to advocate in honor of her son.
“It is time to stop focusing on who stands to profit and focus on who stands to suffer. Robert’s life mattered, and his death matters,” Strang said.
State legislation
Bills to address the sale of kratom are currently pending in Pennsylvania, Michigan, Delaware and Rhode Island.

title: Trump tells Xi that China should buy more US farm goods
text:
Trump tells Xi that China should buy more US farm goods
President Donald Trump meets on Thursday with China’s Xi Jinping and Russia’s Vladimir Putin, a moment that could mark a pivot in world history — or become a quickly forgotten photo op.
Video above: President Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping discuss artificial intelligence at the White House
Trump, who will test his reputation as an expert dealmaker in the trilateral meeting, has promoted his time with Xi and Putin — two of America's leading rivals — as a chance to hash out rules for controlling nuclear arms and to start resolving the wars in Ukraine and Iran. Experts have kept expectations low for major breakthroughs.
Trump had a separate one-on-one meeting with Xi — his third substantial meeting with him this year — right before the trilateral. The U.S. president praised their friendship and their shared interest in having oil shipped through the Strait of Hormuz, which has become a key site of attacks in the Iran war. Trump suggested he would push Xi to buy more agricultural products from America.
“I'll be asking you to do some more for our farmers,” Trump said.
Xi said that Trump's efforts “will be recorded in history” and that he was committed to working with the U.S. president, according to a translation.
Trump also added a separate sit-down with Putin to his schedule, marking the first time the leaders have held talks since their discussions in Alaska last year that failed to broker a deal to ease Russia’s war in Ukraine.
“Wonderful things can come out of this — or at least start,” Trump said after joining Putin for the one-on-one meeting on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation Summit, calling Putin “my friend."
“We’ve had a great relationship for many years,” Trump said after shaking hands with Putin. Their meeting together lasted roughly 40 minutes.
Trump has frequently boasted of his rapport with Putin, even as relations between the U.S. and Ukraine appear to have cratered recently. Trump rejected new Russia sanctions, while Kyiv was undermined by disruptions in satellite support for its drones during the war.
Along for the trip — but so far keeping a low profile — is Elon Musk, whose company SpaceX has intermittently throttled the military-grade Starshield satellite system used by Ukraine for launching its drones and intercepting hits from Russia.
One meeting is unlikely to produce a breakthrough in nuclear talks
Trump has said he wants to talk to the leaders about their nuclear stockpiles. The last nuclear arms pact between Russia and the United States, known as New START, expired in February, and Trump has said he wants “a new, improved and modernized” deal that includes China. But China has less motivation to accept limits given that its arsenal of more than 600 warheads is far smaller than the more than 5,000 warheads believed to be in each of the U.S. and Russian stockpiles.
Daryl Kimball, executive director of the Arms Control Association, said Trump's showmanship could at best start a process that would eventually lead to a sustained set of talks for reducing nuclear arsenals.
“We need more than diplomatic theater and photo opportunities between Xi, Putin and Trump at APEC," Kimball said. “And one meeting will not likely produce dramatic breakthroughs.”
Trump told Fox News in his interview that “it’s a very hard thing to do” to ask a leader to reduce nuclear stockpiles.
Trump boasts about his relationships. But the ties between Xi and Putin are stronger
Putin’s foreign affairs adviser Yuri Ushakov told reporters that Putin, Trump and Xi would likely touch on the war in Ukraine, though the agenda was not fully set. Trump has said he wants to discuss that war — as well as the conflict in Iran.
His ambitions recall an era of great power politics when wealthier countries felt entitled to decide the fate of seemingly lesser nations. Trump is negotiating with China and Russia without the involvement of Ukraine — or countries like Germany, France, the United Kingdom, Japan and South Korea that also have stakes in the outcome of any talks.
The U.S. president has openly pursued a Nobel Peace Prize even as he took military action against Venezuela and Iran. He also threatened earlier this year to take Greenland by force from Denmark, a gambit that led to an agreement for the construction of U.S. military bases.
Video below: Trump administration takes questions on tech outages
Trump has long believed his ability to create personal connections gives him a diplomatic edge. Xi appealed to his ego Wednesday by greeting Air Force One on the airport tarmac, as the two leaders turned their handshake into a one-armed hug.
But Trump does not appear to always have the same deep relationship based on common interests that Xi and Putin share. For all the compliments the U.S. president has showered on the two autocrats, the warmth has not always been mutually effusive.
On Wednesday at APEC, Xi greeted Putin by calling him “my old friend.” The Russian leader responded by declaring Xi to be his “dear friend.” China has helped economically support Russia after its 2022 invasion of Ukraine, providing Putin with a financial lifeline after the U.S. and its allies imposed new sanctions.
“China-Russia relations have remained steadfast through storms while taking a long-term view,” Xi said to Putin. “They have brought greater stability and certainty to a world marked by intertwined changes and turbulence.”
The pair discussed the war in Ukraine during their talks, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov told Russian state news agency RIA Novosti.
By contrast, when Xi came to the White House for a state visit in September, he was far more restrained with Trump, saying they had built a "personal rapport and stayed in touch.” Trump and Xi plan to meet a total of four times this year, with their final time together coming in December at the G20 summit being held at the Trump National Doral Golf Club in Florida.
Ukraine and its European allies are suspicious of the trilateral meeting that could potentially cut them out of the process. German Chancellor Friedrich Merz has said Europeans feared another “Anchorage moment,” a reference to last year's Putin-Trump meeting in Alaska that produced proposals that were rejected by Ukraine and its partners.
Conflicts on AI and trade also hang over the meetings
While Trump views his relationship with China as a positive, it has not necessarily resulted in meaningful changes between the world's two largest economies. China continues to run large trade surpluses with the rest of the world, while the U.S. has almost equally large trade deficits.
And the race between the U.S. and China to master artificial intelligence has grown tense over the past two weeks. Trump ally Jensen Huang resigned last week as the CEO of Nvidia after confessing to an extramarital affair with a woman, Alice Huang, whose company helped to give China access to the company's advanced computer chips used to develop AI models. Beijing has denied that Alice Huang was a Chinese government agent.
Trump held off on imposing tougher restrictions on China's ability to access the chips, suggesting he did not want to insult China and aggravate relations.
Before APEC, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer met with Chinese Vice Premier He Lifeng.
The U.S. officials said afterward that China had not fully honored its commitments made last year in a Trump-Xi meeting to buy more U.S. agricultural products and loosen restrictions on the sale of rare earth minerals needed for electronics.
The trade truce between the U.S. and China reached last year after dueling tariff hikes is set to expire by Jan. 10 next year.
Trump officials have dangled the possibility of opening up highly sanctioned trade with Russia as an incentive for ending hostilities in Ukraine, and Trump has frequently demonstrated that he sees trade as a foreign policy tool.
Meanwhile, both China and Russia have used trade to support Iran, even during the U.S. war on that country, which has pushed up energy prices and reduced global economic growth.
Associated Press writers Darlene Superville and Will Weissert in Washington contributed to this report.

title: Obituary: Ethel T. Price
text:
PORTLAND – Ethel T. Price, 86, passed away suddenly but peacefully at home on Tuesday, Nov. 10, 2026, while knitting an afghan with her beloved dog, Sadie, beside her. The eighth child of Thomas Sylvester Price and Ethel Margaret (Little) Price, Ethel was born in South Portland, Maine on Oct. 14, 1940, five months after her father’s sudden death at just age 42. Nicknamed “Tomie” as a child, she was blessed with “Daddy Mitch” Berube at age 2.
Her early years instilled a fierce independence and the inability to accept “can’t” as a result. Ethel graduated from South Portland High School in 1958 and applied her drive and intelligence to take business classes. She attended the University of Southern Maine part-time to obtain her business degree while working full-time and helping her family succeed. She began her career in accounting in 1959 with Walter and James Ranger. She achieved her CPA license and reveled in her love of numbers and logic and practiced right up to her last day. Also, thanks to Walter, discovered her love of sailing.
She was predeceased by her father, Thomas (d. 1940), mother Ethel (1985), stepfather Mitchell A. Berube (1949); brothers Tom (1988), Peter (2009) and Charles (2011), and sisters Mary E. (2011), Barbara F. (2014), Margaret A. (1987), Carol A. (1990) and Anita L. (2016).
She is survived by three generations of nieces and nephews scattered throughout the country, all having been greatly blessed by Ethel’s loyalty, drive, passion and generosity.
Ethel lived a long, full life and her memory will be treasured by all who knew and loved her. A Catholic Mass Service will be held on Monday, Dec. 7, 2026 at 11 a.m. at St. Pioux Church, 492 Ocean Ave., Portland, Maine. Interment will be at Calvary Cemetery. All are welcome.
In lieu of flowers,
Ethel would be pleased with any donations to:
HART of Maine

title: Boothbay-Wiscasset Regional Adult Education Named Top Performer Again
Former Mattanawcook standout Addison Cyr off to strong start for Husson women’s basketball
text:
Saying freshman center Addison Cyr has made an immediate impact for Husson women’s basketball would be an understatement.
In her first four games, the 6-foot-1 Lincoln native has already posted three double-doubles. She became the first player in Husson program history to score at least 35 points and grab at least 20 rebounds in a game when she notched 37 and 22 in the team’s 69-66 win over Brandeis earlier this week.
She shot 16-for-24 from the floor and sank all five of her free throws. She also had two assists.
She followed that performance with her second double-double: a 19-point, 16-rebound showing in a 72-64 win over St. Joseph’s College. She also added five assists and three blocks.
For her standout performances, she became the program’s first player chosen to the nationwide D3Hoops.com Team of the Week since Bailey Donovan in 2023. She was also selected as the New England Women’s Basketball Association’s Rookie of the Week.
On Tuesday night, she collected her third double-double in a 74-63 loss to No. 20 Bates College in Lewiston. She added 16 points and 10 rebounds, along with three assists, three steals and a blocked shot.
Through her first four games, the former Bangor Daily News All-Maine Schoolgirl Basketball first team selection is averaging 21.3 points and 13.3 rebounds per game. She is shooting 56.5% from the floor and 88.2% from the free-throw line.
She has 11 assists, five blocked shots, and four steals.
“She is definitely talented,” Husson head coach Kissy Walker said. “She has different moves in the post and a soft touch around the rim. She has great hands, she can get up and down the floor, and she can rebound. But the most impressive thing is her great body control. You rarely see a freshman that size with the footwork she has.”
Cyr led Mattanawcook Academy of Lincoln to its first state Class C championship last winter, capping her remarkable career with a 25-point, 23-rebound performance in the Lynx’s 54-40 win over Spruce Mountain of Jay in the state final.
She averaged 25.7 points, 18.1 rebounds and 3.9 assists in guiding the Lynx to a 22-0 campaign.

title: US Army delays detonation of bomb-making chemicals in Iowa after safety concerns raised
text:
DES MOINES, Iowa (AP) — The U.S. Army decided to delay Friday’s detonation of several tons of bomb-making chemicals in southeast Iowa after an outpouring of public concern that a cloud of lead dust could cause environmental contamination and health problems.
The plan is now to carry it out on Monday.
Iowa Gov. Kim Reynolds, who was among those who called for the detonation to be delayed as the clock ticked down Thursday, spoke directly with Acting Secretary of the Army Adam Telle, her office said. Environmental groups filed a lawsuit earlier in the day, seeking emergency court action to halt the plan.
Planning for the detonation at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant began after staff earlier this year found several dozen barrels containing lead azide that had degraded, “creating a highly unstable and dangerous situation,” according to an emergency permit approved last week by the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency. Moving or relocating it posed an unacceptable risk of accidental detonation, a possibility that increases in cold weather.
“This will delay the detonation until the latest possible moment prior to a forecasted temperature drop, which would risk further destabilization of the material,” Telle said in a post on X announcing the push to Monday.
The Army had shared details during a public meeting in Middletown in October, but a public advisory Sunday was the first time other communities — some as far away as 100 miles (160 kilometers) — became aware of the potential impact. Nearly 400 people live in Middletown — about 160 miles (257 kilometers) southeast of Des Moines — but thousands more in surrounding areas could be affected by detonated material that could disperse in the air and land on the ground.
“Public communication is essential to public trust,” Telle said.
Businesses and schools adjusted Friday schedules
Vibrations from the two planned blasts were expected to be quick, but they could break old windows in the Middletown area. That led officials to recommend some residents in Middletown vacate the area.
Iowans in the region were told to stay inside; keep windows and doors closed; bring pets and livestock indoors; and clean cars, windowsills and outdoor surfaces afterward.
“The detonation will result in an air plume with some lead-containing particles which will disperse in the air and deposit on the ground,” an advisory states. “Lead is toxic to humans and animals.”
Many schools throughout the region had already announced closures Friday and would now have to decide how to proceed on Monday.
Lucy Giehl, her husband and two dogs live just about 4 miles (6.4 kilometers) north of the ammunition plant. She first learned of the detonation on Sunday and was still trying to figure out where she’d go during the detonation.
But Giehl, 64, also wondered what happens when she gets home after. She voiced frustration about the lack of information about how to mitigate the risks. Her questions remained Thursday even after the delay.
“What are they going to do during those three days to help people be better prepared?” Giehl asked, asking whether she needs to wear gloves to wipe down surfaces or to keep her dogs from drinking water in their pond. “There’s just so many details that I feel like haven’t been addressed with the public.”
Environmental groups are still pursuing legal action
Environmental groups sued Thursday in an effort to stop the detonation, arguing that the EPA failed to require the Army to consider safer alternatives and that the Army failed to give adequate notice of its plans.
The detonation should be canceled outright, not merely delayed, said Wally Taylor, legal chair for the Sierra Club, one of the groups involved in the lawsuit.
“We don’t want the explosion to take place at all,” Taylor said Thursday after the announcement. “There are ways to do it without all the air quality problems and potential health problems.”
According to EPA and Army documents, alternatives such as neutralizing and decomposing the drums’ contents with other chemicals were considered. But officials said handling the drums would increase the probability of an accidental, fatal detonation.
The Army also says taking no action could lead to an accidental detonation that would result in “the sudden, uncontrolled release of vaporized lead, particulate matter, and toxic combustion gases.” Without planning based on weather patterns, that could cause “severe health impacts,” according to the Army’s environmental assessment.
The Army said a panel of experts in munitions chemistry, engineering and environmental safety prepared the detonation plan.
Experts urged residents to take precautions
Patrick O’Shaughnessy, a professor at the University of Iowa’s Department of Occupational and Environmental Health, said it’s still unknown how much contamination will end up in the atmosphere and on surfaces.
Lead is a neurological toxicant that can harm the brain, nervous system and other organs.
With high doses over a short period, people can be subject to lead poisoning and begin to feel sick, said Andrew Whelton, an environmental engineering professor at Purdue University who has helped communities recover from chemical disasters.
Long-term exposure to low doses can lead to neurological development problems, especially in young children, O’Shaughnessy added.
Iowa State’s Des Moines County Extension field office was busy fielding calls Thursday from concerned residents who have been “deathly afraid” for their health and their animals, said staff member Morgan Hoenig.
“We ran out of soil test kits yesterday,” she said.
___
Hill reported from Las Vegas and Montoya Bryan from Albuquerque, New Mexico.

title: For the first time, UN's highest court finds a country responsible for genocide: Myanmar
text:
For the first time, UN's highest court finds a country responsible for genocide: Myanmar
In a landmark judgment, the United Nations’ top court ruled Thursday that Myanmar committed genocide against the Rohingya minority in a brutal 2017 military operation and ordered the Southeast Asian nation to allow people who fled the violence to return home.
The decision marks the first time the court has ruled that a state committed genocide and comes as the World Court also is handling genocide allegations linked to the war in Gaza and the war in Ukraine.
But it remains to be seen how much of the ruling can be implemented. The court’s rulings are final and legally binding, but it has no way to enforce them beyond reporting noncompliance to the U.N. Security Council.
International Court of Justice President Yuji Iwasawa said the court, in a 9-6 decision, found that Myanmar “has committed genocide against the Rohingya group in northern Rakhine state, in violation of its obligations under the Genocide Convention.”
The 15-judge panel of the World Court, which included Navi Pillay, the respected international jurist who won the Nobel Peace Prize last month, rejected Myanmar’s defense that the 2017 campaign was a legitimate operation against insurgents.
Iwasawa said that “the court finds that Myanmar’s security forces killed thousands of Rohingya civilians, perpetrated widespread acts of sexual violence, as well as acts of extreme violence against children, and attacked fleeing Rohingya as they sought to flee in large numbers.”
Rohingya say the ruling validates the suffering of their community
The atmosphere following the hearing was electric, with lawyers and members of the Rohingya, some of whom had traveled thousands of miles (kilometers) to attend the reading, hugging and crying.
“I’m beyond ecstatic today, hearing the judgment, being read out in detail. A lot of those moments and instances that the judges really went into detail, it really validates the kind of experience that Rohingya have,” said Yasmin Ullah, a Rohingya rights activist who sat in the court’s ornate, wood-paneled Great Hall of Justice for the nearly three-hour reading of the ruling.
In Cox's Bazar, Bangladesh, refugee Mohammad Rofik welcomed the recognition of the plight of the Rohingya.
“Today, the world could recognize and give the victory to the Rohingya community, not only the Rohingya community. It is the victory of the whole community of ... Myanmar," he said.
There was no immediate reaction from the Myanmar delegation in The Hague or from the government in Myanmar.
The court also ordered Myanmar to commit to reparations including allowing Rohingya “safe, voluntary and dignified return to their place of residence.” It ordered Myanmar to investigate, prosecute and punish people found to have committed genocidal acts and to pay compensation to Rohingya. The amount will be decided in later court proceedings.
An umbrella organization of Myanmar opposition groups said in a statement that “the struggle for justice will continue, and this judgment must now be enforced,” calling on the international community to ensure it is fully implemented.
U.N. Secretary-General Antonio Guterres called the ruling “a demonstration of international justice and a reaffirmation that impunity for such horrific acts must not stand.”
Shortly after the ruling was read, U.K. Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband said his government was expelling Myanmar’s defense attache from the U.K. and “calling urgently for a U.N. Security Council session to discuss the judgment.”
Brutal counterinsurgency campaign triggered the killings and expulsions
In August 2017, Myanmar’s military launched what it called a clearance campaign in Rakhine state in response to an attack by a Rohingya insurgent group. The campaign led to accusations that security forces committed mass rapes and killings and burned thousands of homes.
The court said that evidence showed Myanmar forces killed about 10,000 Rohingya.
Under the 1948 convention, to establish that genocide occurred, the court had to find that there was an intent to destroy the Rohingya “in whole or in part.”
About 1.2 million Rohingya refugees now live in Bangladesh, primarily in crowded camps across Cox’s Bazar district, where they endure harsh conditions marked by fire hazards, infectious diseases, monsoon landslides, inadequate sanitation and strict work restrictions.
The case could impact genocide allegations elsewhere
In a 2007 judgment, the court said that Serbia “violated the obligation to prevent genocide” in the 1995 Srebrenica massacre, when Bosnian Serb forces murdered some 8,000 mostly Muslim men and boys in the Bosnian town.
Judges at The Hague-based court have also been asked to rule on other allegations of genocide.
South Africa has accused Israel of breaching the genocide convention during its offensive in Gaza. Israel vehemently denies it. That case is years from completion.
Ukraine also has a case pending against Russia. Shortly after Moscow’s full-scale invasion in February 2022, Kyiv accused Russia of fabricating genocide claims against Ukraine to justify the attack.
“The International Court of Justice’s landmark ruling is long-awaited recognition of the suffering the Rohingya have endured from Myanmar’s military. The ruling also provides a significant precedent for victims of genocide, and other grave crimes, across the world in their own quest for justice,” said Maria Elena Vignoli, senior international justice counsel at Human Rights Watch.
Gambia has a history of persecution of its own
The Muslim-majority nation of Gambia launched the proceedings in 2019, two years after it peacefully ousted a longtime military dictator, Yahya Jammeh, who committed widespread abuses against civilians. Since then, there has been a big push for accountability for the crimes committed by Jammeh’s regime.
Outside the courtroom, Gambian Justice Minister Dawda Jallow paid tribute to the Rohingya.
“The victory belongs to the Rohingya. They survived, they testified, and today they were believed. Many of them are here with our delegation from across the world and from the refugee camps in Cox’s Bazar. Their courage made this judgment possible,” he said.

title: Robbins Lumber faces $54K in fines over deadly Searsmont explosion
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Robbins Lumber faces more than $54,000 in fines after May’s deadly explosion at its Searsmont lumber yard.
The U.S. Occupational Health and Safety Administration has cited Robbins Lumber for five violations related to the explosion and fire, News Center Maine reported. The agency has not released additional details about those violations.
On Thursday, Robbins Lumber acknowledged those violations, saying in a statement that it takes “these findings seriously” and continues to cooperate with agencies to improve safety at its facilities.
“The safety and well-being of our employees, emergency responders, and community have always been important to Robbins Lumber. As we rebuild, we are evaluating our facilities, equipment, procedures, and training with a commitment to improving safety and reducing the risk of another tragedy,” Catherine Robbins-Halsted, the company’s vice president, said in a statement.
The fire broke out about 10:05 a.m. on May 15 at the Robbins Lumber campus off Route 131 in an area where wood shavings are packed in plastic bags and spread to a nearby silo.
At the time, the silo was about 20% filled with sawdust and wood shavings. The silo had a fire suppression system, but it failed to activate because the temperatures at the top had not become hot enough to trigger it.
Smoke could be seen coming from the base, and later an orange glow, prompting firefighters to pour water into the silo and the room at its base, which unbeknownst to them was adding oxygen and stirring up dust suspended in an “explosive mixture,” according to a federal investigation into the disaster.
Then the silo exploded without warning about 11 a.m., throwing, in a blast of pressure and fire, mill employees, firefighters and EMS providers who stood nearby.
Firefighters, many of them critically injured, rushed to pull survivors away from the inferno, as nearly 300 firefighters from 46 departments across four counties scrambled to the lumber yard to contain the blaze and tend to the wounded.
Morrill firefighter Andrew Cross, 27, died at the scene of the fire. Searsmont’s assistant fire chief, Wayne Woodbury, succumbed to his injuries on June 14. The blaze, one of the worst industrial disasters in recent Maine history, also killed one of the company’s co-owners, Alden Robbins, who died on July 2.
At least 10 other people, including first responders, a mill employee and another of the mill’s co-owners, were injured in the fire.
Last week, the Maine Occupational Safety and Health program cited six fire departments for failing to keep track of firefighters’ locations, while another five were cited for issues with personal protective equipment, including breathing apparatuses.
The state waived nearly all $108,000 in penalties so that Appleton, Belmont, Lincolnville, Montville, Morrill and Searsmont can “prioritize their limited resources” to improve firefighter safety.
Robbins Lumber is a leading supplier of eastern white pine products, with roots in Searsmont that stretch back nearly 150 years. It employs more than 100 people.
The mill resumed operations on May 26.

title: Man with traumatic brain injury calls himself the luckiest man alive
text:
EAST LANSING, Mich. (Aging Untold) — A Michigan man who survived a head-on crash that caused a traumatic brain injury calls himself the luckiest man alive.
Jim Lowden is a resident at the Hope Network Neuro Rehabilitation facility in East Lansing. He has been working toward independence since the crash, and said determination helped him get back on his feet.
The crash
Lowden survived a violent crash nearly 11 years ago.
“Eight weeks of my life are gone,” Lowden said. “I don’t remember anything at all.”
He was driving a motor home when a truck traveling the other way blew a tire, went over the median and struck him head-on.
“I was tumbling head over heels through space,” Lowden said. “I remember that. But when I actually came back to Earth, it was in a bed at Oakwood.”
Oakwood is an inpatient transitional rehabilitation center, and Lowden has lived on the campus since the crash.
Lowden’s injuries included a traumatic brain injury, a brain bleed, a fractured skull, broken bones, broken ribs and a punctured lung.
Working toward independence
The man who has never liked needing help found himself being pushed in a wheelchair.
“I never liked people helping me, so this was bad,” Lowden said. “Being pushed around in a wheelchair, I really didn’t like, you know, because you’re not independent.”
He also thought he was going to miss out on something he has done every year since he was 5: go ice fishing. Lowden said he told his cousin he would not make it that year.
“He took me,” Lowden said. “They pulled me out on the ice on a sled.”
Mark Evans of Hope Network Neuro Rehabilitation said Lowden is a powerful story for others.
“Jim really is a powerful story for others to follow because even though he still needs help with some things he’s a pretty independent guy, and he’s a pretty positive guy,” Evans said.
Art as part of recovery
Lowden credits creativity for helping him in his recovery. He creates art on canvas, on cardboard and with metal.
“I think getting to use creativity is really stimulating,” Lowden said. “And if you stimulate your mind, then your body follows it.”
Lowden said he walks with a cane, but he calls himself the luckiest man alive.
“I walk with a cane, but boo hoo, some guy in a wheelchair would be glad to trade with me,” he said.

title: Grand jury indicts Illinois man on terrorism and weapons charges in foiled Hindu temple shooting
text:
Grand jury indicts Illinois man on terrorism and weapons charges in foiled Hindu temple shooting
A 19-year-old man accused of planning a mass shooting at a Hindu temple in a Chicago suburb faces new charges of terrorism and armed violence, according to a grand jury indictment obtained by The Associated Press.
Authorities allege Alexandros Paporakis planned to attack a Hindu temple in Aurora, Illinois, on Oct. 11, the first day of the Hindu holiday of Navaratri. Paporakis' co-workers at a Taco Bell reported to authorities that he told them he planned to “kill Indian people,” and police arrested him that afternoon. He was initially charged with making a terrorist threat and illegally possessing a rifle.
Prosecutors have said Paporakis, of Palatine, Illinois, calls himself a white supremacist and neo-Nazi, and that he wrote a document detailing his fantasies about murdering non-white people. Police have said they recovered a rifle, ammunition, a tactical vest and a patch “displaying imagery associated with white supremacist extremism” from his house.
A grand jury indicted Paporakis on Nov. 5 on six counts of terrorism, two counts of armed violence and two counts of attempted terrorism, all felonies. The jury also added nine more counts of making a terrorist threat.
The indictment also included new weapons-related charges, including possession of a firearm without a serial number and not having a police-issued identification card.
It is not clear why police delayed releasing information about the grand jury indictment.
The indictment alleges Paporakis drove to the Hindu temple with a loaded firearm, “pointed a loaded firearm at an individual and tried to fire” it, which was a “substantial step towards the commission of terrorism.”
Authorities have said Paporakis’ car entered the temple’s parking lot on the day of the thwarted attack. They allege he told his co-worker he left when his gun jammed, but promised to “fix his gun and try again,” according to the indictment.
The indictment also states Paporakis wrote that he wanted to “cleanse the streets of the parasitic infection that is Indian immigration” and intended the attack to scare Indian people away from immigrating to the U.S.
A judge ordered Paporakis to be detained, declaring him a threat to the community. He is due to be arraigned Thursday morning.
Fedor Kozlov, an attorney for Paporakis, told AP in a text message Wednesday that his client is still planning to plead not guilty to the charges.
The thwarted shooting sparked alarm among members of Chicago's Hindu community and South Asian leaders, who said an uptick in racist rhetoric against their community had fueled the threat. U.S. Rep. Raja Krishnamoorthi, who was at the temple that was targeted on the day of the planned attack, urged authorities to charge Paporakis with a hate crime. Authorities have not announced any such charge.
The FBI's Chicago field office said Wednesday there was no additional information about possible federal charges. The U.S. Attorney's Office for the Northern District of Illinois has not responded to a request for comment.

title: St. Peter's Basilica marks 400 years at the heart of Roman Catholicism
text:
St. Peter's Basilica marks 400 years at the heart of Roman Catholicism
St. Peter’s Basilica, the spiritual heart of Roman Catholicism whose commanding dome defines the Roman skyline and is a monument to artistic achievement and perseverance, marked the 400th anniversary of its dedication on Wednesday.
Pope Leo XIV dedicated a Mass “to one of the most celebrated monuments in the world,” telling the faithful gathered beneath the basilica's soaring vaults that “visiting this majestic church always stirs emotion: We are filled with awe, inspired by the sacredness of faith, the power of history and the beauty of art.”
The Chicago-born pontiff also reflected on the scale of the structure, which stretches roughly the length of two American football fields.
Related video: Catholics in Chicago attend Mass and pray for Pope Leo after cancer diagnosis
“The vastness of the Vatican Basilica reflects an enduring vocation to welcome, so that as many people as possible may find a place in the church,” Leo said.
St. Peter's construction spanned 120 years, 20 pontificates and the work of a succession of 12 architects, enduring the Protestant Reformation, which started in 1517, and the Sack of Rome in 1527 before Pope Urban VIII dedicated it on Nov. 18, 1626.
“You walk through those doors and you won’t feel the conflicts and the disasters and the setbacks,” said Elizabeth Lev, a Rome-based American art historian. “You walk through those doors and you see continuity and beauty and achievement and triumph.”
A setting for papal ceremonies and a destination for millions of pilgrims each year, the basilica was built over the traditional burial site of the Apostle Peter, replacing a church that had stood for more than a millennium.
Pope Julius II laid the foundation stone on April 18, 1506, launching a project whose architects included Donato Bramante, Renaissance master Michelangelo and Carlo Maderno, who completed its facade.
Even on the day of its dedication, the basilica’s familiar setting was still taking shape.
“The church facade was complete, but the amazing piazza, which is part and parcel of the church we know today, wasn’t there yet,” Lev said.
“As a matter of fact, you would have heard lots of people complaining about the new facade and how it blocked Michelangelo’s dome,” she said.
Italian sculptor and architect Gian Lorenzo Bernini’s sweeping oval piazza was completed in 1667, its curving colonnades conceived as the welcoming arms of the church. Its 284 columns, arranged in four rows, frame an oval space connected to the basilica by a trapezoidal forecourt.
Inside, the basilica’s architecture draws attention toward its spiritual center: Peter’s tomb beneath the main altar, Bernini’s monumental bronze canopy and Michelangelo’s dome rising overhead. Generations of popes have been entombed in the basilica and the Vatican Grottoes below.
“The inside of St. Peter’s Basilica is marked by unity and magnificence,” Lev said. “So for a church that took 120 years, it’s amazing how each part fits together into something of a unified whole.”
The basilica and its square have witnessed the opening of the Second Vatican Council, papal funerals and the first appearances of newly elected pontiffs. Crowds gather in the square for Sunday blessings, while at Christmas and Easter the pope traditionally delivers his message and “Urbi et Orbi” blessing — Latin for “to the city and to the world” — from the basilica’s central balcony.
In one of the defining images of the coronavirus pandemic, Pope Francis stood before the rain-soaked, deserted square to impart an extraordinary blessing on March 27, 2020.
The basilica also provided the setting for a private meeting between U.S. President Donald Trump and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy before Francis’ funeral on April 26, 2025.
For Lev, the basilica's long history offers a message for another unsettled age.
“I think one of the great lessons about St. Peter’s is that people adapt, the church adapts according to the circumstances,” she said. “And yes indeed, many terrible things happened while they were building that church and they forged onwards and they ended up making something beautiful.”
___
Colleen Barry reported from Milan.

text:
Norway man pleads guilty in theft of 12 guns from Maine sporting goods store
Prosecutors say Grover Lee Harmon admitted his involvement in a March burglary at J&K Sporting Goods in West Paris
Norway man pleads guilty in theft of 12 guns from Maine sporting goods store
Prosecutors say Grover Lee Harmon admitted his involvement in a March burglary at J&K Sporting Goods in West Paris
A Norway man pleaded guilty to federal charges in connection with the theft of 12 firearms from a sporting goods store in West Paris.
Grover Lee Harmon, 41, pleaded guilty Thursday in U.S. District Court in Portland to stealing firearms from a federally licensed dealer and being a felon in possession of a firearm.
According to court records, 12 handguns were stolen from J&K Sporting Goods in March 2026.
Harmon was arrested on unrelated warrants during a traffic stop in April.
Authorities later searched a residence that was used by Harmon and his girlfriend and recovered two firearms stolen during the burglary.
During an interview with investigators, Harmon admitted his involvement in the burglary and acknowledged handling stolen firearms.
Harmon faces up to five years in prison for the theft and up to 15 years for illegally possessing a firearm.
A sentencing date has not yet been announced.

title: ‘Pure anger’: Therapist fired over video that appears to show her hit 7-year-old with autism
text:
ATLANTA (ANF/Gray News) - An Atlanta therapist who works with children on the autism spectrum has been fired after doorbell camera video appears to show her hitting a 7-year-old client.
Lakita Walker and Rameriz Pass say the incident was caught on their neighbor’s Ring camera Tuesday. The video allegedly shows their 7-year-old son’s therapist yanking then hitting him.
“I was distraught. I was heartbroken because I see this all the time, and I couldn’t believe it happened to me,” Walker said.
“It’s like pure anger,” Pass said. “But after that happened, it’s like a kick in the face almost. It hurts.”
Walker and Pass say their son has autism and is nonverbal. He has received in-home applied behavior analysis (ABA) therapy from a licensed therapist with Centria Autism Life Skills Autism Academy since he was 3 years old. The therapy consists of life skills, playing, behavioral management and academics.
The parents say this therapist had only been with him for a month.
“It’s your worst nightmare when you have a nonverbal child dealing with autism. It’s like the last thing you want is someone to mistreat him,” Pass said.
“People think you could trust someone because you hear that they’re trained... That doesn’t mean you can trust them,” Walker said.
The incident happened during the victim’s outside playtime. His parents say he and the therapist were walking around their building when their son ran toward the neighbors’ Ring camera.
“She was too comfortable with what she did in broad daylight in front of my neighbor’s house,” Walker said. “If he looks like he’s been slanged around like a rag doll to me, she’s definitely an adult. She’s more than twice the size. He’s not even 70 pounds.”
Walker says she called police immediately, and they came and took a report. Atlanta police confirmed they are investigating.
“I do feel like she should have been arrested on scene because she struck him twice,” Walker said.
The mother says she then called the therapist’s supervisor with Centria Autism.
“She was shocked. She apologized. She called her boss. They just called and apologized. It was nothing else really said about it,” Walker said.
A spokesperson with Centria Autism provided the following statement to Atlanta News First:
“The individual is no longer employed by Centria, and we remain committed to supporting the child and family affected by this incident. The actions of this individual are unacceptable and do not reflect the values, standards, or expectations of Centria Autism. The safety and well-being of the children and families we serve has always been, and will continue to be, our highest priority.”
The victim’s parents say the therapist being fired is a step in the right direction. The incident has left the whole family traumatized.
“I’m overprotective. Overly protective, and I feel like I let my guard down. It’s already hard for me to trust, and I trusted the company... I trusted what they told me, and they failed. They failed us tremendously,” Walker said.
“The trust is just broken. And when the trust is broken, and my son can’t tell me when he’s being mistreated. So, it’s like, ‘How could I trust anyone right now?’” Pass said.
The parents say they will be talking with their son’s school to get him extra help there. A family member who is a board-certified behavioral analyst has also offered to step in and help.

title: Maine will delay Medicaid work requirements from January to July
text:
Maine state officials on Thursday announced that they will delay the implementation of Medicaid work requirements to July — a change to the health insurance program that was set to launch in January.
The Trump administration notified states last week that they could delay the work requirements provision of the 2025 GOP budget bill known as the One Big Beautiful Bill Act. The new rules are expected to result in 31,000 Maine Medicaid recipients losing coverage.
Rep. Chellie Pingree, D-1st District, said in an interview Thursday that the delay gives new Democratic majorities in Congress an opening to reverse the Medicaid cuts before they take effect.
Democrats swept into control of Congress during the midterm elections, gaining large majorities in the House and Senate.
Pingree said Democrats are going to use their new leverage to try to roll back the cuts, because not doing so will result in millions of people nationwide, including thousands of Maine residents, becoming uninsured and hospitals losing funding.
“The impacts will be like an earthquake,” Pingree said.
The requirements mandate that Medicaid recipients work, volunteer or attend school for 80 hours per month. There are numerous exceptions, including for those who are disabled. The work requirements apply to those aged 19-64 in the expansion population — those in income brackets who became eligible after Maine expanded Medicaid in 2019.
But government estimates expected thousands to lose coverage because they either fail to meet the new requirements or fail to complete the documentation to prove they’re eligible.
Lindsay Hammes, spokesperson for the Maine Department of Health and Human Services, said the state will opt into the delay.
“Maine DHHS plans to use this period to strengthen its eligibility systems, including extensive testing, in order to prepare for full implementation on July 1, 2027,” Hammes said in a statement.
Maine had hired 35 DHHS workers and spent $8 million to implement the requirements.
Federal officials, when announcing the delay last week, said the decision provides “states a transition period to further modernize systems, improve processes, and streamline the applicant and beneficiary experience.”

title: Larry Poindexter, ‘S.W.A.T.’ actor, dies at 66 after tragic accident
text:
(Gray News) - Larry Poindexter died Wednesday at age 66, days after he was hit by a car, Deadline reported.
Poindexter was reportedly crossing the street to pick up food Friday night in the Studio City neighborhood of Los Angeles when he was hit, Variety reported. He died suddenly Wednesday morning, before he was scheduled to undergo surgery for broken ribs.
Poindexter, who has almost 200 acting credits, was best known for his role in the 2003 film “S.W.A.T.” He also appeared in 30 episodes of “Days of Our Lives” and 12 episodes of “General Hospital.” He was a series regular on “The Hard Times of RJ Berger” and had a major recurring role on “JAG.”
He also guest-starred on several shows, including “How I Met Your Mother,” “Friends,” “Weeds,” “The Rookie” and “Hawaii Five-0.”
Poindexter is survived by his wife, Carol Kritzer, and their two sons.
