Central Park's horse-drawn carriage drivers sue NYC over incoming ban
text:
Central Park's horse-drawn carriage drivers sue NYC over incoming ban
Hold your horses: Central Park's horse-drawn carriage drivers sued New York City on Thursday to stop a new law that will ban the iconic tourist attraction, challenging Mayor Zohran Mamdani just minutes after he signed a bill to wind down the industry.
The law — approved after the death of a teenager last spring — is set to stop the carriage rides by June 2028.
But the union representing carriage drivers filed a federal lawsuit in Manhattan attempting to have the ban struck down, arguing the city is taking away their livelihoods.
"The City's approach can be summarized in twelve words: immediately cripple the owners, ignore property interests and contracts, and maybe compensate," the lawsuit reads.
The lawsuit is the latest turn in a long fight over the carriage rides, as animal welfare activists and industry supporters have tussled over whether the carriage rides amount to animal cruelty or are simply a romantic throwback to the city's past.
At a bill signing ceremony at City Hall on Thursday, Mamdani lauded the role of horses in the city's development but said the animals should no longer be hauling tourists around a perpetually busy Central Park among joggers, cyclists and other passersby.
"Our city has changed and now it is time for our laws to change, too," said Mamdani, a Democrat.
City lawmakers reignited their push for a ban earlier this year in response to the death of 18-year-old Indian tourist Romanch Mahajan, who died after jumping from a runaway carriage in what appeared to be the first fatality in a horse carriage accident since they were introduced in Central Park.
Over the years, horses have collapsed or gotten startled and run off into cars or other objects. In response, the city has put various safety regulations in place for the industry, including veterinary checkups, vacation time for horses and a retirement age for the animals.
City Hall has promised to release a career transition plan for those in the carriage industry next April that includes job training, educational pathways and stipends, though drivers argue their future remains uncertain.
"Despite the good intentions of the mayor, the protections he outlined recently should have been written into the legislation," said John Samuelsen, head of the Transport Workers Union, which represents carriage drivers.
The union's lawsuit argues the law is unconstitutional and that the city violated local legal procedures when it approved the law. It names the mayor and various other city officials as defendants.
A spokesperson for the city's law department said it is reviewing the case.

title: 'GTA VI' finally reveals the actors, voices and familiar names behind Vice City
text:
LOS ANGELES (AP) — After years of secrecy, “Grand Theft Auto VI” is finally giving up some of its biggest mysteries.
Rockstar Games kept much of the cast behind its blockbuster video game under wraps before launch, including the performers behind protagonists Lucia Caminos and Jason Duval. Now that players are roaming Vice City and the wider fictional state of Leonida, actors who spent years bound to secrecy are revealing themselves.
The gaming company’s newly released credits are filling in an unusually deep roster of performers, musicians, comedians and broadcasters.
Manni L. Perez plays Lucia and Dylan Rourke portrays Jason, confirming years of fan speculation over the actors behind the game’s central couple. Rockstar’s official credits list both as the leads.
Rourke and Perez marked the reveal together on social media, writing about the years they spent watching developers build the game before finally being able to publicly connect themselves to it.
They are hardly alone.
Former “Saturday Night Live” cast member Bobby Moynihan plays Cal, while Stephen Root, who had previously acknowledged appearing in the game without revealing his role, voices Brian Heder. Taryn Manning, Roselyn Sanchez and Denzel Curry are also among the names buried throughout Rockstar’s sprawling cast list.
The faces behind Lucia and Jason
For years, Rockstar allowed Lucia and Jason to become globally recognizable characters without publicly identifying the actors portraying them.
That created an online guessing game as fans analyzed voices, facial features and past acting credits while Rockstar released trailers but little information about the performers. The official credits finally ended the speculation with Rourke as Jason, a former soldier pulled deeper into Leonida’s criminal world, while Perez plays Lucia, his partner after her release from prison.
The reveal also puts two actors who were hardly household names at the center of one of entertainment’s largest launches.
Rourke said in a joint Instagram post with Perez that they had spent years witnessing what he called some of the hardest-working craftspeople in game development, adding that the pair were honored to be part of the project.
Other actors have described similarly long periods of secrecy. Edwina Rai, who appears in the game, said on Instagram that she first auditioned in April 2022 without even knowing what the project was. She went through three callbacks and a chemistry read before landing a role in what she described as the biggest project of her career.
GTA’s radio stations become their own celebrity universe
Some of the biggest surprises are not walking Vice City’s streets at all. They are coming through its radios and talk shows.
“Weird Al” Yankovic revealed that he hosts Vice City FM, the game’s ’80s station, alongside Brigitte Nielsen. He also wrote in-game commercials and voices Burger Shot advertisements. Rockstar’s credits list Yankovic not only as DJ Al but among the game’s additional writers and original-music contributors.
Charlamagne tha God and Ivy Rivera host the in-game “Early AF” program, while “GTA VI”’s larger radio lineup includes musicians, actors and comedians ranging from Bad Bunny and Burna Boy to Lana Del Rey,Jeremy Irons,Keith Richards and Jason Sudeikis.
The effect is bigger than a conventional video game soundtrack. Rockstar has constructed fictional stations that operate almost like real media ecosystems, with hosts, commercials, talk segments and personalities embedded into the world around the player.
That approach has long been part of the franchise’s satire, but “GTA VI” appears to have expanded it considerably.

title: The Wachowskis Are Working to Get ‘The Matrix’ Rights Back
text:
Report: The Wachowskis Are Working to Get ‘The Matrix’ Rights Back
The Matrix ... reclaimed?
According to a report in Puck, the Wachowskis are “formally notifying Warners they are exercising their copyright termination rights” to their signature sci-fi creation, The Matrix.
“As soon as February 2029, the studio could lose its grip on Neo, Morpheus, et al. in the U.S., and maybe beyond,” the publication adds.
READ MORE: These VHS Tapes Are Worth Shocking Amounts of Money
Warner Bros. does have another Matrix movie in development. Word about the film first emerged in the spring of 2024, when it was revealed that a fifth Matrix, the first that would have been made without directorial involvement of Lana or Lily Wachowski, was being overseen by The Martian writer Drew Goddard.
More than two years later, no additional details have emerged, but the project is mentioned in Puck’s report — along with the tidbit that the Wachowskis have recently been “encouraging of the newest sequel and have even increased their involvement.”
The original Matrix remains of the most beloved science-fiction films of the last 50 years. The sequels ... not so much. The most recent, 2021’s The Matrix Resurrections, reunited original stars Keanu Reeves and Carrie-Anne Moss and was directed by Lana Wachowski, but it was still one of the more expensive flops of the Covid era. It reportedly cost close to $200 million and wound up grossing only about $160 million worldwide.
But we live in a world dominated by IP. (In a few years it may be dominated by squid-like artificial intelligence, but for now it’s just dominated by IP.) Of course Warner Bros., now owned by Skydance, wants to exploit every franchise under its control. That includes The Matrix ... at least for now.

title: Traffic impacts for hours after driver spills coffee, crashes truck hauling French fries in Maine
text:
Traffic impacts for hours after driver spills coffee, crashes truck hauling French fries in Maine
Drivers on Interstate 95 in northern Penobscot County should expect some traffic impacts and delays for several hours on Thursday as crews work to remove a tractor-trailer truck that crashed last Wednesday night.
Maine State Police say the driver of a 2024 Western Star truck hauling French fries spilled hot coffee on his lap at about 11:54 p.m. The driver, a 63-year-old man from Brunswick, lost control and his truck rolled over into the median along the highway in Herseytown Township, which is part of Stacyville.
The driver was not hurt.
Crews started working to remove the truck at about 8 a.m. on Thursday. Police said they expected a lane would be closed for several hours.

title: Former owner of internet-famous squirrel charged with mortgage fraud
text:
One of the owners of an internet celebrity squirrel named Peanut has been charged with numerous felonies including mortgage fraud, a few weeks after the animal’s other owner was detained by ICE.
After New York wildlife officers euthanized the squirrel, also known as P’nut, in 2024, prominent Republicans cited the killing as an example of unnecessary government overreach. The squirrel’s owners, Mark Longo and wife Daniela Bittner, run P’Nuts Freedom Farm Animal Sanctuary in upstate New York and post videos of themselves and their animals to social media.
A New York State Police Special Investigations Unit in Rochester, New York, arrested Longo, 36, on Wednesday following an investigation into residential mortgage fraud, police said. He faces a total of 14 felony charges that also include grand larceny and falsifying business records, said police, who added that Longo is accused of using falsified pay stubs and other documents to obtain a $720,000 residential mortgage.
“The investigation began in December 2024, when State Police received information about financial irregularities involving Longo,” said Beau Duffy, a spokesperson for New York State Police.
Longo did not return messages seeking comment. Police said he was living in Chemung County, on the border of New York and Pennsylvania, at the time of the arrest. He has pleaded not guilty and is due back in Southport Town Court in the Elmira area on Feb. 4, Duffy said.
It’s the second recent setback for Longo and Bittner, as Bittner was arrested by immigration officers in mid-October at a small airport and faced the possibility of deportation to Germany. The Department of Homeland Security, which oversees U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement, said after the arrest that Bittner “chose to overstay her welcome in defiance of our nation’s laws.”
DHS officials did not respond to a request for an update on Bittner’s status on Thursday. A search of an ICE detainee database Thursday turned up no results. Longo has blamed the detention on a paperwork mix-up.
Peanut, who would charm viewers by climbing on his owner’s back and wearing tiny cowboy hats, was a social media celebrity until New York officials responded to complaints that the couple were keeping wild animals in their house as pets. Peanut bit the gloved thumb of a biologist during one inspection and was euthanized to test for rabies.
JD Vance said at a rally before the 2024 election that “Democrats murdered the Elon Musk of squirrels” when Peanut was killed.

title: FEMA facing bed bug infestation
text:
(CNN) - The nation’s Federal Emergency Management Agency is dealing with its own sort of emergency this week -- bed bugs.
The infestation happened at the FEMA headquarters in Washington, D.C.
More than 1,000 staffers are having to work from home while the building is fumigated.
The bed bugs were apparently found on multiple floors.
A memo to FEMA workers alerting them to the problem gave no indication of when staff could return to the building.
This was the second emergency FEMA workers have faced in just a week. They were mobilized by Homeland Security to help with last Friday’s ground-stop on flights.

title: UMaine men’s basketball holds off Quinnipiac
text:
Hudson Franz set a career high in points for the second straight game, scoring 22 points on 7-for-8 shooting as Maine snapped a three-game losing streak with a 69-67 win over Quinnipiac in a men’s basketball game Thursday night in Hamden, Connecticut.
Quinnipiac, which trailed by 19 with 12:37 remaining, nearly erased an 11-point deficit in the last 45 seconds. Lucas Sekasi drained three straight 3-pointers as the Bobcats closed to within 68-67 with three seconds left. Maine’s DeAndre Williams was fouled with .6 seconds remaining and made the first free throw before missing the second one intentionally.
Franz scored 11 of Maine’s first 14 points, helping the Black Bears (2-4) build a 33-21 halftime lead.
The lead grew to 48-29 before Quinnipiac (2-4) began a comeback.
Darius Lopes was the only other UMaine player in double figures, finishing with 10 points.
Keith McKnight scored 18 points and Sekasi had 17 for Quinnipiac.

Sunny stretch continues, even warmer Friday
Temperatures are running 10 to 15 degrees above average, with highs in the 50s and low 60s Thursday afternoon. Temperatures will likely climb a few degrees higher on Friday, after a chilly night in the 30s to low 40s. Sunshine reigns through Saturday, with increasing clouds likely on Sunday. 
The 10-day dry stretch will likely end Monday as a storm moves up the East Coast, bringing tropical moisture toward New England.
An area of low pressure develops along a front off Florida's east coast and could become a subtropical or tropical storm as it moves northward toward the Carolina coast. If it does take on tropical characteristics, it will be given the next name on the list: Kyle. Either way, impacts to Maine would remain the same: Rain, favoring the coast, with a chance for high winds and storm surge.
If the storm moves close enough to the New England coast to create a storm surge, Monday afternoon's high tide would be the one cycle to keep an eye on. Luckily, the month's highest tides are expected in the following days, when the storm will be long gone.

Felony charges dismissed against boxer Floyd Mayweather Jr. over bad check in Las Vegas
text:
Felony charges dismissed against boxer Floyd Mayweather Jr. over bad check in Las Vegas
A Las Vegas court dismissed felony charges against Floyd Mayweather Jr. on Wednesday at the request of prosecutors, following allegations the boxer wrote a bad check to purchase a watch, according to court records.
A hearing in the case that had been scheduled for Thursday was canceled.
Mayweather, 49, was charged in April with theft and passing a check without sufficient funds with intent to defraud.
Prosecutors in Clark County had alleged Mayweather wrote the $200,000 check to Las Vegas designer resale store Gold and Beyond in December 2024 despite having insufficient funds in his account, according to the criminal complaint.
The Associated Press left emails, voice and text messages this week seeking comment with Mayweather’s attorney, Clark County prosecutors and an attorney for Gold and Beyond.
Mayweather, a former five-division world champion, announced his retirement in 2017 with a 50-0 record. After saying earlier this year that he was coming out of retirement, he was scheduled to be in Athens, Greece, for the “Battle of the Legends” boxing match in June. The event was canceled due to a legal dispute with CSI Sports.
CSI sued Mayweather in the Southern District of New York district court alleging breach of contract for allegedly failing to fight Mike Tyson in a separate event. Mayweather denied the allegations in court documents.
Earlier this year, Mayweather was sued in New York over his alleged failure to pay rent at a Manhattan apartment and was in financial disputes with multiple jewelers.
He also filed a lawsuit in New York against his former business manager, alleging a yearslong fraud scheme.

title: AARP says changing economy left Social Security funding plan behind
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
WASHINGTON (Gray DC) - As lawmakers consider how to prevent future cuts to Social Security benefits, a new AARP study says the program’s funding structure has not kept pace with changes in the U.S. economy over the past 40 years.
Sen. Jeff Merkley (D-Ore.) Social Security benefits are a significant source of income for many retirees.
“For about half of American seniors that get these benefits, it accounts for about half to 100 percent of their income,” he said.
Sen. Ron Johnson, (R-Wis.), called on Congress to act.
“Pass a law that prevents the reduction of Social Security benefits, and quit scaring seniors,” he said.
AARP says the program was designed for an economy in which a larger share of the nation’s economic output went to workers, allowing payroll taxes to generate proportionally more revenue.
“We have a shift from workers to capital,” said Rich Johnson of AARP. “So that more money is going to the owners of capital through corporate profits, through investment income than to workers.”
The organization also says the cap on wages subject to Social Security payroll taxes was established when earnings were more evenly distributed.
“That’s currently set at about $184,000. That now covers only about 83 percent of all earnings in the economy. It used to be 90 percent,” AARP’s Rich Johnson said.
Some advocates have proposed eliminating the wage cap to increase revenue or taxing corporate profits to supplement payroll taxes. Lawmakers are weighing possible solutions as they consider how to protect retirees from benefit cuts.

title: University of New England helps business leaders turn AI into action with online graduate course
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Artificial intelligence is reshaping business. The University of New England is helping leaders put it to work.
Following a successful inaugural session, UNE will again offer Leading with AI, an online graduate-level business leadership course designed to help professionals turn AI opportunities into measurable business results. The course returns in spring 2027.
Taught by Mike Wright, director of AI Product Management at Unum, the course helps business leaders navigate critical questions: Where can AI deliver the most value? Which solutions are worth the investment? And how can organizations adopt them responsibly?
Through case studies and hands-on exercises, participants learn to:
● Identify AI opportunities that support business goals
● Evaluate AI technologies, vendors, and tailored solutions
● Assess data integration needs, organizational readiness, risks, and ethical considerations
● Build implementation roadmaps that address technical requirements and coordination across departments
● Define measures of success and plan for scaling AI initiatives
Designed for business leaders at organizations of all sizes, the course connects AI strategy with the technical and operational knowledge needed to put it into practice. Enterprise leaders learn to engage more effectively with IT teams on large-scale transformation, while small and midsize business leaders gain a broader understanding of what successful AI implementation requires.
Students explore machine learning, neural networks and agentic AI systems that can carry out multistep tasks with an emphasis on how these technologies can address business needs. The course examines how tailored AI solutions integrate with organizational data, systems and operations.
A major case study challenges students to develop an AI implementation plan for one of three enterprise-scale scenarios: a major hospital network, a national logistics company or a major entertainment and stadium venue company. Students must work through complex operational demands, departmental constraints, and ambitious AI goals to propose a tailored solution.
“This course helps business leaders evaluate AI vendors, understand applied AI solutions, and make informed decisions about AI adoption, with a focus on operational and technical considerations and an understanding of business risks and opportunities,” Wright said.
Ethics, privacy and responsible AI use are central to those discussions. Wright brings more than 15 years of experience across enterprise and growth-stage technology companies, including Meta, TikTok and early-stage startups. At Unum, a Fortune 500 employee benefits company, he leads AI product strategy and development.
Participants in the inaugural session praised Wright’s engaging teaching style and business experience, highlighting the course’s timely content and practical applications.
“It wasn’t just how to write prompts, for example. It talked about the history of AI, the current AI landscape, and what is projected to come,” participant Alesha Miller said. “The course also taught us about the different types of AI, how they work, governance and regulations, and so on.”
Businesses looking to strengthen AI expertise across their organizations can also enroll multiple employees in Leading with AI. Employers interested in group enrollment can contact mba@une.edu to discuss registration options.
Leading with AI will be offered in spring 2027. For course details and registration information, visit online.une.edu/mba-ce-course.
The University of New England is Maine’s largest independent university, with two beautiful coastal campuses in Maine, a one-of-a-kind study-abroad campus in Tangier, Morocco and an array of flexible online offerings. In an uncommonly welcoming and supportive community, we offer hands-on learning, empowering students to make a positive impact in a world full of challenges. We are the state’s top provider of health professionals and home to Maine’s only medical and dental colleges, physician assistant program and pharmacy school, in addition to a variety of other interprofessionally aligned healthcare programs and nationally recognized programs in the marine sciences, the natural and social sciences, business, the humanities and the arts. Visit www.une.edu.

title: Judge issues 14-day extension of order blocking Trump's memorial arch in DC
text:
Judge issues 14-day extension of order blocking Trump's memorial arch in DC
A federal judge on Wednesday temporarily extended an order blocking the Trump administration from breaking ground on a towering memorial arch in the nation's capital.
The temporary restraining order was due to expire on Thursday, but U.S. District Judge Tanya Chutkan extended it by 14 days. That would keep President Donald Trump's construction project on hold until Dec. 3 or until Chutkan rules on a pending request for a more permanent preliminary injunction.
The decision followed a Nov. 5 order Chutkan issued shortly after a hearing of the National Capital Planning Commission ended with the Trump-heavy commission giving the arch its final approval in an 8-4 vote, despite dozens of witnesses who opposed the construction.
The administration said the work could begin as soon as the approval and the Interior Department issued a final decision authorizing construction and the proper notification was published by the National Park Service.
In issuing the latest delay, Chutkan granted a request by plaintiffs in lawsuits challenging the arch construction. The case has grown more complicated as separate groups have filed lawsuits asking that the project not be allowed to go forward.
Nicolas Sansone, an attorney with the Public Citizen Litigation Group that is representing the plaintiffs in the original lawsuit, said they were "gratified to see that the judge recognized that the circumstances that required emergency relief two weeks ago haven't changed. We're hopeful the additional two-week pause will give the court the opportunity to assess our arguments in favor of a longer-term preliminary injunction that will block construction of the arch while the lawsuit proceeds."
"An activist district court has again blocked the construction of the long-awaited Military Triumphal Arch. The judiciary should not be abused to politicize a structure designed to unite our nation," said White House spokesman Davis Ingle in an emailed statement. "We will continue making the case for this beautiful and fitting monument and are confident we will be fully vindicated as this litigation proceeds."
The District of Columbia and Virginia filed suit Oct. 31. Chutkan consolidated that suit with the original, filed by a group of Vietnam veterans and an architectural historian. Members of the Kennedy family filed a separate lawsuit Nov. 10, citing the impact the 250-foot (76-meter) structure would have on family members buried at Arlington National Cemetery. The Arlington County Board filed a lawsuit Oct. 8 in federal court in the Eastern District of Virginia challenging the speed with which the project was being undertaken and the harm it would cause to the county, which is immediately adjacent to the proposed site.
Chutkan said the 14-day extension of the order is warranted because nothing has significantly changed in the litigation in the two weeks since she issued it. She decided to maintain the status quo pending her ruling on the injunction request.
The arch is one of several projects around Washington that Trump has undertaken as he remakes the city, from renovating one of its storied public golf courses to threatening to demolish the John F. Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts. Those projects could soon face greater scrutiny after the Democrats take control of Congress.
Many of those plans are being challenged in the courts. The federal government Thursday filed a notice of appeal to a 14-day temporary restraining order issued Nov. 14 in the golf course case.
The original plaintiffs in the District of Columbia case — three veterans and a retired architectural historian — had asked Chutkan to prohibit the administration and the National Park Service "from taking any steps to construct, or to direct or facilitate construction of, any structure in Memorial Circle, absent congressional authorization, during the pendency of this litigation."
Critics, including the plaintiffs, argue the administration must seek congressional approval for the arch and say that, once built, it will disrupt the sightlines connecting historic landmarks in the nation's capital. The administration has argued that Congress decades ago cleared the way for a monument at Memorial Circle.

title: Gardens Aglow 2026 lights up Coastal Maine Botanical Gardens
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Maine’s popular light show, Gardens Aglow, returned to Boothbay last Saturday for its six-week run through Jan. 2. Coastal Maine Botanical Gardens invites guests to “Gather, Glow, and Celebrate” with this year’s “Gathered in Maine” theme. New lighted elements feature a maple tapping scene, a landscape fit for mushroom foraging and a larger-than-life anthill with an army of ants carrying leaves and berries. Completely new every year, the in-house design and hand-strung display keep Maine Gardens’ seasonal staff employed into the new year and provide vital funds for the nonprofit’s mission work.
“Our team has been working hard since August on this year’s show. I say this every year, but this year might be the best,” Gretchen Ostherr, president and CEO of Coastal Maine Botanical Gardens, said in a prepared release. “Even though I get to watch — and take part in the light hanging — I am always amazed at how we transform from a green sanctuary into a sparkling wonderland. We can’t wait to celebrate this season with families from Maine and New England.”
For the last handful of years, Maine Gardens have been nominated in the Best Botanical Garden Holiday Lights category, as part of USA TODAY’s 10 Best Readers’ Choice Awards. After landing in the top five in recent years, Maine Gardens hopes to bring the top spot to Maine this year. Event organizers hope that Gardens Aglow fans will show their Maine pride by voting daily to help Gardens Aglow bring the title home.
With price-conscious guests in mind, this year there will be three pricing tiers: Value on weekdays, Standard on Fridays and Sundays, and Premium on Saturdays, allowing guests to pick the night and price that work for them. An additional VIP add-on pass unlocks special Gardens Aglow gifts, free unlimited ticket exchanges, flexible arrival times on your selected date and a cozy fire pit experience.
Ticket prices start at $20 for adults, $18 for seniors and veterans, and $10 for children ages 3-17. Children under the age of 3 are free. Members save 20% on all Gardens Aglow admission tickets. VIP add-on passes are $50 per ticket and are not subject to any discounts. For more information on pricing and time slots, visit gardensaglow.org.
A complimentary park-and-ride shuttle runs Friday, Saturday and Sunday from Boothbay Harbor Town Office, allowing guests to experience Boothbay Harbor’s shopping, dining and lodging delights before and after visiting Gardens Aglow. Shuttle runs begin at 3:45 p.m. The last shuttle back is at 9 p.m.
For a complete calendar of regional offerings, the robust slate of Boothbay Lights events, and park-and-ride details, visit boothbaylights.com.

title: Bowdoin men’s soccer thriving with an adaptable lineup, advancing in NCAA tourney
text:
BRUNSWICK — The 2026 season hasn’t been a smooth ride for the Bowdoin College men’s soccer team, but the Polar Bears have found a way to continue their recent success.
For the third time in five seasons, Bowdoin has reached the third round of the NCAA Division III tournament. After winning two games at home last weekend, the Polar Bears travel to Pennsylvania to face Scranton on Saturday.
Following the graduation in the spring of Tyler Huck, the second-leading scorer in program history, the Polar Bears have patched together enough offense to post a 10-3-5 record. They’ve done so despite several injuries, with several younger players taking on prominent roles.
“We have not had a straight line to where we’re at (this season),” said Bowdoin coach Scott Wiercinski, who has a 124-56-50 record in 13 years leading the program. “We’ve had freshman play, knowing they were good players but not sure what they would contribute. They’ve been forced to play important roles in important games and have performed really, really well.”
The offense has been a group effort. Patrick Brady, a freshman forward from Washington, D.C., has five goals and three assists. Junior forward Adam Prince also has five goals and senior midfielder Alden Mehta has four goals.
“It’s been goals by commission this season,” said Brunswick native Jack Banks, a senior midfielder who has two goals and six assists. “There hasn’t been one guy who did it like Tyler did last year. But this year, everyone has been stepping up in big moments. To be honest, we haven’t scored as many goals as we would have liked this season, but guys like Alden, Adam, Pat Brady, have really stepped up and delivered important goals for us.”
Sophomores Donovan Sinicropi (three goals) and Max Cook have also been in the offensive mix.
Bowdoin’s strength this fall has been on defense. The Polar Bears have allowed 15 goals — an average of 0.83 per game — and have six shutouts.
“We’ve played in different formations and have played with different personnel,” Mehta said. “The willingness for guys to step into different roles and different spots on the team has been hugely helpful.”
Another factor has been the development of sophomore goalkeeper Oliver King, who has played all 18 games. He has 63 saves on the season.
“When you have timely goals and excellent defending, when you do those two things, you’re always going to be in a good situation,” Wiercinski said. “Ollie playing so well in the back has certainly helped us find our way in games that are relatively even.”
Wiercinski is hopeful that Bowdoin’s depth will prove helpful against Scranton (17-1-3), which has outscored its opponents by a 35-8 margin. If the Polar Bears can knock off the Royals, they’d play either Carnegie Mellon or Lynchburg on Sunday, with a trip to the final four in Columbus, Ohio, at stake.
“We’ve been saying all year long, ‘This could be awesome for us if we get deep within the season and have a lot of young guys with experience,'” Wiercinski said. “I’m hoping that’s coming to fruit, and over the next couple of weeks — at least this week —it’ll continue to pay off for us.”

title: Mississippi saw a spike in 'inactive' voters for the midterms. Democrats want answers
text:
JACKSON, Miss. (AP) — Democratic lawmakers in Mississippi are calling for an investigation after a spike in the number of people listed as inactive on voter rolls ahead of this year’s midterm elections — an increase of nearly 60,000 since the presidential election two years ago.
The shift apparently was caused by the integration of data from a major credit reporting agency into the voter roll maintenance process. It came before a historic election for Democrats, who unseated one of the Deep South state’s Republican senators. They want an investigation and legislation to ensure that eligible voters are not mistakenly moved to inactive status, especially as they try to maintain their political momentum ahead of next year’s race for governor.
The Mississippi Legislative Black Caucus has scheduled a news conference Thursday to discuss its demand for legislative oversight committees to investigate how credit reporting data was used to examine voter rolls ahead of the November midterms.
“We need answers to give to our constituents, because the question is still out there: Did my vote count?” said Democratic state Rep. Kabir Karriem, the chair of the caucus. “It was disenfranchisement called by another name.”
Democrats are pressing the issue as they are hoping to build on Democrat Scott Colom’s win in the race for U.S. Senate over Republican incumbent Cindy Hyde-Smith. In addition to the race for governor, Mississippi will hold elections next year for other statewide offices, the legislature and state supreme court. Gov. Tate Reeves, who will be termed out of office, won his 2023 reelection bid by just three percentage points.
Mississippi added Experian data for verifying addresses
Mississippi for years had primarily relied on Postal Service change of address data to maintain its voter rolls. In 2025, Republican Secretary of State Michael Watson announced a partnership with Experian, one of the country’s three major credit reporting agencies, that was intended to “strengthen the integrity” of the state’s elections.
Under the agreement, county elections officials were given access to credit and Social Security data. They were to use that in addition to Postal Service data to verify voters’ addresses.
Mississippi law requires election officials to move voters whose addresses are questioned in the vetting process to inactive status at the same time they mail them a confirmation card, which voters can use to reestablish their active status. Other states do it differently: Policies in Delaware, Maryland, Oklahoma and Rhode Island generally allow voters time to respond to the notice before their status is changed to inactive, according to the MIT Election Data and Science Lab.
Mississippi’s process meant voters may not have known they had been switched to inactive until they showed up to vote, forcing them to cast a provisional ballot.
The number of Mississippi voters listed as “inactive” was 185,000 during the 2022 midterm elections and 171,000 during the presidential election two years ago, according to Associated Press data. Before this year’s election, over 230,000 people were marked as inactive, according to the secretary of state, after the Experian data was included in the verification process.
Colom won the race for Senate against Hyde-Smith by a fraction of that amount. Just over 8,000 votes separated the candidates with 99% of ballots counted.
State moves on from Experian
Elizabeth Jonson, a spokesperson for the secretary of state’s office, said the 230,000 figure was “accumulated over more than five years of maintenance by local officials” and that the state does not classify voters as inactive solely based on the Experian data.
The rise in the number of inactive voters this year was caused by integrating Experian data into the overall verification process, Watson said.
In a social media video, Watson said the state had started using data from a new vendor, Interactive Data, which draws on information for all three major credit bureaus, to maintain its voter rolls.
“I don’t apologize for cleaning voter rolls,” Watson said in an interview. “That is my job.”
Experian has not provided services to Mississippi since early 2025, said Scott Anderson, a spokesperson for the company.
“Decisions regarding voter registration policies, procedures and record updates are made solely by election officials in accordance with applicable local, state and federal laws,” he added.
Voters tagged as ‘inactive’ had to cast provisional ballots
In another video posted to social media, Watson told voters that any “mistakes” made in the voter roll maintenance process could be corrected by casting a provisional ballot — called an affidavit ballot in Mississippi.
Those ballots are reviewed by county election commissioners, who approve or reject the ballots.
Jonson said 21,484 provisional ballots were cast in this year’s midterms, which she said was “nearly identical” to the 21,321 such ballots cast in 2024, a presidential election year in which turnout was higher.
Not all were accepted at the same rate, however. The secretary of state’s office said 75% of provisional ballots had been approved statewide for the November election. But Associated Press data shows that dropped to just 34% in Hinds County, which is majority Black and home to the state capital of Jackson. In the 2024 election, 60% of provisional ballots there were accepted.
It’s not clear whether the use of Experian data played a role in the drop in the acceptance rate.
Democratic lawmakers want answers and change
State Rep. Cheikh Taylor, the chair of Mississippi’s Democratic Party, said he intends to introduce legislation in the new year that would increase transparency in how the credit data is used to verify voter eligibility.
It also would give voters whose records are flagged an opportunity to confirm their identities before they are deactivated.
Taylor said he had not seen evidence that data from Interactive Data would be much different from Experian’s. He added that he hoped to get support from some of his Republican colleagues.
“This is not a partisan issue,” he said. “The right to vote and the freedom to vote belongs to us all.”
He noted the Legislature should move quickly, given Mississippi’s elections next year.
Republican state senator Jeremy England suggested that legislation to increase transparency in the use of credit data on voter lists could draw Republican support.
“I don’t think there was anything nefarious involved with it, but look, Mississippi also does have a dark past when it comes to elections,” England said. “It’s something we definitely need to look at more and make sure that we’re doing it in a better way, so that if someone’s registered to vote, you know, they’re not marked as inactive for a reason they shouldn’t be.”
___
Baker reported from Washington, D.C. Ryan Dubicki, James Bazinet and Tyler Meselsohn of The Associated Press Election Services team contributed to this report.

title: Maine Eviction Prevention Program to close to new applicants amid funding shortage
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
MAINE (WABI) - A program that assists low-income Mainers who are facing eviction from their homes is set to close to new applicants.
The deadline to apply for the Maine Eviction Prevention Program is Monday, November 30 at 5 p.m.
Those who apply by the deadline may not receive funding, however officials with MaineHousing and Project Home said they will make every effort to help all those that sent in their applications on time.
The deadline was announced as the program faces a low amount of available funding due to the number of applicants already on the waitlist.
The Maine Eviction Program has been around since 2024 and has already helped more than 1,400 households.
For more information on the program and how to apply, you can head to the MaineHousing website.

title: US military returns to 2 aircraft carriers in the Middle East
text:
US military returns to 2 aircraft carriers in the Middle East
The U.S. military has gone back to having two aircraft carriers supporting Iran war operations after the USS George Washington departed the Middle East.
A spokesperson for the U.S. Pacific Fleet, Cmdr. Katie Koenig, said Wednesday that the Japan-based USS George Washington was now under its control and “conducting routine operations” in the Asia-Pacific region.
The development is the latest in a shuffling of aircraft carriers in the Middle East. During the Iran war, the carriers have served as the linchpin of a U.S. flotilla that has blockaded all merchant shipping to and from the Islamic Republic as the Trump administration looks to keep squeezing Tehran's economy by preventing its oil from reaching global markets.
Video: Trump speaks on "different approach" during meeting with Putin, Xi
The George Washington departed the Middle East in the same week that the USS Theodore Roosevelt arrived, briefly bringing the number of carriers in the waters off Iran to the unusually high amount of three.
The USS George H.W. Bush, which arrived in the region in April, and the Roosevelt are now the two carriers in the region as well more than a dozen destroyers, cruisers and a littoral combat ship.
The naval presence is helping maintain the blockade on Iran, while the U.S. also has carried out some limited strikes on Iranian targets in the Strait of Hormuz, the critical waterway where nearly a third of the world's oil passed through before the war began Feb. 28. The disruptions to shipping through the strait have raised global energy prices.
The unpopularity of the Iran war and the resulting economic effects contributed to major losses for President Donald Trump’s Republican Party in this month's midterm elections.
Trump has offered mixed signals on whether he plans to return to major combat with Iran, but any negotiated deal to end the fighting appears to be a long way off.
Trump recently has warned Iran that the U.S. military is “locked and loaded” and that the U.S. was keeping an eye on Pickaxe Mountain, a facility linked to Iran’s nuclear program, for signs of activity.
He also has said it was highly unlikely he would need to order new major strikes on Iran, declaring that the war “militarily is effectively over.”
The USS George Washington departed the Middle East following its arrival in August. It had been pulled from a patrol in the South China Sea shortly after reports of mental health and supply issues emerged aboard another long-deployed aircraft carrier in the Middle East — the USS Abraham Lincoln. The Lincoln set a record for uninterrupted time at sea, at more than 240 days.

title: Fiona, famed hippo and social media darling, dead after swallowing child’s hat
text:
Fiona, famed hippo and social media darling, dead after swallowing child’s hat
Fiona the hippo, a beloved Nile hippopotamus who became an internet sensation after her premature birth, has died after swallowing a child’s hat.
She was 9 years old.
Officials with the Cincinnati Zoo announced the news Thursday, days after she swallowed a child’s knit cap.
"It is with extreme sadness that we share with you the devastating news that Fiona did not make it after multiple attempts from our amazing vets and keeper team to help her through what ended up being a medical emergency," a statement from the zoo reads in part. "The vet staff tried everything they could to help her after she ingested a hat that ended up in her habitat by accident last week. Despite multiple attempts to move the hat out of her system, it was ultimately too much to overcome. The team performed necessary supportive care today in an attempt to save her, but it was not successful and she did not recover."
Zoo officials say a bizarre series of events launched the cap into the hippo habitat.
It was tossed into the air in front of the zoo’s hippo enclosure, where it was caught by a massive ceiling fan and then was catapulted through a tiny 1-foot opening above the tank’s 12-foot-tall viewing windows.
“We probably couldn’t make it happen again if we tried,” a zoo spokesperson said of the incident.
Fiona was unable to quickly pass the hat, zoo officials say, and the hat remained inside of her for the better part of two weeks.
The hippo, who weighed around 2,400 pounds, was too large for surgery, but zoo officials say they did everything in their power to help her pass the hat through her system – including acquiring a nine-foot scope to attempt a colonoscopy, and providing laxative-like supplements to “push things through.”
The zoo provided 24-hour care, but said her condition worsened over time. Zoo officials ultimately announced her passing on Thursday saying, "Please keep her keepers and everyone who tried to help her in your thoughts as they try to navigate and come to terms with this shocking news. They are also, understandably, asking for space at this time."
Fiona’s story
Fiona weighed 29 pounds when she was born on Jan. 24, 2017, at the Cincinnati Zoo. She was six weeks premature and weighed about 25 pounds lighter than the lowest recorded birth weight for the species.
Hippos are generally born closer to 100 pounds.
Her tiny size made it difficult for her to stand and nurse, so zoo staff gave her round-the-clock care.
The world watched as caregivers helped her build strength with pool exercises, bottle feedings and plenty of close attention. Fiona steadily grew into a healthy young hippo, and her progress drew fans from around the world.
She became the zoo’s most famous resident, and one of the best-known hippos in the world. Visitors often recognized her by her lively curiosity — and by the way she can make even a routine swim look like a big event.
She became a big sister in 2022 when her mother, Bibi, gave birth to a healthy boy, Fritz.
Fiona and her family were among the zoo’s top attractions, delighting guests by swimming in their habitat known as Hippo Cove and snacking on hippo-appropriate treats like watermelons and, most recently, a whole pumpkin.
Fiona even had her own line of merch at the zoo’s gift shop.

title: Ground stop leads to airport wedding
text:
ATLANTA (KCNC/KTNV) - Flight delays and cancellations left travelers stranded across the country last weekend. But for one couple, a canceled flight threatened to ruin their wedding day, until a chance encounter with a stranger turned their travel nightmare into a day they’ll never forget.
Brelyn Bowman, an ordained minister, said she was on an airplane for more than four hours.
“Everybody was grounded,” Bowman said.
Bowman missed her conference. She said she was not going to make it out of Atlanta that night anyway.
Wedding trip canceled
Jake Hinson and Chelsey Rogers were trying to get to their wedding in Las Vegas. Their flight was delayed more than once before it was canceled.
“Eventually, we get the notification: It’s canceled,” Rogers said. She said no other flights were available that would get them there in time for the ceremony.
Their checked bags had already been sent without them. The couple started their trip home with only a veil in their carry-on.
Meeting the minister
Rogers said she was crying at that point.
“I was so hopeful. I really thought we’d make it, and then we strike up a conversation with Bree,” Rogers said.
“And I made the joke of like, ‘Hey, you know, we can wrap this up now.’ But I never imagined that they would actually say yes,” Bowman said.
They did, and the couple was married shortly after.
‘Humanity really connects’
Rogers said it was at first just the three of them. Then another woman ran up and took pictures from the side.
“And then as the trains were letting people off, people are kind of gathering,” Rogers said.
Bowman said nobody was concerned about the flight at that point.
“I think you have those moments where time just stands still, you know? And you’re just in a moment in space where humanity really connects the way we’re supposed to connect,” Bowman said.
Hinson said the couple spent 13 hours in the airport.
“That’s a bad day, I don’t care who you are,” Hinson said. “And so that just made what had been a really awful experience a highlight of our life.”
Staying in touch
Bowman said she has stayed in touch with the couple. She said she is now the godmother to their children.
The three plan to get together a year from now to celebrate, Bowman said.
Their story is proof that sometimes, the best destination isn’t the one you planned.

title: ‘Vet staff tried everything they could’: What we know about Fiona the hippo's final days
text:
‘Vet staff tried everything they could’: What we know about Fiona the hippo's final days
Fiona the hippo, a Cincinnati Zoo icon, has died after suffering health complications from swallowing a knit hat that was accidentally tossed into her enclosure.
She was 9 years old.
The beloved hippo was born as a preemie and beat the odds of survival with the help of her care team, then nearly 10 years later, found herself fighting again after a freak accident.
Related video above | Tributes pour in remembering Fiona the hippo after her death
Zoo officials say a bizarre series of events launched the cap into the hippo habitat.
It was tossed into the air in front of the zoo’s hippo enclosure, where it was caught by a massive ceiling fan and then was catapulted through a tiny 1-foot opening above the tank’s 12-foot-tall viewing windows.
“We probably couldn’t make it happen again if we tried,” a zoo spokesperson said of the incident.
In the days after, the zoo noticed Fiona had a loss of appetite and her care team stepped in to help.
Over the last 10 days or so, her care team had been working around the clock to provide treatments to help the beloved hippo.
Zoo officials said Fiona, who weighed around 2,400 pounds, was too large for surgery, so they performed treatments to attempt to help pass the hat through her system.
The zoo even brought in a nine-foot scope from the Columbus Zoo to attempt a colonoscopy, but they were unable to reach the hat.
Most recently, they brought in a vibration plate borrowed from a local horse farm, hoping the vibrations would stimulate movement through her digestive tract and help her pass the hat. Fiona stood on the platform several times throughout the day, and her care team will continue providing round-the-clock care.
"The vet staff tried everything they could to help her after she ingested a hat that ended up in her habitat by accident last week. Despite multiple attempts to move the hat out of her system, it was ultimately too much to overcome. The team performed necessary supportive care today in an attempt to save her, but it was not successful and she did not recover," the zoo shared in a statement announcing her death.

title: South Korea’s top court overturns charges against ex-prime minister for his role in martial law
text:
South Korea’s top court overturns charges against ex-prime minister for his role in martial law
South Korea’s Supreme Court on Thursday overturned the conviction of former Prime Minister Han Duck-soo for aiding ousted President Yoon Suk Yeol’s brief imposition of martial law in December 2024.
Han had been convicted of helping legitimize the decree by securing its endorsement at a Cabinet meeting. But the Supreme Court said prosecutors had not sufficiently proven that he intended to help Yoon carry out his unlawful power grab.
The ruling sends Han’s case back to the Seoul High Court, which sentenced him to 15 years in prison in May. It does not free him immediately: The Supreme Court extended his detention by two more months.
Related video: Pro and anti-Yoon rallies in Seoul as impeached president argues against his arrest (2025)
In a separate ruling Thursday, the Supreme Court upheld a four-year prison term for Yoon’s wife, Kim Keon Hee, on corruption charges including stock price manipulation and bribery, the latest development in Yoon’s sprawling saga.
Han and Kim, both currently imprisoned, did not attend the rulings.
Yoon’s martial law decree, announced late at night on Dec. 3, 2024, followed a standoff with liberal opponents controlling the legislature, whom the conservative leader branded as “anti-state” forces obstructing his agenda and paralyzing state affairs.
The power grab collapsed within hours. Lawmakers broke through heavily armed soldiers and police surrounding the National Assembly and gathered enough votes to to overturn the decree, forcing Yoon’s Cabinet to lift it.
Yoon’s powers were suspended on Dec. 14, 2024, when lawmakers voted to impeach him, and the Constitutional Court formally removed him from office in April 2025. After an earlier arrest and release, Yoon was re-arrested in July 2025 and has faced multiple trials over the martial law declaration and other charges, including a life sentence for rebellion that he has appealed.

text:
Residents brace for lead dust cloud as Army plans 5-ton blast in Iowa
Plans by the U.S. Army to detonate about 5 tons of bomb-making chemicals that have become unusable and might explode if moved have residents in southeast Iowa worried that a cloud of lead dust could cause environmental contamination and health problems.
The detonation at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant is set for Friday, and officials recommend that some residents in nearby Middletown begin vacating the area that morning. If they can’t leave their homes, they should stay inside and keep windows and doors closed.
"The detonation will result in an air plume with some lead-containing particles which will disperse in the air and deposit on the ground," an advisory states. "Lead is toxic to humans and animals. The goal of this advisory is to provide the public with actionable information out of an abundance of caution to minimize lead exposure."
Nearly 400 people live in Middletown, but there are thousands more in the path of the plume.
Here's what to know:
Why the Army plans to detonate the drums
The Army said the lead azide degraded and recrystallized while in storage, making it more sensitive. Explosive ordnance disposal personnel directed the Army not to move it.
In its environmental review, the Army said: “Movement, physical handling, or off-site transit over public transportation routes presents an unacceptable risk of accidental, catastrophic detonation.”
The Army decided to detonate the barrel, saying it is the safest way to remove the explosive hazard.
What residents in the area may experience
The Army said two rapid detonations are scheduled for about noon.
University of Iowa mechanical engineering professor Uday Kumar studies shocks and detonations.
"There's a shockwave that comes off of it, and that dissipates as it goes away from the source," Kumar said. "(Damage) can range from shattered windows, if you're close by, and definitely uncomfortable pressure and sound."
The Army says people in Middletown should expect a loud noise, ground vibrations and a visible dust plume. Because of possible window damage, the Army is recommending people in the City Park neighborhood voluntarily evacuate from 8 a.m. to 2 p.m. The Army says dust could remain airborne for up to an hour, depending on wind speed.
While the Army recommends cleaning cars, windowsills and outdoor surfaces, residents have taken to social media to voice concern and question whether that will be enough.
Where lead dust could travel
The Army has released separate maps for potential airborne lead exposure and possible deposition of lead-containing dust on surfaces. The maps are estimates that the Army said it will update 48 hours before the detonation, then again six hours before and hourly until the operation, and then provide a final estimate of the impacted area.
Some schools in the path of the plume have already canceled classes.
How people could be exposed and what the Army advises
The Army identified two main exposure concerns: breathing lead particles while they are airborne and contact with the lead-containing dust after it settles.
Lead is toxic. Exposure can harm the brain and nervous system, particularly in young children; the Environmental Protection Agency said no safe blood lead level has been identified for children.
For people in areas identified by the Army, the advisory recommends staying indoors during the potential exposure period, closing windows and doors, setting heating and cooling systems to recirculate if possible, and avoiding traveling through affected areas. After the Army announces the all-clear, it recommends cleaning surfaces children may touch, such as outdoor play sets, with wet cloths, sponges or mops.
Lead is a neurological toxicant that can decrease brain activity and development, especially in young children, O’Shaughnessy said. He is particularly concerned for toddlers who are at the age of putting everything in their mouth.
According to EPA documents, alternatives such as neutralizing and decomposing the contents of the drums using other chemicals were considered. But officials said any plan that involved handling the drums would increase the probability of accidental, fatal detonation.
What monitoring and sampling are planned
The Army says it will monitor air around the plant during the operation and will take environmental samples in the blast area afterward. The EPA’s emergency permit requires monitoring and sampling before, during and after the detonation, cleanup of contaminated areas and reports to the EPA.
The Associated Press contributed to this report.

title: Possible resolution for Waterfront Park's splashpad proposed
text:
The most hot-button issue in the ongoing debate between the Boothbay Harbor Waterfront Preservation (BBHWP) and abutters Joe and Jill Doyle may be nearing resolution.
In 2020, BBHWP was approved for a splashpad about 25 feet in diameter. However, the project was built larger than the sanctioned size and in the wrong location. The current splashpad is about 26 ft in diameter with an 8-foot-wide apron, totaling a 42-foot diameter, according to a 2021 letter to the planning board. BBHWP returned to the board for a site plan amendment in 2021, which was approved, but was later overruled due to a failure to properly notify abutters.
The current amended site plan application moves the splashpad's western edge uphill 24 feet, 10 inches; adds the eight-foot-wide band (two four-foot bands) to the splash pad's perimeter; and adds a semi-circular stone retaining wall to the upper side.
During the Nov. 16 public merit review hearing, there was back-and-forth about possibly removing the eight-foot bands to reduce the splashpad's size from the Doyles' counsel while BBHWP argued they should be retained for accessibility purposes. Noise concerns were raised. Discussion was tabled.
However, there was a breakthrough after Mary Kaler asserted that noise shouldn't be an issue, since the splashpad's hours would likely not start until around noon and end around 2 p.m.
"If that's the case, thank you for the concession. We'll move the splashpad hours from 9 a.m. to 3 p.m., and we're done," said Joe Doyle. Chair Merritt Blakeslee asked whether Doyle meant he would withdraw his other objections to the splashpad if the hours were limited to 9 a.m. to 3 p.m. or 10 a.m. to 2 p.m. Doyle agreed.
Andrea Neilson said the BBHWP board would have to discuss it and return to the issue next meeting.
Earlier in the evening, the board voted that the park, including the splashpad, may be open each day from dawn until a half hour past sunset, except for permitted events. In a post-meeting interview, Blakeslee said the issue would probably be reintroduced as an amended motion if it was decided the splashpad would have different hours.
On screening (§170-35 (B)), the board agreed that BBHWP must provide solid fencing along the property line, six feet in height, tapering to four feet at the west end of the splash pad, and ending 50 feet from the high-water mark.
Vegetation was split into a separate issue, with abutter John Doyle saying plantings need to be 20 or 30 feet high to provide adequate screening for his 36-foot home. Doyle expressed willingness to work with BBHWP on a proposed vegetation plan and offered to contribute financially. Doyle and Mitch Rasor of Rasor Landscape Architect will confer.
According to a meeting outline, BBHWP argued in an Oct. 23 letter that the planning board lacks authority to impose conditions under §170-70 (conditions attached to site plan approvals). They assert that residential properties in the limited commercial/maritime district should have no right to protections under §170-70 because the district's purpose statement does not mention residential use.
Additionally, they believe that the "decisions about how best to do things in the law are almost always lawmaking decisions ... [that] are outside the adjudicative competence of Maine's planning boards." They cited two cases from the Maine Law Court.
BBHWP attorney Anthony Muri said that he agrees that the board can impose conditions. Still, there are three requirements: 1) There be explicit or implicit authority in the ordinance that gives the board the ability to implement conditions and enable decisions, such as determining times of operation, etc.; 2) There must be a need in the record for the condition; 3) An articulation of policy that gives the board direction to what it can do as to the conditions.
In response, Blakeslee pointed to the language of §170-70, which states that provisions are intended to promote the community's general welfare and minimize nonresidential construction's adverse impacts on adjacent properties, and §170-60, which outlines some areas to which conditions can be attached.
"What then remains is the need for any particular condition, and what we're doing in this proceeding is determining whether there is a need for any particular condition ... that is the point of hearing from the people most directly concerned (BBHWP and the Doyles) ... and that all falls into this category of substantial evidence."
The board decided it has the authority under Maine law to impose conditions under §170-70, if those conditions are supported by record evidence. The motion cited Mick Land Development, Inc v. Town of South Berwick (2026).
An August conversation about public safety and controlling pedestrian crossing resurfaced. Discussion focused on building a barrier to funnel pedestrians and deter children using the splashpad, which is closer to Atlantic Avenue than the original plan, from entering the road. Abutters' attorney Kristin Collins again brought up the need for a sidewalk and crosswalk. However, sidewalk and crosswalk locations are largely under state or town purview
"(A crosswalk) would be dependent on the town applying to the (Maine Department of Transportation), and maybe getting a permit. You can't make that conditional upon us ... We can't control a third party's decisions," said Rasor.
Per § 170-70, the board voted to require a permanent, non-vegetative barrier 4 feet high, running from the northerly property line along Atlantic Avenue to a single pedestrian and vehicular access point south of the Hodgdon House. Additionally, BBHWP will work with the town to apply to DOT to install a crosswalk consistent with the Aug. 28, 2025 TYLin traffic study recommendation at the approximate location of the park's vehicular access point.
They also found no requirements per §170-70 for permitted hours of marina operation, for customary commercial and recreational marine use, such as fueling and dock service.
For lighting, the grocery store was not discussed since it is non-operational and will need to go through its own permitting process before opening. The board found no requirements under §170-70 concerning the proposed lighting plan beyond those already imposed by §170-45 and those imposed by the planning board for events.
In other business, members were surprised to see a proposed split-rail fence on the latest version of BBHWP’s L2 plan, running along the property’s north side between the park and abutters. According to Blakeslee, there was no split-rail fence in the L2 version submitted during BBHWP’s pre-application meeting, nor in the formal application submitted Jan. 9. However, it began appearing in later versions without the board being alerted.
“What concerns me is that ... (if) the current L2 (that shows the fence) is still the version that ends up being approved (then) we've approved a split-rail fence that we didn't really realize was there until the last minute.”
Rasor explained L2 showed a proposed buffering plan and what was approved in 2020. The board in 2020 approved the fence, then required as a visual delineation between the properties.
The board voted that BBHWP provide them with a letter formally stating that it does not seek to place a split rail fence on the north property line as part of the present amended site plan review application, notwithstanding that a fence is shown on the park’s L2 plans of March 31, May 1, Sept. 20, and Oct. 8, 2026.
They also declined to act on an informal Oct. 25 request from BBHWP’s counsel to reconsider its §170-67 compliance decision. This section deals with other required permits. Once a formal, properly briefed request for reconsideration is received, the topic will be placed on the list of issues to be addressed.

title: Judge orders ICE to release 18-year-old arrested during warrantless Maine traffic stop
text:
A man arrested without a warrant by federal agents in Maine this week was released from an immigrant detention center on Thursday after a judge said the arrest was unconstitutional.
The 18-year-old, who has a special immigration status, was one of six people arrested by a U.S. Border Patrol agent during a warrantless traffic stop in Livermore Falls on Monday. The man has no known criminal history and had no order for his removal, according to court documents.
After pulling a work van over because it had Massachusetts license plates and a ladder rack, the agent questioned its occupants about their citizenship and “decided to make a warrantless arrest of the six illegal aliens,” according to an incident report filed in federal court.
In an order filed late Wednesday, U.S. District Judge Stacey Neumann rebuked immigration officials for arresting the man “without an individualized assessment and without justification” despite knowing he had been granted special status for fleeing domestic abuse as a child in Ecuador.
“Congress offered such children a path to lawful status, and a state court found that (the man) qualifies for it,” Neumann wrote. “(Border Patrol) seized him anyway.”
The 18-year-old’s attorney, Tal Rothstein, confirmed that Immigration and Customs Enforcement released the man Thursday morning. They said his personal property, however, had not been returned to him as Neumann ordered.
The American Civil Liberties Union of Washington, D.C., and a number of released detainees sued ICE last month for what they allege is an “ongoing policy” of holding onto detainees’ passports, cash and other objects after their release. A Portland resident whom ICE said it “inadvertently” deported to Guatemala amid an enforcement surge in Maine in January is among the plaintiffs in that case.
A government lawyer had argued on Tuesday that the 18-year old arrested this week was detained “under the authority of a valid arrest warrant,” despite the arresting agent’s incident report noting the detentions were warrantless.
The Department of Homeland Security submitted an administrative warrant, which is signed by immigration officials rather than a judge, as evidence in court on Tuesday. The government’s documents indicate the warrant was drafted after the traffic stop and presented to the man after he had been detained and brought to the ICE facility in Scarborough.
“Where the Government cannot show that a warrant preceded the arrest, the Court treats the arrest as warrantless,” Neumann wrote in her order Wednesday.
Officials from ICE, DHS and Customs and Border Protection have not responded to inquiries about the incident.
Immigration officials are allowed to make warrantless arrests under narrow circumstances. Agents must have reasonable suspicion that the person being arrested is a flight risk or a danger to their community, Neumann wrote.
Neumann said the 18-year-old, who is identified with a pseudonym in court documents, is neither.
According to court records, he fled to the U.S. at 16 to escape physical and psychological abuse from his father in Ecuador. He moved to Rhode Island to live with his brother and was granted special immigrant juvenile status, which is intended to put at-risk youth on a path to citizenship.
“(Immigration officials) have offered no evidence that (the man) is a flight risk or a danger, and no one made that determination before he was seized,” Neumann wrote, adding that he has graduated high school and committed no crimes since he has lived in the U.S.
The man’s petition challenging his arrest was granted by Neumann late Wednesday. She said the arrest violated the Fifth Amendment, and ordered the government to release him by Thursday morning.
“The Constitution does not permit the deprivation of liberty by default,” Neumann wrote. “Nevertheless, they detained him without an individualized assessment and without justification. Due process demands an exercise of reasoned judgment before liberty is taken, not after.”
Court records indicate the man was being held in an ICE detention center in Rhode Island, where he was transferred after being processed at the agency’s Scarborough facility Monday. Neumann had initially ordered the agency not to remove him from Maine while the case proceeded, but agents only received the order after he was en route to the Rhode Island facility.
Rothstein said he was released at the ICE field office in Burlington, Mass.

title: How to make it work when parents move in with adult children
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
(Aging Untold) — When a parent moves in with an adult child, it can bring comfort along with adjustments like new routines, boundaries and expectations.
It’s happening more often: Parent Herald reports a “reverse boomerang effect,” with more parents moving in with their children, driven in part by rising housing costs and caregiving needs.
The Aging Untold hosts talked through where to begin.
Start with why you’re moving in together
Gerontologist Sam Cradduck said the answer begins with the reason for the move.
“First off, I want to know why we’re moving in,” Cradduck said. “Are we moving in so Mom and Dad can help us? Maybe with childcare. Maybe because we’re a dual working family and childcare expenses are astronomical and we need some help. Or are they moving in because Mom and Dad need some help?”
Finances are part of that conversation because expenses go up when more people live in the home, she said.
Families should also decide what the arrangement looks like today and what it will look like in the future.
“Mom and Dad aren’t going to get younger and the kids are going to get older, so the kids are going to need less care, and Mom and Dad are going to need more,” Cradduck said. “So we need to know how we’re going to balance that and who’s going to be responsible for what in this house.”
Expect the relationship to change
“You’re going to have to set expectations and boundaries so you don’t get that resentment,” Dr. Rhea Rogers, a board-certified physician, said. “And then you have to realize that relationship is going to change for both. So you have your children who now maybe are going to be the caregivers, and then the adults who are maybe losing some control.”
Aging expert Amy O’Rourke described how that can feel on both sides. A grown child may feel their space is changing. A parent may feel they are losing independence.
“It’s weird and it’s awkward, and it’s an emotionally, acutely hard to process feeling,” O’Rourke said.
Talk through the details, including privacy
She said everyday details can test a household, including who does the dishes, who cleans, who shops for groceries and what the thermostat is set to.
“I would say designate an area that’s private for you, the child and the parent, so that you have your own place,” O’Rourke said. “And then are you going to knock before you enter? These things have to be talked about.”
Put it in writing and meet weekly
She likes the idea of a “town hall meeting” each week to check in on how everyone is doing.
Aging well coach Katherine Ambrose suggests having something in writing.
“Miscommunication happens because people remember details differently,” she said. “So you put it in writing together and sign it. Now you start your weekly family meeting, and that way you can stay on the same page, because there will be things you don’t think about, like the thermostat, or sounds, how loud someone plays TV, or what they play.”
Ambrose said dating can come up too, including whether adults will feel judged about who they spend time with and where.
Cradduck said the adult children and parents need to treat each other as adults.
“The top of the list on that written out contract or agreement has to say, ‘We are all adults. Do not treat me like I’m a child,’” Cradduck said. “I’m now 40-plus years old. You’re in your late 60s, early 70s, 80s, wherever those ages fall. We’re all adults, and we have to be able to treat one another like adults. So that’s the first rule here.”
Give each other grace
O’Rourke pointed out that slipping into old habits is likely.
“Grace, I think, goes a long way here,” she said. “If you happen to slip into an old behavior, then just kind of wave your hand and say, ‘I’ve just slipped into bad behavior, I apologize,’ or ‘You’re using that tone again.’ Be real direct, because it happens. You know you get around your parent, all of a sudden, you’re thinking, why am I acting like I’m 7 years old again?”
And old wounds can resurface, from childhood or the teenage years.
“You’re going to pop open some old scars,” Cradduck said.
O’Rourke said small acts of generosity matter, such as calling a parent from the grocery store to ask if they need anything.
“A lot can be grown out of compassion and generosity and care for each other,” she said.
An adjustment that can become a gift
While there may be some angst at the beginning, the arrangement can benefit the whole family, especially when younger children are in the home.
“Empathy is learned by helping, by the intergenerational activities and allowing your younger kids to be around their grandparents,” Cradduck said.
“It can be an unexpected blessing, and it’s part of the human journey,” Ambrose said.
Key takeaways
- Create a new norm. Merging households means creating a new way of living together rather than deciding who is right.
- Hold family meetings early. Set expectations about routines and secure private spaces for everyone. Put agreements in writing and check in weekly.
- Treat each other as adults. Make “we are all adults” the first rule of the household agreement.
- Remember that both generations are experiencing loss. Be patient, and respect each other’s autonomy to help everyone coexist in harmony.

title: Could drones help transport organs? Here’s how it might work
text:
ST. LOUIS, Mo. (InvestigateTV) - In 2025, the U.S. saw more organ transplants than ever before with nearly 50,000 transplants. The number of living donors who signed up grew slightly that year too.
Despite this progress, people are still waiting months or even years for the procedure that saves and enhances lives.
Federal data shows that the most common wait time for an organ transplant is between one and two years. Some people can remain on the list for five or more years.
In Missouri, a first-of-its-kind project aims to cut down on the time between identifying and confirming whether a potential donor is an exact match.
Mid-America Transplant is now using drones to transport donor blood samples.
Missouri opened the nation’s first dedicated healthcare drone corridor in April 2026.
The drone path begins near Springfield, Missouri, where blood samples from potential organ and tissue donors will be loaded onto the drone.
After flying around 94 miles, a technician will swap in a fresh battery before the drone completes the 66-mile flight to the St. Louis-area drop point at the Boles Fire Protection District, where the samples will be tested at Mid-America Transplant’s laboratory.
The route follows a defined flight path along existing railway systems several miles north of Interstate 44. The drone flies between 300 and 350 feet above ground level during daylight hours.
Kevin Lee, President and CEO at Mid-America Transplant, said the company expects to cut the travel time down by a third.
Mid-America Transplant said that retrieving a donor blood sample from Springfield previously took more than three hours using ground transport. The drone transport takes less than two hours and costs one-tenth as much.
“Mid-America Transplant has always embraced innovation to enhance donation and transplantation, and this drone corridor represents an exciting step forward,” Lee said. “In our work, every second counts, and faster, more reliable transport of lab samples helps us honor each donor’s gift to its fullest potential.”
If a drone has a malfunction, Lee said it has “multiple redundant systems within them.”
“So, if they have an engine failure, there are backups built into the drone so that it can safely land at a predetermined location by the drone operator. then we will deploy a coordinator to recover that lab sample immediately,” he said.
Right now, the company is only transporting blood samples, but the long-term vision is for the drones to transport kidneys.
