title: Cincinnati Zoo says Fiona the hippo has died, days after ingesting a visitor’s hat
text:
CINCINNATI (AP) — Fiona, the hippo whose premature birth and fight for survival at the Cincinnati Zoo turned her into a global sensation nearly a decade ago, died Thursday from complications after swallowing a knit hat that was accidentally flung into her enclosure. She was 9 years old.
“It is with extreme sadness that we share with you the devastating news that Fiona did not make it after multiple attempts from our amazing vets and keeper team to help her through what ended up being a medical emergency,” the zoo said in a statement.
EN ESPAÑOL | Muere Fiona la hipopótamo tras ingerir un gorro en Zoológico de Cincinnati
The zoo said Monday that it was providing Fiona with round-the-clock care after she swallowed the hat more than a week ago. Specialists had advised that surgery wasn’t an option for a full-grown hippo like Fiona.
Before she died, veterinarians had been keeping Fiona hydrated, giving her treats and monitoring her every move, the zoo said. They borrowed a vibration plate from a horse farm, encouraging her to stand on it several times a day in the hopes that the shaking would help move the hat through her digestive tract.
“Despite multiple attempts to move the hat out of her system, it was ultimately too much to overcome,” the zoo said.
Within an hour of the announcement, visitors began leaving flowers and cards by a hippo statue outside the zoo. “Forever our Fiona,” one note read.
Fans mourn Fiona
Fiona captivated people worldwide after her premature birth in 2017. Her presence was felt all around the zoo, which was scheduled to stay open late Thursday for the first night of its Festival of Lights.
Amy Haacke, a special educator from Dayton, said outside the Cincinnati Zoo that she’s been a “huge fan” of Fiona since she was born because she likes underdogs. Haacke said she uses the Fiona book series in her classroom and owns three Fiona shirts.
“We were coming here anyway, but it kind of means a lot to be here,” Haacke said Thursday. “We were here when she was first born and, I guess, now we’re here when she’s gone.”
Yolanda Gould, who works more than 80 miles (130 kilometers) away in Covington, said she and others in her office left early to travel to the zoo after learning about Fiona’s death. She said outside the zoo that she was feeling “a little devastated” after following Fiona since she was born.
Cincinnati Mayor Aftab Pureval said on social media that Fiona was “a symbol of perseverance and joy” in the city. Ohio Gov. Mike DeWine called her “a true icon.” The Cincinnati Bengals also expressed condolences, dubbing Fiona “the queen of the Queen City.”
In a joint post with U.S. Vice President JD Vance on Instagram, second lady Usha Vance shared a photo of one of their children face-to-face with Fiona through a glass wall of her enclosure. The family has a home in Cincinnati.
“We are so sad to hear the news about Fiona,” she said in the caption. “Our family loved visiting her at the Cincinnati Zoo.”
Fiona was under close care
Fiona swallowed the hat about 11 days ago after a zoo visitor tossed it in the air. A ceiling fan caught and deflected the hat into the hippo enclosure through a small opening above the area’s viewing windows.
It was an accident, zoo spokesperson Michelle Curley said.
Before Fiona died, Mike Wenninger, the zoo’s director of animal health, said veterinarians had sedated her twice to evaluate her condition.
An ultrasound on Tuesday showed some bunching of her intestines, Wenninger said. They also conducted a colonoscopy using a 9-foot (2.7-meter) scope but were unable to detect anything, he said.
The Association of Zoos and Aquariums, the accrediting body for facilities, said in a statement Thursday that the Cincinnati Zoo provided “extraordinary 24/7 care for Fiona throughout this heartbreaking event.”
Surgery would have been challenging
Surgery would have been a major logistical challenge — multiple incisions would have been needed during a very long surgery, as hippos are notoriously difficult to anesthetize and have thick skin, said Jack Kottwitz, assistant professor at Michigan State University’s College of Veterinary Medicine.
The hat and its blend of fibers posed a particular danger despite its relatively small size.
Experts said hippos have a multichambered stomach for digesting plants, and the system makes for a very large gastrointestinal tract through which anything would have to travel.
Jan Hawkins, doctor of veterinary medicine at North Carolina State University, said Fiona’s situation was difficult because it would have been hard to tell where in her body the hat was.
“You can’t do the normal imaging and things that you can do in some of the smaller animals, or even horses,” Hawkins said.
Zoos around the world have warned for years about the dangers posed by objects that are tossed or blown into animal habitats. Two years ago, a rare antelope choked to death after eating the plastic lid from a squeezable fruit pouch at a zoo in Tennessee. A polar bear at a German zoo died in 2014 after swallowing a jacket dropped into his enclosure by a visitor.
Fiona became a sensation after Harambe’s death
Fiona survived her first health scare when she was born six weeks premature. She weighed just 29 pounds (13.2 kilograms), which was less than the lowest recorded birth weight for her species at that time.
She was unable to nurse, so a zoo staffer hand-milked her mother. The zoo recorded her progress with photos and videos, while fans worldwide followed her progress online.
Her story marked an uplifting turn for the Cincinnati Zoo after months of backlash over the shooting of Harambe, the gorilla who became a pop culture phenomenon after he was killed because a child got into his enclosure.
The zoo’s hippo family expanded in 2022 with the birth of Fiona’s baby brother, Fritz.
Fiona’s father, Henry, was euthanized months after her birth as his health badly declined. He had lived 36 years, slightly beyond the average life expectancy for a Nile hippopotamus in captivity.
___

title: 3 UMaine football storylines to follow against New Hampshire
text:
Somehow, a season to forget keeps getting worse for the University of Maine football team. The Black Bears fell to a 37-3 defeat at Albany last week — their worst loss to an Football Championship Subdivision team this season and their second-worst overall after a 55-3 loss to Appalachian State on Sept. 5.
After nine straight losses, there’s one last chance for Maine (1-9, 1-6 Coastal Athletic Association) to salvage something from the 2026 season: a home game against rival New Hampshire (4-7, 3-4) at 1 p.m. Saturday (FloSports). Here are three storylines to follow ahead of the Black Bears’ final game.
Playing for pride
In reality, pride is all that’s been on the line for Maine for much of the 2026 season. Long eliminated from the postseason picture, the Black Bears have spent the past several weeks simply trying to stop the bleeding as the losses continue to accumulate.
A tussle with New Hampshire for the Brice-Cowell Musket provides a chance at a trophy, bragging rights, and maybe even momentum as Maine heads to the offseason. The Black Bears have lost four straight to UNH and 20 of the past 23 meetings. Bucking that trend would be huge.
“We want the musket,” Maine coach Jordan Stevens said in Monday’s teleconference. “(Whether it’s) a trophy case or mantle or whatever it is, there’s a location in each program where it’s supposed to sit, so when it’s not here, it certainly feels like you’re missing a part of the program.”
What’s next?
Prior to 2022, Maine hadn’t won two games or fewer on the field in a full season since 1979 (the 1993 team finished 3-8 but later forfeited all three wins). Win or lose, the Black Bears have now done that three times in five years. With a loss, Maine would finish with its worst on-field record since 1967 (0-8).
The Black Bears fired offensive coordinator Mikahael Waters in early October, yet that unit has continued to struggle (12.2 points per game, 123rd of 124 FCS teams). Could more offensive staff changes be on the horizon? Jordan Stevens is under contract through 2028, so he should be safe — or is he?
Those are the kinds of questions frequently asked after seasons like this.
Cosgrove set for Ring of Honor induction
You’d be hard-pressed to find a single name more synonymous with UMaine football than Jack Cosgrove, who played quarterback for the Black Bears from 1974-77 and was the head coach from 1993-2015. He will be inducted into the Maine Football Ring of Honor between the first and second quarters of Saturday’s game.
Cosgrove, who has coached Colby since 2018 (but has been away from the program since mid-October), is Maine’s all-time winningest coach with 129 victories. He coached the Black Bears to three CAA titles and five FCS playoff berths.

title: This runner has completed over 70 marathons. This year, she ran 7 of them while pregnant
text:
This runner has completed over 70 marathons. This year, she ran 7 of them while pregnant
Deirdre Keane had already run more than 60 marathons when she decided to take on a new challenge of completing the World Marathon Majors. She just didn’t expect to be running them while pregnant.
Earlier this month, the 38-year-old nurse practitioner and management consultant ran the New York City Marathon — her hometown race — in her third trimester. It was the seventh marathon she finished while pregnant and the final race she needed to achieve her goal of running all the World Marathon Majors in the same year.
“I knew how bizarre it was to be running a marathon at 34 weeks, but I also knew how fit I was and self-aware of my body at this point,” Keane said. “And while it is very unusual, I wasn’t the first woman to have ever done this.”
After getting married last year, Keane and her husband Brian began talking about starting a family. Expecting pregnancy to take a while, Keane made other plans for herself in the interim.
“In my mind, 2026 was going to be my year of bucket list items,” Keane recalled. “I was like, this is going to be my last hurrah before settling down and becoming pregnant, becoming a mother.”
She signed up for 11 races: the seven World Marathon Majors, a trail marathon in Ireland, two ultramarathons and an Ironman.
Keane kicked off her quest by running the Tokyo Marathon in March. But when the Boston and London Marathons rolled around in April, she noticed she was running a bit slower than usual and wasn’t quite feeling like herself. So, she took a pregnancy test.
It was positive. But she wasn’t going to let that get in the way of her goals.
She promised her husband she would take the next marathon in Ireland slowly. She also agreed to forgo the Ironman and the second ultramarathon – she had already completed the first before finding out she was pregnant.
“Brian was understandably skeptical and worried at first. Neither of us fully understood the physical limitations of pregnancy and why. The research we found was surprisingly limited and frustrating,” Keane said. “So, we decided to take it one marathon at a time, with me not pushing the pace and keeping walking in my back pocket.”
Keane was initially nervous to tell her OB-GYN about her marathon plans but was relieved when she got the go-ahead.
“I don’t think she thought I would do them towards the end, especially being so pregnant at New York. But I am very stubborn and determined,” Keane said. “Plus I got lucky, I was feeling good. So I was able to do it.”
Exercise is generally considered safe and beneficial during most healthy pregnancies. Experts recommend that pregnant women who were physically active before pregnancy or regularly engaged in vigorous aerobic exercise can continue those activities with approval from their doctor. There is limited research on intensive exercise beyond the recommended amount.
With the approval of her doctor, Keane flew to Australia in August to compete in the Sydney Marathon at 25 weeks pregnant, followed by Berlin at 29 weeks. She then completed the Chicago Marathon at 31 weeks in just under 4 hours and finished with the New York City Marathon at 34 weeks in 4:06.55.
Keane was more worried about the race in New York “because I was starting to look heavily pregnant and feel it too." But she had friends along the course while her husband appeared at multiple spots with water to keep her hydrated.
“The marathon passed a block away from Weill Cornell at mile 16, where I’m delivering, so there were plenty of jokes about just pulling off there to have the baby or testing the medical volunteers’ training on the course with an unusual medical intervention of a delivery,” she said.
Keane’s determination was modeled for her at an early age by her father, John, an Irish immigrant who ran marathons in the 1980s and 1990s.
He died of cancer when she was 13, but continued to run in his final months, completing his final New York City Marathon one day before undergoing surgery to have a tumor removed, Keane said.
Years later, when Keane went to college, she was inspired to run a marathon in her dad’s honor. That’s when she caught the bug.
“I loved marathons from the beginning, because it really shows me what the human body is capable of, not only from a physical standpoint, but from a mental standpoint,” she said. “I realized how much grit I have and how capable I am to overcome hard things.”
Since then, running has become a constant in Keane’s life. She says it helped her cope with the emotional toll of working as a nurse practitioner at Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center in New York during the COVID-19 pandemic.
During the pandemic, feeling isolated and needing something to look forward to, Keane signed up for the World Marathon Challenge: Running 7 marathons on 7 different continents in just 7 days. She completed the challenge in 2023 and was the fastest woman to do so that year.
Now, with the World Majors in her rearview, Keane says she’s taking time to reflect on the past 8 months. Just as she learned from her father’s example, she hopes to pass the lessons running has taught her on to her son.
“I want to teach my son resilience and that he can do hard things,” she said. “And that when life inevitably gets tough and throws challenges at him, he will push through them and see the other side of them, whether we elect to do them like a marathon or some things that are way beyond our control.”

title: High school valedictorians to get custom Nike Air Force 1s thanks to Sen.-elect Scott Colom
text:
(AP) - Nike is gifting high school valedictorians across the country with a pair of custom sneakers after Mississippi’s incoming senator appealed to the company on social media.
Scott Colom, who is poised to become the state’s first Black U.S. senator since Reconstruction, called on the sneaker giant to honor his historic election by giving every high school valedictorian in his state a pair of custom Air Force 1s -- his favorite style. The sneakers cost between $90 and $180 on the company’s web site.
“It would encourage MS students to hit the books the rest of the year! #justdoit,” the Democrat suggested Monday on X, referencing Nike’s famous slogan.
The company accepted the challenge and took it one step further.
“The athlete mindset makes things possible, including this idea,” Oregon-based Nike responded Tuesday on X. “@scott_colom, we’ll do you one better… For this year, 2026/2027 high school valedictorians from across the U.S., let’s go!”
Nike said more details would be forthcoming, but Colom has already suggested the custom sneaker should give a nod to Hiram Revels, a fellow Mississippian who was the first African American to serve in Congress when he took office in 1870.
“I’m so proud of @Nike for stepping up to motivate students across the country in this historic moment. This is the #justdoit mentality that makes your company great,” he wrote on X on Tuesday. “Please consider honoring Hiram Revels in the design.”
Colom, a 43-year-old local prosecutor, narrowly defeated Republican Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith in this month’s midterm elections.
When he takes office in January, he’ll become the state’s third Black senator, following Revels and Blanche Kelso Bruce, who was the only formerly enslaved person to serve in the U.S. Senate when he took office in 1875.
Colom’s victory marked a major shift in the Magnolia State, which has the nation’s largest proportional share of Black people but for decades has largely been controlled by white conservatives. The last time Mississippi chose a new Democratic senator was 1947; the winner was a staunch segregationist.

title: School district suspends 2 hockey teams during police investigation
text:
FAIRBANKS, Alaska (KTVF/KTUU/Gray News) — Police are investigating allegations of kidnapping and sexual assault involving two Alaska high school hockey teams during a tournament earlier this month
Police consider charges against 5 individuals
Amanda Graham, the public information officer for the Wasilla Police Department, said authorities are considering charging five individuals.
“The alleged incidents occurred in Wasilla while the teams were in the Valley for the Stars and Stripes tournament,” Graham said. “Two Wasilla detectives recently traveled to Fairbanks to conduct interviews as part of the ongoing investigation.”
Palmer High School hosted the Stars and Stripes Hockey Tournament from Nov. 5 through Nov. 7.
School district suspends hockey activities
The Fairbanks North Star Borough School District said it is investigating an incident involving students from the North Pole High School and Lathrop High School hockey teams.
“The district has initiated an investigation and is coordinating with law enforcement. As an interim administrative safety measure, all hockey activities involving the two teams have been suspended,” a district spokesperson said.
“This temporary pause is not a disciplinary determination and is intended to support student safety and the integrity of the investigation,” the spokesperson said.
The spokesperson said the district cannot share additional details at this time because the investigation is active and involves students.
“The district takes matters involving student safety and well-being seriously and is committed to a thorough and fair investigative process,” the spokesperson said.
District addresses community interest
In a separate statement Wednesday, a spokesperson said the district is working through the investigative process, including determining appropriate disciplinary consequences for those involved.
“We recognize there has been significant community interest in this incident and that many rumors and inaccurate accounts are circulating. We encourage our community to avoid speculation, particularly when it involves students. It is important that the investigative process moves forward thoroughly and fairly based on the facts rather than rumors,” the spokesperson said.
Athletic association responds
The Alaska School Activities Association, the governing body of high school sports, said Wednesday that it is aware of the ongoing investigation and will support the outcome from law enforcement and the Fairbanks North Star Borough School District.
“ASAA appreciates the Fairbanks North Star School District informing us of this incident and the need to shutdown both teams until they have the time to fully and fairly investigate. We have total faith in their ability to properly deal with this issue,” an Alaska School Activities Association spokesperson said.
No names have been released because the people involved are minors.

title: Janet Reingold
text:
Janet Reingold, strategist, writer, founder, and the quiet force behind more public policy than most people will ever realize, passed away earlier this month. She was a part-time resident of Southport.
She wrote for four U.S. presidents, governors, cabinet secretaries, and corporate, academic, and philanthropic leaders, and founded Reingold, Inc. an impactful management and strategic communications firm. Her deepest legacy is the people she taught. Much of what is now common practice in strategic consulting and communications began as her teaching.
An introvert who loved getting out into the world, she was equally happy reading a research paper by the fire, hiking in the Alps, or bringing in lobster traps. She was a devoted daughter, niece, aunt, and wife. Her marriage to Philip Yasinski was a wonderful love story between two eccentric people who balanced each other. We will miss her.
Celebration of Life will be Friday, Dec. 4 at 2 p.m. at Columbia Country Club, 7900 Connecticut Ave, Chevy Chase, MD 20815.
In lieu of flowers please consider a donation in Janet’s memory to: The ALS Association: https://www.als.org/ways-give, or Johns Hopkins Greenberg Bladder Cancer Institute, 600 N. Wolfe Street, CMSC 130, Baltimore, MD 21287. Please note GBCI on the memo line of your check.

title: Taylor Swift returns to the CMA Awards stage for the first time in 13 years, Ella Langley wins big
text:
Ella Langley completely sweeps the 2026 CMA Awards, wins entertainer of the year
It didn't take a crystal ball to see: The 2026 Country Music Association Awards were always going to be all about Ella Langley.
The Alabama-born-and-raised singer was named entertainer of the year during Wednesday's event — beating the host of the evening and last year's winner Lainey Wilson, as well as Cody Johnson, Luke Combs and Chris Stapleton, for the top prize.
“At this point, I'm sick of me," she started her acceptance speech with a joke, after having spent so much of the show on stage. “I could quit tomorrow and have the best career of my life.” Wilson emerged with a bedazzled broom because, “I told you, you was going to sweep, girl!” she said as she embraced Langley.
Related video above: Dolly Parton's philanthropic impact felt in Massachusetts
It really was Langley's night from the jump. The 60th annual CMA Awards, broadcast live from Nashville’s Bridgestone Arena, started and ended with her. Langley accepted the first award of the night, single of the year, for her history-making “Choosin’ Texas.”
Competition was fierce: Taylor Swift’s song for the “Toy Story 5” film, “I Knew It, I Knew You,” was also nominated in the category, as were Langley’s own “Be Her,” Wilson’s “Somewhere Over Laredo” and Johnson’s “The Fall.”
And then Langley was back on stage almost immediately afterward — to perform her joyous “Loving Life Again” with a string quartet and to pick up another award, when “Choosin’ Texas” was named song of the year.
“This song is the gift that keeps on giving,” she said in her speech.
She also won female vocalist as well as album of the year, the latter for her thrilling, old-soul country “Dandelion.”
“My lip is already quivering,” she said. “I’m at a loss for words.”
The return of Taylor Swift and a tribute to Dolly Parton
Swift was in the building. The pop powerhouse lit up the CMA Awards by performing “I Knew It, I Knew You” with a bit of her 2006 country hit “Our Song” mixed in for good measure.
She began her set in the back halls of the arena before hitting the stage — joined by Keith Urban on banjo, no less — as if no time had passed.
But it's been 13 years since Swift last performed at the CMA Awards, a decade after her last appearance there and 17 years after being named the youngest entertainer of the year in the show’s history.
Consider it a treat in a night full of them. The show began with a powerful tribute to the larger-than-life Dolly Parton. The American icon died in August at age 80, and her legacy will be felt for many decades to come.
Host Wilson got the celebration started, duetting Parton's “I Will Always Love You” with the legendary singer-songwriter Vince Gill.
Then she was joined by singer Brad Paisley in a funny opening monologue where the pair sang modern parodies of famous country songs: Loretta Lynn's “Coal Miner's Daughter” became “Data Miner's Daughter,” and Willie Nelson's “Always On My Mind” was transformed into “Always On My Phone.”
No shortage of awards and performances here
A standout set arrived early: Kacey Musgraves and Miranda Lambert duetted “Horses & Divorces” — a song from Musgraves’ latest album, “Middle of Nowhere,” that doubles as a delicious resolution from the pair of former frenemies — with its norteño accordion and shout-along lyrics. The stage was set to look like an ’80s beauty parlor, recalling one of Parton’s most famous acting roles: the 1989 film “Steel Magnolias.”
Tim McGraw brought it back to the ’90s, singing “Don’t Take the Girl.” Megan Moroney slowed things down with her big-hearted ballad “Beautiful Things.” Tucker Wetmore was joined by a brass band for a bit of his single “Who Told You That” before launching into some of Hank Williams Jr.'s 1984 hit “All My Rowdy Friends Are Coming Over Tonight."
Combs tackled his song “Miss You Here.” Lambert and Langley brought some country-disco with “Snakeskin Boots.” Mumford & Sons teamed up with Stapleton for “Here.”
Later, Stapleton would hop back on stage to join Stephen Wilson Jr. — and to be awarded male vocalist of the year, for a ninth time in his career.
Lainey Wilson performed a brand new one, the full-throated “Just A Woman."
It was a bit of a theme: The modern traditionalist Zach Top also debuted a new track, the bluegrass-y “Moonshine.” Before he left the stage, Dierks Bentley joined in for a tribute to the late John Anderson. They sang his 1983 single “Swingin’”.
Best new artist went to Stephen Wilson Jr.; vocal group went for a second year in a row to the Red Clay Strays, who also performed their song “Revival.”
Brooks & Dunn took home vocal duo for the 17th time.
“I love to hear myself talk, and I've actually run out of things to say,” Kix Brooks said in his acceptance speech. “Thanks for making us famous.”
“Follow the yellow brick road,” added Ronnie Dunn.
Later in the night, they received the Willie Nelson Lifetime Achievement Award. Halestorm, Marcus King, Brothers Osborne, Hardy and Luke Bryan paid tribute to the legendary country music duo, covering some of their biggest hits: “Boot Scootin’ Boogie," “Rock My World (Little Country Girl),” “Hard Workin’ Man,” “Hillbilly Deluxe” and “Play Something Country.”
Prizes are nominated and voted on by members of the Country Music Association, which includes music executives, artists, publicists, songwriters and other industry professionals.

title: ‘Vanderpump Rules’ star Jax Taylor shares cancer diagnosis
text:
(Gray News) - Former “Vanderpump Rules” star Jax Taylor shared his cancer diagnosis on Wednesday.
Taylor, 47, revealed on Instagram that he went to the hospital in July for pain he thought stemmed from a kidney stone.
“What I thought was just a kidney stone turned into something I never imagined. My CT scan also showed a tumor on my left kidney. After many tests and appointments, I found out it was cancer,” he said.
Taylor said Wednesday that he had surgery to remove the tumor, which was “larger and deeper than originally expected,” and is now waiting for the pathology results.
Taylor, who shares a 5-year-old son with reality star Brittany Cartwright, said he just wants “to be healthy and be here to watch my son grow up.”
“If there’s one thing I hope people can take away from this, it’s never to take your health for granted. I did for many years and I won’t ever do that again,” he said.

title: Alleged gang member, in the U.S. illegally, admits role in ATM scheme in Maine, across New England
text:
Alleged gang member, in the U.S. illegally, admits role in ATM scheme in Maine, across New England
A man whom federal prosecutors call an illegal alien from Venezuela and an alleged member of the violent transnational criminal organization Tren de Aragua (TdA), has pleaded guilty in connection with an ATM jackpotting scheme that included robberies and attempted robberies in Maine, Massachusetts, New Hampshire, Connecticut and Rhode Island.
ATM jackpotting schemes typically involve a crew of individuals who travel to targeted ATMs and install malware directly to the ATM’s software programming to force the ATM to dispense all its cash.
Moises Alejandro Martinez Gutierrez, 29, pleaded guilty in federal court in Boston on Wednesday to two counts of conspiracy to commit bank theft and damaging a protected computer. He was initially charged in February 2026 and will be sentenced on Feb. 11, 2027.
Crimes Across New England
Prosecutors say Martinez Gutierrez was arrested in Augusta in February following an attempted ATM jackpotting robbery there. Prosecutors say they then identified him as having participated in five prior attempted and completed jackpotting robberies across New England, including completed robberies on Dec. 31, 2025, in Norwich, Conn.; Jan. 20, 2026, in Braintree, Mass.; and Jan. 30, 2026, in Rochester, N.H.; as well as attempted robberies on Jan. 14, 2026, in Coventry, R.I., Jan. 19, 2026, in Stoneham, Mass. and the Feb. 5, 2026 case in Augusta.
To carry out these thefts, prosecutors say Martinez Gutierrez would approach the ATM, access it with an ATM key, and appear to interact with it using a cellphone. In the completed robberies, prosecutors say Martinez Gutierrez would eventually return to the ATM in a car and remove significant amounts of cash from the machine. Bank security videos recorded Martinez Gutierrez and alleged co-conspirators carrying out these thefts and attempted thefts. Martinez Gutierrez and, allegedly, his co-conspirators used cell phones and other electronic devices to inject malware into the ATM, causing it to override its withdrawal limits.
The charge of conspiring to commit bank fraud carries a sentence of up to five years in prison, up to three years of supervised release and a fine of up to $250,000. The charge of damaging a protected computer carries a sentence of up to 10 years in prison, up to three years of supervised release and a fine of up to $250,000. Martinez Gutierrez is subject to deportation proceedings upon completion of an imposed sentence.
Multi-year Nationwide Investigation
Over the last two years, prosecutors say federal law enforcement has been investigating a nationwide conspiracy, believed to be coordinated and committed by members of TdA, to steal money from ATMs using malware.
TdA is a violent transnational criminal organization that originated in Venezuela in the mid-2000s. TdA has expanded its criminal network throughout the Western Hemisphere and established a presence in the United States. Prosecutors say TdA’s criminal activities include human smuggling, extortion, drug trafficking, kidnapping, and robbery.
Prosecutors say TdA has used ATM jackpotting in the United States to steal millions of dollars from financial institutions.

title: NSB branches in Brunswick and Topsham holding Giving Tree initiative
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
What better place to support a Giving Tree than a branch?
Three Norway Savings Bank locations will host Giving Trees from Nov. 27 through Dec. 21. All are encouraged to visit the branches, take a wish tag, purchase the listed item and help those in need while spreading holiday cheer in the process.
All gifts collected will be donated to three local nonprofits doing great things for the community: the Midcoast Youth Center, which is a Bath-based organization that offers a diverse array of programs and services designed to improve the lives of youth and prevent youth suicide in Sagadahoc County, Brunswick and Harpswell; the Brunswick Area Teen Center, which provides a free and safe space for teens to engage in creative outlets, share their talents, hang out with friends, and participate in an abundance of activities; and The Gathering Place, which maintains a safe, welcoming and comfortable space in downtown Brunswick for people who live alone, seniors on fixed incomes, individuals with disabilities, people who are homeless and families.
Tags can be grabbed and gifts dropped off at the Maine Street branch, 83 Maine St., Brunswick; the Cook’s Corner branch, 14 Gurnet Road, Brunswick; and the Topsham branch, 47 Topsham Fair Mall Road.
In addition, NSB is currently holding the Share and Care Food Drive at all of its branches in Maine and New Hampshire through Dec. 14. All customers and community members are encouraged to drop nonperishable food items in special designated areas at each branch, with all items collected to be hand delivered by NSB team members to local food pantries and food banks located in each respective community.

title: Robbins Lumber cited for five serious safety violations after deadly mill fire
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
SEARSMONT, Maine (WABI) - Robbins Lumber has been cited for five serious safety violations and faces $54,691 in proposed penalties after the deadly May 15 explosion and fire at its Searsmont mill, according to the U.S. Department of Labor.
A serious violation is the second most severe penalty the agency can issue. OSHA defines a serious violation as involving a hazard that “could cause an accident or illness that would most likely result in death or serious physical harm, unless the employer did not know or could not have known of the violation.”
A spokesperson for the Department of Labor says the company has 15 business days from receiving the citations to comply, request an informal conference with the Occupational Safety and Health Administration’s area director or contest the findings before an independent review commission.
The Department of Labor did not disclose the specifics of the citations. WABI has requested more information into the nature of the violations.
OSHA opened an inspection into the mill on the day of the deadly explosion and fire. The incident killed two firefighters and injured mill co-owner Alden Robbins, who later died from those injuries. Ten others were also left with burn injuries.
The Maine State Fire Marshal’s Office ruled the fire to be accidental and said it likely started in the unloader mechanism at the base of a silo. Investigators believe that the explosion was caused by suspended particulate material rapidly igniting inside the silo.
A prior OSHA citation
Robbins Lumber faced several fires and an OSHA citation even before the May 15 disaster.
8 Investigates found at least three fires connected to the mill in recent years, as well as a 2025 OSHA citation for failing to follow preventative safety procedures and failing to conduct an annual inspection of its energy-control procedures.
Company’s response
Robbins Lumber co-owner Catherine Robbins-Halsted released a statement Thursday morning, saying in part: “For nearly 145 years, Robbins Lumber has been part of this community. The outpouring of compassion and support we have received during these extraordinarily difficult months has meant more to us than words can express. We remain deeply grateful to our employees, our neighbors, the first responders, and the many people who have stood beside us. We cannot change what happened on May 15, but we can honor those affected by continuing to learn, improve, and do everything within our power to help prevent another tragedy.”
You can read her full statement below:
The events of May 15, 2026, forever changed Robbins Lumber, our families, our employees, and our community. The loss of life and the injuries suffered that day are heartbreaking, and the impact of this tragedy will be felt for generations. Our hearts remain with the families who lost loved ones, those who were injured, and everyone whose lives have been forever altered. We recognize that while buildings and equipment can be replaced, lives cannot. As we work to rebuild our business, we know that our lives, and the lives of so many others, will never be the same.
We acknowledge the citations issued by the Occupational Safety and Health Administration (OSHA) following its investigation into the May 15 incident. We take these findings seriously and continue to work cooperatively with the appropriate agencies as we review the circumstances surrounding this tragedy and identify opportunities to strengthen our safety practices.
The safety and well-being of our employees, emergency responders, and community have always been important to Robbins Lumber. As we rebuild, we are evaluating our facilities, equipment, procedures, and training with a commitment to improving safety and reducing the risk of another tragedy.
For nearly 145 years, Robbins Lumber has been part of this community. The outpouring of compassion and support we have received during these extraordinarily difficult months has meant more to us than words can express. We remain deeply grateful to our employees, our neighbors, the first responders, and the many people who have stood beside us. We cannot change what happened on May 15, but we can honor those affected by continuing to learn, improve, and do everything within our power to help prevent another tragedy.
Our thoughts remain, first and foremost, with those who lost their lives, those who were injured, and the families who continue to carry the weight of that day.

title: ‘I’m not sure what MAGA means’: Elon Musk backs away from Trump’s brand after GOP’s midterm defeats
text:
ATLANTA (AP) — Elon Musk was on the front row at Donald Trump’s second inauguration and has spent hundreds of millions of dollars trying to help the Republican president and his “Make America Great Again” allies win elections.
Now, after Republicans’ midterm thrashing by Democrats, the world’s richest man insists he’s not a MAGA acolyte after all and feels “pretty foolish” for spending so much money on the cause.
It’s the latest example of billionaire tech executives shifting their stances as Democrats prepare to take control of Congress and many more U.S. statehouses in January after they spent months promising a regulatory and oversight crackdown on artificial intelligence firms, their data center expansion and their interactions with the Trump administration.
“I mean, I’m not MAGA,” Musk told The New York Times on Wednesday during the newspaper’s DealBook Summit.
“I’m not sure what MAGA means,” added the Tesla and SpaceX CEO, who once sported a black MAGA hat in the Oval Office and coined the “Dark MAGA” label. “But I, I don’t think I’m, like, if, if that means sort of blind adherence to a set of policies by the Republican Party,” Musk continued, “then I certainly don’t have that. I think there are, there, there are positives and negatives in both parties.”
Trump takes Musk’s shift in stride
Trump, whose relationship with Musk has ranged from ally and trusted adviser to pariah, reacted Thursday with a seeming shrug.
“He’s a friend of mine,” Trump told NBC News in a telephone interview, similar to how the president described Russian President Vladimir Putin when they met earlier in the day in the Chinese tech hub of Shenzhen. “Elon is — Elon’s got very good intentions. I mean, he was with me the whole — he traveled with me.”
Musk, who has based himself and several of his companies in Texas, spent more than $400 million on Trump-aligned Republicans running in November. That included around $200 million backing Texas Senate nominee Ken Paxton, who lost to Democrat James Talarico.
Democrats scored sweeping victories after making Musk, other tech titans and the proliferation of artificial intelligence and AI data centers a campaign focus. They plan new scrutiny on the industry, including congressional investigations into tech firms’ dealings with Trump and his administration. That leaves Musk and others scrambling to rebrand themselves after spending years aligning closely with Trump and his fellow Republicans as they sought government contracts and favorable policies on everything from taxation to AI regulation.
Palantir co-founder and CEO Alex Karp, whose AI software company counts the Pentagon among its lucrative government clients, earlier this month raised eyebrows when he insisted to Politico that he’s always been a progressive.
“I’ve been a Democrat my whole life. I grew up in a far-left environment,” he said. “I know more about being a progressive than almost anybody on the planet, and I absolutely believe Palantir — all of our products are essentially progressive.”
Karp, a donor to Trump’s White House ballroom project who has adopted the president’s rhetoric to describe his own business as “anti-woke,” said he’s willing to support a Democrat for president in 2028.
At the Times’ event, Musk said if he had a do-over, he “probably” would have “spent less money” on the midterms.
“I feel pretty foolish about having spent so much money and not seeing much for it,” Musk told columnist Andrew Sorkin. “Or maybe it would’ve been much worse without that. But it certainly shows that American elections are not just about money.”
Democrats and Trump offer takes on Musk’s future
Musk sat alongside other Big Tech billionaires at Trump’s inauguration and led the president’s Department of Government Efficiency, a post that for months made him the most high-profile figure in the administration other than Trump himself.
Hours after Trump was sworn in on Jan. 20, 2025, Musk appeared at a Trump rally in Washington, where he enthusiastically embraced the president’s agenda and his supporters.
“This was no ordinary victory,” he said. “This was a fork in the road of human civilization. OK? There are elections that come and go. Some elections are important, some are not. But this one really mattered. ... It is thanks to you that the future of civilization is assured.”
Some Democrats were unimpressed with Musk’s change in tenor.
Responding to Musk’s turnabout on X, the social media platform that Musk owns, Sen. Ruben Gallego of Arizona was concise: “You are still getting a subpoena.”
Trump, his friendly remarks notwithstanding, offered his own prediction about Musk’s future.
“MAGA, to me, means something very specific,” the president said, without elaborating, “and when people veer from it, they don’t do very well.”
___
Follow the AP’s coverage of Elon Musk at https://apnews.com/hub/elon-musk.

title: Woman missing since 1994 identified in decades-old cold case
text:
GREENBRIER COUNTY, W.Va . (WDTV/Gray News) - Authorities have made a breakthrough in a decades-old cold case involving a Virginia woman who disappeared in 1994.
Investigators identified the woman as Elizabeth Jean Acton, who had been reported missing from Colonial Beach, Virginia.
The investigation began May 9, 2001, when a West Virginia Paving employee discovered skeletal remains near an interstate exit in Greenbrier County, West Virginia.
Investigators determined the remains belonged to a woman who was approximately 37 to 47 years old and about 5 feet tall. Her identity was unknown, and she became known as “Greenbrier County Jane Doe.”
Investigators learned that Acton was 41 when she was last seen on Aug. 24, 1994, in Colonial Beach.
The case was entered into the National Missing and Unidentified Persons System and the Combined DNA Index System, but no matches were found.
For more than two decades, state police continued to investigate and followed numerous tips and leads.
In September 2024, state police submitted the case to Marshall University for additional DNA testing. On Aug. 12, 2026, the West Virginia Office of the Chief Medical Examiner notified investigators that the remains had been identified as Acton.
West Virginia State Police and the Colonial Beach Police Department are working together to determine how Acton traveled from Virginia to the roadside dump near U.S. Route 60 and the Interstate 64 Alta exit in Greenbrier County.

title: A path to bring back parole in Maine emerges as a receptive governor steps in
text:
A state commission teed up a plan on Wednesday to reinstate parole in Maine, a move the incoming governor is open to after opposition from the previous executive.
The majority of the commission recommended that if the state decides to bring back the conditional early release program it should be applicable to both people incarcerated in the future and those already incarcerated, under specific circumstances. However, members disagreed on what those circumstances should be, punting a core question to the incoming Legislature which will settle the specifics.
Maine was the first state to abolish parole 50 years ago and is one of 16 states that remain without it today. A proposal to reinstate the program last session failed to gain committee support, though opposition had less to do with the policy itself and more to do with how to implement such a change.
So lawmakers instead opted to examine the intersection of parole and current sentencing practices through a study commission, which held its final meeting on Wednesday, lasting eight hours, to set recommendations for the next Legislature. Rep. Nina Milliken (D-Blue Hill), who introduced the parole bill last session and sat on the commission, said she plans to pursue it again when session begins in January.
Previous efforts to reinstate parole were expected to fail, because outgoing Gov. Janet Mills, a former prosecutor and state attorney general, consistently opposed such a program. The next iteration will be considered by Gov.-elect Hannah Pingree, who told Maine Morning Star she supports reinstating parole, as long as it is established in a way that weighs evidence of rehabilitation alongside risk.
Parole is not automatic but a condition granted by a parole board for someone to serve the remainder of their sentence supervised in the community, while adhering to specific rules.
“An effort to reinstate parole should focus on whether someone has demonstrated readiness to return to the community — through education, treatment, behavioral progress, and a clear plan for reentry — and ensure that decisions are made in a way that is fair, consistent, and proportionate to the individual’s circumstances,” Pingree said in a statement.
She added that, “critically, this work cannot stop at the point of release. If we expect people to succeed when they return to the community, we must ensure that the conditions for success are in place: stable housing, access to health care, pathways to employment, and strong community connections.”
Who should be eligible?
One of the key questions the commission was asked to settle was whether parole should be applied only to people convicted after a parole law is passed or also to people currently incarcerated.
Four members voted to recommend retroactive application for all crime types, with a higher evidentiary standard of rehabilitation for sexual assault and crimes against family and household members. Four members voted to recommend retroactive application with exclusions and/or a higher standard for retroactive application (leaving the specifics of both up to legislators).
No members voted for an option to allow retroactive application for all crime types without exceptions, and one member voted to not allow retroactive application at all. One member abstained.
“I want people to think that this is not just a question of whether the incarcerated person has done good work for themselves and are in a better place,” Francine Garland Stark from the Maine Coalition to End Domestic Violence told the commission on Wednesday. “I certainly hope that they are, but the harm that they have caused has not been rehabilitated. They may themselves be in a better place, but what has happened remains.”
Garland Stark and other victims’ advocates, who did not have a seat on the commission, offered suggestions during the final meeting, overwhelmingly urging the group not to pursue reinstating parole retroactively specifically for cases that include elevated, aggravated assault, attempted murder, manslaughter, and murder cases.
While people with violent offenses are eligible for parole in some other states, Maine would be an outlier if it included these types of sentences in parole retroactively.
Pointing to the Maine Department of Corrections’ mission statement to rehabilitate and the low recidivism rate touted by the department, Sen. Rachel Talbot Ross (D-Cumberland) questioned why certain cases should be excluded, if the department and a parole board were to deem the incarcerated person rehabilitated and no longer a threat to society.
Milliken added that putting such exclusions into statute doesn’t offer the nuance that exists among people who commit serious offenses. Victims’ advocates similarly emphasized during the meeting that victims are not a monolith.
“What the challenge of retrospect application does is it upends what people currently working on that healing process thought was going to be the parameter of their span of peace,” Garland Stark said.
Pointing to Maine’s supervised community confinement program, Christopher Laliberte, a currently incarcerated person who sits on the commission, said early release through that program is not accounted for in a judgment, because “it’s not a guarantee — it’s an opportunity.”
Supervised community confinement allows people to serve the final few months of a sentence in the community supervised by the department through probation. It is available to people in the last 30 months of their sentence, up from 18 months after a change in 2021.
“I view parole very much the same way,” Laliberte said. “It’s not taking away a judgment that a jury or a judge has given. It’s providing an opportunity for relief for someone who has done the work to prove that they have ‘rehabilitated’ themselves.”
But victims’ rights advocates said they discuss the implications of supervised community confinement with victims at length before and after sentencing, pointing out how that would not be possible if parole became retroactively eligible to people already serving sentences today.
Other commission recommendations
A key point of confusion during debate of reinstating parole last session was what would happen if conflicts arose between the administration of parole and probation violations.
The commission recommended on Wednesday that the probation violation take precedence if it falls under Maine’s split sentences statute.
The commission punted on the policy question of whether a judge should be able to issue a life sentence without parole, instead voting to recommend that a future parole bill not be passed without lawmakers addressing it.
The majority of the commission also recommended parole not replace the supervised community confinement program.
During consideration of the parole bill last session, the Maine Department of Corrections argued the current system was sufficient in part because of supervised community confinement. Long-timers in Maine State Prison told Maine Morning Star that the prospects of early release through that program are too far out to have a tangible impact on motivation.
In 2026, 81 people eligible to apply for supervised community confinement did not, with 41% citing housing as a barrier and 58% reporting they weren’t interested, according to data the Department of Corrections provided the commission.
The overarching money question
Discussion of various aspects of reinstating parole made clear inadequacies in the current system, specifically when it comes to funding.
“Victim notification in our state currently is woefully underfunded and under-resourced, and fails on the regular,” said Cara Cookson, director of victim services for the Maine Office of the Attorney General.
Maine didn’t enact victim notification requirements until 1995, which continues to present challenges for DOC Victim Services getting contact information to notify people, Cookson added. The ability of victim witness advocates to do their work in a timely way also depends on prosecutors, and Maine has faced ongoing staffing shortages and heavy caseloads.
The commission recommended on Wednesday that any parole system established include the financial and human resources necessary to have a robust victim notification system.
Maine relies heavily on the federal Victims of Crime Act to fund victim services. That federal funding has declined in recent years and the state has tried to pick up the tab.
“I think the Legislature has done a really insufficient job, and I think that’s being generous, in caring for the programs that you guys are all running,” Milliken said to victims’ services advocates during Wednesday’s meeting. “And frankly, that’s Democrats’ fault, and I’m going to say that on mic because we have been responsible for running the budget for the state for several years now and we have not done an adequate job to make sure that you guys can continue to provide the life saving services that you do for the state of Maine.”
Along with its specific recommendations regarding how to reinstate parole, the commission also agreed to include a statement in its final report recognizing that the success of the programs within a parole system would require financial investment by the legislature.
Correction: This story was updated to clarify that the commission recommended a parole structure, should the state decide to reinstate the program.

title: Maine Will Have The Earliest Sunset in The Nation Next Month
text:
The summer stuff has been put away and the winter flannels have made their way out of storage.
It's about this time every year that people from Maine really begin to plan for the forthcoming winter.
The nights will get colder and soon the weather forecasts will feature snowfall maps and wind chill advisories.
Another clear sign that winter is nearly upon us is the shortened amount of sunlight Maine receives.
For 2026, the earliest sunset of the year will actually arrive before winter is even official.
Aroostook County in Maine Will Have The Earliest Sunset in The Nation For 2026
According to data pulled together from the NOAA solar calendar, Aroostook County in Maine is set for the earliest sunset in the nation on December 10. The sun will drop below the horizon that day at 3:46pm.
If you compare that to another state along the eastern seaboard, it gets a little depressing. The earliest sunset in Florida for 2026 will happen in Miami on December at 5:31pm. That's nearly a two-hour difference in sunlight.
The earliest sunset of the year arrives 11 days before the winter solstice, which happens on December 21 this year.
Other Parts of Maine Will See A Little Bit More Sun
While The County will feel the pain with the earliest sunset in the nation, other parts of Maine will see a little more sunshine before it sets behind the horizon.
The earliest sunset for Portland, Maine, will be on December 9 at 4:03pm.
The earliest sunset for Augusta, Maine, in 2026 will happen on December 7 at 3:59pm.
The earliest sunset for Bangor, Maine, in 2026 will also be December 9 at 3:54pm.

title: ‘Vanderpump Rules’ star Jax Taylor shares cancer diagnosis
text:
(Gray News) - Former “Vanderpump Rules” star Jax Taylor shared his cancer diagnosis on Wednesday.
Taylor, 47, revealed on Instagram that he went to the hospital in July for pain he thought stemmed from a kidney stone.
“What I thought was just a kidney stone turned into something I never imagined. My CT scan also showed a tumor on my left kidney. After many tests and appointments, I found out it was cancer,” he said.
Taylor said Wednesday that he had surgery to remove the tumor, which was “larger and deeper than originally expected,” and is now waiting for the pathology results.
Taylor, who shares a 5-year-old son with reality star Brittany Cartwright, said he just wants “to be healthy and be here to watch my son grow up.”
“If there’s one thing I hope people can take away from this, it’s never to take your health for granted. I did for many years and I won’t ever do that again,” he said.

title: Trump posthumously pardons MLB hits leader Pete Rose
text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — President Donald Trump on Thursday said he had posthumously pardoned Pete Rose more than two years after the baseball star’s death and a year after he was reinstated by Major League Baseball Commissioner Rob Manfred.
“I have just given a Complete and Total Pardon to the Late, Great Pete Rose, a true Baseball SUPERSTAR & LEGEND,” Trump posted on social media.
Rose, baseball’s career hits leader at 4,256, entered guilty pleas on April 20, 1990, to two counts of filing false tax returns, admitting he failed to report $354,968 during a four-year period. That was about eight months after Rose agreed to a permanent ban from baseball.
″I know I’m not a bad person, but I did make some mistakes and it’s in the eyes of the judge,″ Rose said that night during his weekly talk show on WCKY-AM in Cincinnati. ″All you can say is it’s up to the judge.″
The pardon comes after Manfred issued a sweeping decision last May that opened a pathway for Rose to be considered for baseball’s Hall of Fame. Manfred declared that individuals on MLB’s permanently ineligible list would have their statuses restored at death, a ruling that impacted 17 people, most notably Rose and Shoeless Joe Jackson.
Under a rule adopted by the Hall’s board of directors in 1991, anyone on the permanently ineligible list can’t be considered for election to the Hall. The earliest Rose or Jackson could now be inducted would be in 2028.
Rose agreed to his permanent ban in August 1989 after Major League Baseball investigator John M. Dowd concluded he bet numerous times on the Cincinnati Reds while playing on and managing his hometown team from 1985-87.
Facing a sentence of up to six years in prison and $500,000 in fines, Rose was sentenced on July 19, 1990, by U.S. District Judge S. Arthur Spiegel in Cincinnati to five months in prison. He also was fined $50,000 and ordered to perform 1,000 hours of community service as a gym teacher’s assistant with inner-city youths in Cincinnati as part of a one-year probation period. The first three months of the probation were to be spent at the halfway house.
Rose repaid the Internal Revenue Service $366,042.
“History and the tincture of time will decide his place among the all-time greats of baseball,” Spiegel said. “With regard to Pete Rose, the individual, he has broken the law, admitted his guilt, and stands ready to pay the penalty. Under our system of law and sense of fairness, when he has completed his sentence, he will have paid his debt to society and should be accepted by society as rehabilitated. Only time will tell whether he is to be restored to his position of honor for his accomplishment on the ball fields of America.”
Rose reported that Aug. 10 to the U.S. Penitentiary Marion Camp in Illinois, a minimum security facility, and was released Jan. 7, 1991. He entered Talbert House to start serving his probation and departed on April 5.
A 17-time All-Star during a playing career from 1963-86, Rose was the 1963 National League Rookie of the Year, 1973 MVP and 1975 World Series MVP. A three-time NL batting champion, he broke the prior hits record of 4,191 set by Ty Cobb from 1905-28.

title: Desert Shield Thanksgiving at Loring
text:
PRESQUE ISLE, Maine (WAGM) - Thanksgiving is usually a time for family, but for hundreds of people at Loring Air Force Base, that family looked a little different while loved ones were deployed for Operation Desert Shield. It’s the focus of this week’s Throwback Thursday with Brian Bouchard.
For military families, the holidays can be especially difficult when someone they love is serving far from home. In this week’s Throwback Thursday, we dial the time machine back to 1990 to Loring Air Force Base, where more than 400 people gathered for Thanksgiving dinner while many airmen were deployed for Operation Desert Shield.
They invited a few friends over for Thanksgiving dinner at the Loring Air Force Base Rec Center today. Well, maybe saying a few friends is not quite accurate. They actually invited more like 400 people to attend a Thanksgiving dinner.
“With so many of our men deployed and so many of the families still here, we thought this would be a great way to celebrate Thanksgiving together as a family. And there are so many people who are interested in helping.”
For those whose loved ones are deployed in Operation Desert Shield, family can be very important, especially during the holidays. And while the people seated next to them today may not have been actual relatives, you can’t help but feel a real sense of family.
“We decided a lot of our friends and family at Loring are here and we wanted to come and spend Thanksgiving with them.”
“Oh, well, he’s not at home. So we decided to have Thanksgiving dinner with this other couple that decided to come also.”
“You’re a volunteer, so you’re here to help out. Why’d you decide to help?”
“I really couldn’t. It just sounded like a nice thing to do, help out these people with their, you know, family deploy. You know, they help so.”
“Everyone is away from their immediate families. And so here we don’t have grandma and grandpa and mom and dad and cousins and sisters. So we all learn to be a family with each other. So when there’s problems, we have people to go to. And right now we’re dealing with something and dealing with it very, very well.”
For the news, I’m Joe Cloukey, reporting from Loring Air Force Base.

title: Scientists discover possible CTE marker in patients' blood
text:
Scientists discover possible CTE marker in patients' blood
Scientists stumbled onto a hint that measuring a toxic protein tied to Alzheimer’s disease just might one day be useful in diagnosing a different brain disease in football players and others who have suffered repeated blows to the head.
Doctors evaluate symptoms such as mood swings and memory loss to try to tell if patients may have CTE, or chronic traumatic encephalopathy, a disease linked to concussions and other brain trauma. But other diseases cause similar symptoms, and a CTE diagnosis can only be confirmed by examining the brain after death.
Now, two small studies are highlighting a new clue — that a blood test being developed to spot abnormal tau in the brains of Alzheimer’s patients seems to also detect buildup of that protein in people with advanced CTE.
Tau normally supports neurons but in Alzheimer’s, it tangles inside those nerve cells. Scientists are developing a blood test to track those tangles by detecting a particular tau fragment called eMTBR-tau243. But researchers at Washington University in St. Louis got a surprise when using autopsy records to study the new test – finding someone with high levels of that biomarker who didn’t have Alzheimer’s but CTE instead.
The researchers turned to a larger collection of autopsied brain and blood samples, eventually testing blood stored from 11 people classified as having CTE.
Compared to samples stored from healthy people, levels of eMTBR-tau243 were higher in those with advanced CTE, said study co-author Chihiro Sato, a WashU assistant neurology professor. That biomarker couldn’t reliably identify early-stage CTE, the research team reported at a dementia meeting in Japan last week.
Separately, researchers at Boston University and Arizona’s Banner Health were studying the same question using blood stored from 21 former professional or school football players who also donated their brain for research after death. Autopsies found 16 died with advanced CTE, two with earlier-stage CTE and three didn’t have the disease.
Blood levels of that tau biomarker were significantly higher in the athletes with advanced CTE, the researchers reported Thursday at a scientific meeting in Boston. Adding to the complexity, five of those with CTE also had Alzheimer’s disease, resulting in the highest levels of that tau biomarker.
Both studies were published in the medical journal JAMA.
The possible CTE link is interesting but very preliminary, requiring much larger studies to see if there’s a real connection, cautioned Northwestern University neuropathologist Dr. Rudolph Castellani, who wasn’t involved with the research.
Abnormal tau is found in several additional brain diseases, which can overlap in older adults. Moreover, tau buildup in CTE is different from the type that occurs in Alzheimer’s, Drs. Günter Höglinger and Carla Palleis of Germany’s Ludwig Maximilian University of Munich wrote in an accompanying editorial in the journal.
They also stressed the need for far more research, while saying the two studies together “represent an important step” in the quest to one day detect CTE in living patients.

title: FEMA facing bed bug infestation
text:
(CNN) - The nation’s Federal Emergency Management Agency is dealing with its own sort of emergency this week -- bed bugs.
The infestation happened at the FEMA headquarters in Washington, D.C.
More than 1,000 staffers are having to work from home while the building is fumigated.
The bed bugs were apparently found on multiple floors.
A memo to FEMA workers alerting them to the problem gave no indication of when staff could return to the building.
This was the second emergency FEMA workers have faced in just a week. They were mobilized by Homeland Security to help with last Friday’s ground-stop on flights.

title: Iran War costs surpass $48B as lawmakers demand unreleased estimates on base damage
text:
Iran War costs surpass $48B as lawmakers demand unreleased estimates on base damage
The costs of the Iran War have risen to an estimated $48.3 billion as of Nov. 13, but because that total does not include damage to U.S. bases attacked in the Middle East, lawmakers are pushing for the Pentagon to provide those figures.
Arthur Miller, a Pentagon budget official, provided the latest overall cost estimate Thursday to the Senate Armed Services Committee, which is considering his nomination to be Navy comptroller. The $48 billion figure includes the costs of military operations, as well as for replacing equipment and munitions.
Democratic Sen. Richard Blumenthal of Connecticut pressed Miller for an estimate on damage to U.S. installations, which Miller said he didn't have. Republican Sen. Roger Wicker of Mississippi, the committee's chair, directed Miller to try to provide an answer as soon as possible.
An Associated Press analysis found that Iran attacked aircraft hangars, systems that detect incoming strikes, warehouses, troop housing and more, causing billions of dollars in equipment damage.
The war's price tag has been a flashpoint in Congress, with debates over costs intensifying as the Trump administration asks lawmakers to pass a $1.5 trillion defense budget. After the unpopular war and its economic effects contributed to severe Republican losses in the midterm elections, financial battles over the conflict will only escalate once Democrats take control of Congress in January for the remainder of President Donald Trump's term.
The Pentagon has faced growing calls from Democrats to release estimates on the damage Iran has done to American bases in the Middle East through missile and drone attacks.
Sen. Elizabeth Warren, a Democrat from Massachusetts, grilled acting Navy Secretary Hung Cao on the costs of the war at his confirmation hearing Tuesday for the permanent job.
Citing independent estimates and media reports, Warren said the U.S. naval blockade on Iranian shipping costs about $32.5 million a day, while an Iranian attack on the Navy's regional headquarters in Bahrain did at least $400 million in damage.
Cao confirmed the figure for the blockade but said he could not offer a full damage assessment in Bahrain because "it's a nonpermissive area for us to go." Cao told a reporter months ago that Iran "blew the hell out of Bahrain."

title: Toyota issues recall for thousands of vehicles due to airbag degradation
text:
Toyota issues recall for thousands of vehicles due to airbag degradation
Toyota has issued a recall for more than 314,000 cars, trucks and vehicles, the U.S. National Highway Traffic Safety Administration said on Wednesday.
According to the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration, the vehicles are being recalled over a potential issue with Takata Corporation airbags. The NHTSA said that the passenger-side airbags could spray metal shards throughout the vehicle cabin, which may result in serious injury or death.
Related videos above: How to stay ahead of recalls
Models affected include the 2002-2010 Lexus SC430, 2011 IS250, 2017 GX460, 2003-2008 Toyota Corolla, 2005-2006 Tundra, 2005-2007 Sequoia, and 2016-2017 4Runner vehicles.
Owner notification letters are expected to be mailed beginning Dec. 28.
Owners can contact Toyota's customer service at 1-800-331-4331. Toyota's numbers for this recall are 26TB25, 26TA25, 26LB11, and 26LA11.

title: Maine business climate hurt by high costs, low productivity: report
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Rising energy and housing costs, along with low productivity and a heavy state and local tax burden, are casting a cloud over Maine’s business climate, according to a report released Wednesday.
The latest “Measures of Growth” barometer, published by the Maine Development Foundation and the nonpartisan Maine Economic Growth Council, showed positive economic signs in rising wages, growth in the labor force and better access to broadband.
“Maine has extraordinary advantages — our natural resources, innovative businesses and a spirit of collaboration that sets us apart. But we can’t afford to let persistent challenges in education, productivity and the cost of living undermine those strengths,” said LuAnn Ballesteros, a member of the Maine Economic Growth Council who heads external and government affairs at the Jackson Laboratory in Bar Harbor.
“We’ve spent years identifying what needs to improve,” she added. “Now we need to turn that knowledge into action that delivers measurable results for Maine people and businesses.”
Resource for policymakers
The annual barometer, which aims to serve as a resource for policymakers at all levels, tracks 31 indicators measuring Maine’s economic strengths and areas in need of improvement.
Among businesses featured in the 48-page report for turning the state’s unique assets into competitive advantages are OystHERS, an oyster farm and raw bar in Bath, and the University of Maine Business and Law Clinic in Portland. Pleasant River Lumber and Elmet Technologies also received shoutouts.

title: Grieving parents call for kratom crackdown
text:
WASHINGTON (Gray DC) - Rebecca Strang’s life turned upside down a few months ago.
“I’m here today as a mother who lost Robert to kratom 58 days ago,” Strang said.
She’s in Washington advocating for a kratom crackdown, and describes her new reality.
“The worst day of my life has suddenly become my life’s work,” Strang said.
What the DEA says about kratom
According to the DEA, the leaf-derived powder creates stimulant effects in low doses and sedative effects in high doses. The DEA said it can quickly develop into psychological and physical dependence.
Industry criticism
Dean Francis criticized the kratom industry.
“The greed of a nefarious industry that exploits loopholes in our dietary supplement laws to masquerade a highly addictive and deadly drug as a plant based herbal supplement,” Francis said.
Francis said the industry lures vulnerable groups, including young people and veterans, with promises of an energy boost. He said the industry then addicts them for profit.
Regulation status
The USDA has not issued guardrails or guidelines on kratom. The agency does warn against using it for medical purposes.
The Department of Health and Human Services has taken only initial steps toward regulation.
Support from Congress
The group’s call for a crackdown is supported by Iowa Sen. Chuck Grassley.
“We know that kratom is an opioid that kills people, and we have to have strong enforcement of that,” Grassley said.
Strang said she will continue to advocate in honor of her son.
“It is time to stop focusing on who stands to profit and focus on who stands to suffer. Robert’s life mattered, and his death matters,” Strang said.
State legislation
Bills to address the sale of kratom are currently pending in Pennsylvania, Michigan, Delaware and Rhode Island.

title: Body camera video shows arrest of mother after toddler nearly dies from fentanyl overdose
text:
CHANDLER, Ariz. (KPHO/Gray News) — Police in Arizona have released body camera video showing the arrest of a mother after her toddler nearly overdosed on fentanyl this summer.
Police said the boy’s grandmother called 911 at about 4:45 p.m. on June 27 from a home in Chandler.
Officer Zach Hardman was the first to arrive.
A woman who identified herself as the boy’s grandmother handed him the toddler.
“He was just so limp. He was breathing, but it was getting worse at the time,” Hardman said in a video shared by Chandler police.
According to court documents, the 17-month-old child was pale and limp, his eyes had rolled back, and he was breathing abnormally.
Hardman gave the boy Narcan, a medication used to reverse opioid overdoses.
“Once I administered that Narcan, his trend definitely started to get better,” Hardman said.
The boy was taken to a hospital and recovered from the reported overdose.
Police said the toddler’s mother, 28-year-old Alexis Sipple, had left the home before officers arrived.
Home surveillance video showed the mother leaving, and court documents said she appeared to be trying to evade police by attempting to take an Uber out of the neighborhood.
Officers found Sipple hiding next to a trash can in a neighbor’s backyard. Body camera video showed officers telling her to stand up. Sipple can be heard asking, “Is he OK?”
Officers then handcuffed her and placed her in a police vehicle.
Sipple was arrested on a felony child abuse charge.
“When you put your child in danger like that, you deserve to face justice,” Hardman said.
During a search, detectives noted finding drug paraphernalia in the bedroom Sipple shared with her two children.
Court documents said officers found aluminum foil and a black straw between the mattress and box spring, as well as two bottles of methadone.
Sipple pleaded guilty to felony child abuse.
On Oct. 13, Sipple was sentenced to one year in jail and 10 years of probation, with credit for time served and early release granted for an inpatient substance abuse treatment program, court documents stated.
Court records also showed Sipple had three prior felony convictions.
“My main goal is to better myself for my children, to go to treatment, and go back into college so I can pursue my dreams,” Sipple said during sentencing. “I have definitely learned my lesson.”
Hardman said he has children around the same age as the toddler involved.
“I have children that age, so it hit home a little bit more for me,” he said. “So, I was just so relieved that he was going to be OK. It just means a lot to be able to be there, to be able to provide care and aid to this kid.”

title: Zoo trying 'new approach' to help Fiona the hippo pass swallowed hat
text:
Zoo trying 'new approach' to help Fiona the hippo pass swallowed hat
The Cincinnati Zoo care team is trying a "new approach" to help their beloved hippo Fiona after she swallowed a hat that was tossed into her enclosure.
The zoo care team borrowed a vibration plate from a local horse farm and encouraged Fiona to stand on the platform several times throughout the day.
"The hope is that the vibrations will help encourage movement through her digestive tract and help the object pass," the zoo shared in an update.
The team is continuing to work around the clock, and Fiona remains off habitat as she receives treatment.
"Her care team even offered her a sniff of coffee, a scent she has always liked, and they were happy to see her respond. Thank you for your continued love and concern for Fiona and her dedicated care team," the zoo shared.
Not Fiona’s first health challenge
Born six weeks premature at the Cincinnati Zoo on Jan. 24, 2017, Fiona weighed only 29 pounds at birth — 25 pounds less than the lowest recorded birth weight for her species.
She survived because of her animal care team's tireless efforts to save her and has inspired many to care about her species and wildlife.
Now, she's one of the most well-known animals not just in Cincinnati or the country, but around the world.
Community rallies support for beloved hippo
Many took to social media to share their support and love for Fiona as she undergoes treatment.
Timothy the hippo, otherwise known as Fiona's biggest admirer, shared a message via San Antonio Zoo for Fiona.
"We’re sending lots of love from Texas to the most beautiful hippo in the world. Hope you’re feeling more like yourself soon!" a post from the zoo reads.
Plenty of other zoos shared messages of support in the comments of the Cincinnati Zoo's health update post.

title: Larry Poindexter, ‘S.W.A.T.’ actor, dies at 66 after tragic accident
text:
(Gray News) - Larry Poindexter died Wednesday at age 66, days after he was hit by a car, Deadline reported.
Poindexter was reportedly crossing the street to pick up food Friday night in the Studio City neighborhood of Los Angeles when he was hit, Variety reported. He died suddenly Wednesday morning, before he was scheduled to undergo surgery for broken ribs.
Poindexter, who has almost 200 acting credits, was best known for his role in the 2003 film “S.W.A.T.” He also appeared in 30 episodes of “Days of Our Lives” and 12 episodes of “General Hospital.” He was a series regular on “The Hard Times of RJ Berger” and had a major recurring role on “JAG.”
He also guest-starred on several shows, including “How I Met Your Mother,” “Friends,” “Weeds,” “The Rookie” and “Hawaii Five-0.”
Poindexter is survived by his wife, Carol Kritzer, and their two sons.
