title: The Latest: Cincinnati Zoo says Fiona the hippo has died, days after ingesting a visitor’s hat
text:
Fiona the hippo, whose premature birth in 2017 and tenacious fight for survival at the Cincinnati Zoo turned her into a global sensation, has died, the Cincinnati Zoo announced on Thursday.
Veterinarians and staff tried for days to help the hippo safely digest and pass a knit cap she swallowed, but the efforts were ultimately unsuccessful.
The Nile Hippopotamus swallowed the hat on Nov. 8 after a zoo visitor tossed it in the air and a ceiling fan deflected the hat into the hippo enclosure through an opening above the area’s viewing windows. Zoo spokesperson Michelle Curley said it was an accident.
Fiona captivated and inspired fans worldwide after she was born six weeks premature in January 2017, weighing 25 pounds (11.34 kilograms) less than the lowest recorded birth weight for her species at that time. As millions followed her recovery and progress online, her popularity grew and inspired books, clothing and even a marriage proposal in front of her exhibit.
Here’s the Latest:
Surgery would have been a major logistical challenge for many reasons, specialists said
Hippos have a digestive system that would make Fiona’s situation tricky, Jack Kottwitz, an assistant professor at Michigan State University’s College of Veterinary Medicine, said before her death was announced.
“They have a multichambered stomach for digesting plants — sort of like a cow — but they don’t regurgitate and chew cud like a cow does. Those multiple chambers, tissue folds, fluid, and digesting food easily ‘hide’ the hat, making removal with an endoscope from the stomach chambers very difficult,” Kottwitz said.
In order to find the hat, multiple incisions might be needed during a very long surgery, he said. But hippos are notoriously difficult to anesthetize and have skin over 2 inches (5 centimeters) thick in places. Hippos also really need access to water, and Fiona would have needed to be kept out of the water for several days post-surgery to allow any incisions to heal, he said.
Fiona fans commiserate on social media
Comments flooded in Thursday on a Facebook fan page for Fiona, with people expressing a mix of sadness and frustration.
Some posters urged people to avoid directing their anger at the family of the zoo visitor who flung the knit hat that landed in Fiona’s enclosure. Others shared happy memories of visiting Fiona throughout their lives.
Cincinnati mayor mourns Fiona’s loss
Mayor Aftab Pureval described Fiona as a symbol of perseverance and joy who brought smiles to many faces.
“Our city is heartbroken, but we couldn’t be more grateful that she was part of our lives and our community as a whole,” he said in a social media post sharing the news of Fiona’s death.
Fiona became a sensation after Harambe’s death
Fiona survived her first health scare when she was born six weeks premature in 2017. She weighed just 29 pounds (13.2 kilograms), which was less than the lowest recorded birth weight for her species at that time.
Fiona was unable to nurse, so a zoo staffer hand-milked her mother. The zoo recorded her progress with photos and videos, while fans worldwide followed her progress online.
Her survival brought an uplifting turn for the Cincinnati Zoo after months of backlash over the shooting of Harambe, the gorilla who became a pop culture phenomenon after he was killed in 2016 because a child got into his enclosure.
Cincinnati Zoo Gorilla Death (4872×3248, AR: 1.50)
Even without Fiona in ‘Hippo Cove,’ her presence was felt
There’s a holiday-themed Fiona statue just outside the entrance to the Cincinnati Zoo, and the gift shop has an entire Fiona-themed wall. It’s filled with hippo-themed shirts, coffee mugs, shot glasses and books, including “A Very Fiona Christmas” and “You’ve Got This, Fiona.”
How did the hat get into Fiona’s enclosure?
Fiona swallowed a knit hat about 11 days ago after a zoo visitor tossed it in the air, at which point a ceiling fan caught and catapulted the hat through a small opening above the area’s viewing windows.
It was an accident, said zoo spokesperson Michelle Curley.
Fiona had been cared for around-the-clock before her death
Veterinarians had been keeping Fiona hydrated, giving her treats and monitoring her every move, the zoo said. They even borrowed a vibration plate from a horse farm, encouraging her to stand on it several times a day in the hopes that the shaking would help move things along through her digestive tract.
Before she died, Mike Wenninger, the zoo’s director of animal health, said veterinarians had sedated her twice to evaluate her condition.
An ultrasound on Tuesday showed some bunching of her intestines, indicating she was still trying to pass the obstruction, Wenninger said. They also conducted a colonoscopy using a 9-foot scope, but were unable to detect anything, he said.
Cincinnati Zoo says Fiona the hippo has died
Fiona, the hippo whose premature birth and fight for survival at the Cincinnati Zoo turned her into a global sensation nearly a decade ago, died Thursday from complications after swallowing a knit hat that was accidentally flung into her enclosure.
“It is with extreme sadness that we share with you the devastating news that Fiona did not make it after multiple attempts from our amazing vets and keeper team to help her through what ended up being a medical emergency,” the zoo said in a statement.
The zoo said Monday that Fiona was undergoing care around the clock after swallowing the hat more than a week ago.

title: Cony football draws on past defeats for motivation ahead of Class B title game
text:
Our Communities. Our Teams. Our Future.
We’re proud to make high school sports coverage free for everyone, because these moments matter. At Maine State Credit Union, we’re here for the people and places that make Maine strong. Let’s go! Learn more at mainestatecu.org. 
AUGUSTA — As a sophomore last year, Drew Lindquist played on some Cony High teams that enjoyed remarkable successes. How those seasons ended, though, still eats at him.
Lindquist was a backup quarterback last fall for the Cony football team, which fell 40-20 to Westbrook in the Class B championship game. He also was part of the Cony team that lost 4-3 to Fryeburg Academy in the state final this past June.
“Those bus rides home after those two losses, that’s a familiar feeling that I don’t want to feel again,” said Lindquist, now Cony’s starting QB. “We want a different feeling this year — we want to know the feeling of holding up the Gold Ball.”
Cony is close again, having reached the Class B title game again after repeating as Northern Maine champion last week. Fueled by past championship defeats, the Rams (9-1) are hoping for redemption against Marshwood (9-1) at 2:30 p.m. Saturday at Fitzpatrick Stadium.
Now that it’s been a year, the Rams can admit it: They handled last year’s state championship game poorly. Lindquist said Cony was cocky going into the game, thinking it would easily defeat Westbrook. Quickly, the Rams found themselves in a battle they didn’t expect.
Late in the game, as Westbrook charged toward victory, things began to spiral for Cony. The Rams got down on themselves, displayed poor attitudes and committed personal fouls out of frustration. Eventually, coach BL Lippert benched the entire defense to send a message.
“I was sick of seeing the penalties, and I got flack from a lot of the parents and a lot of the players — ‘It’s my last game; why are you taking me out?’ — but my message was, ‘We’re not going down like this,’” Lippert said. “I think this year, the team has gotten that message, and it’s felt like we have a little more mental toughness.”
That’s shown all season. When Cony trailed late against Fryeburg and Skowhegan early in the year, it responded with game-winning drives. The Rams almost beat Lawrence despite trailing 28-7 at halftime in Week 5.
All of the Rams’ success this fall has come with Anderson Noyes, possibly their best player, being in the lineup for just three games.
The Westbrook loss a year ago was far from Cony’s only heartbreak of 2025-26. The Rams had the No. 1 seed in boys basketball but fell to rival Gardiner in the Class B North title game. Then the baseball team lost to Fryeburg in a nail-biter.
“Seeing our seniors last year so sad, that was a tough feeling, and I don’t want us to be the seniors who are feeling sad like that,” said senior Ian Lasselle, who also plays for the Cony basketball team. “We worked hard to get back here, and we want to get it done this time.”
They’ve earned the right to be here. Since that Week 5 defeat at Lawrence, the Rams have outscored opponents 216-21 over five games, posting shutouts against Camden Hills (37-0), Skowhegan (47-0) and Fryeburg (28-0). The regional final against Fryeburg was Cony’s closest game during that span.
Before last season, Cony’s only trip to a football state final was its comeback win over Kennebunk in 2013. The Rams rattled off seven consecutive winning seasons from 2017-24 but failed to win the regional crown each time.
“You just never know when you’re going to get here again,” Lippert said. “Last year, on the field after the game, I thought, ‘Boy, we might not be here for a while.’ We’re fortunate to be back here already, and, hopefully, we can take advantage of it and play a little bit better than we did last year.”
The Rams know now what being on the big stage feels like. Before last November, Cony had not played in a state championship game in any boys sport since 2013. Between football and baseball, Saturday’s showdown with Marshwood will mark the third such instance in 12 months.
It would mean everything for Cony to do it in football, where the Rams have been knocking on the door for a while. The Rams reached their first regional title game under Lippert three years ago. Last year, they were one win from a state championship. A Gold Ball would be the next step.
“It would be unimaginable — everything we’ve ever dreamed of as kids,” Lasselle said. “We’ve always waited for this moment. We thought we were going to get it last year, and we didn’t, but we’re hoping to get it this year.”

title: State cuts nearly $180K of promised funding to Bangor’s largest warming shelter
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
MaineHousing cut more than 40% of the state funding the Brick Church warming shelter expected this winter after learning it planned to use part of the money to buy its building, an expense the agency says the grant doesn’t cover.
The Brick Church’s funding award was cut from $427,650 to $248,850 after the shelter submitted a detailed budget during the contracting process, which happens after grant awards are announced, according to MaineHousing spokesperson Scott Thistle.
That budget showed that nearly $180,000 of the money would have gone toward buying the building on Union Street under its rent-to-own agreement. The application doesn’t specifically bar recipients from using the money to buy a building, but “the intent is that the funding is for operating costs,” Thistle said. The application gives MaineHousing some leeway to adjust the award, he said.
The shelter says it will still be able to stay open this winter, but the cut raises questions about the long-term future of Bangor’s largest overnight warming center, which has space for 70 people. Local warming center leaders say they’re seeing more visitors in their first week open than in previous years, though fewer centers are open every night this year.
MaineHousing determined that the funding could be used for lease payments during the winter months, but not for a building purchase, because the purchase would have paid for the shelter’s space year-round, including months when it isn’t open.
“We appreciate the warming shelter work they’re doing. It’s really important,” Thistle said. “But that just wasn’t allowed under the grant.”
The money cut from the Brick Church’s award was never disbursed, so it remains in the state’s Emergency Housing Relief Fund, he said.
The Brick Church is open every night from mid-November to mid-April. The Bangor Area Homeless Shelter also received state funding for five warming shelter beds, but the two other Bangor warming centers that applied this year, the Mansion Church and the Together Place recovery center, were not awarded state funding.
Leon Licata, pastor of the Brick Church, said he found out last week about the cut but is staying positive. “There are other options out there” for funds, he said, noting that he plans to apply for a loan and explore other possible avenues.
It’s unclear what the setback means for the shelter’s ability to open in future years, although Licata said it will still be able to operate through mid-April. It needs to raise $176,000 by the end of December to pay off the debt on its building.
“Eventually the building has to be paid off, but how that is going to happen we don’t really know right now,” Licata said.
The shelter opened Sunday night, and by Tuesday night 44 people were staying there. That’s higher than usual, Licata said, adding that nightly counts hovered in the low teens for the first few weeks of the season last year, when there were more warming centers operating every night.
The Mansion Church has received state funding for a shelter in previous years but was denied the funding this year because it couldn’t stay open through April as required by the program. But the church is still operating the shelter this year and also opened Sunday night. It can fit 25 people, or 30 if needed, according to pastor Terry Dinkins, who was recently elected to the City Council.
The shelter already had 18 people Monday night, which Dinkins said was higher than in past years.
“People are really stepping up,” he said, adding that despite the church’s lack of state funds, it’s received many donations of blankets, pillows and food and has cots for people to sleep on this year for the first time. “Everything helps,” he added.
The city also stepped in earlier this fall, after grant awards were announced, to fund an as-needed warming shelter at the Together Place recovery center on nights when temperatures drop below 15 degrees. That will cover up to $106,000 in expenses, mostly with a community development block grant.
“We remain committed to delivering that vital service for unhoused residents and patrons this winter,” said Shea Mullaney, Together Place board president, adding that his organization will do everything it can to support the Brick Church and the rest of the warming centers in the city.
“Lives are at stake,” he said.

title: 'I was ready to die': COPD patient shares lung cancer scare
text:
'I was ready to die': Patient recounts COPD diagnosis as women are getting lung cancer younger
People who have chronic obstructive pulmonary disease also have a fivefold increased risk of developing lung cancer.
November is both Lung Cancer and COPD awareness months.
Dr. Albert Polito, a pulmonologist who is the medical director for The Lung Center at Mercy Medical Center in Baltimore, Maryland, told Hearst sister station WBAL that he is seeing more women — even younger women — being diagnosed with lung cancer.
"Traditionally, when we think of COPD and lung cancer, a lot of times, (we see) the image of a man, an older man, who's been smoking and hacking away for years," Polito said. "I think we've got to keep it in mind that women get this; they oftentimes get it at earlier ages as well."
Polito also said lung cancer symptoms are initially silent, unlike the signs of COPD.
"You wheeze, you're short of breath, you have a cough. Those are the classic things. Maybe some chest tightness," Polito said.
Lourdes Hyatt, 70, said she started to have issues when she experienced trouble breathing.
"If I get up to do something and I'm up five or 10 minutes and doing anything, I have to sit down for 15 minutes to catch my breath," Hyatt said.
Hyatt was diagnosed with COPD. Coupled with her being a smoker, the protocol is that she undergoes regular lung scans.
"We have been doing once-a-year CT scans on her for the purpose of lung cancer screening, and earlier this year, she had a nodule that showed up on the scan that we biopsied and it was cancer," Polito said.
"When I first heard, I was like, I was ready to die. I was like, so scared," Hyatt said.
Polito said that while many nodules are benign, Hyatt's was an early-stage cancer.
"He said it's the primary source of it, so it's nowhere else, which was a relief. And it was Stage I, which was very good, too," Hyatt said.
Hyatt has undergone radiation, and "so far, so good" as she awaits another follow-up scan in January.
"There are smokers who actually don't have COPD, but the ones who get COPD actually have a higher risk of developing lung cancer than the ones who don't have COPD," Polito said.
Polito said it's important to monitor one's health and check in with the doctor.

title: How Mainers can plan ahead to make flight cancellations less painful
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Friggatriskaidekaphobia! Fear of Friday the 13th! After the full ground stop at 3:45 on Friday, Nov. 13, hundreds of thousands of folks had their weekend plans disrupted and may now be a bit superstitious about Friday the 13th. Flight cancellations seem common these days, and we need to be prepared. Frequent flyers know what steps to take, but many of us are flummoxed when we see the departures board at the airport list our flight as canceled.
Here are some suggestions of actions to take before you fly and several steps to take when you find yourself stranded. Fortunately, our mobile devices can help us navigate this issue.
BEFORE YOU GO
• Book early flights and fly non-stop when possible. These two actions help to lessen the chance of being stranded.
• Be sure to download the app for airline, train, or bus company. You will receive timely updates.
• Practice using apps like Uber or your airline’s app before you leave. Build your confidence with the apps so anxiety does not slow you down when you are making alternative plans.
• Think about your luggage. Can you manage it by yourself? Smaller airports and train stations may not have services to help you.
• You might want to carry extra cash. We saw this week that customers of several major banks were unable to access their accounts.
• Check the weather so you are prepared for weather-related delays.
• Check the status of your flight before leaving for the airport (airports’ websites and airline apps will keep you up to date).
• Pack snacks. If there is a massive delay across a region, food vendors may run out of food.
IF YOU FIND YOURSELF GROUNDED
• Don’t panic — you will not be stranded forever, though it may feel like it.
• Find a quiet spot to gather your thoughts — whom do you have to notify? What’s your timeline? Make a plan.
• Listen carefully to announcements and check your airline app frequently — do you need to pick up luggage? Has your gate changed?
• Keep your phone charged. It is your lifeline to rebooking, rides, and hotel reservations.
• Rebook online, not in person. It’s much faster and less frustrating than waiting in a line with a hundred irritated people.
• Rebook before delays are lifted because once they are, websites and phone lines become clogged quickly.
• Check the airport maps to find gates, food, restrooms, first aid, and help desks. Both Apple Maps and Google Maps show the internal setup of airports.
• Here are a couple of helpful sites and apps that track flights: Flight Aware and Flighty.
• Be sure to check nearby airports for alternative flights. Google Flights might be useful in this search.
• Check alternative means of transportation:
1. Amtrak: If you are on the East Coast, you can get back to Maine.
2. Buses: Concord Trailways, Greyhound, FlixBus, and Megabus are good alternatives. They may be slower, but faster than two or three days at the airport.
3. Rome2Rio is an app that will show you alternative means of transportation from point A to point B. Some reviews state it is not as accurate as it used to be; however, it will certainly show you some possibilities.
4. Uber and Lyft: You may need to use them to get to a hotel or bus station. Be aware that prices will probably skyrocket when there is a major shutdown like last Friday evening. If you have practiced using the app beforehand, booking a ride should go smoothly.
• Check local hotels and book rooms before 6 p.m. You can reserve a room via their website. If there is a major delay, they will fill up quickly. A canceled hotel room fee is better than sleeping on the airport floor.
Euripides: “Experience, travel — these are as education in themselves.”
Mark Twain: “Travel is fatal to prejudice, bigotry, and narrow-mindedness.”
Seneca: “Travel and change of place impart new vigor to the mind.”
Hans Christian Andersen: “To move, to breathe, to fly, to float, to gain all while you give — to roam the roads of lands remote — to travel is to live.”
Helen Keller: “Life is either a daring adventure or nothing.”
People across the centuries have touted the benefits of travel, and they must have faced challenges as difficult as a full ground stop. Explore the world, and have plans B and C, just in case.

title: Who will pay for proposed southern Aroostook County transmission line?
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
AROOSTOOK COUNTY, Maine (WAGM) - A proposed transmission line in southern Aroostook County drew a question about who will pay for it at a county commissioners’ meeting.
A resident asked why the public would have to help pay for the line, which is associated with a proposed wind project.
Project details
County Administrator Justin Tibbitts said the wind project could generate about 800 megawatts of electricity.
He said the company behind the project, Clearway, has expressed interest in working with the county on community improvement projects, but nothing is firm. Tibbitts also said Clearway expects to bring several thousand construction jobs to the area.
Transmission costs
Commissioners discussed a possible 11% public share of transmission costs. They said they were unsure exactly what costs that share would cover.
Tibbitts said the board is trying to get answers about the cost and hopes to work with government partners.
Commissioners’ role
Tibbitts said commissioners do not have direct oversight of the project and have not taken a position for or against it.
The board plans to hold town hall meetings in southern Aroostook to hear from residents.

title: Mental competency at issue in US criminal case against Meghan's father
text:
TAMPA, Fla. (AP) — A judge scheduled a mental competency hearing Thursday for the 82-year-old estranged father of Meghan, the Duchess of Sussex, two weeks after he was arrested in Florida and charged with storing child sexual abuse material in California.
Thomas Markle was released after his arrest at a senior care center but was ordered to jail four days later, on Nov. 10, when authorities accused him of cutting off his electronic ankle monitor. A judge also ordered him to be examined by a mental health professional.
A hearing was set for Thursday afternoon in federal court in Tampa, Florida. Prosecutors declined to comment Wednesday. Markle’s lawyer did not reply to an email seeking comment.
Markle’s arrest in Lakeland, Florida, followed the seizure of approximately 78 items from storage units in the Los Angeles area, including slides, film negatives and books that contained suspected child sexual abuse images, the FBI said in a court filing.
Some images appear to depict him with children, the FBI said.
Markle had a stroke earlier this year while living in the Philippines and had to have his left leg amputated. That forced him to return to the U.S. and settle in Florida.
The Sun, a British tabloid newspaper, reported that Meghan’s half brother found child sexual abuse images while clearing out their father’s home in the Philippines. The discovery led to a search of the two U.S. storage units in California, which Markle had rented since 2008.
Meanwhile, in the Philippines, Markle is under investigation for possession and intent to distribute images. The Women and Children Protection Center, a branch of the Philippine National Police, filed a formal criminal complaint against Markle on Monday, police spokesperson Brig. Gen. Allen Rae Co said in a written statement.
The complaint was filed with the prosecutor’s office following an investigation into digital devices found at Markle’s former home in Cebu City, the statement said. The prosecutor’s office will assess the case for possible charges.
Markle did not attend his daughter Meghan’s 2018 wedding to Prince Harry at Windsor Castle. She said at the time he needed to tend to his health. Meghan is an American citizen who starred in the U.S. television drama “Suits.”

title: Here’s who’s eligible for money in the $32 million class-action GoodRx settlement
text:
(Gray News) - GoodRx has agreed to a $32 million settlement in a class-action lawsuit that alleged the company disclosed customers’ personal and health information.
The lawsuit alleged GoodRx, a telehealth and prescription coupon company, disclosed customers’ personal and health information to advertising and analytics companies, including Criteo, between at least 2017 and 2020.
Both GoodRx and Criteo denied these allegations but agreed to a $32 million settlement. Now, some GoodRx users may be eligible to receive a payment.
Filing a claim
Settlement class members include those who used a website, app or service made available by or through GoodRx before April 20, 2024, according to the settlement’s website.
Settlement class members have until Dec. 29 to file a claim either by mail or online. You also have until the same date to exclude yourself from the settlement.
If you’re not sure whether you’re included in the settlement class, you can email info@goodrxprivacysettlement.com or call 1-877-888-9232 for more information.
The amount of each payment will depend on the number of claims approved.
A final hearing on the settlement is scheduled for Feb. 11, 2027.

title: Democrats won big. Now we must make room.
text:
Pious Ali is a Portland at-large councilor. The opinions expressed here are his own.
We won.
Across the country, Democrats delivered significant victories in the 2026 midterm elections. But winning an election is not the same as building a lasting political coalition. The question before our party is simple: what will we do with the power voters have entrusted to us, and will we make room for the people who helped us win?
Our victories reflect the diversity of experiences, backgrounds and communities that make up the Democratic Party.
In Michigan, Abdul El-Sayed, the son of Egyptian immigrants, won a seat in the U.S. Senate. In Colorado, Melat Kiros, an Ethiopian immigrant and lawyer, won a congressional seat. In Georgia, Everton Blair Jr., the son of Jamaican immigrants and an openly gay Black leader, won a seat in Congress. In California, Dr. Aisha Wahab, an Afghan American, won election to the U.S. House. In Maryland, Adrian Boafo, a Ghanaian American, was elected to Congress.
Here in Maine, Troy Jackson brought another important perspective to our victory. A fifth-generation logger from Allagash and longtime union member, Jackson entered politics through the struggles of working people. His experience organizing alongside fellow loggers over wages and working conditions reminds us that the labor movement remains central to the Democratic Party’s identity and future.
These victories represent more than individual candidates winning office. They reflect the broad coalition that makes our party strong.
We must also recognize the extraordinary role of Black women in delivering Democratic victories. For generations, Black women have been among our most consistent voters, organizers, advocates and candidates. They have mobilized communities, defended voting rights and helped carry our party through difficult elections.
We cannot continue celebrating their contributions on election night while failing to give them meaningful influence over our leadership, policies and priorities.
Our winning coalition includes organized labor, immigrants and their families, Black voters, Latino and Asian American communities, women, young people, LGBTQ Americans and working families who believe the government should improve their lives.
These communities are not simply voting blocs to be mobilized every two or four years. They are partners who deserve a meaningful voice in shaping our party’s future.
Power has an expiration date.
As Democrats, we should understand that electoral victories are opportunities, not permanent endorsements. We cannot afford to repeat the mistakes that followed 2020, when we failed to fully sustain the energy, relationships and expectations of the coalition that brought us victory.
We have the next year and a half to demonstrate that we have learned those lessons.
That means investing in local organizers, strengthening relationships with labor unions, supporting emerging leaders and opening the doors of party leadership to people whose lived experiences have too often been overlooked.
It also means connecting our political victories to the everyday concerns of Americans: affordable housing, rising grocery prices, healthcare, wages, education and the cost of raising a family.
People need to see that their votes make a difference in their daily lives.
We must also resist the temptation to demand ideological uniformity. A broad Democratic coalition will naturally include people who disagree about policies, priorities and strategies. That diversity should be a strength, not a reason to exclude people from the conversation.
Our party must become more comfortable with disagreement and more intentional about creating opportunities for people from different backgrounds to shape our direction.
I believe the future of the Democratic Party depends not only on who we elect but also on whom we invite into the rooms where decisions are made. We should be recruiting candidates from immigrant communities, working-class neighborhoods, labor organizations and communities that have historically been underrepresented in political leadership.
We should be listening to young organizers, Black women and emerging leaders long before we need their votes. And we should be willing to share responsibility, influence and power.
We won because our coalition was broad enough to bring people together across differences. Now we must prove that our party is big enough to make room for them.
Winning gave us power. Our future depends on how we share it.

title: FCC gives state prisons the go-ahead to jam signals from contraband cellphones
text:
FCC gives state prisons the go-ahead to jam signals from contraband cellphones
The Federal Communications Commission on Thursday acted to allow state prisons across the United States to jam the signals of cellphones smuggled to inmates as the federal government cracks down on devices that authorities say are the No. 1 security threat in the nation’s correctional facilities.
The vote was unanimous among the commissioners meeting in Washington.
State prison officials for years have sought the right to jam, arguing that blocking the signals of contraband phones would halt inmates’ ability to use the devices to run drug rings, coordinate prison riots and even order acts of violence such as attacks on guards.
Under the new rule, prisons are not required to use the jamming technology, they must conduct multiple tests to make sure cell signals outside prisons are not affected and they have to notify officials if the jamming devices are moved.
FCC Chairman Brendan Carr, who spoke in favor of the measure, visited this week with officials in South Carolina, whose prison directors have led efforts to obtain permission to jam.
Cellphones have been smuggled inside hollowed-out footballs, whisked in by corrupt employees and sometimes even dropped by drone. The signal-jamming technology was already allowed in federal facilities but needed FCC permission, due to a nearly century-old communications law, to be available for state prisons.
U.S. Attorney Bryan Stirling, who headed South Carolina's Corrections Department for more than a decade, led an effort from many of his counterparts across the country to gain use of the technology. South Carolina Attorney General Alan Wilson, elected this month as the state's next governor, organized fellow prosecutors to press Congress to change the law but they were unsuccessful.
FCC chair says it's ‘ready to take action’
While in South Carolina, Carr stood alongside Stirling, Wilson and other South Carolina officials before a display of hundreds of confiscated cellphones and massive drones used to ferry the contraband over prison fencing. He said many people might not perceive the danger.
"People really don’t understand the threat that these pose," Carr said, noting that 25,000 cellphones were confiscated in the nation's state and local prisons each year. “We’re going to put a new tool in the hands of law enforcement, and it’s going to make a dramatic difference.”
Carr cited the case of Robert Johnson, a South Carolina corrections officer who was nearly killed at his home in 2010 in a hit that officials said was orchestrated by a prisoner using a contraband cellphone.
After nearly three dozen surgeries and now in “pain 24/7,” Johnson said Wednesday that he refers to the phones as “weapons of mass destruction” because of the potential dangers for which they can be used. He has testified in previous FCC hearings over jamming requests and often spoken out on the issue.
“No one should have to go through what I went through,” Johnson said. “But I also believe that the Lord chose my wife and I to go through this because someone had to carry the banner, and he chose us to do it.”
South Carolina tested the tech in 2008
South Carolina has been the testing ground for state prison cellphone jamming. In 2008, the FCC allowed the state to conduct a one-time test of a jamming system at a maximum-security prison. A briefcase-sized device emitted a frequency that immediately shut down cellphones around an auditorium; outside, service was uninterrupted.
Another test took place at a different state prison in 2019, a first-time collaboration between federal officials and state prison officials. A year earlier, seven South Carolina inmates had died in the worst U.S. prison riot in 25 years, in what officials said was a gang fight arranged in part using illegal cellphones.
The FCC has shown willingness to work on eradicating prison cellphones, holding a 2016 field hearing in South Carolina and hosting meetings with members of Congress, prison officials and representatives of the wireless industry.
Groups that advocate for inmates' rights have opposed the move, arguing that the high rates inmates must pay to use official prison phones have pushed them toward using contraband cellphones just to stay in touch with family. The telecommunications industry has long argued against it, too, saying that jamming technology risks interfering with legitimate communications.
Carr said in South Carolina that he felt the industry was softening on jamming, in part due to recognition of the problem's size as well as agencies' experiments with targeted technologies.
“We aren’t considering jamming outside this unique context," Carr said. "Maybe people aren’t cheering it on from industry, but the opposition has receded substantially.”

title: There is no going back 'to the way it was before' the Iran War's energy shock, IEA says
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
There is no going back 'to the way it was before' the Iran War's energy shock, IEA says
The greatest energy shock in history and growing climate change concerns are reshaping how the world will power homes, drive cars and fuel industries, said an International Energy Agency report released Thursday.
The repercussions from the Iran war will “leave lasting marks" on the world's energy sector, said the Paris-based IEA, founded after the 1973-74 oil crisis.
Energy-hungry nations will prioritize the security and affordability of their electricity, the report said, which will benefit renewable technologies, like solar energy, and other alternatives, like nuclear power. But it also reinforces the case to keep coal as a backup for times of crisis.
This is especially true in coal-rich Asia, which went into energy triage when the Iran war cut off the Strait of Hormuz, a narrow passageway where about a fifth of the world’s traded oil flowed.
The report looks “past the current turmoil to explore the range of energy futures that could emerge from today’s upheaval,” said IEA Executive Director Fatih Birol, who warned that “the longer the crisis lasts, the deeper the effects will be.”
“I don’t see any credible pathway for the energy world to return to the way it was before," he said.
The annual United Nations climate talks in Turkey, known as COP31, are in their final week. Before these negotiations, the U.N. announced the world is dangerously close to missing its goal of limiting global warming to 1.5 degrees Celsius (2.7 degrees Fahrenheit) above pre-industrial temperatures.
Electrification — the process of powering homes, cars and industries with electricity — and moving away from planet-warming fossil fuels are major issues at COP31.
“For the first time, we are actually seeing the policies used to respond to energy security concerns being very strongly aligned with policies needed for energy transitions,” said IEA Director of Sustainability Laura Cozzi in an interview with The Associated Press. “This is a unique convergence that sees electrification at the heart of crisis response.”
Flagship report projects energy future
The IEA is the world's leading intergovernmental energy organization, with more than 30 member countries. Its flagship report this year analyzes government and private data to project various future scenarios based on whether countries stick with current policies or drastically shift because of ongoing crises.
There is a clear before and after the Iran war for the energy sector, experts said. In March, the IEA coordinated the emergency release of 400 million barrels of crude oil stocks to stabilize global markets.
“When we look at how energy crises change the world over the long term, governments are only just beginning to get their head around just how much things will change,” said Dave Jones, co-founder of the think tank Ember.
Conflicts, trade tensions, climate risks and cyberattacks are increasing the number of possible energy futures, and the IEA said the “drive to diversify” fuel supplies will reshape the energy trade.
“The world will not look the same after this crisis, but how we will look exactly, this still depends, and we will see in the next few months," Cozzi said.
The IEA projects the Middle East will still be the world's largest oil exporter, but nations will likely reduce dependence on the Strait of Hormuz. The IEA projects the amount of oil passing through the strait could go from 20 million barrels per day before the Iran war to 8.5 million barrels in 2030, and even under 2 million barrels by 2035.
While fossil fuels still dominate energy mixes, the IEA said solar and nuclear power are the “biggest beneficiaries” of governments prioritizing domestic energy sources.
“This crisis has exposed the price of fossil fuel dependence,” said Mohamed Adow, director of Power Shift Africa. “It’s crazy that a conflict thousands of miles away can send energy bills soaring at home.”
Energy security concerns, however, may lead nations to rely on coal as a fallback option. Michelle Manook of FutureCoal, an industry-backed group formerly known as the World Coal Association, said “for coal-rich economies, domestic coal remains an important energy security asset."
“We see coal has a momentum,” said the IEA's Birol. “We will see if it is long-lived or not.”
Climate talks eye electrification
COP31 follows a year rattled by the Iran war, as well as several climate-induced disasters, like Europe’s deadly heat waves and Nepal’s devastating flooding. Global warming is adding pressure to rising electricity demand.
In what the IEA called a “striking milestone,” energy demand for cooling overtook energy demand for heating for the first time this year. Cozzi said this is “the beginning of the trend that will last for the next decade and beyond.”
India, the world’s most populous nation, will account for more energy demand growth over the next decade than anywhere else in the world. China, already one of the world’s most electrified economies, may see electrification grow from 32% last year to 43% by 2035, the highest among major economies.
At COP31, Turkey wants the world to increase the share of electricity in total global energy consumption from roughly 21% today to 35% by 2035.
While Turkey prefers this to come from renewables, U.N. documents on the negotiating table don't spell this out. That means power plants running on coal and other fossil fuels could be used to supply power grids, at least initially.
“The IEA’s latest report makes clear that the fossil energy crisis unleashed by the U.S.-Israel war on Iran has irrevocably changed the global energy system, adding to the many reasons why countries would benefit from a rapid transition to clean energy,” said Rachel Cleetus, climate program director at the Union of Concerned Scientists, who is at COP31.

title: What happened during the historic trilateral summit between Trump, Xi and Putin?
text:
What happened during the historic trilateral summit between Trump, Xi and Putin?
President Donald Trump joined China's President Xi Jinping and Russia's President Vladimir Putin in China for a trilateral summit focused on nuclear weapons, global conflicts, and world peace.
What happened during the historic trilateral summit between Trump, Xi and Putin?
President Donald Trump joined China's President Xi Jinping and Russia's President Vladimir Putin in China for a trilateral summit focused on nuclear weapons, global conflicts, and world peace.
President Donald Trump met with China's President Xi Jinping and Russia's President Vladimir Putin in China for a historic trilateral summit aimed at addressing nuclear weapons, global conflicts, and world peace.
Trump expressed optimism at the start of the meeting, hoping it can reduce the number of nuclear weapons.
At the start of the summit, Xi said: "We will be having discussions on the theme of promoting world peace."
China and Russia say they have agreed with the United States on U.N. reforms, boosting fuel supplies, and dialogue around reducing nuclear risks.
"Too often past leaders avoided talking to nations with whom they had disagreements, and we feel the opposite," Trump said.
The declaration from the meeting did not mention the wars in Ukraine or Iran, issues that Trump said he would bring up with the leaders.
The summit comes after the expiration of the Strategic Arms Reduction Treaty (START) between the U.S. and Russia in February, which had capped nuclear weapons for more than a century. The expiration lifted limits on the world's largest nuclear arsenals. Trump rejected a Russian proposal to extend the treaty for another year and instead called for a new agreement that includes China.
China has less motivation to accept nuclear limits given that its arsenal of warheads is much smaller than the more than 5,000 believed to be in each of the U.S. and Russian stockpiles.
While analysts do not expect significant changes from this meeting, Trump is expected to meet with Xi again before the end of the year.

title: Man with traumatic brain injury calls himself the luckiest man alive
text:
EAST LANSING, Mich. (Aging Untold) — A Michigan man who survived a head-on crash that caused a traumatic brain injury calls himself the luckiest man alive.
Jim Lowden is a resident at the Hope Network Neuro Rehabilitation facility in East Lansing. He has been working toward independence since the crash, and said determination helped him get back on his feet.
The crash
Lowden survived a violent crash nearly 11 years ago.
“Eight weeks of my life are gone,” Lowden said. “I don’t remember anything at all.”
He was driving a motor home when a truck traveling the other way blew a tire, went over the median and struck him head-on.
“I was tumbling head over heels through space,” Lowden said. “I remember that. But when I actually came back to Earth, it was in a bed at Oakwood.”
Oakwood is an inpatient transitional rehabilitation center, and Lowden has lived on the campus since the crash.
Lowden’s injuries included a traumatic brain injury, a brain bleed, a fractured skull, broken bones, broken ribs and a punctured lung.
Working toward independence
The man who has never liked needing help found himself being pushed in a wheelchair.
“I never liked people helping me, so this was bad,” Lowden said. “Being pushed around in a wheelchair, I really didn’t like, you know, because you’re not independent.”
He also thought he was going to miss out on something he has done every year since he was 5: go ice fishing. Lowden said he told his cousin he would not make it that year.
“He took me,” Lowden said. “They pulled me out on the ice on a sled.”
Mark Evans of Hope Network Neuro Rehabilitation said Lowden is a powerful story for others.
“Jim really is a powerful story for others to follow because even though he still needs help with some things he’s a pretty independent guy, and he’s a pretty positive guy,” Evans said.
Art as part of recovery
Lowden credits creativity for helping him in his recovery. He creates art on canvas, on cardboard and with metal.
“I think getting to use creativity is really stimulating,” Lowden said. “And if you stimulate your mind, then your body follows it.”
Lowden said he walks with a cane, but he calls himself the luckiest man alive.
“I walk with a cane, but boo hoo, some guy in a wheelchair would be glad to trade with me,” he said.

Optional heat pump rate could save Maine electric customers hundreds of dollars
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Optional heat pump rate could save Maine electric customers hundreds of dollars
Data from the U.S. Census Bureau’s American Community Survey show about half of Maine households still use heating oil as their primary source of heat, but that share has fallen nearly 20% since 2018.
At the same time, electricity use for home heating has nearly doubled. Gov. Janet Mills has said the shift is being driven by the surge in high-efficiency heat pump installations. Now, the Maine Public Utilities Commission has reinstated a seasonal heat pump rate for Central Maine Power customers, which is designed to help reduce the amount that residential customers pay for electricity.
Customers can choose to sign up for this rate starting on Dec. 1. The new rate would appear on their bill the following month.
Related video above: Maine received $43 million in March to support heat pump installations
Efficiency Maine reports that heat pumps not only perform well in cold climates but also save families hundreds of dollars a year compared to oil. State and federal rebates have helped accelerate adoption, and Mills has set a goal of installing 275,000 heat pumps statewide by 2027.
A previous pilot program for the heat pump rate was popular and helped reduce costs.
CMP says the rate can provide meaningful savings for customers who heat their homes with heat pumps in cases where a customer's usage drops in the summer cooling season and increases during the winter heating season.
CMP says this rate could help eligible customers save hundreds of dollars on the delivery part of the electric bill over the course of the year. That is the only portion of the electric bill controlled by CMP.
On Tuesday, the Maine PUC announced the new Standard Offer electricity supply rate that will take effect on Jan. 1, 2027. The rate for residential and small business customers will rise from 12.72 cents to 13.63 cents per kilowatt-hour.
For an average residential customer using about 550 kilowatt-hours a month, that will add about $5 to the monthly bill, but that rate is negotiated and set by the state, not the utility company.
"We've listened to our customers and took action to help them save," said Linda Ball, President and CEO of Central Maine Power. "We know Mainers value having options to manage their electric bills, especially during the coldest and darkest months of the year. Bringing back the Seasonal Heat Pump rate and asking to keep the Electric Technology rate available to all customers are two ways we're advocating for options that can help our customers."
The Office of the Public Advocate, the Efficiency Maine Trust, the Natural Resources Council of Maine, AARP, and Acadia Center all stated opposition to reinstating the Seasonal Heat Pump rate.
In 2025, 96,020 Central Maine Power households received at least one disconnection notice.
Utility companies in Maine cannot disconnect customers between Nov. 15 and April 15.

title: How to make it work when parents move in with adult children
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
(Aging Untold) — When a parent moves in with an adult child, it can bring comfort along with adjustments like new routines, boundaries and expectations.
It’s happening more often: Parent Herald reports a “reverse boomerang effect,” with more parents moving in with their children, driven in part by rising housing costs and caregiving needs.
The Aging Untold hosts talked through where to begin.
Start with why you’re moving in together
Gerontologist Sam Cradduck said the answer begins with the reason for the move.
“First off, I want to know why we’re moving in,” Cradduck said. “Are we moving in so Mom and Dad can help us? Maybe with childcare. Maybe because we’re a dual working family and childcare expenses are astronomical and we need some help. Or are they moving in because Mom and Dad need some help?”
Finances are part of that conversation because expenses go up when more people live in the home, she said.
Families should also decide what the arrangement looks like today and what it will look like in the future.
“Mom and Dad aren’t going to get younger and the kids are going to get older, so the kids are going to need less care, and Mom and Dad are going to need more,” Cradduck said. “So we need to know how we’re going to balance that and who’s going to be responsible for what in this house.”
Expect the relationship to change
“You’re going to have to set expectations and boundaries so you don’t get that resentment,” Dr. Rhea Rogers, a board-certified physician, said. “And then you have to realize that relationship is going to change for both. So you have your children who now maybe are going to be the caregivers, and then the adults who are maybe losing some control.”
Aging expert Amy O’Rourke described how that can feel on both sides. A grown child may feel their space is changing. A parent may feel they are losing independence.
“It’s weird and it’s awkward, and it’s an emotionally, acutely hard to process feeling,” O’Rourke said.
Talk through the details, including privacy
She said everyday details can test a household, including who does the dishes, who cleans, who shops for groceries and what the thermostat is set to.
“I would say designate an area that’s private for you, the child and the parent, so that you have your own place,” O’Rourke said. “And then are you going to knock before you enter? These things have to be talked about.”
Put it in writing and meet weekly
She likes the idea of a “town hall meeting” each week to check in on how everyone is doing.
Aging well coach Katherine Ambrose suggests having something in writing.
“Miscommunication happens because people remember details differently,” she said. “So you put it in writing together and sign it. Now you start your weekly family meeting, and that way you can stay on the same page, because there will be things you don’t think about, like the thermostat, or sounds, how loud someone plays TV, or what they play.”
Ambrose said dating can come up too, including whether adults will feel judged about who they spend time with and where.
Cradduck said the adult children and parents need to treat each other as adults.
“The top of the list on that written out contract or agreement has to say, ‘We are all adults. Do not treat me like I’m a child,’” Cradduck said. “I’m now 40-plus years old. You’re in your late 60s, early 70s, 80s, wherever those ages fall. We’re all adults, and we have to be able to treat one another like adults. So that’s the first rule here.”
Give each other grace
O’Rourke pointed out that slipping into old habits is likely.
“Grace, I think, goes a long way here,” she said. “If you happen to slip into an old behavior, then just kind of wave your hand and say, ‘I’ve just slipped into bad behavior, I apologize,’ or ‘You’re using that tone again.’ Be real direct, because it happens. You know you get around your parent, all of a sudden, you’re thinking, why am I acting like I’m 7 years old again?”
And old wounds can resurface, from childhood or the teenage years.
“You’re going to pop open some old scars,” Cradduck said.
O’Rourke said small acts of generosity matter, such as calling a parent from the grocery store to ask if they need anything.
“A lot can be grown out of compassion and generosity and care for each other,” she said.
An adjustment that can become a gift
While there may be some angst at the beginning, the arrangement can benefit the whole family, especially when younger children are in the home.
“Empathy is learned by helping, by the intergenerational activities and allowing your younger kids to be around their grandparents,” Cradduck said.
“It can be an unexpected blessing, and it’s part of the human journey,” Ambrose said.
Key takeaways
- Create a new norm. Merging households means creating a new way of living together rather than deciding who is right.
- Hold family meetings early. Set expectations about routines and secure private spaces for everyone. Put agreements in writing and check in weekly.
- Treat each other as adults. Make “we are all adults” the first rule of the household agreement.
- Remember that both generations are experiencing loss. Be patient, and respect each other’s autonomy to help everyone coexist in harmony.

title: Oxford Hills football eager for rematch with Bonny Eagle
text:
Our Communities. Our Teams. Our Future.
We’re proud to make high school sports coverage free for everyone, because these moments matter. At Maine State Credit Union, we’re here for the people and places that make Maine strong. Let’s go! Learn more at mainestatecu.org. 
PARIS — When the Oxford Hills and Bonny Eagle football teams squared off in the regular season on Oct. 9, Bonny Eagle won handily, 45-6.
On Saturday, Oxford Hills will try to produce a much different result when the teams meet again with a Gold Ball up for grabs in the Class A championship game.
How are the Vikings preparing to play an opponent that was so dominant the last time the teams met? They’re accepting the challenge and embracing the opportunity.
“I’m not going to lie, the boys were hoping Bonny Eagle made it so they could play those guys again and prove to themselves that they can play with a team like Bonny Eagle,” said coach Nate Danforth. “And they’re looking forward to it.”
In the regular-season game, Oxford Hills (9-1) accumulated 219 yards, while Bonny Eagle (10-1) more than doubled that total, finishing with 497 yards. Senior quarterback Lucas Klehn ran 10 times for 170 yards and four touchdowns and completed 4 of 5 passes for 91 yards and a touchdown.
“Against (Bonny Eagle), it was a tough battle last time,” said Carter Davis, a junior. “I’d say we weren’t as prepared as we should’ve been, and we’re going to come more prepared this week. And we know that they’re just going to keep trying to feed (Klehn) the ball, and we just (have) to stop it, stay in our gaps.”
Oxford Hills also needs to sustain longer drives, improve on special teams, and be better with its positioning and physicality.
“When Bonny Eagle got up a few touchdowns, it was like, ‘Where are we, guys? How are we going to respond to that?’” Danforth said. “And Bonny Eagle just started rolling and made it hard for us to focus on what we needed to do, and next thing you know, the game’s over and they put 45 on us.”
The Vikings believe they’re a better team now.
Their resilience was on full display when they rebounded from their loss by shutting out a fellow North contender Portland, 29-0, on Oct. 17. That started what is now a five-game winning streak.
“(Losing to Bonny Eagle) was definitely a wake-up call,” said Gunner Truman, a senior. “I know after that Bonny Eagle week, we were out here for two and a half hours every day, and the coaches got hard on us, and ever since then, I think we’re setting the tone better … we’ve had a run since then.”
Standout running back Keegan Ridley only played on defense in the first game against Bonny Eagle, so the Vikings know they have another weapon to unleash when they take the field Saturday at Fitzpatrick Stadium.
Ridley has rushed 135 times for 854 yards and 10 touchdowns. Against Windham in the A North final, he ran for three touchdowns and returned a kickoff for a score.
His presence will boost the offense led by quarterback Toby Oufiero, who has proven to be a threat in the run and pass games. The junior has 1,501 yards and 17 touchdowns through the air, and he is second on the team in rushing yards with 579 and first in rushing touchdowns with 13.
“It’s gonna give us confidence, just having everybody in our normal spots,” said Ridley, a junior. “And last time we played (Bonny Eagle), we had guys moved around, kids were out, so this week we’re going to be full strength and ready to put up a fight.”
Perhaps Oxford Hills can following the example set by Bonny Eagle, which lost to Thornton Academy, 49-14, in the regular season on Oct. 24, then flipped the outcome in the playoffs, winning 35-28 in the South final.
“It’s definitely something we can look at, and in the past, there’s been upsets in the championship games,” Truman said. “… So, yeah, it’s definitely a message out there that we could take, and I think it’s definitely possible.”
The Vikings are seeking their second state title, having won in their last trip to the Class A final in 2022. Bonny Eagle has won seven championships, most recently in 2019.

title: Susan Smith denied parole again 32 years after drowning her sons in a South Carolina lake
text:
COLUMBIA, S.C. (WCSC/Gray News) — Susan Smith was denied parole for a second time, 32 years after she drowned her sons in a lake in South Carolina.
Smith, who is now 55, strapped her 14-month-old son, Alex, and her 3-year-old son, Michael, into her car and let it roll into John D. Long Lake in October 1994.
Smith told investigators that a Black man had carjacked her and taken the children. For nine days, Smith made several tearful pleas asking that Michael and Alex be returned safely before confessing to drowning her sons.
The car was found at the bottom of the lake with the boys still inside.
A jury convicted Smith on July 22, 1995, and she was sentenced to life in prison with the possibility of parole after 30 years.
Prosecutors have long argued that Smith killed her sons because she believed they were the reason the wealthy son of the owner of the business where she worked broke off their affair, according to the Associated Press.
During her trial, Smith and her attorneys said her mental health was to blame.
She was denied parole for the first time in November 2024. At that parole hearing, she said God had forgiven her and cried, saying that what she did was horrible and she would give anything to bring her sons back.
Smith can ask for parole again in 2028.
During Thursday’s parole hearing, Smith said her sons were innocent children who did not deserve to die. She said she has so much remorse for killing them and asked the board to give her a chance to get out of prison and do good for the world.
“I know that David didn’t get to see Michael and Alex grow up. You didn’t get to see him ride a bike or go to school. And I’m really, really sorry for that, and I would go back and change all of that if I could, I would, OK? I’m not the same person I was 32 years ago,” she said.
The boys’ father, David Smith, and original prosecutors oppose her release.
“She took away one of the greatest gifts God gives us – life. She did that deliberately. It wasn’t an accident, it wasn’t a mistake. She did it deliberately,” he said in testimony Thursday.

title: Prosecutor declines to charge a police officer who fatally shot a Black man in Wisconsin
text:
Prosecutor declines to charge a police officer who fatally shot a Black man in Wisconsin
The Wisconsin police officer who shot and killed a 38-year-old Black man in Madison in July, sparking racial justice protests and renewed calls for police reform, will not face criminal charges, a prosecutor announced Thursday.
Kiel Baitinger-Peterson, an officer with more than a decade of experience in law enforcement, fired the shots that killed Corey Ruiz on July 22. Baitinger-Peterson was one of four officers who responded to calls about someone checking out parked cars and an alleged burglary attempt, police said. They surrounded Ruiz, who was on a bicycle.
“I conclude it was reasonable for the officer to use deadly force when this person resisted officers, produced a knife, and was not affected by multiple attempts to use Tasers while officers attempted to take him into custody,” Dane County District Attorney Ismael Ozanne said in a statement announcing his decision.
Video below: Corey Ruiz's mother speaks after Wisconsin officer cleared in his death
The Wisconsin Department of Justice said immediately after the shooting that two officers attempted to use a Taser on Ruiz but weren’t successful. Ruiz “brandished a knife and injured” Baitinger-Peterson, the department said.
Civil rights attorney Ben Crump, who represents the Ruiz family, said in a statement that there was nothing in the videos that the district attorney showed them on Thursday to justify the shooting.
“The medical examiner told the family that if the officer had not fired that shot to his head, Corey would have survived,” Crump said. “It was clearly an excessive use of force. This police killing in Madison, Wisconsin, was unjustifiable, unreasonable, unnecessary, and unconstitutional.”
Video below: Corey Ruiz's daughter speaks after Madison officer cleared in his death
Prosecutor shows the Ruiz family video of the shooting
Ozanne said he reached his decision after reviewing evidence that included police reports, diagrams, surveillance videos, police squad car videos and citizen videos. Madison police officers do not wear body cameras.
“In the video you see they tackle him, they tase him, they kick him and then the police officer executes him,” Crump said during a news conference. “The video is the objective unbiased witness here.”
Crump said it is one of the worst excessive force cases that he has worked on.
“When you are shooting a man who is on the ground, three (times). It hits him in his chest and the kill shot hits him in his head,” he said.
Crump said the medical examiner told the Ruiz family he would have survived had the third shot not been fired and hit him in the head.
Ozanne said his decision was a correct interpretation of the law.
“A person does not have to like and/or agree with the law, however I am sworn to apply the law to the facts at hand,” the prosecutor said. “The law applies equally to members of law enforcement and to those who are not.”
The victim's brother, Adam Ruiz, told reporters that the prosecutor has “mistreated” his family.
“We’re destroyed,” he said. “We won’t accept this.”
Days of protests followed the shooting
Baitinger-Peterson has not replied to an email seeking comment.
Executive Director Jim Palmer of Wisconsin Professional Police Association, the police union, said in a statement the decision that the officer's use of deadly force was legally justified “is supported by the evidence and consistent with the legal standards governing the use of force by law enforcement officers.”
It was the third time since 2012 that Madison police had shot and killed someone in the same neighborhood. The killing sparked days of protests and forced the city to reckon with calls for police reform to address racial justice issues.
Baitinger-Peterson and the other three officers who interacted with Ruiz that day have been on paid administrative leave since the shooting.
While bystanders captured the confrontation on video, there is no body camera footage because Madison police officers don’t wear them. All Madison police officers could be equipped with body cameras by the end of 2027 thanks to a $350,000 donation from a local nonprofit that city officials announced in September.
The donation will help cover operational expenses, while other costs are being funded through grants and other means.

title: Here's 20 Maine Christmas Events Worth Making Time For This Holiday Season
text:
20 Maine Christmas Events to Add to Your 2026 Holiday Bucket List
The holidays in Maine are probably my kids' favorite time of the year, and thankfully, there are so many activities to choose from to get us all in the Christmas spirit.
From November into December 2026 (and in a few cases, further into January and even February 2027), there are stunning light shows, Christmas festivals, Polar Express train rides, and magical performances to check out in the state.
Sure, a bunch are family-friendly, but you can just as easily hit up these events with friends, your special loved one, or go solo like Buddy the Elf on a mission. I've rounded up 20 of some of the best spots to make sure to put on your holiday list of fun for this season.
What are some fun Christmas events in Maine?
Going out and seeing Christmas lights feels like an obvious choice for the holidays, but that's also because there are some pretty spectacular displays.
You can drive through millions of lights, like the Maine Celebration of Lights in Cumberland, or you can go for a stroll through an illuminated holiday woods walk, like the Nyte Walk in Lebanon.
There are also train rides like the Polar Express in Portland, which offers an immersive experience as you head to the North Pole to see Santa.

title: How to turn a business anniversary into a marketing opportunity
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Every business has milestones worth celebrating. Whether you’re marking five years or 35 years, an anniversary offers more than an opportunity to throw a party or thank your customers. It’s also a chance to reflect on how far you’ve come, reconnect with the people who helped you get there and build momentum for the next chapter.
Here are five ways any business owner can turn an anniversary into a meaningful marketing opportunity.
Take stock of your brand and what it represents today. An anniversary is a perfect opportunity to ask whether your logo, messaging, website and marketing materials accurately reflect who you are today and where you’re headed. Consider gathering feedback from employees, customers and trusted colleagues. What three words would they use to describe your business? What makes you different from your competitors? Does your brand communicate those qualities clearly?
Make sure your website is working as hard as you are. An anniversary provides a natural deadline for a website refresh. Review your content, update employee biographies, showcase recent work and make sure your contact information is easy to find. Most importantly, consider how people are discovering businesses today. Search engine optimization remains important, but AI is changing how people find information. Increasingly, prospective customers are asking AI tools for recommendations rather than typing keywords into traditional search engines. Your website should clearly communicate your expertise, services, location and credentials so both people and AI-powered search tools can understand what makes your business valuable.
Tell the stories behind your success. Anniversaries provide wonderful opportunities for storytelling, and stories are the foundation of effective public relations. Rather than simply announcing that you’ve been in business for a certain number of years, think about the people, challenges and turning points that shaped your organization. Consider sharing these stories through blog posts, social media, newsletters or short videos. Remember that the most compelling anniversary stories aren’t necessarily about how successful you’ve become. They’re about what you’ve learned and how you’ve helped others along the way.
Use your experience to establish yourself as a thought leader. One of the greatest assets of a longtime business owner is accumulated knowledge. You’ve witnessed changes in your industry, navigated challenges and developed insights that could help others. An anniversary is an ideal time to share that expertise. Consider writing an opinion column, contributing articles to industry publications, appearing on podcasts or speaking at conferences. You might even have enough material for a book.
Celebrate the people who made your success possible. No business reaches a significant anniversary alone. Employees, customers, mentors, vendors and community partners all contribute to its longevity. Consider hosting a celebration, recognizing longtime employees, sharing customer success stories or supporting a nonprofit that reflects your company’s values. A handwritten thank-you note to an important customer or mentor can be just as meaningful as an elaborate anniversary event. These gestures strengthen relationships while reminding everyone involved that your business is about more than transactions. It’s about people, trust and shared accomplishments.
Celebrate the past while investing in the future. Business anniversaries should inspire gratitude, but they should also spark ambition. The marketplace continues to evolve, technology keeps changing and customer expectations never stand still.
Whatever milestone you’re celebrating, resist the temptation to treat it as a finish line. Instead, use it as a launching pad for your next chapter. After all, the best way to honor your business’s history is to make sure it has an exciting future.

title: Nuggets rally in second half to beat Celtics
text:
DENVER — Nikola Jokic had 24 points, nine assists and eight rebounds, Jamal Murray had 21 points, seven rebounds and four steals, and the Denver Nuggets overcame a 17-point first-half deficit to defeat the Boston Celtics 105-101 on Wednesday night.
Murray drained a jumper with 6.4 seconds remaining to extend the Nuggets’ lead to 104-101, and Celtics star Jayson Tatum was called for a technical foul after he tossed the ball from the baseline to a referee standing near midcourt. Murray sank the ensuing free throw to seal the win.
Five Denver players scored in double figures, including DeMar DeRozan, who had 13 of his 18 points in the fourth quarter.
The Nuggets rode a 20-4 run in the third quarter that included a scoreless stretch of 4:35 for Boston to take their first lead of the night, 69-67, on a Cameron Johnson jumper. From there, the teams traded the lead 15 times in the final 16:10 before a pair of DeRozan free throws with 49 seconds remaining gave Denver the lead for good.
The win was the Nuggets’ fifth in their last seven games, while the Celtics dropped back-to-back regular-season games for the first time since March 10-12.
Tatum finished with 24 points for Boston but scored only four points in the second half and had a season-high six turnovers, four of which came during Denver’s third-quarter comeback. Neemias Queta added a season-high 17 points and 10 rebounds, while Payton Pritchard scored 15 points.
Boston, which was making 38.2% of its 3-pointers this season, missed 33 of its 44 shots from beyond the arc.

title: AARP says changing economy left Social Security funding plan behind
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
WASHINGTON (Gray DC) - As lawmakers consider how to prevent future cuts to Social Security benefits, a new AARP study says the program’s funding structure has not kept pace with changes in the U.S. economy over the past 40 years.
Sen. Jeff Merkley (D-Ore.) Social Security benefits are a significant source of income for many retirees.
“For about half of American seniors that get these benefits, it accounts for about half to 100 percent of their income,” he said.
Sen. Ron Johnson, (R-Wis.), called on Congress to act.
“Pass a law that prevents the reduction of Social Security benefits, and quit scaring seniors,” he said.
AARP says the program was designed for an economy in which a larger share of the nation’s economic output went to workers, allowing payroll taxes to generate proportionally more revenue.
“We have a shift from workers to capital,” said Rich Johnson of AARP. “So that more money is going to the owners of capital through corporate profits, through investment income than to workers.”
The organization also says the cap on wages subject to Social Security payroll taxes was established when earnings were more evenly distributed.
“That’s currently set at about $184,000. That now covers only about 83 percent of all earnings in the economy. It used to be 90 percent,” AARP’s Rich Johnson said.
Some advocates have proposed eliminating the wage cap to increase revenue or taxing corporate profits to supplement payroll taxes. Lawmakers are weighing possible solutions as they consider how to protect retirees from benefit cuts.

title: Woman says she found maggots crawling on her LongHorn Steakhouse meal, lawsuit says
text:
TRUSSVILLE, Ala. (WBRC/Gray News) - An Alabama woman is suing LongHorn Steakhouse, claiming she found maggots on broccoli she ordered from the restaurant.
Alexandria Eatman said she picked up a to-go lunch for herself and coworkers from the Trussville restaurant around noon on Oct. 27. That’s when she and a coworker noticed something crawling on her food.
“We noticed I had maggots crawling on my broccoli,” Eatman said.
Her attorney, Antonio Spurling, said she had eaten much of her meal before noticing what was on the broccoli.
Eatman said she returned to the restaurant, where a manager told her someone would reach out. She said no one contacted her that day.
The next morning, Eatman said, she became ill and went to a hospital, where she spent about half a day receiving medicine and fluids.
“I had a lot of nausea, diarrhea. I was very weak for days. It just took a lot out of me,” she said. “I wasn’t able to work.”
Spurling said her illness is documented.
Eatman said she posted pictures of the meal on Facebook, and a corporate representative contacted her the next day. She said the representative apologized, told her there was a problem with the broccoli supplier and offered her a $100 gift card.
“I think I was very disappointed after they only decided, like, we’ll give you a $100 gift card,” Eatman said. She then began looking for an attorney.
A manager at the Trussville location declined to comment when contacted by WBRC.
Longhorn restaurant operator Darden Restaurants released the following statement to WBRC:
“What was shown in the image was moth larvae. Unfortunately, it can occasionally be present in fresh broccoli. We take food safety seriously and we immediately discarded all broccoli as soon as we became aware.”
Eatman is suing LongHorn Steakhouse, Darden Restaurants and RARE Hospitality International. The lawsuit, filed Nov. 5 in Jefferson County Circuit Court, alleges negligence in handling food and seeks compensatory and punitive damages. It does not specify an amount.
The latest inspection report on the department’s website, from March 2026, gave the restaurant a score of 90 and noted food temperature and handwashing violations. The inspection took place months before the incident Eatman described.

title: A van Gogh with a complex past sells for a record $190 million at auction
text:
A van Gogh with a complex past sells for a record $190 million at auction
A vibrant landscape painted by Vincent van Gogh weeks before his death has sold for $190.4 million at auction, a record for a work by the artist.
“Châtaigniers en fleurs” (Chestnut Trees in Flower) exceeded its $180 million estimate at a Sotheby’s auction in New York on Wednesday. The sale went ahead after an agreement between its current owners and the heirs of a Jewish family that sold it in Nazi-era Germany.
A day before the auction, Sotheby’s announced an agreement between the Blaquier-Arrieta family, which has owned the painting since 1975, and the descendants of Hedwig and Samuel Fischer, who sold it in 1936.
Related video: A painting was buried in a New York apartment closet. It could sell for up to $5 million
A lawyer for the Fischer heirs had asked for the sale to be postponed until Sotheby’s showed the painting had not been sold under duress.
The auction house said that “in recognition of the painting’s complex Nazi-era history and the suffering endured by the Fischer family during the Holocaust, the two families have reached a mutually satisfactory resolution.” It did not disclose details of the agreement.
The Fischer heirs said they were “grateful for the trusting and fair negotiation and collaboration with Sotheby’s and the Blaquier-Arrieta family, which make it possible to acknowledge the suffering of the Fischer family during the Nazi era.”
Van Gogh painted “Châtaigniers en fleurs” in a burst of creativity after his release from a psychiatric asylum in May 1890. He took his own life two months later.
The previous record for a van Gogh was $117.2 million paid for “Verger avec cyprès” (Orchard with Cypresses) at a Christie’s auction in 2022.
Paul Cézanne’s portrait “Arlequin” sold for $111 million in Wednesday’s sale of a dozen Impressionist and post-Impressionist works amassed by the late Argentine art collector Nelly Arrieta de Blaquier and her sugar magnate husband, Carlos Pedro Blaquier.
The 12 works sold for a total of $412 million.

A South Portland man pleaded not guilty to four charges stemming from a 2025 crash involving a school bus in Belfast.
Kyle Young, 41, made his first court appearance by Zoom Wednesday afternoon. He is being held on $1,000 bail and, if released, has been ordered not to drive, among other conditions.
A Waldo County grand jury indicted Young last week on charges of aggravated criminal OUI, reckless conduct with a dangerous weapon, endangering the welfare of a child, and driving to endanger.
The crash
Prosecutors say Young was high on drugs when he crashed into an RSU 71 school bus in June 2025.
About two dozen students were on the bus. Two students, Young and his then-4-year-old child, who was in the car with him, were hospitalized.
The state said delays involving the lab and the investigation contributed to the time it took to bring charges.
Bail arguments
Young’s attorney asked for $1,000 unsecured bail, saying Young had no cash and wanted to return to his job. The attorney said Young has been sober for nine months and had stable employment before his arrest.
The state asked for $1,000 secured bail. Prosecutors acknowledged it was a low request for the charges, but cited the length of time between the alleged incident and the charges.
Young has one prior OUI on his record. He was also convicted of a felony drug charge in November 2025 and sentenced to 30 days in jail.
