title: Man’s wife, daughter arrested 4 years after his severed head was found in a trash bag
text:
CITRUS HEIGHTS, Calif. (KXTV) - Authorities say a California man’s wife and daughter have been arrested four years after his severed head was found in a trash bag.
A person walking a dog found a severed head in a trash bag in the Todd Valley area of Foresthill on Sept. 28, 2022, according to the Placer County Sheriff’s Office. Detectives couldn’t identify the victim at the time because of the state of decomposition.
In 2024, a private lab’s DNA analysis – along with help from the FBI – finally led investigators to relatives and to a name: 73-year-old Paul Wesley Fitzmaurice Jr.
“The investigation continued once we had him identified, and we realized that Paul had never been reported missing,” Placer County Sheriff Wayne Woo said.
The victim was last known to be living in Citrus Heights with his wife, 75-year-old Georgia “Gwenn” Fitzmaurice, and their daughter, 45-year-old Mary Fitzmaurice.
Detectives served a search warrant Tuesday at the family’s home, and Mary and Gwenn Fitzmaurice were arrested later that day. Investigators allege the former was responsible for killing her father before she and her mother conspired to dispose of his remains.
“We discovered that Gwenn and Mary had kept up the façade to family and friends that Paul was still alive, and in fact, they were still receiving Paul’s Social Security benefits and his CalPERS [California Public Employees’ Retirement System] pension,” Woo said.
Investigators say Mary Fitzmaurice was booked on murder charges, while her mother was booked on accessory charges. Both women are being held in jail on no bail.
One of the family’s neighbors, who didn’t want to be identified, said he noticed Paul Fitzmaurice’s absence.
“I wondered what happened to Paul a few years ago,” the neighbor said. “I hadn’t seen him around. I asked how he was doing, and nobody ever even said he passed or he died or he was sick or anything. They just stopped talking.”
Investigators are still processing evidence to learn how Paul Fitzmaurice was killed and where the rest of his body is located. As for a motive, the sheriff says it’s too early to say.

title: Christmas Bazaar and Wreath Sales Nov. 28
New program aims to keep Portland area families in their homes
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
A Portland nonprofit is launching a new pilot program aimed at preventing child homelessness and keeping kids with their parents, organizers announced Wednesday.
Project Home, which works with low-income households to secure stable housing, is partnering with the John T. Gorman Foundation to expand its work with families who are homeless or at risk of losing their housing.
The program is expected to serve about 1,100 children and adults from 300 families. It expands Project Home’s school-based prevention work, which began in Portland Public Schools in 2020. The nonprofit will now work with the South Portland, Westbrook, Scarborough and Windham school departments to identify people experiencing housing instability and connect them to support.
Project Home will also work with the state to connect with families already involved with Office of Child and Family Services caseworkers.
Victoria Morales, Project Home’s executive director, said the goal is to keep families in their homes or help them secure stable housing before their circumstances worsen and they become homeless. Some are already living in cars, staying at shelters or doubling up with others, she said. Most are working but struggling to pay their bills.
According to U.S. Census data, 12% of Maine households are below the federal poverty level. But many more households — about 28% across the state — are part of a population called ALICE (Asset Limited, Income Constrained, Employed) and have a hard time covering basic expenses, including housing, according to data released this year by the United Ways of Maine.
“The majority of the families are earning too much income to qualify for most services but don’t earn enough to afford the cost of living,” Morales said. “A lot of the families we’re working with are being raised by single moms. It makes it incredibly difficult to raise enough money to support the cost of rent, food and healthcare.”
In Cumberland County, 65% of households headed by a single woman and 61% headed by a single man are below the ALICE threshold. Data from United Way shows that a household with a single adult and one child in childcare needs to make nearly $66,000 annually to cover a basic survival budget.
Morales said many of the people who will be served by the program have a hard time securing housing because they may have low credit scores and incomes, no renting history or have a past eviction. Project Home, which partners with more than 1,000 landlords across Maine, will help families find and secure apartments by guaranteeing leases for which they might not otherwise qualify.
Inadequate housing was cited as a factor in about 18% of cases in which children were removed from their families and placed into foster care, according to a 2024 report from the Maine Children’s Alliance. And while state lawmakers the following year took the “important step” of enacting legislation that makes clear that poverty alone does not constitute neglect, Morales said, housing instability can still contribute to removals.
“Now we have an opportunity to build on that progress by reaching families earlier, addressing housing instability before it becomes a crisis, and giving parents the support they need to keep their children safely at home,” she said.
The John T. Gorman Foundation is supporting the pilot program through a $750,000 grant, said president and CEO Nicole Witherbee. She is excited about the opportunity to work on this program with Project Home, which she said has a “terrific track record” for helping families stay in stable housing.
“When you have a family without housing, things get precarious very quickly,” Witherbee said. “We worry about what happens to that family and their ability to stay together.”
Morales said many families coming out of crisis situations into stable homes don’t have consistent access to healthcare. Once they are housed through the program, a visiting nurse will work with families to assess their needs and help connect them to primary care. They’ll also have access to financial coaches and employment support.
Project Home plans to collect data to help determine how to expand the model to other communities. Witherbee is excited about the impact the program could have on Maine families.
“Housing is the great stabilizer. It’s the thing that ensures access to school, your ability to work, to healthcare,” she said. “Finding smart, creative ways to ensure that families stay housed feels absolutely essential, especially in these times.”

title: Looking back week of Nov. 26
text:
Bar Harbor
Jim Coffman, a senior scientist at Mount Desert Island Biological Laboratory, was part of an international group that sequenced the genome of the purple sea urchin, a west coast cousin of the green sea urchin found along the eastern seaboard. Having the genome decoded will save scientists months of work preparing for an experiment before actually initiating it, said Dr. Coffman. Because humans and sea urchins share a common ancestor, the urchins are not only an excellent and accessible model for studying embryonic development, but also a model that has been used for the last 150 years or so, said Dr. Coffman. They are easy to fertilize; all it takes is mixing a little sperm with some eggs. In a few minutes the eggs are fertilized. Two other factors make sea urchins important in studying embryotic development: they are optically transparent and develop synchronically. This latter characteristic allows researchers to harvest cells and get a snapshot of a particular developmental stage.

title: Dolly Parton’s niece wears dress made for her late aunt to this year’s CMA Awards
text:
NASHVILLE, Tenn. (CNN) — Dolly Parton never got to wear a dress designed for her to the 2026 Country Music Association Awards.
However, her niece, Danielle Parton, 50, honored her late aunt by wearing it to the ceremony at Nashville’s Bridgestone Arena in her place.
Parton’s estate named Danielle Parton its new brand ambassador last month. She said Dolly Parton never got to wear the dress.
The white and gold dress had long sleeves, a scoop neckline and a fringe skirt with silver sequins and gold metallic trim.
Dolly Parton died in August at age 80. A tribute performance for her also took place at Wednesday’s awards ceremony.

title: He was shot while deer hunting in Maine. It changed his life forever.
text:
Outdoors
The BDN outdoors section brings readers into the woods, waters and wild places of Maine. It features stories on hunting, fishing, wildlife, conservation and recreation, told by people who live these experiences. This section emphasizes hands-on knowledge, field reports, issues, trends and the traditions that define life outside in Maine. Read more Outdoors stories here. 
This story was originally published in November 2022.
The small car bounced wildly along the rutted gravel road. Chad Thompson of Milford lay in the back seat, bleeding profusely, as his two friends raced to get him help.
The Old Town High School students were deer hunting on the last day of firearms season on Nov. 28, 1992, when one of them accidentally fired his rifle while loading it. The bullet tore through the left upper thigh of the then-18-year-old Thompson, severing his femoral artery.
“You almost felt it before you heard it, because it happened so quick. I had blood shooting out of my leg, and steam,” said Thompson, who somehow stayed on his feet.
He described the ensuing scene as chaos, but his friends acted quickly.
“They knew enough to tie a tourniquet on my thigh, which saved my life,” Thompson said.
Looking back as the 30th anniversary of that day approaches, Thompson is amazed he survived the catastrophic wound. Quick thinking, a lucky encounter with would-be rescuers, vital medical intervention and his own will to live changed his life in ways he never could have imagined — including his ongoing friendship with the man who fired the rifle.
“Beyond the fact that it was a terrible accident, someone was looking over me that day,” Thompson said.
Thompson was in trouble. They were 30 miles from Old Town, well off the Stud Mill Road, and there were no cellphones.
While speeding down the dirt road, the car’s oil pan was gashed by a rock. Then the engine seized up just as they came upon a group of hunters gathered at a pickup truck.
John Fahey Jr., Bruce Nickerson and Jeff Fahey were returning to their hunting camp on the rainy morning when they heard panicked shouts from down the road.
They raced to the car and found Thompson hunched over in the back seat. John Fahey was shocked, and said the exit wound in the front of the leg — packed with clothing to stem the bleeding — was the size of a grapefruit.
“I didn’t think he was going to make it out,” Fahey said. “The amount of blood was just unbelievable.”
They put Thompson in the bed of John Fahey’s truck and told his friends to apply pressure to the wound and keep him warm during the desperate ride. Fahey drove as fast as he could while Nickerson made sure the teens kept Thompson awake.
“I’m laying on my back, but I felt like I hadn’t slept in a month. I was so tired,” Thompson said.
Once back on asphalt in Milford, Nickerson jumped out at a house to call 911 while Fahey sped into Old Town. There they were stopped by police, who had paramedics and an ambulance waiting to transport Thompson to Eastern Maine Medical Center in Bangor.
Despite being in critical condition after blood transfusions and undergoing several hours of surgery, Thompson amazingly survived.
“From the minute that gun went off, everything went his way,” Fahey said. “He was very fortunate.”
Thompson spent two months at EMMC. Nine days into his stay, he developed bleeding that forced doctors to present him with a terrible decision.
Leaning on the support of his parents, Sam and Kathy Thompson, and his family and friends, Thompson opted for amputation of his leg below the knee rather than complicated restorative measures that might fail in the long run.
“I said, I am not going to live life having an issue that is going to prevent me from doing the things that I want to do,” he said.
During his recovery, Thompson was released briefly a few times. That included Christmas Mass at St. Joseph’s Church in Old Town, where he received a standing ovation. One of the unexpected hurdles was withdrawal while being weaned off the morphine that had been used to ease his pain.
The former three-sport athlete, an avid hunter and angler, was forced to adjust to life with a prosthetic limb. Thompson took a year off before enrolling at Maine Maritime Academy in Castine, where before the accident he had been recruited to play soccer. He battled chronic pain and discomfort with his prosthesis and withdrew prior to his junior year.
He tried to remain active alongside his friends in the years that followed, but it came at a price.
“I may have had a smile on my face, but at the end of the day I was gritting my teeth,” Thompson said. “I didn’t want it to dictate what I could do and what I couldn’t do, so I would just suffer through it.”
He attended the University of Southern Maine, but withdrew because of a leg infection, and then the University of Maine. Eventually he started a hydroseeding business, then ran a car wash for eight years in Old Town.
Thompson was back hunting about 10 years after the accident, although hearing gunshots initially made him flinch.
“It was mind over matter. I got used to the pain and discomfort every day. In my mind, I thought that’s what life was going to be like,” he said.
Thompson eventually visited a prosthetics company in Oklahoma, where he met renowned prosthetist Kevin Carroll. A few years later, Carroll referred Thompson to Dr. Jan Ertl, who discovered that Thompson’s pain was caused by the type of amputation he’d had.
Ertl modified Thompson’s amputation, and the results were astounding. Thompson was able to do things that had been excruciating in the past, including playing with his children in the backyard.
“One of the kids pitched me the Wiffle Ball and I hit it. I instinctively ran to first base and everybody just stopped and looked at me,” Thompson said. “I got emotional. Everybody got emotional.”
Thompson’s moment of joy inspired him to write a letter to Carroll expressing appreciation for helping him get his health and his life back. Three weeks later, he was offered a job at Hanger Clinic, the nation’s largest network of orthopedic and prosthetic clinics.
“Chad is the real deal, just an amazing human being,” Carroll said from his home in Ireland. “It’s really an honor to know him for such a long time, and he’s a guy that I would definitely call a friend.”
Thompson has worked with Hanger Clinic for 18 years and serves as its area business manager for offices in Bangor, Augusta and Rockport. The job provides him with daily reminders of his ordeal and how he overcame it.
His experience as an amputee helps him counsel patients who are transitioning to prosthetics.
“He’s such a positive soul and gives so much to the community of persons with limb loss and other physical challenges,” Carroll said. “He’s a big deal and a very modest individual.”
Thompson, who also is a firearms safety advocate, is active with programs that provide amputees with the chance to participate in recreational activities.
“My motivation is making sure that those who have the surgery know that they’re not alone, that there are other people who have gone through what they’ve gone through, so they can work toward being able to function with a prosthesis and live life at any pace that they want to live it.”
In the years after the accident, Thompson bowhunted for deer, then took up duck hunting. Now, he’s again pursuing deer with a rifle.
“I’ve always been extremely passionate about nature and the outdoors,” said Thompson, who in 2021 shot a six-point buck on his land at Rocky Pond in Otis.
Thompson’s life isn’t the only one that was changed on that rainy November day. He remains friends with the man who shot him, and at one point they even shared an apartment in Portland.
“He’s a victim, too,” Thompson said. “He didn’t mean to do it, and he has to live with it the rest of his life. I’ve never, ever, held a grudge against him.”
The frightening images and experiences are burned into Fahey’s memory.
“I couldn’t tell that story for five years without crying,” said Fahey, who hunted deer only a handful of times after the accident, then gave it up.
Someone who meets Thompson and doesn’t know his story likely wouldn’t be aware that he is an amputee. He still hunts, fish, skis, snowshoes and enjoys other activities.
He believes that everything worked out the way it was intended.
“It’s been quite a journey,” Thompson said. “The fact that I’m able to do those things wearing a prosthesis and having the capability of helping someone drag a deer out, or putting up my own treestand, I just love it.”

title: Motorcyclist killed in Alton crash
text:
A motorcyclist is dead after a crash with a passenger vehicle Thursday afternoon in the Penobscot County town of Alton.
The crash was reported at about 4 p.m. on Bennoch Road. Police initially said it was near 8600 Bennoch Road. Alton is north of Old Town.
The driver of the motorcycle, who has not been publicly identified, was pronounced dead at the scene as a result of injuries from the crash. The driver of the passenger vehicle sustained minor injuries, according to the Penobscot County Sheriff’s Office.
The investigation is ongoing, the sheriff’s office said.
Bennoch Road was closed after the crash and police asked drivers to find alternative routes.

title: Joe Quinn wins VFW Commander's Special Project Gun Raffle
text:
The Veterans of Foreign Wars (VFW) Department of Maine is pleased to announce that Joseph "Joe" Quinn is the winner of the Department Commander's Special Project Gun Raffle.
The raffle was conducted as a fundraising initiative to support Maine Paws for Veterans, the Department Commander's Special Project for the year. Maine Paws for Veterans provides service dogs and support to Maine veterans, helping improve their quality of life through greater independence, confidence, and companionship.
The fundraiser was made possible through the generous support of VFW members, community supporters, and friends of the organization from across the state. Proceeds from the raffle will help Maine Paws for Veterans continue its mission of providing vital services and support to Maine veterans.
"The success of this raffle demonstrates the strong commitment of our VFW members and supporters to improving the lives of veterans throughout Maine," said Department leadership. "Every ticket purchased contributed directly to a worthwhile cause and will help make a meaningful difference for veterans in need."
Following the official drawing, Joe Quinn's ticket was selected as the grand prize winner. The Department of Maine VFW extends its congratulations to Quinn and its sincere appreciation to everyone who participated in and promoted the fundraiser.
The Veterans of Foreign Wars Department of Maine remains committed to supporting veterans, military families, and programs that make a lasting and positive impact on the lives of those who have served our nation. Fundraising efforts such as the Department Commander's Special Project help ensure that organizations like Maine Paws for Veterans can continue their important work across the state.
For additional information about the Department Commander's Special Project and Maine Paws for Veterans, please contact Brad Drummond, chairman of the Department Commander's Special Project, at 207-462-1364.

Noah Wyle and FIGS partner to erase $200 million in medical debt for Americans
text:
Noah Wyle of 'The Pitt' partners with scrubs company FIGS to help erase $200 million in medical debt for Americans
Actor Noah Wyle is again proving that he wants to be more than just a TV doctor through his ongoing advocacy work.
Wyle, star of "The Pitt," is partnering with the scrubs company FIGS to tackle more than $200 million in American medical debt, translating into more than 150,000 Americans getting out of the red.
"There is a company that purchases medical debt for about a penny on the dollar, and I stumbled upon them last year and thought, what a great multiplier. What a bargain," Wyle told CNN during an interview.
Wyle and FIGS will each commit to donating $1 million over the next three years to the nonprofit organization Undue Medical Debt, according to a news release.
The effort was announced this week.
"So right now, about one in three Americans is carrying medical debt to the tune of about $220 billion in this country. The average is not a lot, but it's enough to keep you in poverty," Wyle said.
He also challenged anyone who believes in the cause to donate to the nonprofit to make the reach go even further and spread some welcome holiday cheer.
His advocacy work has also included meeting with politicians to help frontline health care workers, CBS News previously reported.
Before Wyle's stardom on "The Pitt," he starred on the '90s medical drama "ER."

title: South Thomaston fire chief says only small amount of firefighting foam discharged in Owls Head
text:
SOUTH THOMASTON, Maine — The South Thomaston fire chief issued a detailed report to the Select Board over the discharge of firefighting foam in neighboring Owls Head on Nov. 2.
Chief David Elwell said there was only residual foam in the truck that was later rinsed out at a hydrant at the intersection of North Shore and Ash Point drives in Owls Head. He said in his conversation with the Maine Department of Environmental Protection, the representative advised that, based on the information provided, no cleanup would be required.
“He also indicated that there were currently no established procedures or specific state protocols in place to address this type of incident involving the newer PFAS-related foam concerns,” Elwell said in his report.
Later in the report, the chief said the Department of Environmental Protection representative said that this discharge was nothing like the spill that occurred in Brunswick on the airfield.
The incident has been sharply criticized by Owls Head officials.
“It just boggles my mind with all the attention of what happened with the Brunswick discharge,” Owls Head Town Administrator Rodney Mason told the Select Board at its Monday meeting.
The Owls Head incident occurred the night of Nov. 2 at the intersection of Ash Point and North Shore drives. Mason said he noticed a fire truck using a hydrant at that location and spraying water. He thought it was an Owls Head truck and called the chief to ask what was going on, and was told it was not an Owls Head truck.
Mason said he then returned and videotaped what the South Thomaston truck and crew were doing because he noticed they were washing away gravel and loam he had put down at the former Grange Hall property that he and his wife had purchased.
The town, including the fire department, was not notified that South Thomaston would be coming to their town, Mason said.
Mason said the foam was being discharged into a culvert and with the water from the fire hydrant at the intersection, it spread the chemical across his property and across North Shore Drive. Some of the homes in that area get their water from wells.
The town administrator said the foam was clearly visible the following day.
The town administrator said he notified the Department of Environmental Protection and someone came down and did some soil testing the next day.
In his report, Elwell said on the evening of Nov. 2, members of the South Thomaston Fire Department were conducting the department’s regularly scheduled monthly apparatus and equipment inspections. During the inspection, a department member was assigned to Engine 51 and was completing the monthly equipment checks. Engine 51 is equipped with two separate foam systems: one containing Class A foam and the other containing Class B foam.
While circulating the pump and inspecting the apparatus compartments, the firefighter inadvertently activated the Class A and Class B foam system switches. He believed he was operating the switches for the apparatus floodlights to verify their proper operation. However, the switches he activated controlled the two foam systems, the report stated.
Shortly after the switches were activated, members observed foam discharging from the water tank overflow. The situation was immediately recognized, and personnel proceeded to the pump panel and shut off both foam system switches.
Several years ago, the department drained the Class A and Class B foam tanks on Engine 51, as the department was no longer carrying foam on this apparatus. However, it is believed that a residual amount of foam may have remained in one or both tanks following the draining process, the report stated.
For several years, the foam tank gauges have consistently indicated that both tanks were empty. The department had not been aware of any remaining foam in either tank.
Upon recognizing that the foam systems had been inadvertently activated, the chief said he immediately contacted Maine Water to request guidance regarding an appropriate hydrant location where he could send the truck to be refilled with water.
Maine Water recommended using the hydrant located at the intersection of North Shore and Ash Point drives in Owls Head, Maine to fill the truck, the chief said in his report.
The chief said he initially had thought about sending the truck out back of the fire department to the fire pond and using that as a water supply. Due to the drought, there was not enough water to flush this truck.
“I also thought about the wetland portion around the pond and including the pond. I decided it was not a good idea to flood that wet area with the foam due to animals and the wetlands. I thought it would be a better spot to do this where there is city water and no wells in the immediate area of the hydrant,” the chief said.
The urgency of this response was based on the potential consequences of the two foam products mixing within the apparatus plumbing and pump system. Class A and Class B foam products can react when mixed, potentially creating a gel-like substance that can cause significant damage to the pump and associated plumbing, the chief said in his report.
The department has experienced a similar issue with this apparatus in the past, which resulted in repair costs totaling well into the tens of thousands of dollars. Given this previous experience, it was important to take immediate action to remove any remaining foam from the system and prevent additional damage to the apparatus, the chief said.
“Due to the immediate concern of preventing damage to the apparatus, I made the decision to proceed with flushing the system at the recommended hydrant location before I had an opportunity to notify all applicable authorities,” the chief said.
Elwell said he received a telephone call from the Owls Head fire chief advising that he had received a complaint from the property owner where the hydrant was located. The owner is Owls Head Administrator Mason.
“Before I was able to contact the Maine Department of Environmental Protection, the property owner had already contacted the DEP regarding the incident,” the South Thomaston chief stated.
On Nov. 9, the Department of Environmental Protection representative came out and tested the truck. He looked in the foam cells and there was no foam in them that he could test. The main drain to the pump was opened and there was a little residual foam laying in that drain that he was able to get samples of, the chief said in the report.
The test results were expected to take a couple weeks.
To prevent an accidental activation of either foam system in the future, the department’s next step will be to disconnect the foam activation switches at the pump panel, the chief said.
This story appears through a media partnership with Midcoast Villager.

title: UMaine women’s ice hockey coasting early in Hockey East play
text:
The University of Maine women’s ice hockey team is off to one of its best starts in program history in Hockey East play.
The Black Bears, under first-year head coach Alex Gettens, were 4-1-1 in Hockey East games entering Thursday night’s game against fifth-ranked Northeastern at Boston University’s Walter Brown Arena.
The two teams will play again Friday at Bentley University.
UMaine, 7-6-1 overall, took a five-game unbeaten streak (4-0-1) into the game against the 10-1-2 Northeastern (7-0-1 in Hockey East).
“I couldn’t be more proud of how the team is. They are playing so hard every weekend, regardless of the opponent,” Gettens said. “They’re feeling confident in themselves, individually, which is really cool. They are playing an ultimate team game.
During the five-game unbeaten streak, UMaine has allowed only three goals.
Junior goalie Kiia Lahtinen has posted a goals-against average of .059 and a save percentage of .978 in those five games.
Several players have played important roles in the team’s success, with points co-leader Gracie Hanson (two goals, eight assists) leading the list.
“Gracie has been phenomenal in a lot of ways,” Gettens said. “She leads Hockey East in faceoff winning percentage right now [67.4%] and her game continues to blossom every weekend. She is always finding new things to bring to the table, and she has a lot of confidence in herself.”
The other co-points leader, Lily Fetch (three goals, seven assists), set a school record with four assists in a 4-1 win over Holy Cross.
Freshman Julie Jebouskova had three goals and an assist in last weekend’s sweep of Holy Cross and now has three goals and five assists.
Lila Shea doesn’t have any points yet, but Gettens said she has “stepped up into a huge role and has elevated her game big-time” to help compensate for the injury losses to Mackenzie Podewell and Stephanie Jacob.
Gettens is hoping to get both back in the near future.
Raegan Wurm is the team’s leading scorer with five goals. Mikayla Boarder has produced three goals and three assists.
The blue line corps has done its job defensively, and the team’s defensive players have also chipped in offensively, with eight goals and 19 assists led by Kendall Sundby (three goals, six assists) and Lulu Rucinski (three goals, four assists).
Gettens knows his team is facing a huge challenge against Northeastern. He added, however, that a tough early-season schedule, including losses to No. 2 Minnesota and No. 6 Quinnipiac, will prove beneficial.
“Northeastern is a phenomenal team. They play a high-tempo game,” Gettens said. “For us, playing those really difficult games at the beginning of the year, this is where it pays dividends. We’ve bought into what we want to do and the way we want to play. That’s what we’re going to lean on this weekend.”

title: Grand Theft Auto VI could outsell Taylor Swift’s entire Eras Tour in its first week, report says
text:
(Gray News/AP) – The global rollout of “Grand Theft Auto VI” is underway, with presales for the highly anticipated release hitting $1.65 billion as of Wednesday, according to Sensor Tower.
The franchise has already sold more than 470 million games worldwide, including 230 million copies of “Grand Theft Auto V,” which was released in 2013.
Wall Street Journal reports third-party analysts anticipate “Grand Theft Auto VI” to have the “biggest-ever launch for a video game.” It’s projected to sell more than 30 million copies by the end of its fiscal year, the Wall Street Journal reported.
Analysts expect the video game’s global launch-week sales to hit $3.3 billion, the Wall Street Journal reported. To put it into perspective, the Eras Tour’s box office sales reached $2.2 billion over 21 months.
At $80 or more per copy, ultimately, the game could earn well over $10 billion.
GTA VI trailers draw millions of views, award nominations
The first “GTA VI” trailer drew more than 93 million YouTube views in its first 24 hours, while Take-Two Interactive, Rockstar’s parent company, has said the second trailer generated more than 475 million views across platforms in a day.
The game also has attracted awards attention before most players have had a chance to explore it.
“GTA VI” received eight nominations Tuesday for the Game Awards, including game of the year, game direction, narrative, art direction, score and music, audio design, action/adventure and performance. The awards will be presented Dec. 10.
Who are the main characters in GTA VI?
Rockstar returns to Vice City, its fictionalized version of Miami, with two new protagonists, a sprawling Florida-inspired world and the pressure of following one of the most successful entertainment products ever released.
At the center of “GTA VI” are Lucia Caminos and Jason Duval, a couple whose attempts to improve their lives pull them deeper into the criminal underworld of Leonida, Rockstar’s fictionalized version of Florida.
Lucia has recently been released from prison, while Jason is a former soldier who became involved with drug runners in the Leonida Keys. When a criminal job goes wrong, the pair become entangled in a wider conspiracy.
The focus on their relationship marks a major departure from “Grand Theft Auto V,” which followed three playable protagonists.
Where is GTA VI set?
Rockstar has promoted Leonida as its largest and most detailed open world yet, extending beyond Vice City to beaches, highways, wetlands, nightlife districts and smaller communities inspired by South Florida.
Developers immersed themselves in the region while building the game, driving through Miami, the Florida Keys and surrounding communities, flying over the Everglades and researching the area’s history and architecture.
What remains unknown about GTA VI?
Despite years of trailers and promotional material, Rockstar has kept significant portions of “GTA VI” under wraps.
The full voice cast has not been revealed, including the performers behind Lucia and Jason. Actor Stephen Root has confirmed to The Associated Press that he appears in the game, though Rockstar has not publicly identified his role.
Questions also remain about the full range of characters, locations, activities and gameplay systems waiting inside Leonida.

title: Obituary: Patricia Elizabeth Regan
text:
PORTLAND – Patricia Elizabeth Regan, 71, of Portland, passed away on Nov. 11, 2026, leaving behind a family who will miss her dearly.
Patricia was born on August 30, 1955, in Portland, Maine to Leonard and Mary (Gallant) Regan. She was one of eight daughters. She attended Catherine McAuley High School, graduating with the Class of 1974. One of the highlights of her senior year was a class trip to Paris, a special experience she fondly remembered over the years.
Patricia shared three children with her longtime partner, Harold Joseph Brown Jr.: Joseph, Elizabeth, and Marc Regan. Her family was an important part of her life, and she took great pride in her children and grandchildren.
Throughout her working years, Patricia enjoyed a variety of positions, including retail sales and working at a newspaper distribution center.
Those who knew Patty will remember her as an amazing person who always looked for the good in others. She was an empathetic and compassionate soul, often described as a good egg. She lived by the values of family, kindness, and sacrifice. She found a sense of belonging and connection within her community, where she built meaningful relationships.
She had many hobbies including making jewelry, crafting, shopping for the best deals and spending as much time as she could with her grandchildren. She wore her Irish heritage on her sleeve and instilled those values in us.
“When Irish eyes are smiling, Sure they steal your heart away”
Patricia was predeceased by her parents, Leonard and Mary, and her sister, Joan Hedrick.
She is survived by her children, Joseph and his wife Erin Regan of Barrington NH, Elizabeth Regan and her longtime partner Gilbert Bastardo of Portland Texas, Marc and wife Nicole Regan of South Portland Maine; her sisters, Marie Charleston, Ann Regan, Dorothy Regan, Barbara Hogg, Rita McDonough and Teresa Regan; and her beloved grandchildren, Lilah, Easton, Gavin Bastardo, and Ruby Regan.
Her family is deeply saddened by the untimely passing of their mother and extends their heartfelt thanks to everyone who has offered kind words and support during this difficult time. They find comfort in knowing that Patricia passed peacefully and has been reunited with her parents and sister, Joan. She will be remembered with love by all who knew her.
Visiting Hours will be held from 3 p.m. to 5 p.m. on Monday, Nov. 23, at the Conroy-Tully Walker Funeral Home of South Portland, 1024 Broadway with a service starting at 5 p.m. Interment will take place at 10 a.m. on Tuesday, Nov. 24, at Calvary Cemetery, 1461 Broadway, South Portland.
To view Patty’s Memorial Page or to share an online condolence, please visit http://www.ConroyTullyWalker.com.

title: Here's 20 Maine Christmas Events Worth Making Time For This Holiday Season
text:
20 Maine Christmas Events to Add to Your 2026 Holiday Bucket List
The holidays in Maine are probably my kids' favorite time of the year, and thankfully, there are so many activities to choose from to get us all in the Christmas spirit.
From November into December 2026 (and in a few cases, further into January and even February 2027), there are stunning light shows, Christmas festivals, Polar Express train rides, and magical performances to check out in the state.
Sure, a bunch are family-friendly, but you can just as easily hit up these events with friends, your special loved one, or go solo like Buddy the Elf on a mission. I've rounded up 20 of some of the best spots to make sure to put on your holiday list of fun for this season.
What are some fun Christmas events in Maine?
Going out and seeing Christmas lights feels like an obvious choice for the holidays, but that's also because there are some pretty spectacular displays.
You can drive through millions of lights, like the Maine Celebration of Lights in Cumberland, or you can go for a stroll through an illuminated holiday woods walk, like the Nyte Walk in Lebanon.
There are also train rides like the Polar Express in Portland, which offers an immersive experience as you head to the North Pole to see Santa.
READ MORE: L.L. Bean in Freeport, Maine, Unveil 8 Special Holiday Weekends
And of course, there's a bunch of festivals across the state, including some that have been around for decades. Just take Kennebunkport's Christmas Prelude. According to its website, it started all the way back in 1982. That's over 40 years of festive fun!
That's clearly just a hint of all the holiday options you can pick. Take a look to see what you feel like doing this season, or if you love Christmas so much, maybe all of them.

title: School district suspends 2 hockey teams during police investigation
text:
FAIRBANKS, Alaska (KTVF/KTUU/Gray News) — Police are investigating allegations of kidnapping and sexual assault involving two Alaska high school hockey teams during a tournament earlier this month
Police consider charges against 5 individuals
Amanda Graham, the public information officer for the Wasilla Police Department, said authorities are considering charging five individuals.
“The alleged incidents occurred in Wasilla while the teams were in the Valley for the Stars and Stripes tournament,” Graham said. “Two Wasilla detectives recently traveled to Fairbanks to conduct interviews as part of the ongoing investigation.”
Palmer High School hosted the Stars and Stripes Hockey Tournament from Nov. 5 through Nov. 7.
School district suspends hockey activities
The Fairbanks North Star Borough School District said it is investigating an incident involving students from the North Pole High School and Lathrop High School hockey teams.
“The district has initiated an investigation and is coordinating with law enforcement. As an interim administrative safety measure, all hockey activities involving the two teams have been suspended,” a district spokesperson said.
“This temporary pause is not a disciplinary determination and is intended to support student safety and the integrity of the investigation,” the spokesperson said.
The spokesperson said the district cannot share additional details at this time because the investigation is active and involves students.
“The district takes matters involving student safety and well-being seriously and is committed to a thorough and fair investigative process,” the spokesperson said.
District addresses community interest
In a separate statement Wednesday, a spokesperson said the district is working through the investigative process, including determining appropriate disciplinary consequences for those involved.
“We recognize there has been significant community interest in this incident and that many rumors and inaccurate accounts are circulating. We encourage our community to avoid speculation, particularly when it involves students. It is important that the investigative process moves forward thoroughly and fairly based on the facts rather than rumors,” the spokesperson said.
Athletic association responds
The Alaska School Activities Association, the governing body of high school sports, said Wednesday that it is aware of the ongoing investigation and will support the outcome from law enforcement and the Fairbanks North Star Borough School District.
“ASAA appreciates the Fairbanks North Star School District informing us of this incident and the need to shutdown both teams until they have the time to fully and fairly investigate. We have total faith in their ability to properly deal with this issue,” an Alaska School Activities Association spokesperson said.
No names have been released because the people involved are minors.

title: Fiona’s death gives parents a chance to teach kids about grief — and life
text:
For many children, the death of Fiona, a beloved hippo at the Cincinnati Zoo, may be their first experience with losing an animal they have grown to love, even if they never met her in person.
Fiona, who was 9-years-old, died Thursday from complications after swallowing a knit hat that was accidentally flung into her enclosure. Her death has sparked an outpouring of love from around the country for the Nile hippopotamus, with zoo visitors leaving flowers and cards by the statue outside the entrance.
Samantha Haines, a mother in St. Petersburg, Florida, said she initially kept the news that Fiona had swallowed a hat from her 10-year-old daughter, who loves hippos, because she “didn’t want to worry her.” But she told her daughter about Fiona’s death Thursday.
Psychologists and grief specialists say when animals die, the experience can provide opportunities for parents to help children understand death and navigate difficult emotions, including grief.
Haines said they cried together for about 20 minutes before she told her daughter she could add her Fiona-themed ornaments to the Christmas tree in her room. When her daughter emerged, she was distracted by a book about dragons and didn’t want to talk about the hippo.
“I think she just needs a distraction right now,” Haines said. “We have recently experienced a heavy death in the family and have been on the roller coaster of the grieving process already.”
Experts recommend using clear, age-appropriate language to explain that Fiona died and will not be coming back. Phrases such as “went to sleep” can confuse or frighten younger children.
Caregivers also do not need to have every answer. Acknowledging uncertainty and making space for questions can help children feel comfortable expressing their emotions.
Parents can also acknowledge their children’s feelings and share their own sadness with them. Experts say there is no single right way to grieve, and children may need time and repeated conversations to process the loss.
“People are so averse to talking about death and grief, but it is the one thing that is guaranteed: We are all going to die. We need to be open to talking about that,” Deirdra Flavin, CEO of the National Alliance for Children’s Grief, previously told The Associated Press.
Kaitlyn Hermsen, a mother of four in Oconomowoc, Wisconsin, says her 8-year-old daughter would visit zoos to see hippos, and became obsessed with Fiona’s story, especially because she and the beloved animal were close in age.
“Her love for hippos is so big that we traveled all the way from Wisconsin to Cincinnati to visit her,” Hermsen said.
She said telling her daughter about Fiona’s death was heartbreaking.
“Through the sadness, she found comfort in imagining Fiona in heaven with our dog, Loki, and her favorite cow, Betsy.”
Comments flooded a Facebook fan page for Fiona, with people expressing a mix of sadness and frustration. Some urged others not to direct their anger at the family of the visitor whose hat landed in Fiona’s enclosure, while others shared happy memories of visiting her.
Remembering Fiona through drawings, photographs, favorite videos or stories about her life can also provide comfort and a sense of closure. Such activities can help children celebrate the joy Fiona brought to others while beginning to understand that death is a permanent but natural part of life.
___
Mumphrey reported from Flagstaff, Arizona.
